author: acdlite
message:
Prefetch scheduler mirrors the navigation's tree walk (#98975)

The prefetch scheduler's static walk decided at the parent which child
was still part of the current page and which began the new part of the
route, and it fetched the head through two functions of its own that
copied the per-segment decision (a static attempt, then a runtime deopt
if that wasn't enough) for a node that hangs off the route root instead
of sitting in the tree.

Give the walk the same shape as the navigation's. The walk over the part
of the route the current page also has owns the comparison for its own
node — first whether the route position still matches, then whether any
of its params changed — and hands off to the walk over the new part of
the route when either fails, so the root enters the shared walk like
every other node. The per-segment decision, a static attempt or a
runtime deopt, lives in one function that the new-part walk calls for
every segment, and the runtime request's walk gets the same split
between iterating the children and deciding for one node.

The head is a one-node route tree like any other segment now, so it goes
through the same functions: the new-part static walk and the direct
runtime fetch it already had.

This is a pure restructuring and issues the same requests as before: a
segment the navigation keeps is still prefetched at the ordinary static
tier without a runtime deopt, the head is still fetched whenever
anything is, and a chain of inlined segments is still dropped where a
Shell-phase walk crosses from a kept node into the new part. A later
change uses the shape to prefetch only what the navigation would fetch.

author: acdlite
message:
Separate route structure comparison from param comparison (#98974)

Changing a page’s search params doesn’t change which page it is, but it
may change the data that page needs. The router currently mixes these
concerns by appending search params to `__PAGE__` segments. Remove that
encoding so we can compare which route is being rendered separately from
the param values used to render it.

Param values are now compared through the existing VaryPath data
structure, while route structure is compared during the existing tree
traversals. Each traversal can decide which comparisons matter for the
work it’s doing.

Client-side comparisons and history restoration still need the search
params, so store them in a separate FlightRouterState slot for now. As
before, previous-page search params are stripped from normal request
headers. This is a temporary step that lets us migrate incrementally.
Eventually, FlightRouterState will be replaced by a type that represents
the route and its params more directly.

This is mostly a refactor, though it fixes an accidental inconsistency
in search-param handling compared with regular route params, avoiding
some redundant prefetch work.

Fully cached pages already track their vary params correctly. This
separation prepares us to do the same for partially dynamic segments
during navigation, so changing an unrelated param won’t require
rendering their dynamic content again.

author: acdlite
message:
Store the head as its own CacheNode (#98973)

Throughout most of the client router implementation, the head is treated
as if it belongs to the page segment. For example, CacheNode has
separate `rsc` and `headRsc` fields, and the page's CacheNode owns both.
This had led to a bunch of special cases related to the head.

The Segment Cache largely (though not entirely) avoids this by instead
modeling the head as a special kind of segment. It has its own vary
path, its own SegmentCacheEntry, etc. There are still a few places where
treatment of the head is special, because it doesn't exist inside the
normal route tree structure. But we treat it like segment wherever
possible.

This PR updates the navigation implementation to use the same model:
treat the head as a segment that is a sibling to the route segment tree.

This is a large diff but the changes are almost entirely mechanical.
Although the added/removed balance is about even, that includes a new
test case. The net number of implementation lines has gone down.

author: acdlite
message:
Record which params a CacheNode's data depends on (#98972)

Adds a `varyParams` field to CacheNode. When present, they represent the
set of params that the data for that segment varies by. (When null, the
set is unknown.)

Currently, the vary params are only known when the data is fully cached;
vary params are not recorded during a dynamic render. However, this will
change in a future PR once we've integrated with the experimental
Ledgers feature in React.

author: acdlite
message:
Use RouteTree<T> for CacheNode tree (#98971)

Refactors the CacheNode tree to use the RouteTree<T> data type.
CacheNode used to be a tree-shaped object, with a similar structure to
RouteTree<T>. CacheNode is now a data container instead, embedded inside
a RouteTree structure.

So the usage sites change from CacheNode to RouteTree<CacheNode>.

As a result, we can now diff against the render tree directly during
prefetches and navigations, instead of diffing against
FlightRouterState. This gets us closer to migrating everything away from
FlightRouterState to our shared data types.

author: acdlite
message:
Remove the page/layout distinction from RouteTree (#98970)

Part of a series of internal refactors to improve param tracking on the
client.

A route tree node used to come in two variants, a layout and a page,
distinguished by an isPage flag that every constructor had to keep
consistent with the VaryPath it built. The variants only differed in
whether the vary path carried a search params entry, and the code that
needed to know either checked the flag or read the vary path's shape
positionally.

Collapse them into one RouteTree type with one VaryPath type. The few
places that still care whether a node is a page derive it from the
segment. When something needs to read the search params, they can be
accessed from the RouteTree or VaryPath like we do for other params.

This is a pure refactor of the existing code. It reads more naturally
with a single tree type and a single vary path type, which the rest of
this stack builds on.

author: lukesandberg
message:
Fix root predicates (#98942)

Fix the definition of GC roots to account for all transient references

There was a categorical mistake in how `uppers` and
`collectible_dependents` were interpreted. Both of these refer to a task
above us and this is it is a reference but the reference might be
comming from transient or persistent tasks. This is what kept confusing
the 'root' definition

So the new definition is simply

* You are collectible if there are no references (persistent or
transient)
* You are a root if there are only transient references, which includes
transient uppers and collectible_dependents


The old definition expected roots to have no uppers at all, which isn't
correct. A `run_once` task becomes an aggregation root and so the nested
persistent tasks reference it as an upper. Those tasks should become gc
roots since they are on the transient <--> persistent boundary and the
only thing retaining them is references from transient tasks.

author: lukesandberg
message:
[turbopack] only remove followers if they are actually removed as children (#98843)

## What

When removing edges, only enqueue `lost follower` jobs when we actually
remove children.

## Why

GC can race with other kinds of task completion which also remove
outgoing edges.

If task completion drops a child from a task that also becomes
collectible. Then it is possible for there to be an enqueued
CleanupOldEdges job at the time GC runs. Then we will have two jobs that
remove children, only one will succeed but both will enqueue
`InnerOfUppersLostFollowersJob` for all the chidren. This can lead to
panics since one of those jobs will fail to remove the follower

The fix is simple, only remove tasks as followers when you actually
removed them as children.

author: lukesandberg
message:
turbo-tasks-backend: simplify the collectibility predicate and collect transient tasks (#98615)

Fix refcounting for transient tasks
- ensure transient tasks refcount each other correctly, and are eligible
for collection
- ensure root tasks are born with a transient_ref_count of 1

Also drop some ultimately harmful conditions from the gc predicate
- don't consider `cell_dependent`. cell dependencies form cycles and are
subsumed by ancestors
- to read a cell you have to read it from a child (covered by
parent_count) or be passed it from a parent. For the parent to have
passed it to you it must have a child dependency on the producer or be
passed it by its parent (recursively). So the task that passed you the
vc must be holding ownership over both tasks.
- therefore a stale cell_dependency can only exist within a task that is
effectively dead, however because we do not reliably clean up all tasks
in a session (due to leaking root tasks), we cannot fully exclude the
existence of stale cell_dependency edges. We just know they must only
exist within unreachable tasks.

author: lukesandberg
message:
turbo-tasks-gc: Invalidating a deleted task should be a no-op (#98614)

Make invalidating deleted tasks a no-op.

Invalidators now represent a 'weak' reference to a task, and
invalidations don't assert task existence. We know that the task exists
when the invalidator is created but by the time an invalidation occurs
it might not exist anymore. So treat the dependency as weak.

Take care to not create 'blank' tasks when querying for them, this can
confuse assertions that occur later.


## Why is this safe?

Currently it is safe because we never reuse task ids, so invalidating a
deleted task is perfectly reasonable, much like invalidating a
non-active task, there is nothing to do

In the future if we start reusing task ids, then this becomes an ABA
problem. An invalidator can point at a new task. This is also not too
bad, a spurious invalidation is self healing. Also most invalidators are
not actually persisted which limits the risk.

So we can either decide to build a mechanism to tear down these stale
edges or tolerate spurious invalidations. I think we could make
invalidator users subscribe to a 'deleted task id bus' which would allow
them to drop references, this could be useful and then the few cases
where we _persist_ invalidators (by way of `State` objects) would need
to devise a new mechanism (or decide to tolerate the spurious
invalidations)

Avoid decoding prerender matcher parameters twice (#99121)

## Summary

Avoid decoding route parameters a second time while selecting prerender
metadata. This fixes valid percent-containing URLs returning 500,
including both build-generated closed routes and runtime-generated open
routes.

For example, a request for
`/open/docs/space%20here/with%2Fslash/fallback%25` is already normalized
for manifest lookup before reaching `PrerenderManifestMatcher`. Its
final parameter now contains a literal `%`. The matcher previously used
`getRouteMatcher`, which tried to decode the captures again and threw
even though this call only needed to determine whether the route
structure matched.

Test the existing, lazily constructed route regular expression directly
instead. Matcher precedence, source-page filtering, and the current
server parameter encoding behavior stay unchanged. This does not
introduce a new manifest or adapter contract.

The open fallback is requested twice to cover generation and reuse. The
existing fixture uses `dynamicParams = false` and remains excluded from
the Cache Components matrix, which does not support that configuration.

This is an independent prerequisite for #97393: the failure reproduces
without the parameter-matching API and should be fixed for existing apps
too.

## Verification

- Before the fix, the new closed and open catch-all requests returned
500 with a parameter-decoding error. After the fix, both return 200 and
retain the existing encoded server parameter values.
- The focused matcher unit suite passes all six tests.
- The three encoding regressions pass with production Webpack after
restacking. The API routing suite also passes all 36 tests with
fresh-native production Turbopack above this prerequisite, including its
existing percent-containing URL cases.

author: sokra
message:
Turbopack: chunk each layout segment once in production (#99100)

### What?

Stops Turbopack from re-chunking every App Router layout segment once
per page in production builds. The manually constructed server-utilities
chunk group is now only created in development.

### Why?

A production build should chunk each shared layout segment exactly once.
Instead, a layout segment was chunked again for every endpoint below it.
On a small app with four endpoints, the root layout was chunked 4 times
and a nested `dashboard` layout 2 times. The emitted output was still
shared, so this was wasted build work rather than bigger bundles, which
is why output-based tests never caught it.

Production already builds a single module graph for the whole app, so
the module graph is not what differs between endpoints. The difference
comes from the server-utilities chunk group that seeds the
layout-segment chain:

- It is a `SharedMerged` group whose parent is the current endpoint's
entry chunk group.
- A merged group's parent is part of its identity, so every endpoint
gets a different group (5 chunkings on the same app).
- Its result seeds the availability info passed to each layout segment
after it. Availability info is part of the chunking task key, so each
shared segment ended up with a different key per endpoint and was
chunked again.

The code comment already said this manual shared chunk exists mainly to
help development. That makes sense there: each endpoint has its own
module graph in development, and without the group layout segments would
share very little across pages.

This is PR 0 of the chunk-group stack. The PRs above it are:

1. #98733 — canonical chunk-group identity
2. #98734 — graph-derived output groups
3. #98823 — Pages Router dev client graph chaining
4. #98685 — chunk-group availability bitmaps
5. #99050 — keyed chunk-group index lookups

### How?

The manual server-utilities group is now created only in
per-page-module-graph mode, which is development. In production the
layout-segment chain starts from an endpoint-independent state, so
sibling endpoints produce the same chunking task key for a shared
segment. The server utilities are then chunked with the entry through
the whole-app graph. Development behaves exactly as before.

On the same four-endpoint app, a production build now chunks the root
layout and the nested layout **once each**, and the manual
server-utilities group is gone. Development still creates the group and
chunks segments per page, which is expected for on-demand compilation.

Adds `test/e2e/app-dir/layout-segment-chunk-sharing`, a root layout and
a nested layout that share one module across two sibling pages. It
asserts two things:

- **Output sharing (Turbopack dev and production):** the shared module
is emitted into exactly one server chunk. Webpack builds a
self-contained server bundle per route, so this assertion is gated on
the bundler, not the mode.
- **Work sharing (Turbopack production only):** output sharing alone
does not prove the chunking *task* was reused, since a segment could be
re-chunked per page with an identical result. The test builds with
tracing enabled and uses `next internal query-trace` to count executions
of the nested layout's chunking task, which must be exactly one. A cache
hit produces no execution span, so the count equals the number of real
executions. Development compiles pages on demand with a module graph per
page, so repeated chunking is expected there and the assertion is
skipped.

With the fix reverted, the work-sharing assertion fails with 2
executions, while the output-sharing assertion still passes.

### Performance

Measured on a synthetic App Router app: a root layout and a nested
`section/layout.tsx`, each importing M modules (~20% `'use client'`),
with N trivial sibling pages under `section/`. Cold `next build` with
release native builds of both commits (`192fcaf7` vs this PR, one shared
JS build); paired runs in ABBA order on an 8 vCPU / 16 GB Vercel Sandbox
VM; 95% Student-t intervals on the paired differences.

At **800 pages × 1,000 modules per layout**, a dedicated 12-pair run:

| metric | Δ | 95% CI | pairs improved |
|---|---|---|---|
| Turbopack compile time | **−6.3%** (−767 ms) | [−968, −565] ms | 12/12
|
| total `next build` time | **−2.2%** (−764 ms) | [−1241, −287] ms |
9/12 |
| Turbopack process peak RSS | **−4.2%** (−104 MB) | [−141, −68] MB |
12/12 |

In traces of that build, the nested layout goes from 800 chunking
executions to 1, the root layout from 802 to 1, and the server-utilities
group from 803 to 0 (Node.js chunking spans overall: 7,223 → 1,617).
Smaller configurations (50–800 pages × 200 modules, 200 pages × 1,000
modules; 8 pairs each) showed no detected difference in time or
Turbopack memory, so the gain matters mainly for large apps.

**Trade-off:** without the manual shared group, a few server utilities
(the `*-async-storage.external` and `runtime-reacts.external` wrappers,
the vendored `react-rsc` getter and a small `bytes` helper) are now
inlined into each page's SSR entry chunk instead of being emitted once.
That adds about **2.3 KB of server output per App Router endpoint**
(+0.9% to +4.4% of server JS in these fixtures). Client JS is
byte-identical. Keeping these modules shared in production without
per-endpoint identity would be a possible follow-up.

### Verification

- Trace measurement on the fixture (production): root layout 4 → 1,
nested layout 2 → 1, server-utilities group 5 → 0; dev unchanged
- Production build renders and serves every route with the shared
module; the shared module is still emitted into exactly one server chunk
- `layout-segment-chunk-sharing` — Turbopack production (3 passed),
Turbopack dev (output assertion passed, trace assertion skipped),
webpack production (Turbopack-only assertions skipped)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings -A deprecated`,
`cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `turbopack-core` + `next-core` unit tests (252 passed);
`turbopack-tests` snapshots (126 passed, no changes)

author: lukesandberg
message:
turbo-tasks-gc: Defer most aggregation graph management until after GC has settled (#98591)

Fix AggregationGraph updates during GC.

During GC we aremoving a lot of edges so this can trigger a lot of
aggregation graph churn. Because of the highly parallel nature of GC
this can end up with multiple queues fighting over updates which can
exceed various retry limits and lead to things like trying to turn nodes
into `followers` that are actively being deleted.

Instead we just don't rebalance the aggregation graph during GC, instead
we buffer every `rebalance` request and set the `optimize` budget to
zero. Then after GC settles we process all the rebalances at once,
taking care to filter out any tasks that have been since deleted.

Because GC is only removing edges it can lead to inefficient graphs (too
many interior nodes) but not violate graph invariants.

Alternatives considered:

The initial idea was to ensure GC had finished with all 'children' of
the node before processing rebalance requests, but this was only a
partial solution (and complex!), since it didn't handle the case of an
aggregating node having multiple children become collectible in the
initial scan, this could still trigger 'optimization contention' and
turning dead nodes into followers.

Testing:

The test/benchmark are enhanced to produce non-trivial aggregation
graphs which improves test coverage (though the issue of racing deletes
was trivially found by CI also)

author: sokra
message:
Use graph-backed codegen for client proxies and WASM loaders (#99115)

### What?

Generate **both RSC client-reference proxies and WebAssembly loaders**
under their graph-backed wrapper module identities, using one shared,
higher-level content helper. Remove both generated-path exceptions from
`BindingUsageInfo::used_exports` and the earlier proxy-specific export
filter.

### Why?

The wrapper is the module in Turbopack's graph, but its chunk item
previously delegated code generation to a separately processed virtual
JS module. Export-usage lookup for that proxy/loader missed the graph
and fell back to “all exports used.” In a `sideEffects: false` barrel
this could register a pruned client export and request a missing
`<locals>` module ID. The WebAssembly loader had the same graph-identity
mismatch, hidden by a separate filename-based fallback.

Canary's #99102 now guards against the client-reference missing-ID
symptom by checking pruned references. This PR fixes the upstream
identity mismatch instead so `expand_exports()` sees real usage;
#99102's independent safety checks remain in place.

### How?

`chunk_item_content_with_code_from(graph_module, code_source, ...)`
takes the generated source's analyzed program, references, exports,
source map and async behavior while using the wrapper for the *whole
code-generation module context*. Both client-reference and WASM wrappers
call it. This replaces the public low-level `with_module_context`
setter; it does not change module IDs, WASM output assets, React Flight
registration, or the existing single-chunk WASM rejection. sokra's
`ResolvedVc` suggestions are also applied.

#99090's pruned-reexport-source guard remains necessary: removing it
independently still fails its execution fixture. #99082 proposed
reverting all of #98617 and closed unmerged; it was not a separate fix
to delete.

The neutral production proxy regression and two supplemental
pruned-source execution fixtures remain in the PR.

### Verification

- **WASM can-fail/can-pass:** all 3 existing WASM execution fixtures
pass before removing the fallback; with the fallback removed but old
loader delegation retained, all 3 fail `export usage not found
...wasm_.loader.mjs`; with the shared helper, all 3 pass (instantiation,
imported functions/memory, and `?module` compilation).
- **Proxy can-fail/can-pass:** without the wrapper-context path and
proxy fallback, the production fixture fails `export usage not found
.../__nextjs-internal-proxy.mjs`; with the fix it passes.
- **Rust/build:** 1,282 tests pass across affected crates; clippy (`-D
warnings`), rustfmt and `pnpm build-all` (18/18 tasks) pass.
- **Next.js integration:** Turbopack production 6 suites/12 tests
(proxy, used client references, #99102 regression, edge WASM and WASM
output tracing); development 3 suites/8 tests (proxy, used client
references and edge WASM). Client-reference chunking 1/1. After rebasing
onto current canary, `pnpm build-all` and focused proxy/edge WASM
production tests (3 suites/7 tests) pass again.

author: lubieowoce
message:
[PPF] Instant validation for `ensureStatic = "shell" | "prefetch"` (#98249)

Adjusts Instant Validation internals to validate the `ShellStatic` stage
instead of `ShellRuntime` when `ensureStatic >= "shell"`. If that's the
case, the client will do a static request (and extract the shell from
it), so the app shell cannot access session data (unlike the PPF
default, where we use a runtime shell).

Note that in some cases, this might seem more restrictive than needed.
For `ensureStatic >= "shell"`, the client will do a static prefetch that
goes up to the `Static` stage which resolves more things, like static
`params`, `prefetch()` ( in the `PrefetchStatic` stage) and
`navigation()` (in the `NavigationStatic` stage). However:
1. The client expects to be able to rewind the static prefetch into a
shell and reuse it across the whole route, so we should be validating
that the shell is actually useful.
2. For `ensureStatic = "shell"`, we might still do a *runtime* prefetch
(with `<Link prefetch={true}>`), which will not have `navigation()`, and
validating `ShellStatic` catches that.

### Implementation notes

- I've renamed `RequestStore.needsAppShell` to
`RequestStore.needsRuntimeShell` (undoing a previous rename), because
the `ShellStatic` stage can _also_ be an App Shell, just not a _runtime_
one. The flag controls whether or not we're delaying link data until the
runtime stages, which we don't need to do if the shell is static.
- If we have `ensureStatic >= "shell"` set, we _won't_ set
`RequestStore.needsRuntimeShell` anymore, which means that the main
render can once again be re-used for both IV and SSV.
`prepareValidationInputsInPartialPrefetching` is changed accordingly.
We'll also set `revealAfterStage` to `StaticShell` to match what the
client would have prefetched.
- We add a new mode in instant validation,
`ValidationPrefetchKind.StaticAppShell`, which checks the prefetch at
the `ShellStatic` stage. This is enabled if we have `ensureStatic >=
"shell"`. the PPF default mode`ValidationPrefetchKind.RuntimeAppShell`
uses `ShellRuntime` instead.





### Tests

- IV should show an insight for unguarded `cookies()` if `ensureStatic
>= "shell"` (unlike the default behavior of app shells)
- IV should *still* show an insight for unguarded static `params`,
`prefetch()`, and `navigation()` regardless of `ensureStatic` (same as
default)

author: sokra
message:
Tune Node server chunking for require overhead (#99120)

### What?

Tune production Node.js server JavaScript chunking to use a lower
estimated cost for loading a chunk, a smaller soft minimum chunk size,
and no per-group chunk-count target. Client, CSS, Edge, and development
chunking remain unchanged.

### Why?

Server chunks are loaded with Node.js `require()`, not network requests.
Measurements across synthetic JavaScript chunks found roughly 0.1 ms of
fixed load overhead, equivalent to approximately 2.5–25 KB of parsing
work depending on code density. The existing 200 KB estimate overweights
each server-side load and encourages unnecessary merging.

### How?

Apply the server-specific tuning to both Node production chunking
contexts while keeping the existing maximum merge size. The values are
an initial estimate from the benchmark; representative application
builds and cold-start measurements can refine them.

`deploy-tarball` job is skipped on docs-only canary pushes or on
production tag pushes
(https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/35075211933). The
`upload-preview-tarballs` workflow then failed when downloading the
artifact.

This change lets the download step fail without failing the job and
skips the upload step in that case, so a missing artifact no longer
turns the workflow red. The failed-but-tolerated download step still
leaves an error annotation on the green run. Real breakage still
surfaces in build-and-test, which waits on the published tarballs.

author: eps1lon
message:
[cd] Retry preview tarball uploads with backoff and richer diagnostics (#99060)

The `upload-preview-tarballs` workflow aborted its entire run when a
single tarball upload hit a transient network error, and the logged
error did not identify which package or request had failed. One observed
run failed with `TypeError: fetch failed` (`UND_ERR_SOCKET`) after the
~78MB `next` tarball body had been written but before the response
arrived (e.g.
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/35721116824/job/106724007428#step:4:19).

`scripts/upload-preview-tarballs.js` now wraps each package's upload in
a retry with exponential backoff (5 attempts, 1s/2s/4s/8s). Every
failure is retried, including network-level rejections without an HTTP
status. Error messages now name the package and the failed request
phase, and non-OK responses include a truncated response body alongside
the status and response headers such as `x-vercel-id`, so the next rare
failure is actionable. A package that exhausts its retries no longer
aborts the remaining uploads; all failures are collected and reported at
the end as an `AggregateError`.

author: sokra
message:
Add experimental custom webpack support (#98862)

### What?

Add the experimental `customWebpack` configuration option so
webpack-mode applications can use a project-installed webpack version
instead of the version bundled with Next.js. Webpack is now an optional
`^5.98.0` peer dependency, and the new option is documented with
end-to-end coverage for webpack 5.98.0 and 5.111.0.

### Why?

Next.js currently redirects webpack imports to its bundled
implementation. This prevents applications from opting into newer
compatible webpack releases or validating upgrades independently. The
new option provides an explicit escape hatch while preserving the
bundled implementation as the default.

### How?

After configuration is resolved, webpack-mode startup redirects the
existing webpack require-hook aliases to the package resolved from the
application. The selection is propagated to webpack build workers
through the existing local-webpack runtime switch. If the optional peer
cannot be resolved, Next.js restores its bundled aliases and reports an
actionable installation error.

The implementation only activates for webpack, leaving Turbopack and
Rspack unchanged. It also handles the resolver stack API exposed by
external webpack versions. The test matrix verifies the selected
compiler version, rendering in development and production, the
build-worker path, missing-peer diagnostics, and bundled fallback
behavior when the option is disabled.

message:
Preserve error boundaries in on-demand partial prerenders (#99051)

An on-demand prerender failure still throws when its recovery output
requires a resume. This hides the route's error boundary behind a
generic error response, even when healthy parts of the page could
continue rendering.

Failures now retain their original error and serialized postponed state.
Self-hosted servers append a separate continuation for each document
request. Adapter deployments use the existing platform transport to
resume with the actual request.

In `next start`, a failed partial prerender follows the same prerender
and resume flow as a successful PPR cache miss. Failed preludes are not
persisted, so later independent requests retry prerendering before
resuming. Concurrent requests can share the pending prerender, and each
document request owns its resume.

The response retains status 500 and non-cacheable headers. Failed output
is not persisted as a successful ISR entry. Build failures and recovery
without a usable Flight result continue to throw.

The tests cover errors inside and outside Suspense, request-specific
dynamic content, navigation after failed prefetches, same-URL recovery,
successful-page retention, and original-error reporting.

Preserve error boundaries during on-demand prerendering (#99037)

In production, an error while generating an App Router page on demand
can return a generic 500 response or a Pages Router 500 page instead of

invocation, without changing existing in-flight batching. Failed output

platform's `waitUntil` when available.

scope for this PR and continues to throw. A follow-up PR will preserve
and resume that partial recovery output.

The fix applies to self-hosted production servers and adapter-based
Vercel deployments. The legacy Vercel deployment path retains its
existing behavior of replacing the response with a generic error page.

failures, pending I/O inside Suspense, same-URL recovery,
successful-page retention, and original-error reporting.

author: gnoff
message:
Preserve closed-route admission across cache misses (#98964)

## Summary

Keep route admission independent of ISR cache contents. With Cache
Components disabled, a route using `dynamicParams = false` and
`generateStaticParams()` can currently return 200 for a build-generated
URL, then incorrectly return 404 after `revalidatePath` expires its
cache entry. An empty external cache causes the same failure on the
first request.

For example, if the build generated `/products/known`, that URL remains
allowed after invalidation; `/products/unlisted` remains disallowed
regardless of cache state. If a later build removes `/products/known`,
it must immediately stop matching, even if an external cache still holds
that URL's old response.

The request handler now rejects unlisted closed URLs before looking up
their ISR entries. This prevents both serving an old cache hit and
generating a new response for a URL the current build does not admit. An
admitted build path whose matched fallback is `false` regenerates using
a blocking render when necessary.

The two decisions stay separate: the manifest determines whether the URL
may match, while the response generator chooses how to produce an
admitted response. We do not share mutable fallback-mode state between
those stages.

### Preserved exceptions and adapter behavior

- **Server Actions:** forwarding can invoke a worker at
`/products/[slug]`, not a concrete page URL. Action calls retain their
existing exemption from page admission checks. A retained action must
still work after the user navigates away from its closed route.
- **Draft mode:** an unpublished URL can be previewed without admitting
it publicly or replacing its public cache entry.
- **Minimal mode:** the platform router remains responsible for
admission before invoking the renderer.
- **Adapters:** rendering a routing 404 now happens outside the response
cache. The previous placement could successfully send a 404 and then
throw `cache entry required but not generated` because it returned no
cache entry for a non-null cache key. The new adapter fixture reproduces
this on the parent runtime.

This uses the existing prerender manifest and does not change its format
or the adapter contract. The most specific matched dynamic route
continues to determine the policy for open URLs, so specialized matchers
can admit an open suffix without admitting an unknown closed prefix.

## Regression coverage

Real fixtures cover:

- Repeated invalidation, ordinary and optional catch-all paths,
time-based ISR, concurrent regeneration, and serving a stale response
while regenerating in the background.
- Empty external caches and an external cache retained across two real
builds. The latter verifies that the removed path's old entry still
exists but is never consulted.
- Document, HEAD, navigation, prefetch, bot, rewritten, and
overlapping-route requests.
- Direct and forwarded Server Actions, draft previews, and direct
minimal-mode renderer invocations.
- Adapter-specific 404 handling and regeneration of admitted paths.
- The distinction between routing rejection and content that calls
`notFound()`: an admitted URL can transition from 200 to 404 and back,
including when its build render returned 404.

These legacy `dynamicParams` fixtures are excluded from the Cache
Components matrix because that configuration does not support the API.

## Stack

This is an unflagged correctness fix, placed after #98950 and before the
parameter-matching API in #97393. It can land without committing to that
API. The API's mixed-prefix and dynamic-tail lifecycle coverage belongs
in the API layer.

## Verification

- Before the original fix, the two initial regression fixtures failed 11
checks while the open-route and time-based controls passed.
- Against the parent runtime, the new adapter fixture reproduces the
cache-entry invariant on document, navigation, prefetch, and bot
requests, plus the invalidation regression.
- The retained Server Action regression passes on the parent runtime,
fails on the earlier PR revision without the exemption, and passes with
the explicit action exemption. It also passes in development with the
exemption.
- Local production runs before replaying the follow-up onto the rebased
stack: all 49 tests across seven suites pass in both Webpack and
fresh-native Turbopack, including the existing closed-parameter
navigation suite. The follow-up patch applied unchanged; CI will verify
the rebased head.
- Development Turbopack request-mode coverage: 10 passed; the
public-cache reuse assertion is production-only.
- Repository TypeScript, Next.js declaration generation, changed-file
formatting/ESLint, and `git diff --check` pass.

No live deployment verification. A separate `revalidate-if-generated`
hang with an always-empty custom cache reproduces on both this PR and
its parent; its diagnostic is retained for a separate follow-up, not
included or silently skipped here.

message:
Keep cached root parameters out of generic fallback shells (#98950)

## Summary

Replace #98892 with a fix for both ways root-dependent content can enter
a generic fallback shell: reusing an existing Resume Data Cache entry
and executing a fresh cache fill.

For example, cached English content produced for `/en/items/one` remains
reusable in `/en/items/[slug]`, but must be absent from
`/[lang]/items/[slug]`. When reusing that concrete prerender as a seed,
clone its cache map and replace entries whose recorded
`readRootParamNames` intersect the unknown roots with omission markers.
The original seed is unchanged.

Keep those markers in the cache map itself, not a separate collection
that must stay synchronized. They carry the reason for a hole between
prerender passes and are never serialized into the persisted RDC.
Preserve canary's distinction between URL data and session data when
computing shell and prefetch hints.

invocation, including cached components with an internal Suspense
boundary. Affected nested caches use independently cancellable

omission marker: the nested leader has no RDC of its own. Otherwise the
final prerender sees an unexplained miss and loses the fallback's

author: sampoder
message:
[turbopack] Track members across namespace re-exports (#96396)

## What?

This PR closes a missed tree-shaking opportunity for libraries that
expose a module namespace as a named export. One real-world example is
Zod, whose public API has a structure similar to the following (and this
pattern also appears in v0's codebase):

```js
// user.js
import { z } from './lib.js'

console.log(z.object(), z.string(), z.defaultLocale)
```

```js
// lib.js — mirrors zod/index.js
import * as z from './external.js'

export * from './external.js'
export { z }
export default z

// external.js — mirrors zod/v4/classic/external.js
import en from './locales/en.js'

export * as locales from './locales/index.js'

export const object = () => 'object'
export const string = () => 'string'
export const defaultLocale = en
```

The analyzer can now preserve the information that only `object`,
`string`, and `defaultLocale` are read from `z`, and use it after
resolving that named export to the namespace of `external.js`.

This PR is now standalone on `canary`. Its two former prerequisites have
landed: #98680 introduced the independently reviewed
`EsmAssetReferenceOptions` constructor refactor, and #96282 integrated
CommonJS and ESM whole-namespace forwarding with canary's generic
`ExportUsage::Passthrough` fixed point.

## Why?

Previously, Turbopack knew that the named export `z` was used, but lost
the static member information from expressions such as `z.object()`.
Once `z` resolved to a namespace object, the optimizer therefore kept
every export of `external.js` — including `locales` and all of
`./locales/index.js` in this example.

The optimization must remain conservative in several cases:

- a computed property whose name cannot be determined statically, such
as `z[key]`;
- a namespace binding that escapes to unknown code, such as passing `z`
to another function;
- static and opaque uses of the same binding, where the opaque use must
dominate narrowing;
- live exports and method calls, whose binding and receiver semantics
must not change.

It must also avoid changing ordinary named-import behavior. A property
read on an imported value is not proof that the value is a module
namespace; narrowing and namespace provenance are valid only after
re-export resolution proves that fact.

## How?

### Represent namespace-member requests explicitly

The module-part model now has explicit states for this operation:

- `ExportedNamespaceMember { export, member }` represents a static
member read on a named export before re-export resolution;
- `RenamedNamespaceMember { export, member }` represents the case after
that export resolves to a module namespace.

This avoids overloading an ordinary `Export` or an optional `member`
field with two meanings. It also keeps existing `Export` and
`RenamedNamespace` identities unchanged; the new variants have distinct
hashes only for the new states.

Multiple static reads and multiple aliases are tracked as independently
keyed references, so `z.object`, `z.string`, and `z.defaultLocale` all
survive rather than overwriting one another.

### Narrow only after proving the export is a namespace

The analyzer records a statically known member on an imported binding
while leaving the emitted member expression intact. Re-export following
first resolves the outer named export:

1. If it resolves to a namespace object, Turbopack synthesizes a
namespace-member reference to the resolved module and contributes
`PartialNamespaceObject({ member })` there.
2. If it resolves to an ordinary named export, it continues to behave
like a normal named read of the outer module. It does not mark the
module as namespace-observable or unnecessarily disable export-name
mangling.

Dynamic property access and escaping bindings do not produce a narrowed
member part, so they continue to retain the full namespace. When static
and opaque uses are joined, the full-namespace use wins.

The explicit module-part variants are threaded through both fragment and
non-fragment infrastructure so they remain valid graph identities. The
new `ExportedNamespaceMember` rewrite itself currently runs only when
module fragments are disabled. A dedicated `moduleFragmentsEnabled:
true` fixture verifies the supported existing split behavior without
claiming that this new rewrite is active there.

While rebasing, canary moved follow-reexport canonicalization into
`turbopack-ecmascript` so lazy dynamic imports can carry the same
canonicalization policy. Namespace-member handling now lives in that
canonicalization helper as well, preserving both the new
lazy-compilation path and this PR's namespace rewrite.

## Testing

Enabled coverage includes:

- the Zod-shaped snapshot showing only `object`, `string`, and
`defaultLocale` retained while the unused locale namespace is removed;
- multiple static members on one namespace-valued export;
- dynamic access, escaping use, and mixed static/opaque use retaining
the full namespace;
- direct `export * as`, including an enabled used/unused precision
assertion;
- computed-string, parenthesized, optional, and missing-property reads;
- `this`-sensitive method calls;
- default-exported and renamed namespace values;
- live bindings read and mutated through multiple aliases, with single
evaluation;
- nested namespace runtime behavior and top-level-await targets;
- scope-hoisted, non-scope-hoisted, and module-fragment configurations;
- export-name mangling safety and non-pessimization across #96282's
forwarding edges.

Development coverage updates both a value behind the CommonJS forwarding
edge and a statically read namespace member, verifying HMR observes each
new value without stale exports or runtime errors.

One optimization-only limitation is documented under
`__skipped__/namespace-value-reexport-nested`: member narrowing
currently stops after the first namespace level for a read such as
`z.locales.en`. The full nested runtime behavior is covered by the
enabled `namespace-value-reexport` fixture.

Local verification on the standalone canary rebase passes affected-crate
and `next-core` checks, 14 focused execution/snapshot tests, the merged
passthrough/annotation unit tests, 60 analyzer graph tests, `build-all`,
and the development/HMR test. A throwaway ordinary object-valued
named-import fixture also verified that the pre-resolution path
preserves property values and `this` for getters and methods; it was
removed after review.

author: lubieowoce
message:
[PPF] Implement `unstable_ensureStatic = "shell" | "prefetch"` (#98191)

Builds on #98129, where we made it possible for shells to be static
while the prefetches depending on where runtime data is accessed:
- `ensureStatic = "shell"` simply defers all runtime tracking until the
prefetch (semantically, it's as if it was gated by `await prefetch()`).
this means that the shell will always be considered static (although the
prefetch can still be runtime)
- `ensureStatic = "prefetch"` is analogous, but means that the prefetch
should be static (semantically, it's as if it was gated by `await
navigation()`). this effectively skips the tracking altogether, and
*both* the shell and the prefetch will be static.
- notably, in this mode, accessing fallback params in an ISR fallback no
longer sets `needsRuntimeRequest` either, because the config disallows
runtime prefetches, even if it'd let us skip waiting for the ISR
prerender to finish.

note that "static" here means "statically prerendered", as opposed to
"rendered on demand via runtime prerender". both options still allow the
prerender to have dynamic holes. disallowing dynamic holes altogether
will be handled by `ensureStatic = "navigation"` in a follow up.

### Implementation notes

i've also renamed `walkNeedsRuntimeCompleteness` to
`walkCanUseRuntimeRequests` -- in practice, the function checks "is this
a PPF route", but being PPF no longer means that runtime completeness is
required, because `ensureStatic` deliberately gets rid of it.
`walkCanUseRuntimeRequests` is a bit more accurate, because it tells us
whether runtime requests are possible at all. This change (and the
associated changes in comments) are in a separate commit for ease of
review.

author: lubieowoce
message:
[PPF] Validate `unstable_ensureStatic` nesting (#98357)

`ensureStatic` forms a hierarchy: `"auto" < "shell" < "prefetch" <
"navigation"`, with each value being more contrained than its
predecessor.

1. A child segment cannot relax constraints set by a parent segment, it
can only tighten them
- so `shell` in a layout and `prefetch` in a page is fine, but the
opposite is not
- note that setting `"auto"` in the child *is* allowed, because it means
"unconstrained" and is compatible with all the other configs
2. We can't have two conflicting levels set by two parallel slots (but
`auto` is compatible with any other constraint, so it's allowed, same as
above)
3. If a segment sets `ensureStatic = false`, then no other segments on
that route are allowed to constrain the route by setting anything higher
than `auto` (this is meant as a signal for e.g. "this segment
DELIBERATELY uses a runtime shell and should not be overridden to be
static")

Also adds exhaustive tests for all of these scenarios.

message:
refactor(turbo-rcstr): drop unsupported 16-byte pointer width (#98355)

## What?

Removes turbo-rcstr's 16-byte/128-bit pointer representation and the
unused `atom_size_64` feature plumbing. Unsupported pointer widths now
fail with an error that names the supported 32-bit and 64-bit widths.

## Why?

This follows up on review feedback from #97577. The previous negative
cfg made unknown pointer widths fall through to the 64-bit
representation, while the 16-bit implementation and `atom_size_64`
features had no users. Making both supported widths explicit keeps
representation assumptions visible and produces a useful failure for
unsupported targets.

## How?

The narrow tagged-value layout is now specific to 32-bit targets, and
the pointer-sized layout is specific to 64-bit targets. `atom_size_128`
remains unchanged. The dead feature declarations are removed from
turbo-rcstr and its proc-macro crate.

author: sokra
message:
test(turbo-tasks-backend): run the db_versioning tests on wasm (#97901)

### What?

Makes `turbo-tasks-backend`'s `db_versioning` tests run on
`wasm32-wasip1-threads` instead of being
skipped, by routing temporary-directory creation in tests through a
small helper that does not depend
on `std::env::temp_dir()`.

Twelve test instances that were previously skipped now execute on wasm.
Three related
`kv_backing_storage` instances remain skipped, but for a different — and
verified — reason (see below).
Native behaviour is unchanged: the same tests run exactly as before, and
nothing is newly skipped there.

The wider WASI suite also exposed an unrelated intermittent stall in
`test_unbounded_busy_queue_does_not_churn_workers`: passing isolated
runs finish in about 0.25 seconds,
while repeated runs can stop making progress indefinitely. That stress
test is now ignored only on
WASI, with the observed reason recorded; native coverage remains enabled
while the underlying
multi-threaded runtime stall is investigated separately.

### Why?

These tests were skipped with the reason `no temp directory on WASI`,
which turned out to be only half
true. WASI genuinely has no notion of a system temp directory —
`std::env::temp_dir()` is hard-coded to
`unsupported()` in `std/sys/paths/wasi.rs`, so it panics regardless of
`TMPDIR` — but the *filesystem
itself works fine*. A WASI guest can use any directory the host preopens
for it.

So the blocker was in how the tests asked for a directory, not in the
platform. Asking WASI where "temp"
is fails; creating a directory inside a path the host already granted
succeeds.

This matters beyond tidiness: skip reasons are the primary record of
what does and does not work on
wasm, and an inaccurate one is worse than no reason at all, because it
makes a fixable problem look like
a platform limit and quietly discourages anyone from trying.

Fixing it also uncovered the *real* limitation underneath. With temp
directories working, the three
`kv_backing_storage` tests get further and hit a genuine platform gap:
`memmap2` ships `unix.rs`,
`windows.rs` and a stub for every other target, so `turbo-persistence`
cannot open a database on WASI
at all (`Failed to mmap: platform not supported`). Those three are still
skipped, now with that cause
recorded instead of the temp-directory one. That is a real, separate
piece of work — persistent caching
cannot function on wasm until `turbo-persistence` grows a non-mmap read
path — and it is now visible
rather than hidden behind a misleading reason.

### How?

A single test-only helper owns the platform difference, so the ~11 call
sites stay identical in shape
and no test carries its own `cfg`. On native it delegates to
`tempfile::tempdir()`, preserving today's
behaviour byte for byte, including having `TempDir` own cleanup. On wasm
it creates the directory inside
a preopened path instead of consulting the environment. The helper is
crate-private and compiled only
for tests, so it adds nothing to the shipped crate, and it returns
`tempfile`'s own error type rather
than erasing it.

Two deliberate choices are worth calling out for review:

- **Every remaining skip is justified by an observed failure**, not by
inference. Each of the three
`kv_backing_storage` tests was run individually and traced to
`memmap2`'s stub before being skipped
again; the twelve `db_versioning` ones were confirmed to pass. Nothing
is skipped speculatively.
- **Skips use `ignore` with a reason rather than `cfg`**, so they appear
in test output as
`ignored, <reason>` instead of silently vanishing from the run. That is
what keeps the count of
what-doesn't-work-on-wasm honest and reviewable, and it is asserted that
the native run still has
  zero ignored tests.

The wasm coupling is documented at the helper: it relies on the host
preopening a directory, which the
repository's Node wasi test host does. A different runner must provide
the same, or update the helper.

author: sokra
message:
fix(turbo-tasks): let parking_lot block on wasm instead of panicking (#97860)

### What?

Makes `parking_lot` locks actually block on wasm instead of panicking,
and removes 33 of the 35
`ignore`s that panic had forced onto the wasm test suites.

### Why?

`parking_lot_core` picks its thread parker in `thread_parker/mod.rs`.
The working wasm parker
(`wasm_atomic.rs`, built on `memory_atomic_wait32` /
`memory_atomic_notify`) is selected only under

```
all(feature = "nightly", target_family = "wasm", target_feature = "atomics")
```

Otherwise it falls back to `wasm.rs`, whose `park()` is
`panic!("Parking not supported on this platform")`.
`wasm32-wasip1-threads` **does** report
`target_feature = "atomics"`, so the only missing piece was the feature
— every contended lock
panicked, which is why so many tests were ignored on wasm.

### How?

Two changes, and **neither alone is sufficient**:

- bump `parking_lot_core` 0.9.8 → 0.9.12, because 0.9.8's atomic parker
needs `feature(stdsimd)`,
  removed from Rust long ago;
- enable `parking_lot`'s `nightly` feature **for wasm targets only** (it
forwards to
`parking_lot_core/nightly`). 0.9.12 *still* gates the atomic parker
behind it, so a bump on its own
  keeps selecting the panicking stub silently.

Verified on the resolved feature graph rather than the manifest —
`nightly` is present for
`wasm32-wasip1-threads` and absent for the host.

### Testing

`contended_mutex_blocks_and_hands_over` is built so it cannot pass
vacuously: a barrier guarantees the
waiter actually contends, the waiter must block for a measurable
interval, and it must observe the
holder's write. **Negative control**: with the feature removed it fails
at
`parking_lot_core-0.9.12/src/thread_parker/wasm.rs:26` with *"Parking
not supported on this platform"*.

```
turbo-tasks          54 pass / 28 ignored  ->  72 pass / 11 ignored
turbo-tasks-backend  66 pass / 32 ignored  ->  82 pass / 15 ignored
native                     0 ignored, unchanged
```

Two of the old ignores remain, under a different and verified cause:
their work completes in ~500 ms
of an 800 ms serial sum, so the parallelism is real, but dropping a
multi-thread tokio runtime while
their blocking helpers are still alive deadlocks on wasm. That was
previously hidden because
`panic = abort` killed the process at the failing assertion before
teardown ran. It is fixed in the
follow-up runtime layer.

Also fixes a latent bug unrelated to wasm:
`test_parallel_try_for_each_mut` asserted every element was
incremented, which only holds when the chunk size is 1. Chunking comes
from
`available_parallelism() * 4` and each chunk stops at its first error,
so with parallelism 1 the chunk
size is 2 and every second item is skipped — it would fail on any
single-core machine. It now asserts
the parallelism-independent contract.

author: sokra
message:
test(turbo-tasks): run the wasm tests with a Node wasi host (#97789)

### What?

Adds a Node host so `wasm32-wasip1-threads` test binaries can run, and
wires the `turbo-rcstr`, `turbo-tasks`, and `turbo-tasks-backend`
library tests into the WASI CI job.

It also provides the WASI allocation symbols expected by the `lz4-sys`
dependency introduced by the base PR, allowing those test binaries to
link.

### Why?

The Rust test binaries require host functionality that stock WASI
runners do not provide. Turbopack stores its link-time task registries
in WebAssembly custom sections and imports a host callback to read them.
Its multithreaded runtime also requires shared memory and thread
spawning through Node Workers.

The base PR replaces `lzzzz` with `lz4`. `lz4-sys 1.11.1` compiles its C
sources against custom allocation shims on `wasm32-wasi*`, but excludes
the Rust implementations when the target OS is WASI. Without equivalent
symbols supplied by the consuming crate, test links fail on unresolved
malloc, calloc, and free shims.

Running these suites in CI gives the remaining WASI layers direct
regression coverage instead of relying on native-only tests.

### How?

The Node cargo target runner provides WASI preview1, imported shared
memory, and the complete two-phase [`link-section` custom-section
protocol](https://github.com/mmastrac/linktime/blob/ae29e51d94a955df2442ed6418b8a712c1f2bfb3/link-section/docs/PREAMBLE.md#wasm).


[`@emnapi/wasi-threads`](https://github.com/toyobayashi/emnapi/tree/main/packages/wasi-threads)
supplies Worker lifecycle, compiled-module transfer, load/start
ordering, and cleanup for the
[`wasi.thread-spawn`](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-threads)
import that Node's WASI runtime does not provide. The module is compiled
once, then the structured-cloneable `WebAssembly.Module` and shared
memory are sent to Workers. A small adapter around the package's
lower-level `ThreadManager` and `ThreadMessageHandler` APIs preserves
Rust's original one-argument ABI: the high-level `WASIThreads` wrapper
requires guest `malloc`/`free` exports for that ABI, and Rust test
binaries do not export them. Worker identifiers come from a shared
atomic counter because Tokio Workers can spawn additional Workers while
the main WebAssembly thread is parked.

On WASI, `turbo-persistence` supplies the three allocation symbols
required by liblz4 and forwards them to WASI libc, keeping allocation
and deallocation within the same allocator. Native builds do not compile
these wrappers.

Tests that depend on unavailable platform behavior remain visible as
WASI-only ignored tests with explicit reasons. Native runs keep the full
test set enabled. A following stacked PR replaces the unsupported
`parking_lot` parker and re-enables the corresponding contention tests.

The workflow installs and builds the workspace before running the host
because both the package dependency and compiled production support used
by a later stack layer must be available.

### Verification

- Node 20 host unit tests: 9/9
- Exact combined WASI CI command: `turbo-rcstr` 12 passed / 1 ignored;
`turbo-tasks` 68 / 44; `turbo-tasks-backend` 65 / 35
- Full 111-test `turbo-tasks` binary through the package-managed host:
95 passed / 16 ignored
- No Worker-side `WebAssembly.compile`; the compiled module is
transferred by `ThreadManager`
- `pnpm install --lockfile-only --offline` with a frozen lockfile

author: sokra
message:
Turbopack: mangle exports behind an escaping namespace via the facade (#97770)

### What?

Allows Turbopack to keep mangling a module's internal export keys when
its namespace object escapes. A facade preserves the original public
names while forwarding each one to the mangled key in the locals module,
matching webpack's materialized-namespace behavior.

This PR is stacked on #98617. That lower PR now owns the generic
synthetic-facade compact registration, including empty evaluation
groups, descriptor reuse, scope-hoisted factories, pruned references,
and cycle/async fallbacks. This PR creates those facades for escaping
namespaces, so the generic path is exercised at scale here.

### Why?

A namespace import or dynamic import whose reads cannot be enumerated
currently disables mangling for the entire target module. That makes one
broad consumer lose the size benefit for every otherwise-static consumer
of the module.

Materializing the original namespace surface keeps ESM semantics intact
— including live values and `Object.keys()` — while allowing internal
consumers to use shorter names.

### How?

The facade's synthesized per-export references participate in the module
graph, so named usage propagates to the locals module. Its structural
locals edge carries evaluation usage only, while each forwarded name
carries its own export usage. Part-reference code generation also honors
references pruned by the graph, matching ordinary ESM references.

Modules with no exports are not split, async modules retain the existing
path, and real export-cycle circuit breakers avoid compact registration
because they require their getters to be visible before imports run.
Namespace grouping includes the SWC syntax context so scope-hoisted
modules cannot accidentally share the wrong generated binding.

### Testing

- `cargo test -p turbopack-ecmascript -p turbopack-tests` — **590 unit,
303 execution, 3 auxiliary, and 131 snapshot tests passed** on the
current stack
- `cargo clippy -p turbopack-ecmascript -p turbopack-core -- -D
warnings`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `pnpm test-dev-experimental-turbo
test/development/app-dir/lazy-dynamic-imports/lazy-dynamic-imports.test.ts`
— 9/9 passed
- `pnpm test-dev
test/e2e/app-dir/instant-validation/suspense-boundaries.test.ts` — 38/38
passed
- `pnpm test-start-turbo
test/production/app-dir/barrel-optimization/mui/index.test.ts` — 1/1
passed
- `pnpm test-start-turbo
test/e2e/app-dir/cache-components-allow-otel-spans/cache-components-allow-otel-spans.test.ts`
— 4/4 passed
- `pnpm test-start-turbo
test/e2e/404-page-custom-error/404-page-custom-error.test.ts
test/e2e/app-dir/app-esm-js/index.test.ts
test/e2e/app-dir/app-esm-js/standalone.test.ts` — 9/9 passed
- Existing materialized-namespace fixtures verify namespace values, key
enumeration, dynamic imports, CommonJS consumers, and liveness through
the locals module
- A callable CommonJS namespace fixture regression-tests the compact
registration path after facade materialization
- The full execution suite specifically caught and now covers pruned
locals references and merged evaluation-only locals references in the
generic #98617 implementation

### Bundle-size measurements

Incremental effect of enabling `turbopackMangleExportNames` on this
stack. Both sides use the same native binary and retain #98617's compact
re-export registration; only mangling is toggled. Client reports raw and
deterministic gzip (`gzip -9 -n`, sorted files); server reports raw only
because Node.js consumes server code uncompressed. JavaScript files
only; source maps, CSS, and license sidecars are excluded.

#### Scope hoisting disabled

| benchmark | client raw | client gzip | server raw |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `basic-app` | −17,380 B | −1,131 B | −61,155 B |
| `heavy-npm-deps` *(three-dependency variant: lodash + Mantine +
Mermaid)* | −47,537 B | −6,720 B | −82,326 B |
| `module-cost` | −223,816 B | −2,113 B | −596,419 B |

#### Scope hoisting enabled

| benchmark | client raw | client gzip | server raw |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `basic-app` | −22,658 B | −7,634 B | −32,805 B |
| `heavy-npm-deps` *(three-dependency variant: lodash + Mantine +
Mermaid)* | −14,118 B | +1,291 B | −20,956 B |
| `module-cost` | +30 B | −785 B | −7,265 B |

The `heavy-npm-deps` rows use a modified benchmark fixture with Mantine
and Mermaid enabled alongside lodash; the committed fixture enables

test(dev): add dedicated compiler polling coverage (#97673)

### What?

Adds a dedicated development integration test for compiler file watching
in polling mode under both webpack and Turbopack.

It also removes obsolete `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING` / `CHOKIDAR_INTERVAL`
variables from the unrelated `read-only-source-hmr` suite, which remains
focused on read-only source semantics and normal watcher behavior.

Stack: **5/5** · Previous: #98737

### Why?

Next.js did not have an e2e/development test dedicated to
`watchOptions.pollIntervalMs`. Existing Rust coverage checks watcher
modes, while the filesystem-watcher fuzzer is manual rather than part of
the normal development-test matrix.

The test also regresses notify-rs/notify#981. Older PollWatcher versions
stored ordinary-file mtimes at whole-second precision, so a second edit
in the same second compared equal and was permanently dropped. The
preceding stack layer upgrades to `notify 9.0.0-rc.5`, which preserves
nanosecond precision for regular files without content hashing.

### How?

The dedicated pages-directory fixture configures only
`watchOptions.pollIntervalMs`:

- webpack maps it to compiler `watchOptions.poll`;
- Turbopack passes it to notify and selects PollWatcher.

It intentionally does not set `WATCHPACK_POLLING`, create/delete routes,
or test the dev-server route watcher, keeping the test focused on
compiler-level polling.

The test writes two versions of an already-loaded page with controlled
mtimes at +100 ms and +200 ms inside the same future whole second. It
waits for the first HMR update before making the second write, requiring
two distinct watcher events rather than allowing changes to coalesce.

A negative control with the older npm-provided native binary observes
the first update but permanently misses the second. A fresh local native
build from the full stack passes both updates. The dedicated test and
`read-only-source-hmr` pass under both Turbopack and webpack; Prettier

message:
build(turbopack): upgrade notify to 9.0.0-rc.5 (#98737)

### What?

Upgrades the Turbopack filesystem-watcher dependency from `notify 8.1.0`
to the published `9.0.0-rc.5` release candidate.

Stack: **4/5** · Previous: #98863 · Next: #97673

### Why?

notify-rs/notify#981 fixes PollWatcher dropping multiple edits to the
same regular file within one second. The old implementation stored file
mtimes at whole-second precision; with content hashing disabled, a
second write in the same second compared equal and produced no event.
This is the root cause behind #96982.

rc.5 keeps nanosecond mtime precision for ordinary files without
enabling content hashing. It remains a pre-release, so the pin should be
revisited when notify 9.0 stable is available.

### How?

The workspace dependency is pinned to exactly `9.0.0-rc.5`, and Cargo
regenerates the lockfile. No Rust source compatibility changes are
required: `turbo-tasks-fs` uses a narrow notify API surface and does not
rely on removed APIs.

The lockfile update includes notify's current backend dependencies
across Linux, macOS, and Windows; cross-platform CI remains important
because local runtime verification is Linux-only.

### Filesystem-watcher fuzzer impact

The preceding stack layer adds `--poll-interval-ms` to `turbo-tasks-fuzz
fs-watcher`, which provides a direct before/after control for this
dependency update. Using a 100 ms polling interval, a 1,000 ms
observation window, and no directory recreation:

| Fuzzer mode | notify 8.1.0 | notify 9.0.0-rc.5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--track-read-writes` | **230/288 iterations had mismatches** over
five minutes | **0/291 iterations had mismatches** over five minutes |
| ordinary reads | same-second changes can be missed depending on timing
| **0 missing invalidations across 295 iterations** over five minutes |

The read/write mode is the strongest comparison: it repeatedly produces
an external edit after a read-derived write in the same-second window,
so notify 8 fails consistently while rc.5 remains clean.

Two findings are intentionally unchanged by this PR:

- polling symlink mutations can still be missed within one second
because rc.5 retains whole-second mtime precision for non-files; the
fuzzer documents this limitation;
- directory recreation can produce recoverable `PathNotFound`
diagnostics while PollWatcher scans deleted subtrees. A 60-second
resilience run completed 500 iterations with no panic or terminal error.

A fresh native SWC/Turbopack build also passes the upper integration
suite's rapid subsecond HMR case without timestamp workarounds.

Fixes #96982

test(turbopack): fix filesystem watcher symlink expectations (#98983)

### What?

Makes the filesystem-watcher fuzzer's expected symlink invalidations
reflect net target changes over each iteration.

Stack: **2/5** · Previous: #98982 · Next: #98863

### Why?

Symlink indices are sampled with replacement, so one link may be changed
multiple times before the dependent task re-reads it. A later mutation
can restore the iteration-start target. The old expectation retained
that path after the first intermediate mutation and incorrectly reported
a missing invalidation even though the task observed no net value
change.

### How?

The fuzzer snapshots symlink targets at the iteration boundary and
removes expected paths whose final target matches the snapshot. All
unlink/recreate operations and watcher timing remain unchanged; only the
expected observable result is reconciled.

Behavioural tests cover untouched links, restored targets, repeated
mutations, and genuine net changes. Five-minute recursive and
nonrecursive directory-symlink runs complete without missing
invalidations.

test(turbopack): fix filesystem watcher read-write tracking (#98982)

### What?

Replaces the filesystem-watcher fuzzer's obsolete pure-write tracking
mode with a tracked read-derived write mode.

Stack: **1/5** · Next: #98983

### Why?

Pure write effects are no longer watcher dependencies after #92300
removed write-invalidation tracking and added effect-value
deduplication. The old fuzzer mode therefore expected behavior the
runtime intentionally does not provide and reported mismatches on every
iteration.

### How?

The new mode reads each regular-file path to establish a real watcher
dependency, then writes an idempotent value derived from the observed
external content. An external edit changes the derived effect value, so
the task reruns without restoring removed product semantics or entering
a write/invalidation loop. Symlinks remain read-tracked.

recursive/nonrecursive stress runs complete without mismatches.

author: acdlite
message:
Don't re-request the App Shell to upgrade an ISR fallback (#94808)

When a page hasn't been prerendered with concrete params yet, the server
answers a per-segment prefetch with the fallback shell and flags it as
upgradeable, and the client records that on the cache entries so a later
prefetch of the same route can retry and pick up the concrete prerender
once the server has generated it. The scheduler runs that retry from its
Fulfilled-entry branch: any prefetch task that finds an
upgradeable-fallback entry and hasn't retried yet spawns a revalidation
for its own URL.

That's right for the concrete static walk, where the retry can bring
back the param-dependent content the fallback omitted. It's wrong for
the Shell-phase walk under Partial Prefetching. A shell request asks for
shell-stage content, and the fallback render already produced all of it:
a concrete prerender's shell stage omits the same param-dependent
content the fallback omitted, so the retry can only return the shell the
cache already has.

This shows up with root params. The shell varies only on the root params
it reads, so a shell fetched for `/en/uk/posts/1` whose root layout
reads `lang` but not `region` is keyed with `region` as a fallback, and
a link to `/en/gb/posts/1` finds it in the cache. With the retry gate
on, revealing that link re-requested the identical shell, once per link
whose root params the shell doesn't read.

The fix gates the ISR fallback retry on the walk's strategy, next to the
Pending and Rejected branches that already skip revalidations during a
static shell attempt. The per-task retry loop that the original fallback
response starts is unchanged.

The included test reveals three links from `/en/us`: `/en/uk/posts/1`
fetches the shell, `/en/gb/posts/1` (same `lang`, different `region`)
fetches nothing, and `/fr/uk/posts/1` (different `lang`) fetches a new
shell.

This PR originally narrowed the shell's cache key to the root params the
server reported. That change landed separately in "Convert per-segment
prefetches to NavigationFlightResponse format" (#96877); rebasing onto
it left the test, which then caught this.

message:
Remove redundant unsafe_ignore annotations (#98961)

## What?

Remove 54 redundant `#[turbo_tasks(unsafe_ignore)]` field annotations,
reducing the field-annotation total from 136 to 82 (39.7%). Fields that
no longer carry the exemption now participate in the generated
`NonLocalValue` or `OperationValue` assertions.

This is stacked on #98953, which renames the former tracing attribute to
`unsafe_ignore` and leaves it solely as a marker-trait assertion escape
hatch.

## Why?

Most annotations predated the removal of `TraceRawVcs` and were only
needed to exclude fields from recursive VC tracing. Keeping those
exemptions would unnecessarily bypass compile-time marker checks after
tracing is gone.

The remaining annotations fall into these categories:

- 47 foreign, standard-library, or runtime types that cannot receive
marker implementations because of Rust's orphan rules
- 29 workspace-local helper or state types that do not currently
implement the marker
- 4 unconstrained trait objects or opaque futures
- 1 local `OperationValue` contract gap
- 1 macro fixture that tests the exemption itself

The local helper/state group is the meaningful follow-up area; unlike
foreign types, those types could gain separately reviewed marker
implementations in their owning crates.

## How?

Every field exemption was evaluated against the existing generated
marker assertions. An annotation is removed only when the field already
satisfies the appropriate marker bound. `debug_ignore` remains intact
where it serves an independent purpose.

No new `unsafe impl`, wrapper type, macro opt-out, or weakened assertion
is introduced, so this change removes redundant unsafety rather than
relocating or widening it.

author: acdlite
message:
Fix prefetch loop when a predicted route redirects (#98998)

A full or runtime prefetch (e.g. `router.prefetch(url, { kind: 'full'
})` or `<Link prefetch={true}>`) of a URL that matched a learned route
pattern but is redirected by the server (e.g. `/docs/changelog` →
`/changelog` while `/docs/alpha` renders `[collection]/[...slug]`)
caused the client to re-issue the same prefetch indefinitely, at
whatever rate the network allowed, until the tab was closed.

When the server contradicts a route prediction, the client is supposed
to remember that the URL shape can't be predicted and resolve it on the
server from then on. We were storing this information
(`hasDynamicRewrite`) in the wrong place: on the predicted route cache
entry, rather than the optimistic routing table that's used to generate
predictions.

The fix moves the `hasDynamicRewrite` flag to the optimistic routing
table so it applies to all subsequent optimistic routing predictions.

Fixes #98345.

author: lubieowoce
message:
[PPF] Separate tracking of runtime data accesses for shells and prefetches (#98129)

Expands the static tracking from #96095 to track shells and prefetches
separately. We split the `ShouldAttemptStaticPrefetch` hint into
`ShouldAttemptStaticShell` and `ShouldAttemptStaticPrefetch`, which the
client router considers separately depending on whether we need a shell
or a prefetch.

The server-side tracking of `needsRuntimeRequest` becomes a bit more
subtle.

First, a runtime data access should only affect the shell if we're in
the `ShellStatic` render stage. If we're already in the `PrefetchStatic`
stage, then that content is not conceptually part of the shell, and
should not deopt the shell to runtime, so we only unset
`shouldAttemptStaticShell` if we're still in the shell stage.

Second, accessing data that would only resolve in the prefetch (params,
search params, short-stale caches) should **not** affect whether the
shell can be static. `makeRuntimeDataHangingPromise` has been split into
variants that match this:
- `makeSessionDataHangingPromise` - data that affects the shell (and the
prefetch), e.g. `cookies()`
- `makeURLDataHangingPromise` - data that only affects the prefetch,
e.g. `params`
- `makeUnknownRuntimeDataHangingPromise`, used for private caches -- we
omit these during build so we don't know whether they should affect the
shell or only the prefetch, so we conservatively affect both (unless a
private cache is only used in the prefetch stage)
  
The server-side `needsRuntimeRequest` promise is now resolved such that
data that only resolves in the prefetch does not affect the shell. If
we're accessing data that only resolves in the prefetch, we will delay
the promise's resolution to the `PrefetchStatic` stage, which means that
when the client rewinds the static response to a shell, it will see an
unresolved promise and consider the response as not having used runtime
data. (see `markRuntimeDataAccessWhenStageReached`)

message:
Turbopack: trace static project files referenced by packages (#98712)

### What?

Allow Turbopack's native asset tracer to follow fully static
application-root file references originating in packages, while
continuing to block dynamic package references from traversing the
application.

Patterns containing alternatives retain only their fully static branches
for project-root tracing. Branches containing any dynamic segment are
discarded. A focused node-file-trace fixture covers a package loading an
application-owned config through `path.resolve()` and `fs.existsSync()`.

### Why?

Turbopack currently redirects every working-directory-relative reference
from `node_modules` to the package directory. This protects builds from
dynamic package expressions accidentally tracing much or all of the
application, but it also prevents safe static configuration lookups such
as `next-i18next.config.js` from reaching standalone output.

The dynamic safeguard should remain, but known static files do not carry
the same risk and should follow runtime working-directory semantics.

Related to #98628.

### How?

Add a pattern-level operation that extracts fully static alternatives
from a normalized reference pattern. The tracing root selection uses
that filtered pattern to choose the configured project working
directory; dynamic-only patterns retain the existing package-directory
fallback.

The shared root-selection path applies this consistently to filesystem,
path, worker, child-process, and specialized traced references. Existing
outside-base and `node_modules` filtering tests continue to cover the
safeguard.

### Verification

- `cargo fmt -- --check`
- `cargo test -p turbopack-core resolve::pattern`
