author: taras-janea
message:
[Windows] Disable constexpr std::mutex ctor so wheels load with msvcp140.dll older than 14.40 (#169429) (#196987)

Fixes
- #169429

## Root cause

Since 2.9.0 the Windows wheels are built with MSVC 14.42 (the CI AMI moved from VS 2022 LTSC 17.8 to LTSC 17.12 in pytorch/test-infra#6968). Starting with VS 2022 17.10 (MSVC 14.40) the STL gives `std::mutex` a `constexpr` constructor that zero-initializes the mutex instead of calling `_Mtx_init_in_situ`, and relies on `msvcp140.dll` >= 14.40 to understand that layout. Microsoft documents this as a binary-compatibility requirement (microsoft/STL#4730, microsoft/STL#4978).

When an older `msvcp140.dll` is already loaded in the process, the first lock of a global mutex during `c10.dll` static initialization faults inside `mtx_do_lock` in `msvcp140.dll`. The loader reports that as `[WinError 1114] A dynamic link library (DLL) initialization routine failed`, naming whichever DLL `torch/__init__.py` happened to try first. This happens
when:
- the system VC++ redistributable is older than 14.40 (the original report had 14.36 installed), or
- a package that bundles an old copy is imported first.

## Fix
Define `_DISABLE_CONSTEXPR_MUTEX_CONSTRUCTOR` for MSVC in the top-level `CMakeLists.txt`, in the existing `if(MSVC)` flags block. This is Microsoft's documented escape hatch; it restores the classic constructor so the binaries work with any 14.x runtime. It goes into `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS` and `CMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS` before `Dependencies.cmake` is included, so third-party code statically linked into `torch_cpu.dll` gets it as well. whisper.cpp, z3, tesseract, RapidFuzz and Firefox apply the same define for the same reason.

## Test Plan
Reproduced on the 2.9.0 and 2.14.0 CPU wheels and on a local MSVC 14.42 build by preloading the `msvcp140.dll` 14.26 before importing torch.

author: alexmalyshev
message:
[torch] Make Dynamo's per-region eval-frame flags thread-local (#196637) (#196637)

Summary:

Four flags in `eval_frame.c` describe "the Dynamo region the calling thread is
currently inside", but were stored process-wide:

- `current_isolate_recompiles_id`
- `skip_guard_eval_unsafe`
- `fullgraph_compiled_frame_count`
- `fullgraph_error_on_nested_compile`

`compile_wrapper` save/restores each of them around every call to a compiled
function, so with two threads the save/restore pairs interleave.  Thread A
enters its region, thread B overwrites the global, and thread A now runs the
rest of its call under B's value; when they unwind in the other order, B's
"prior" value is A's, and the wrong value is left behind for good.

The consequences differ per flag. `current_isolate_recompiles_id` picks the
cache bucket in `ExtraState::cache_entry_map`, so a leak sends one region's
compilations into another region's bucket.  `is_skip_guard_eval_unsafe` is
worse: a thread inside `set_stance(skip_guard_eval_unsafe=True)` turns guard
evaluation off for every other thread, which is a silent-wrong-results bug.

This is not free-threading specific, it reproduces under the GIL. Free
threading only makes the window wide enough to hit reliably.

Each flag becomes a `Py_tss_t` slot holding a tagged scalar, and the three that
`eval_frame_cpp.cpp` read via `extern` become accessors, matching the
`get_current_isolate_recompiles_id` that was already there.  `Py_tss_t` is used
instead of `__thread`/`__declspec(thread)` so the extension stays portable
across dlopen and Windows configurations.  A fresh thread now starts at the
inactive defaults rather than inheriting whatever another thread last set.

Test Plan:
The two deterministic scenarios from `free_threading_scenarios.py` fail before
this change and pass after, on both interpreters:

```
for t in free_threading_scenarios free_threading_scenarios_ft; do
  for s in tls_isolate_id tls_skip_guard_eval; do
    buck2 run fbcode//mode/dev-nosan //caffe2/test/dynamo/fb:free_threading:$t -- --scenario $s
  done
done
```

Before, all four report a leak, e.g. `isolate_recompiles id leaked across
threads: this thread set 111, another thread set 222, this thread now reads
222`. After, all four exit 0.

message:
[profiler][xpu] Test that ac2g CPU->GPU flow arrows end on the device (#194904)

## What
Add an XPU profiler regression test that asserts CPU→GPU ("ac2g") flow arrows
end on the device, in `test/profiler/test_xpu_profiler.py`.

## Why
`ac2g` means *async CPU→GPU*: a flow starts at a host launch and must end at
the device op, so no flow may both start and end on the host. On XPU the
exporter could attach flow endpoints to host-side Level Zero (`ze*`) driver /
overhead subspans, producing redundant host→host arrows and orphan host
finishes that break CPU→GPU trace correlation. This test locks the invariant so
the class of bug cannot regress.

## How
Profile a small workload, export a Chrome trace, and check every ac2g flow
finish lands on a GPU device track. GPU tracks are the pids labelled `"GPU …"`
in the trace's `process_labels` metadata; a finish on any other (host) track is
malformed. The check is type-agnostic (it does not enumerate record kinds), so
it catches any nested host subspan. A sanity assertion ensures the workload
actually produced ac2g flows.

## Notes
- **Draft on purpose:** the underlying fix lives in Kineto
  (pytorch/kineto#1549); this test will only pass once that fix is pulled into
  `third_party/kineto`. Ready to un-draft after the Kineto PR lands.
- Validated on Intel GPU hardware: the test correctly fails on the current
  (unfixed) trace and passes on the fixed one. XPU-gated (`TEST_XPU`).

[cuda][nccl] Use `ncclAlltoAllv` on ROCm too (#199124)

Summary:
Applies the same treatment as the previous diff to
`all2all_single_unequal_split`. RCCL deprecated `ncclAllToAllv` in 2.28; like its
scalar sibling it is a forwarding shim that logs and calls the same
function-table entry (`misc/api_trace.cc:499`):

```
ncclResult_t ncclAllToAllv(...) {
    WARN("Please note that ncclAllToAllv is deprecated, please use ncclAlltoAllv instead");
    return ::rccl::RcclGetFunctionTable()->ncclAlltoAllv_fn(...);
}
```

Split out from the scalar change because the ladder shape differs and the
reasoning is not the same. The scalar version could put the version check first
unconditionally, since NCCL and RCCL both grew `ncclAlltoAll` at 2.28. Here
`USE_ROCM` has to stay conjoined to the version check: upstream NCCL never added
a lowercase `ncclAlltoAllv`, and per D115510405 NCCLX's capital-T
`ncclAllToAllv` is its canonical name and is not deprecated, so that spelling
has to keep working for NCCLX indefinitely. Only ROCm moves.

The cost is that the nine-argument call is now spelled out in two arms. A
`#define` or a function-pointer alias would avoid the duplication, but at the
price of a preprocessor indirection in the middle of the call; the explicit
version reads closer to the scalar ladder above it. Happy to switch if reviewers

author: A-Kokolis
message:
[torch][inductor] Add RAIIAtenRecordFunctionHandle profiling to remaining uncovered kernel paths (#179700) (#179700)

Summary:

This adds `RAIIAtenRecordFunctionHandle` profiling to 4 kernel call paths that
previously had no profiler events, making them visible in GPU traces with
"External id" linkage:

1. `generate_fallback_kernel_with_runtime_lookup_aot` (`cpp_wrapper_cpu.py`):
 AOT ProxyExecutor dispatch via `aoti_torch_proxy_executor_call_function`

2. `generate_fallback_kernel_with_runtime_lookup_nopython` (`cpp_wrapper_cpu.py`):
 Non-AOT dispatcher via `aoti_torch_call_dispatcher`

3. `generate_fallback_kernel_with_runtime_lookup_python` (`cpp_wrapper_cpu.py`):
 GIL-acquiring Python fallback via `PyObject_CallObject`

4. Non-Triton GPU template kernels (`cpp_wrapper_gpu.py`):
 CUTLASS/ROCm kernels via `kernels.{name}()` direct call

Every site is gated on `kernel_profile_enabled()`, which requires
`config.cpp.enable_kernel_profile` *and* a platform whose generated code carries
the handle's declaration; the config flag alone is not sufficient. With
profiling off the generated code contains no `RAIIAtenRecordFunctionHandle` at
all.

All four sites build the declaration through one helper,
`_record_function_handle_line`, which `write_record_function_handle` also uses.
That leaves a single spelling for the recorded name and for the C++ identifier
derived from it, and every path records `str(op_overload)`, so one operator is
not reported as `aten::mm` on one dispatch path and `aten.mm.default` on
another.

The two sites that own their braces (the AOT ProxyExecutor call and the
non-Triton GPU call) open them with `EnterKernelProfileScopeLine` /
`ExitKernelProfileScopeLine` instead of writing `{` and `}` as raw lines. Both
blocks are inert as written - everything they reference is materialized before
the brace, and the scheduler emits buffer frees after the call returns - but a
raw brace is invisible to the memoized-declaration scoping, which is what lets a
later line name a variable that died at the closing brace.

On the Python fallback the record is emitted ahead of
`py::gil_scoped_acquire_simple`, so the event covers waiting for the GIL.
Acquiring the GIL is frequently the dominant cost of that path, and an event
starting after it would hide the thing being profiled.

On the JIT `cpp_wrapper` GPU path, `write_get_raw_stream` declared
`stream{idx}` inline at the first kernel call and memoized the name, so when that
call sat inside a profiling block the declaration died at its closing brace and
every later kernel named a variable that no longer existed. The declaration now
comes once from the entry function prologue, as dual-wrapper mode already did,
and `write_get_raw_stream` only returns the name. Subgraphs are inlined into the
same function and share the parent's `device_idxs`, so that one declaration
covers them too, which is why the subgraph-specific stream name upstream added is
no longer needed. Pure AOTI is untouched: it takes the stream as a function
parameter and skips the prologue declaration entirely, which also keeps backends
with no stream type to query, such as MTIA, off this path. `CppWrapperMps`
declares none, since Metal kernels are dispatched without a raw stream.

Two things deliberately left alone. These four records carry no argument
metadata (`nullptr` where the c-shim path passes a
`std::vector<C10IValueHandle>`), so they report no Input Dims; deriving it means
re-deriving each argument expression, and for a `ReinterpretView` that mints a
tensor handle whose only owner is the returned string, so reusing the expression
already handed to the kernel call would double-free it. Separately, CUTLASS and
ROCm kernels now sit inside two nested blocks, since the parent diff already
wraps `call_kernel` in a `kernel_profile_scope`; the inner block is redundant but
removing it would widen the event to the whole outer scope.

Test Plan:
Unit tests, `mode/dev-nosan` on H100. The default asan config cannot initialize
CUDA ("CUDA with nvcc does not work well with ASAN"), which silently skips every
GPU variant, so the no-sanitizer config is the one that actually exercises them.

```
buck2 test mode/dev-nosan fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:test_aot_inductor -- \
--regex 'profiler|kernel_profile'
```
75 passed, 0 failed, 32 skipped (MPS, plus the cpu-only / non-cpu-only fallback
cases).

Four tests cover the paths above, each parametrized over `enable_kernel_profile`:
- `test_aoti_profiler_proxy_executor` for the AOT ProxyExecutor path
- `test_aoti_profiler_nopython_dispatcher` for the non-AOT dispatcher path
- `test_aoti_profiler_python_fallback` for the Python fallback path. Its custom op returns `Tensor[]`, not just takes one: `_compatible_with_cpp_boxed_dispatch` accepts a `Tensor[]` *argument* (`arg_supported` recurses into `ListType`), so an op that only takes a tensor list is routed to the boxed dispatch path and never reaches `PyObject_CallObject`. Only the *return* type is restricted to `Tensor`, `Tensor?` and `()`, so a `Tensor[]` return is the cheapest schema that lands on the Python fallback. The op registers `CompositeExplicitAutograd` only, which also covers Meta and so supplies the shape propagation tracing needs; a separate Python fake impl would additionally require a companion C++ `m.set_python_module` call in fbcode.
- `test_aoti_profiler_gpu_non_triton` for the CUTLASS/ROCm GPU path
- Existing `test_aoti_profiler` and `test_kernel_profile` tests pass

Each check is anchored on the generated handle's own identifier
(`record_<sanitized>_(`) and ordered against the call it wraps, so a record
emitted anywhere else in the file cannot satisfy it. The GPU test asserts that a
non-Triton kernel was selected rather than branching on it; branching let it
pass having checked nothing whenever autotuning did not choose CUTLASS.

Non-vacuity, run with the parent commit's `cpp_wrapper_cpu.py` /
`cpp_wrapper_gpu.py` and this diff's tests:
- `test_aoti_profiler_nopython_dispatcher` fails
- `test_aoti_profiler_python_fallback` fails
- `test_aoti_profiler_gpu_non_triton` fails; the generated code has
`kernels.cutlass_fused_mm_t_<hash>(` and no record handle beside it

`test_aoti_profiler_proxy_executor` still passes against the parent, because its
recorded name was already `str(op_overload)` - the change there tightens an
assertion rather than covering new behaviour.

MPS and MTIA. The JIT stream declaration lives in `_codegen_jit_stream_declarations`, which pure AOTI skips (it takes the stream as a parameter, and MTIA -- registered with `CppWrapperGpu` -- has no stream type to query) and `CppWrapperMps` overrides to do nothing (Metal kernels never take a raw stream). Without that, OSS CI failed `test__int_mm_mps`, `test_addmm_mps` and `test_lite_mode_cpp_wrapper_optional_device_arg_mps` with `NotImplementedError`. `test_prologue_stream_declaration_per_backend` reproduces it on Linux: CUDA JIT declares `stream0`, MPS JIT and MTIA AOTI declare none. It fails with `NotImplementedError` with the fix removed, and again with only the pure-AOTI early return removed (the MTIA case), and passes with it.

```

buck2 test mode/dev-nosan fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:test_aot_inductor -- \
  --regex 'test_aoti_profiler|test_kernel_profile|KernelProfileNumelScope|KernelProfileScopeMemoryPlanning'
buck2 test mode/dev-nosan fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:control_flow -- --regex 'CppWrapper|cpp_wrapper'
```

[inductor] remove_noop_ops: keep a copy of an input that is mutated before the copy's user runs (#198132)

Fixes #198131

`remove_noop_ops` replaces `aten.copy(dst, alias(src))` (and `aten.clone`) by `src`. When `src` is a graph
input that is mutated later in the graph (its functionalization write-back `copy_` precedes the write-back
that consumes the removed copy), the consumer now observes the mutated value:

```python
def fn(dst, src):
    dst[0:, :] = src[0:, :]
    src.add_(1)
```

lowers to `copy_(src, add); copy_(dst, src)` and copies the *updated* `src` into `dst` (eager and aot_eager
copy the old value). Static and dynamic shapes, any in-place op on `src`, 2.14.0 and current nightly.

This PR records the earliest in-graph `copy_` mutation of every input storage and skips the replacement
for a non-view noop whose source aliases such an input when one of the node's users is ordered after that
mutation. View noops (`alias`, full `slice`, `view`) are unaffected, and copies whose users all run before
the mutation are still removed, so the extra copy is only kept where it is needed for correctness.

static and dynamic).

message:
[Dynamo] Trace property __isabstractmethod__ truth testing (#198726)

Related to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/195901.

## Problem

Dynamo evaluates `property.__isabstractmethod__` directly on the Python property object during tracing. If an accessor's `__isabstractmethod__` attribute has a user-defined `__bool__` that raises, the exception becomes an `InternalTorchDynamoError` instead of being handled by the compiled function's exception handler.

## Fix

Add a polyfill that checks the truth value of each accessor's `__isabstractmethod__` attribute, returning early when one is true. Route `PropertyVariable` through this polyfill so Dynamo traces the truth testing and handles its exceptions within the compiled program.

## Tests

Add `test_property_isabstractmethod_raises`, covering exceptions from truth testing for `fget`, `fset`, and `fdel` with `backend="eager"` and `fullgraph=True`.

- All three cases fail with `InternalTorchDynamoError` using the original getter and pass with this change.
- `python test/dynamo/test_misc.py -v -k property`: 7 tests passed.
- `lintrunner -m origin/main`: passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

## Remaining limitation

The original CPython test, `PropertyTests.test_property___isabstractmethod__descriptor`, still encounters an unsupported sourceless-object conversion for the `NotBool` instance created inside a local class body. Its expected-failure entry remains unchanged. This PR addresses exception handling for property objects that Dynamo can already track.

I used ChatGPT Codex to help investigate the issue and draft the implementation, regression test, and PR description. I applied the changes and ran the tests locally and fully reviewed all codes/description including modifying.

author: fegin
message:
[Pipeline] Add explicit send wait actions (#196726)

## Summary

Add `WAIT_SEND_F` and `WAIT_SEND_B` as first-class pipeline schedule actions.

Each send now has an explicit matching wait. The runtime keeps the P2P operations, work handles, source tensors, and optional output-release callback alive until that wait executes.

## Motivation
Pipeline sends are nonblocking. Their work handles and source tensors must remain alive until communication completes.

Implicit end-of-step waits cannot express earlier ownership release and are unsuitable for static CUDA graph capture. Explicit actions make send lifetime part of the schedule.

This PR is stacked on #196963, which lets forward output ownership be released without breaking backward autograd connectivity.

## Design

For generated schedules:

  - Insert one wait for every send.
  - Place a forward-send wait after the matching backward action when available.
  - Place backward-send waits and unmatched forward-send waits at schedule end.

  For pre-lowered `compute_comms` schedules:

  - Require one ordered wait for every send.
  - Reject duplicate sends, missing waits, and waits without a pending send.

  At runtime:

  - Track each send by direction, stage, and microbatch.
  - Retire a send only when its explicit wait executes.
  - Release forward output ownership after the forward send completes.
  - Drain pending sends only when action execution fails.
  - Do not poll for communication completion.

  The schedule simulator also understands send-wait dependencies and requires he peer receive to be posted before a wait can complete.

  This PR does not enforce an outstanding-send count. A later PR can move these explicit waits earlier to satisfy a memory budget.

[Dynamo] Fix getattr on builtin types raising AttributeError when attribute is missing (#198330)

author: weicheng-hsu
message:
[dynamo] Match CPython repr for self-referential UserList and UserDict (#198512)

I confirmed that under Dynamo, `repr()` of a self-referential `UserList` or `UserDict` differs from CPython. The cause is that Dynamo's `generic_repr()` registers every object for cycle detection, while CPython only registers inside the reprs of C containers such as `list` and `dict`. I think the most fundamental fix is to align with CPython and move the registration from `generic_repr()` into those container reprs, but that touches several files, so for now this PR skips the registration for `UserList` and `UserDict` (including subclasses that do not override `__repr__`). If maintainers are open to changing the registration logic, I'm happy to do that work.

> AI-assisted PR description:
>
> ## Issue
>
> Towards #195901. Implements the `UserList` / `UserDict` items of my [claimed self-referential container repr subtask](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/195901#issuecomment-5800751713) (`test_userlist.py::UserListTest::test_repr`, `test_userdict.py::UserDictTest::test_repr`). The set item is #198476.
>
> ## Summary
>
> ```python
> l = UserList([1, 2]); l.append(l)
> repr(l)  # eager:  [1, 2, [...]]
>          # dynamo: [1, 2, ...]
> d = UserDict(); d["self"] = d
> repr(d)  # eager:  {'self': {...}}
>          # dynamo: {'self': ...}
> ```
>
> In CPython, cycle detection is done by the container reprs, not by `repr()`:
>
> - [`PyObject_Repr`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.3/Objects/object.c#L734-L779) has no cycle detection, only a recursion-depth check (`_Py_EnterRecursiveCallTstate`).
> - C container reprs call `Py_ReprEnter` on themselves and return their own placeholder: [`list_repr_impl`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.3/Objects/listobject.c#L584-L591) returns `"[...]"`, [`dict_repr_lock_held`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.3/Objects/dictobject.c#L3208-L3211) returns `"{...}"` (see also the [comment on `Py_ReprEnter`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.3/Objects/object.c#L2730-L2740)).
> - [`UserList.__repr__`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.3/Lib/collections/__init__.py#L1232-L1233) and [`UserDict.__repr__`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.3/Lib/collections/__init__.py#L1162-L1163) are pure Python (`return repr(self.data)`), so they are never registered and the cycle is caught by the inner list or dict.
>
> Dynamo's `generic_repr` registers every object in `_repr_running`, so the second visit to the `UserList` is caught at the `UserList` itself. It is not in the sentinel table (`list`, `dict`, `deque`), so it falls back to the default `"..."` and the inner list never gets to catch the cycle.
>
> This PR skips the registration in `generic_repr` when the type's `__repr__` is `UserList.__repr__` or `UserDict.__repr__`, so it also covers subclasses that do not override it. All other types, including subclasses that override `__repr__`, behave exactly as on main. The two expected-failure markers are removed.
>
> I did not use an `issubclass` check. It would also skip subclasses whose own `__repr__` never reaches `repr(self.data)` (e.g. one that formats `self.items()` itself), and for a self-referential instance of such a subclass nothing would register: main's `"..."` output would become `InternalTorchDynamoError` (wrapping `RecursionError`) during tracing.
>
> <details>
> <summary>Call chain in CPython vs Dynamo</summary>
>
> ```
> CPython:
> repr(u) -> UserList.__repr__ -> list_repr(u.data)        [registers u.data]
>   -> repr(u) -> UserList.__repr__ -> list_repr(u.data)   [already registered -> "[...]"]
>
> Dynamo (main):
> repr(u) -> generic_repr [registers u] -> UserList.__repr__
>   -> generic_repr [registers u.data] -> ListVariable.tp_repr_impl
>   -> repr(u) -> generic_repr [u already registered -> "..."]
> ```
>
> </details>
>
> ## Question for reviewers
>
> The underlying mismatch is broader than `UserList` / `UserDict`: Dynamo registers at the `repr()` entry point, while CPython registers inside the C container reprs. A prototype that moves the registration into the container VTs' `tp_repr_impl` also fixes list/dict subclasses, tuples, `super().__repr__()` and `a.__repr__()` cycles, but touches about five files and changes cycle handling for every container. Would you prefer that approach instead, here or as a follow-up?
>
> <details>
> <summary>Prototype details (two alternatives, not in this PR)</summary>
>
> **A. Skip registration whenever `type(obj).__repr__` is a Python function.** Rejected: it guesses at the entry point whether a C repr will run, and a Python `__repr__` can reach a C repr through a path that bypasses `generic_repr`, so nothing registers:
>
> ```python
> class L(list):
>     def __repr__(self):
>         return "L" + super().__repr__()
>
> a = L([1]); a.append(a)
> repr(a)  # eager:         L[1, L[...]]
>          # main:          L[1, ...]
>          # alternative A: InternalTorchDynamoError: RecursionError
> ```
>
> `super().__repr__()` dispatches through the slot wrapper (`_wrap_unaryfunc`) straight to `ListVariable.tp_repr_impl`, not through `generic_repr`.
>
> **B. Register inside the C container VTs' `tp_repr_impl` (list, tuple, deque, dict, OrderedDict, dict views, set, frozenset, SimpleNamespace) and drop registration from `generic_repr`.** This mirrors CPython. The prototype matched eager for every case in this table (all measured with `fullgraph=True`):
>
> | case | eager | main | this PR | B |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | `UserList` / `UserDict` cycle | `[1, [...]]` / `{1: {...}}` | `[1, ...]` / `{1: ...}` | ok | ok |
> | user object whose `__repr__` formats a list that contains the object | `Box([Box([...])])` | `Box([...])` | same as main | ok |
> | `L(list)` using `super().__repr__()` | `L[1, L[...]]` | `L[1, ...]` | same as main | ok |
> | `a.__repr__()` on a self-referential list | `[1, [...]]` | `[1, [1, [...]]]` | same as main | ok |
> | list / dict subclass cycle | `[1, [...]]` / `{1: {...}}` | `[1, ...]` / `{1: ...}` | same as main | ok |
> | tuple cycle | `([(...)],)` | `([...],)` | same as main | ok |
>
> A self-referential `defaultdict(list)` graph breaks on main, with this PR and with B, because the repr of its `list` factory hits `tp_repr_impl not implemented` for `type`. With a `None` factory it prints `defaultdict(None, {1: ...})` on main and with this PR, and B matches eager. A `__repr__` that recurses forever raises `InternalTorchDynamoError` (wrapping `RecursionError`) with B instead of printing `"..."`; CPython raises `RecursionError`.
>
> With B, `test/dynamo/test_repr_protocol.py` and the CPython `test_userlist`, `test_userdict`, `test_list`, `test_dict`, `test_tuple`, `test_deque`, `test_set`, `test_ordered_dict` and `test_collections` suites had no new failures (compared at the summary level). The only changes were unexpected successes for the two `UserList` / `UserDict` tests and, because the prototype also added the set placeholders from #198476, three set `test_cyclical_repr` tests.
>
> #195177 also touches how unbound `__repr__` calls reach `generic_repr` so that `Py_ReprEnter` still sees self-references, so it may be relevant.
>
> </details>
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> Run on CPU with Python 3.13. The new `test_self_ref_userlist_repr` / `test_self_ref_userdict_repr` use `fullgraph=True`, because a graph break would run `repr()` eagerly and hide the wrong output. With `generic_repr` from main, both fail with the `"..."` output shown above.
>
> ```bash
> python test/dynamo/test_repr_protocol.py -v -k userlist -k userdict
> python test/dynamo/test_repr_protocol.py
> PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_userlist.py -v
> PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_userdict.py -v
> lintrunner -a torch/_dynamo/variables/object_protocol.py test/dynamo/test_repr_protocol.py
> ```
>
> I also compared the outcome of every test (2258 on main) in related Dynamo and CPython container suites between main and this branch. The only differences are `UserListTest.test_repr` and `UserDictTest.test_repr` (skipped -> ok) and the two new tests. Cases that do not run `UserList.__repr__` / `UserDict.__repr__` behave exactly as on main, including the gaps listed in the prototype details.
>
> <details>
> <summary>Regression comparison commands</summary>
>
> ```bash
> for t in test_repr_protocol test_dicts test_sets test_list; do
>   python test/dynamo/$t.py -v
> done
> python test/dynamo/test_misc.py -v -k repr
> python test/dynamo/test_repros.py -v -k repr
> for t in test_userlist test_userdict test_userstring test_list test_dict \
>          test_dictviews test_set test_ordered_dict test_tuple test_deque \
>          test_collections test_defaultdict test_types; do
>   PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/$t.py -v
> done
> ```
>
> </details>
>

author: bottler
message:
Fix missing cp.async drain in memory-efficient attention forward kernel (#198922)

Fix a race condition in the CUTLASS memory-efficient attention forward kernel,
reported by turboderp in https://github.com/facebookresearch/xformers/issues/1392
as nondeterministic NaNs with head_dim >= 256 on Ampere, Ada and Blackwell
consumer hardware, hitting roughly a third of runs on an RTX 3090. This is the
same fix @danthe3rd made in xformers in 2023, "[cutlassF] fix race condition":
https://github.com/facebookresearch/xformers/commit/55a4798d99c350eca9d225a14003f226775e5f76
This copy of the kernel never picked it up.

## History and how this happened

The kernel was vendored from xformers in #86157 (Oct 2022), nine months before
the upstream fix landed (July 2023). None of the syncs after that picked the fix
up: it is absent from #100583, #103704, #112267 and #127090 alike.

The commented-out call site sitting in the tree today came from somewhere else
entirely. #123571 (Apr 2024) backported the sliding-window feature, copying that
region of `kernel_forward.h` across from an upstream source that was by then
post-fix. The region happened to contain one line of the race fix. That line
could not compile, because the `drain_cp_asyncs()` definition it calls lives in
`mma_from_smem.h` and was never backported, so it was commented out with "TODO
figure out if this is needed for correctness" and left there.

So nothing was reverted -- the fix simply never arrived, and one orphaned
fragment of it was later smuggled in by an unrelated feature port. Other copies
of this kernel, including CUTLASS example 41, do have the fix; this one is the
outlier.

## Details

`MmaMultistageFromSharedMemory::operator()`, the `attn @ V` GEMM, ends its
mainloop on `cp_async_wait<kNumStagesConcurrentLoad - 1>()` and never issues a
final `cp_async_wait<0>`, so up to `kStages - 1` async copies into the V staging
buffer are still in flight when it returns. `__syncthreads()` does not wait for
`cp.async`. `AttentionKernel::SharedStorage` is a union in which `mm0` overlaps
all of `after_mm0` (`si`, `mm1`, `epilogue`), so those late-landing writes can
clobber shared memory that `prologueV(blockN + 1)`, the epilogue, or the next key
block's `Q * K^T` GEMM is already reading or writing.

`CustomMmaMultistage` (the `Q * K^T` GEMM) appears to drain at the end of its own
mainloop, but that block is guarded by
`SharedMemoryClear == SharedMemoryClearOption::kZfill`, and `find_default_mma.h`
pins `SharedMemoryClear` to `kNone` for every attention kernel. It is a
compile-time-false branch, so in practice nothing drains at all.

This adds `drain_cp_asyncs()` (`cp_async_fence(); cp_async_wait<0>();
__syncthreads();`) to both from-shared-memory Mma variants -- a no-op stub on
`MmaPipelinedFromSharedMemory`, which issues no `cp.async` -- calls it at the
three points in `kernel_forward.h` that need it, and drops the dead `kZfill`
block that the explicit calls replace.

A narrower fix would be a single `cp_async_wait<0>` at the end of the multistage
mainloop. I matched the upstream change instead so this copy stays diffable
against the xformers and CUTLASS ones, since silent divergence is what produced
the bug.

Worth noting for severity: this kernel is also reachable from plain
`F.scaled_dot_product_attention`, which applies no upper bound on head_dim for
the mem-efficient backend while flash and cuDNN both cap at 256, so head_dim 512
selects it with no opt-in.

Test Plan:

`compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck` on the affected kernel, before and after,
using this script:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

q, k, v = (
    torch.randn(1, 8, 129, 512, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    for _ in range(3)
)
with torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel(torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION):
    F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

```
compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck --racecheck-detect-level info python repro.py
```

On an H100, varying head_dim and seqlen, reported hazards in
`fmha_cutlassF_f16_aligned_32x128_gmem_sm80`:

```
                              before              after
m=129 k=128  (nBlockN=1)   0 hazards           0 hazards
m=129 k=256  (nBlockN=2)   0 err,  8 warn      0 err,  8 warn
m=129 k=512  (nBlockN=4)   8 errors            0 err,  8 warn
m=64  k=512  (nBlockN=4)   4 errors            0 err,  4 warn
m=129 k=512  float32       8 errors            0 hazards
```

Every race error is eliminated. Hazard count tracks
`nBlockN = ceil(head_dim / MM1::ThreadblockShape::kN)` and is zero at
`nBlockN == 1`, which is exactly when `prologueV(blockN + 1)` is never reached --
one of the three restored call sites. Reverting brings the 8 errors back, so this
is not a build artifact.

Correctness, same machine, fp16 and bf16, seqlen in {129, 256, 257, 1024} x
head_dim in {128, 256, 512, 1024}, 30 runs each with the caching allocator
poisoned with NaN between runs: no NaNs and bitwise-identical output across runs,
before and after.

```
                      before      after
m=1024 k=128         0.421 ms   0.428 ms
m=1024 k=256         0.989 ms   0.981 ms
m=1024 k=512         2.250 ms   2.266 ms
m=4096 k=128         6.298 ms   6.273 ms
m=4096 k=256        16.027 ms  16.030 ms
m=4096 k=512        37.632 ms  38.115 ms
```

Maximum deviation 1.3%, sign inconsistent across configurations, so the added
synchronization is not measurable above run-to-run noise.

Those measurements were taken before the `kZfill` block was removed. Since the
branch is compile-time false for every attention kernel, removing it cannot
change the generated code, so the numbers stand for the change as a whole.

I could not reproduce the reported NaNs on an H100 across 2000 runs at the
reporter's exact shapes. Every reproduction in the issue is on a consumer part
with substantially lower memory bandwidth, which plausibly widens the window.
The author of the original xformers fix likewise noted they could not reproduce
it. The race itself is present regardless, as the sanitizer results show.

Formatting checked with the repo's pinned clang-format 19.1.4 restricted to the
changed line ranges; note that neither CLANGFORMAT nor CLANGTIDY currently
includes this path in `.lintrunner.toml`.

This change was authored with the assistance of an AI coding agent (Claude).
The analysis, sanitizer runs and measurements above were performed and reviewed
before submission.

author: taras-janea
message:
[Windows] Re-enable FBGEMM on x64 and fix MSVC AVX flag detection (#198490)

Fixes:
- #169816.

## Root cause

FBGEMM has been silently disabled on every Windows x64 build since #158210.
`CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR` is `AMD64` on Windows, but the gate introduced there only allows `x86_64|aarch64`, so `set(USE_FBGEMM OFF)` fires unconditionally it also overrides `USE_FBGEMM=1` from the environment. Windows is left with `onednn` as the only quantized engine, so torchvision's pretrained quantized models (which pin `backend="fbgemm"` via `weights.meta`) fail with `RuntimeError: Quantized backend not supported`.

## Changes

**`CMakeLists.txt`**: allow `AMD64`, and restore the 32-bit exclusion #158210 dropped. The pointer-size check is required because 32-bit Windows also reports `AMD64`. It additionally excludes 32-bit `-m32`/x32/ILP32 builds. No 64-bit platform changes.

**`cmake/Modules/FindAVX.cmake`**: MSVC exposes AVX intrinsics without any `/arch:` flag, so the no-op `" "` candidate won and cached `CXX_AVX*_FLAGS=' '`. fbgemm reuses those cache variables, so its AVX targets built without `/arch:`, `__AVX2__` went undefined, and the kernels guarded by it failed to compile (`error C3861: 'transpose_kernel_mxn_sse'`). Probe the real flag first on MSVC. The non-MSVC branch is unchanged.

## Behavior change

Default qengine on Windows moves from `onednn` to `x86`, matching Linux.

## Test Plan

```
cmake -U "C_AVX*" -U "CXX_AVX*" -U "C_HAS_AVX*" -U "CXX_HAS_AVX*" -U USE_FBGEMM -S . -B build

author: albmalamd
message:
Fix get_free_port() returning ports in use on other addresses (#199015)

## Summary

`get_socket_with_port()` probed with `bind(("localhost", 0))`, which usually resolves to `[::1]`, so the kernel only checked loopback for conflicts. Callers (`create_c10d_store`, rendezvous, the DCP async process executor, the launcher tests) hand the port to a TCPStore server, which binds the wildcard address. A port already listening on another address, e.g. NCCL/RCCL bootstrap and proxy sockets on the NIC IP or Gloo on the hostname IP, could be returned, and the server bind then failed with `EADDRINUSE`. This showed up as a flaky `test_async_process_executor.py::test_checkpoint_save_failure_continues_serving` (`port: 34091, useIpv6: false, code: -98, name: EADDRINUSE`).

Probe the dual-stack wildcard `[::]` (`IPV6_V6ONLY=0`, fallback `0.0.0.0`) instead, matching the TCPStore bind. Drop `listen(0)`: a wildcard listener would accept, and never serve, connections meant for the server while the port is reserved (`test_port_already_in_use_on_worker` hangs otherwise). A plain bind still reserves the port.

`torch/distributed/elastic/utils/api.py` had its own copy of `get_socket_with_port()` with the same bug; it is the one exported as `torch.distributed.elastic.utils.get_socket_with_port`. It now delegates to the `distributed.py` implementation. It stays a `def` in `api.py` rather than a re-import, since `api.py` has no `__all__` and a foreign `__module__` would trip `test_public_bindings`.

The old `listen(0)` is also why `test_port_already_in_use_on_worker` is skipped on MI200. In the MI200 run where it was last enabled (#166517), it hung (`Command took >30min, returning 124`, 3 attempts, `FAILED CONSISTENTLY`) while MI300 passed. The runner's hostname resolved to the loopback address the probe listened on, so the TCPStore client connected to the reservation socket, which never replies, and the client doesn't apply its timeout in that state. Without the listener the client is refused and times out after 1s as intended, so the skip is removed.

Fixes #168435
Fixes #168434

Related to the rendezvous port fixes in #195994.

## Test Plan:

New `test_get_socket_with_port_reserves_all_addresses` reserves a port through both the `distributed.py` and the exported `elastic.utils` function, and checks that binding it on `127.0.0.1`, `127.0.0.2` and `::1` fails with `EADDRINUSE`. Addresses the host can't bind are skipped. Before: fails 20/20. After: passes 20/20.

| Implementation | New test |
|---|---|
| `main` (loopback probe in both copies) | fails (IPv4 cases, both functions) |
| `distributed.py` fixed, `api.py` copy unfixed | fails (`elastic.utils.api` cases) |
| IPv4-only probe (`0.0.0.0` only) | fails (`::1` cases) |
| `IPV6_V6ONLY=1` probe | fails (IPv4 cases) |
| this PR | passes |

```
python test/distributed/elastic/utils/distributed_test.py -v
```

Before: the new test fails. After: 9/9 pass.

`test_port_already_in_use_on_worker` with `socket.gethostname()` pointed at loopback names (the MI200 condition):

| `gethostname()` | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| real hostname (`127.0.1.1`) | pass | pass |
| `localhost` / `::1` | hangs (killed at 180s) | pass (~5s) |
| `127.0.0.1` | pass | pass |

MI200 confirmation comes from `ciflow/periodic-rocm-mi200` on this PR.

End to end, with 5000 extra listeners held on 127.0.1.1 to raise the natural ~0.1% collision rate, 20 runs of:

```
python -m pytest test/distributed/checkpoint/test_async_process_executor.py -k test_checkpoint_save_failure_continues_serving
```

Before: 6/20 failed with `EADDRINUSE`. After: 20/20 passed. `get_free_port()` with 3000 listeners on another address, 5000 calls: before 1087 busy ports returned, after 0.

Also pass with the fix: `test_launcher.py`, `launcher/launch_test.py`, `launcher/test_run.py`, `rendezvous/static_rendezvous_test.py`, `rendezvous/c10d_rendezvous_backend_test.py`, `test_async_process_executor.py`. `test_public_bindings.py -k test_correct_module_names` reports nothing new.

author: aorenste
message:
[CooR] Make stream observations rank-portable under compile_on_one_rank (#196940)

Dynamo recorded a stream's tracing-rank device and guarded stream inputs by
their exact identity. Reusing a compile_on_one_rank artifact on another rank
could therefore expose the original device index or recompile even when the
same current-stream relationship held.

Carry runtime-relative device provenance through stream variables and guard
stream equality by whether the input is the current stream. Default and
indexless constructors are normalized to the current device; CPU streams are
left unchanged, and explicit device indices (including negative ones) are
still refused under compile_on_one_rank as before.

Stream comparisons against a current stream are evaluated with eager
semantics: the traced current stream is given the type its API returns (e.g.
torch.cuda.Stream), so mixed-type ==/!= dispatch as in eager, and ordering
ops raise eager's TypeError. CURRENT_STREAM_MATCH checks the ambient stream
itself, so it is listed as an unmodelled guard for precompile.

Stream inputs whose .device or .device_index is read still guard on the
concrete index and recompile per rank; that is left for a follow-up.

author: egeboy35
message:
Fix silent parallel_for corruption on MSVC: stop mixing vcomp and libomp OpenMP runtimes (#193792)

Fixes #193784. Also fixes #176091, the SDPA symptom of the same defect.

On MSVC x64 `torch_cpu` imports two OpenMP runtimes at once.
`-openmp:experimental` compiles `#pragma omp parallel` into `_vcomp_*` calls and
links VCOMP140 by itself, while this module's library search finds the
`libomp.lib` shipped with Visual Studio and adds it to the link line. The two
runtimes share no state, so inside a vcomp team every worker asks libomp and is
told `omp_get_num_threads() == 1` and `omp_get_thread_num() == 0`.
`ParallelOpenMP.h` then hands every worker the whole range and
`at::get_thread_num()` returns 0 on all of them, so each one runs the entire
chunk and any non-idempotent kernel body silently accumulates N times.

The fix skips both library searches when the compiler id is MSVC - the generic
one and the `OpenMP_PREFIX` one. There is nothing for them to find: cl.exe links
the runtime matching its `-openmp` flag on its own, so naming a library is
redundant at best, and naming libomp is the defect. The prefix search needs the
guard too because `HINTS` adds to the default search paths rather than replacing
them, so any non-empty `OMP_PREFIX` - even one pointing at a directory that does
not exist - still finds the Visual Studio `libomp.lib`.

The compiler id is checked rather than `MSVC`, because `Platform/Windows-Clang.cmake`
sets `MSVC` for clang-cl too, and clang-cl emits `__kmpc_*` calls that do need
libomp. For the same reason the MSVC ARM64 special case is removed: it was
guarded on bare `MSVC`, so on clang-cl ARM64 it linked vcomp for a compiler that
needs libomp, and on cl.exe ARM64 the new check already covers it.

### Rebuilding

The fix is invisible to an in-place reconfigure. `OpenMP_<LANG>_FLAGS`,
`OpenMP_<LANG>_LIB_NAMES` and `OpenMP_libomp_LIBRARY` are cache entries. This
module skips detection while the first two are cached, and even when detection
reruns, both guarded searches start with `NOT OpenMP_libomp_LIBRARY`, so a cached
libomp path is reused. An existing build directory therefore keeps linking libomp.
Delete the build directory, or clear the entries first:

```
cmake -U "OpenMP_*" <build-dir>
```

### History

I first sent this extending the ARM64 branch to find vcomp explicitly.
@frost-intel pointed out that linking vcomp explicitly is redundant and that
`MSVC` is too broad a guard. #196730 by @taras-janea implemented that suggestion
and also removes the ARM64 block, which is adopted here with co-authorship. @ezyang's review of #196730 caught the unguarded `OpenMP_PREFIX`
search.

### Test Plan

Windows 11, MSVC 14.44.35207, CPU-only, no MKL.

**The module in isolation, each configure in a fresh directory.** A minimal
project that runs `find_package(OpenMP)` under the real MSVC environment and
prints what the module selects:

| case | `OpenMP_CXX_LIB_NAMES` |
|---|---|
| main | `libomp` |
| this PR | empty |
| previous revision of this PR, `OMP_PREFIX=C:\nonexistent` | `libomp` |
| this PR, `OMP_PREFIX=C:\nonexistent` | empty |
| configured with main, then reconfigured in place with this PR | `libomp` (stale cache) |
| same directory, reconfigured with `-U "OpenMP_*"` | empty |

**Full build, 8 intra-op threads.** Integer addition is exactly associative, so a
wrong integer sum cannot come from reassociation:

```
python -c "import torch; y = torch.ones(40_000_000, dtype=torch.int64); print(sorted({y.sum().item() for _ in range(8)}))"
```

```
before:  [600000000, 640000000]      # 15x and 16x the true 40000000
after:   [40000000]
```

```
python test/test_transformers.py TestSDPACpuOnlyCPU TestSDPAFailureModesCPU
```

```
before:  FAILED (failures=3108, skipped=58)
after:   OK (skipped=58)             # 3203 tests
```

```
dumpbin -imports build/bin/torch_cpu.dll
```

```
before:  VCOMP140.DLL and libomp140.x86_64.dll
after:   VCOMP140.DLL only, zero __kmpc_* imports
```

Where these full-build numbers came from: the first revision of this change
(generic-search guard only), on main as of `7744b78e00e`, in an existing build
directory with the `OpenMP_*` cache entries cleared before reconfiguring - the
`cmake -U "OpenMP_*"` equivalent, not a deleted build directory. The later
revisions only remove the ARM64 block and guard the `OMP_PREFIX` search. On x64
without `OMP_PREFIX` they select the same libraries, as the fresh-directory table
above shows, so the link line is unchanged and rebuilding did not relink
`torch_cpu.dll`.

`cmake/public/mkldnn.cmake:20-30` relies on `caffe2::openmp` to give binaries that
pull dnnl objects their OpenMP runtime, because oneDNN adds no link dependency of
its own. With an empty MSVC library list `caffe2::openmp` carries no library, so
those binaries could fail to resolve `omp_*`. All 125 executables under
`build/bin` - the C++ tests plus `protoc` and two benchmarks - were deleted and
linked fresh, with no unresolved externals. `test_jit` is the only one that links
dnnl directly (`test/cpp/jit/CMakeLists.txt:129`). It links, loads and runs: 563 of
590 pass, and none of the 26 failures involves OpenMP - 14 are test backends this
Windows build does not register, 9 are `pinv`/`tensorinv` in a build without
LAPACK, 2 cannot read a model archive, and 1 matches an error message.

The change touches no compiler flag, so nothing recompiles; the full
`pip install -e . -v --no-build-isolation` takes about fifteen minutes.

MSVC ARM64 is covered by CI rather than by me: `windows-arm64-binary-wheel` built
the previous revision of this PR (`e27f297`), which already dropped the ARM64
block, with `USE_MKL` off, `BLAS=apl` and `-openmp:experimental`, and it linked.
That was the real risk of removing the block - no vcomp on the link line and
unresolved `_vcomp_*` symbols - so the autolink holds on ARM64 too. It shows the
link, not runtime behaviour. clang-cl is untested, for lack of the toolchain;
the reasoning is above.

Developed with AI assistance (Claude), which also ran the measurements on my
Windows machine; I reviewed the change and the results.

author: anijain2305
message:
[inductor] Prefetch Inductor cache keys at torch.compile() time (#198747)

`torch_key`/`triton_key` hash the torch and triton sources the first time an
FX graph cache key is computed, which blocks the first compile for ~140ms
even on a warm cache. They already support `prefetch()` via
`prefetchable_cache`, but nothing called it.

`codecache.prefetch_cache_keys()` starts both in a background thread (once).
torch.compile(backend="inductor") calls it as soon as the wrapper is created,
so the hashing overlaps with everything before the first call (model init,
data loading) as well as Dynamo and AOTAutograd tracing. Dynamo's `_compile`
also calls it for Inductor backends reached without torch.compile (e.g.
torch._dynamo.optimize). The prefetchers are bound at codecache import so
tests that `mock.patch` `torch_key` keep working; `TestCacheKeyStrategy`
now clears `triton_key` in setUp because it assumed nothing earlier in the
process had computed the real value.

The cost is importing torch._inductor.codecache inside torch.compile()
instead of inside the first compile, which would have imported it anyway.
Starting only from `_compile` was the first version, but with small
compiled regions Dynamo tracing is too short to hide the hash. Making
torch_key itself faster is complementary and wouldn't remove the wait.

process wall 3.37s -> 2.99s.

author: mlazos
message:
Fix #187340: [torch.compile][Inductor][CUDA] torch.nextafter is incorrectly compiled as no-op (#196578)

Adds numerically accurate lowering for nextafter.

> **AI-assisted draft for that independent GitHub review:**
>
> ## Summary
>
> Fix Inductor's `torch.nextafter` lowering so compiled results match eager semantics for fp16, bf16, fp32, and fp64, including exact non-NaN bit patterns, non-contiguous inputs, and signaling-NaN quieting.
>
> Fixes #187340
>
> ## Root cause
>
> The generic numeric pointwise lowering widened fp16 and bf16 operands before taking a one-ULP step. The widened result could round back to the original low-precision value, making compiled `nextafter` a no-op. In addition, the libdevice fp32 path can flush subnormal steps around zero instead of producing the next representable value expected by eager execution.
>
> ## Fix
>
> - Add a dtype-aware lowering shared by ATen and prims, with `NO_OPMATH` dtype propagation.
> - Preserve fp16 and bf16 operands through code generation regardless of the global load-upcast setting.
> - Route Triton through `triton_helpers.nextafter`, using unsigned bit-pattern stepping for 16-bit and 32-bit values, fp64 libdevice handling, and explicit NaN quieting.
> - Remove `nextafter` from the operations expected to require fp32 upcasts.
> - Route MPS and Halide through a per-call native ATen fallback, as well as low-precision calls on backends without the specialized Triton path.
> - While adding backend fallbacks, restrict Halide detection to CPU and CUDA so CUDA configuration cannot redirect MTIA to ATen.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> Applicability: Applicable
>
> Description: ATen and prims registrations share one lowering that owns dtype preservation and backend selection. Supported Triton calls flow to one runtime helper that owns IEEE bit stepping; incompatible backend paths use a local native fallback without changing Inductor's global fallback set. The Halide backend check consults configuration only for CPU and CUDA.
>
> Examples: A non-contiguous CUDA fp16 call is handled by the shared lowering, kept in fp16, and emitted through `triton_helpers.nextafter`. A float32 MPS prims call instead becomes an ATen fallback node and never reaches the unsupported Metal pointwise override. An MTIA call continues through its registered Triton scheduling even when the unrelated CUDA backend is set to Halide.
>
> ## Example
>
> Before this change, compiling the following fp16 operation could return the input unchanged. It now returns the same next-representable bit patterns as eager execution (`[1, 15361]` when viewed as `int16`):
>
> ```python
> x = torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0], device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
> y = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0], device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
>
> expected = torch.nextafter(x, y)
> actual = torch.compile(torch.nextafter, fullgraph=True)(x, y)
> torch.testing.assert_close(actual.view(torch.int16), expected.view(torch.int16))
> ```
>
> ## Testing
>
> - `PYTHONPATH="$PWD${PYTHONPATH:+:$PYTHONPATH}" python test/inductor/test_torchinductor_opinfo.py -k nextafter -q` on an NVIDIA H100: 42 total, 40 passed, 2 expected skips.
> - `PYTHONPATH="$PWD${PYTHONPATH:+:$PYTHONPATH}" python test/inductor/test_op_dtype_prop.py -q`: 620 tests passed.
> - `PYTHONPATH="$PWD${PYTHONPATH:+:$PYTHONPATH}" python test/inductor/test_pallas.py PallasLoweringTests.test_nextafter_halide_config_does_not_affect_mtia PallasLoweringTests.test_low_precision_nextafter_falls_back`: 2 tests passed.
> - MPS and Halide runtimes were unavailable locally. Their committed test entry points exited without executing device/backend tests; fake-device lowering checks verified that MPS produces a `FallbackKernel`, Halide produces a `FallbackKernel`, and MTIA remains a computed pointwise buffer when CUDA is configured for Halide.
> - `lintrunner -a` twice on `torch/_inductor/lowering.py` and `test/inductor/test_pallas.py`, followed by a plain `lintrunner`: no lint issues.
>

author: fegin
message:
[Pipeline] Defer FSDP gradient reduction waits (#196725)

**Split pipeline FSDP gradient reduction into explicit start and wait actions.**

`REDUCE_GRAD` starts asynchronous FSDP gradient finalization and stores its public `GradientReductionHandle`. `WAIT_REDUCE_GRAD` waits for that handle and completes gradient scaling. Every reduction has exactly one matching wait, and each pipeline rank may have at most one pending reduction.

By default, the wait remains adjacent to its reduction, preserving existing behavior. With `defer_reduce_grad_wait=True`, schedule lowering moves only the wait to immediately before the next local reduction or to the end of the schedule. The reduction remains at its existing causal point, allowing its communication to overlap with the next local stage's backward computation.

For pre-lowered compute-comms schedules, the action stream is the source of truth. Their `REDUCE_GRAD` and `WAIT_REDUCE_GRAD` ordering is validated regardless of the constructor option.

Non-final outer gradient-accumulation steps skip both actions. Deferred waits reject FSDP stages that share a communication context because another stage cannot safely use that context while a reduction is pending.

[rpc] Fix dangling this in RRef::handleError static map (#192960)

The static errorHandlers map in RRef::handleError() used lambdas that captured this. Since the map is initialized once, all subsequent calls from any RRef instance would use the first caller's this pointer.

This can cause a use-after-free if the first RRef is destroyed first, and even if not, the wrong RRef's timedOut_ flag is set, leading to incorrect error handling.

Pass this as a parameter to the lambdas instead of capturing it.

Also update _test_remote_message_delay_timeout to use timeout=3 instead of 2. The faulty agent delays PYTHON_REMOTE_CALL by 2 seconds in pipeWrite, which is called synchronously from send(). With timeout=2, rpc.remote() returns around the same time the creation timeout fires, so to_here(0.001) may race with the timedOut_ update. Using timeout=3 provides enough margin for to_here() to consistently take the intended fetch timeout path.

author: guilhermeleobas
message:
Remove `_base_vt` (#193679)

Consider the following example:

```python
class MyList(list):
    def append(self, item):
        super().append(item)
```

Dynamo represented this inheritance by storing a `_base_vt` object on `UserDefinedObjectVariable` (UDOV), pointing to a `ListVariable`. This composition-based approach had limitations:

* Storage lived in a separate location (`_base_vt`), while dispatch logic remained on the UDOV itself.
* The `_base_vt` object was unaware it was serving as the base for a user-defined object, which broke identity/equality semantics in edge cases like:

```python
>>> class F(frozenset): ...
>>> f = F()
>>> id(f) == id(f.copy())
False
>>> h = frozenset()
>>> id(h) == id(h.copy())
True
```

Because the underlying `_base_vt` had no notion of being wrapped by a user-defined object, Dynamo's `.copy()` incorrectly returned the same identity in both cases.

Rather than composition, this PR uses inheritance to directly extend the behavior of the base type. The VT inheritance for a class `class MyList(list)` is `UserDefinedList` -> `UserDefinedObjectVariable` -> `ListVariable` -> `VariableTracker`. The reason for this choice is:

* `UserDefinedObjectVariable` is the `PyHeapType` and knows how to redirect any custom method calls to the appropriate user-defined implementations.
* `ListVariable` contains the builtin behavior for a list type.
* Inheritance gives a single MRO instead of two separate objects, so `isinstance` checks and attribute/method lookup fall through naturally to the builtin behavior without needing a separate `_base_vt` redirect.

Each commit in this stack migrates a specific user-defined object from composition to inheritance, but only the top commit ([#193679](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/193679)) is relevant for CI. Before merging, I'll squash everything into a single commit.

author: CodersAcademy006
message:
Fix int32 overflow in CUDA bincount/histogram bin index (#189685)

Fixes #189666

## Root cause

`getBin` in `SummaryOps.cu` computes the histogram bin as an `int64` `IndexType` but casts the intermediate to `(int)` first, truncating it to 32 bits:

```cpp
IndexType bin = (int)(((bVal - minvalue)) * nbins / (maxvalue - minvalue));
```

For `bincount`, `minvalue = 0` and `maxvalue = nbins`, so the bin equals the input value. Any value above `INT_MAX` (2147483647) wraps to a negative bin index. That negative index becomes a negative atomic offset in `kernelHistogram1D`, giving the reported illegal `__global__` atomic well before the output allocation.

With the repro value `2147484647` the bin wraps to `-2147482649`, i.e. `-17179861192` bytes, which matches the address in the sanitizer report exactly.

## Fix

Cast to `IndexType` instead of `(int)`, keeping the full 64-bit range. `histc` is unaffected since its bin is always `< nbins` and small.

## Test

Added `test_bincount_int32_overflow` reproducing the issue. The output histogram needs `INT_MAX + 1001` int64 bins (~17 GB), so it is gated with `@largeTensorTest("18GB", "cuda")`. Before the fix it aborts with an illegal memory access under compute-sanitizer; after, it returns a count of 2 at the large bin.

Note: I could not build/run CUDA locally, so the regression test is validated by CI.

Approved by: https://github.com/Skylion007

author: jansel
message:
Fix cuDNN/MIOpen RNN backward reading the saved output with assumed strides (#198773)

Fixes #198652.

_cudnn_rnn_backward_input and _cudnn_rnn_backward_weight (and their MIOpen
twins) passed the saved forward `output` to the library as-is, implicitly
assuming that after the batch_first transpose it is (T, B, H)-contiguous. The
other inputs are normalized: `x` and `dy` go through .contiguous() and
`hx`/`cx` are TORCH_CHECKed. Eager never violates the assumption because
_cudnn_rnn returns `output` as a transposed view of a (T, B, H) buffer, but
any caller that hands the kernel a differently strided copy of the same
values gets silently wrong gradients: cuDNN reads the recurrent inputs
h_{t-1} from `y` in its backward passes, so for LSTM/RNN the weight_hh
gradient is wrong and for GRU dx, weight_ih and the biases are wrong as well.
torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks returning contiguous copies
reproduces this with no compiler involved.

Under compiled autograd with the inductor backend this is exactly what the
issue hits: _cudnn_rnn_backward has no meta kernel, so the first
CudnnRnnBackward0 node graph-breaks and runs eagerly (correct), while the
second one is lowered through inductor's
make_fallback(aten._cudnn_rnn_backward, require_contiguous), which feeds the
kernel a (B, T, H)-contiguous copy of the first LSTM's saved output. That is
why two chained cuDNN LSTMs are needed and only the first one's weight_hh_l0
is corrupted.

The fix makes the kernels call .contiguous() on `output`, mirroring `x` and
`dy`; it is a no-op in the eager path. Alternatives considered: dropping
require_contiguous from the inductor fallback or tagging the op with
needs_fixed_stride_order would only shield one caller and leave saved-tensor
hooks and other producers of restrided saved tensors broken; adding a meta
kernel for _cudnn_rnn_backward is an independent improvement that would not
remove the stride assumption. The MIOpen kernels have the identical pattern
and get the same change; they could not be exercised here, but ROCm CI runs
both new tests.

Test Plan:

Both new tests fail on a build with the fix reverted
(test_cudnn_rnn_backward_saved_output_layout: LSTM/GRU/RNN all mismatch,
test_chained_cudnn_lstm: 211/256 mismatched elements) and pass with it.

```
python test/test_nn.py -k test_cudnn_rnn_backward_saved_output_layout
python test/inductor/test_compiled_autograd.py -k test_chained_cudnn_lstm
python -m pytest test/test_nn.py -k "cudnn or rnn or lstm or gru" -q
lintrunner -a aten/src/ATen/native/cudnn/RNN.cpp aten/src/ATen/native/miopen/RNN_miopen.cpp test/test_nn.py test/inductor/test_compiled_autograd.py
```

The reproducer from the issue now matches eager (cudnn=True: OK) on a B200
with cuDNN 9.26.

This change was authored with the help of an AI assistant (Claude).

author: bobrenjc93
message:
[dynamo] Add PrecompileSession, the caller-driven multi-graph capture (#198137)

**Problem.** `torch/_dynamo/precompile_package.py` held the pieces of a multi-graph capture -- the guard filter, the compiler configuration, the guard classification, the summary builder -- but nothing drove them, so no caller could record a function's compiled variants.

**Fix.** Add `PrecompileSession`, a context manager that compiles the function into a fresh `CompilePackage` under a recording guard filter and reports what the calls covered as a `PrecompileSummary`, with `precompile_capture(fn, *, backend, guard_filter_fn, recompile_limit, dynamic)` as its entry point.

**Summary.** The module had `default_guard_filter_fn`, `_capture_config`, the guard classification and `_summarize`, but no driver, so nothing under `torch/` could capture a function's variants. `PrecompileSession` is that driver: entering it compiles `fn` through `torch._dynamo.optimize` with a fresh `CompilePackage`, a filter that records every kept and dropped guard slot, the caller's `dynamic` and `recompile_limit`, and `isolate_recompiles=True`, and hands back a callable whose calls run under `_capture_config`. That callable records any exception a call raised for the summary and, after every call, takes the bundled AOTAutograd artifacts filed under its backend ids out of `PrecompileContext` with the new `take_artifact`, so another capture's `clear()` between calls cannot lose them. The key constraint is that the filter runs once per compilation, spells every slot through `_normalize` so the kept, dropped and risky sets and the facts compare with each other, and keys its `GuardFact` set by the code object the new `CompilePackage.current_entry` property names, which lets `summary()` report a dropped slot whose source held different values across a frame's variants as risky. Rendering the session as an artifact behind the coverage and guard gates is the next PR; the guard-drop invariance policy, the drift probe and the installed serving mode of the reference stack are out by design, and `truncated` is always empty.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR adds `PrecompileSession`, the multi-graph capture that the multi-call `DynamoTracer` front-end of `capture()` (#198138) is built on.

## Entering a session

The new test drives a graph-breaking step at two shapes and reads the summary inside the block:

```python
from torch._dynamo.precompile_package import precompile_capture

def step(model, x):
    y = model(x)
    torch._dynamo.graph_break()
    return y.sum(dim=0) + y.shape[0]

model = torch.nn.Linear(4, 4)
x2, x3 = torch.ones(2, 4), torch.ones(3, 4)
session = precompile_capture(step, backend="eager")
with session as call:
    call(model, x2)   # compiles step and its graph-break continuation
    call(model, x3)   # recompiles both for the second shape
    summary = session.summary()
call(model, x2)       # PackageError: "PrecompileSession is not active"
```

`__enter__` does one thing:

```python
self._compiled = torch._dynamo.optimize(
    self._backend,
    package=self._package,              # a fresh CompilePackage(fn)
    guard_filter_fn=self._guard_filter_fn,
    dynamic=self._dynamic,
    recompile_limit=self._recompile_limit,
    isolate_recompiles=True,
)(self._fn)
return self._call
```

`isolate_recompiles=True` gives the package its own cache region: a function captured (or compiled) earlier in the process would otherwise serve its existing cache entries and this package would record nothing. The test pins this by opening a `second` session on the same `step` after the first and checking `second.summary().guarded_codes >= 2`. A session cannot be re-entered: the test re-enters the finished `session` and expects `PackageError` ("cannot be re-entered; start a new capture").

## Each call runs under the capture configuration

The configuration is per call, not per block, so user code between calls (`optimizer.step`, data loading, a later `save()`) runs in the ambient configuration:

```python
def _call(self, *args, **kwargs):
    if self._compiled is None or self._finished:
        raise PackageError("PrecompileSession is not active")
    limit = max(self._recompile_limit, torch._dynamo.config.accumulated_recompile_limit)
    try:
        with _capture_config(), torch._dynamo.config.patch(accumulated_recompile_limit=limit):
            return self._compiled(*args, **kwargs)
    except Exception as e:
        message = f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
        if message not in self._capture_errors:
            self._capture_errors.append(message)
        raise
    finally:
        self._take_backend_artifacts()
```

The ambient `accumulated_recompile_limit` is raised to at least the per-frame limit so the explicit `recompile_limit` is the effective one. An `Exception` is recorded once (deduplicated by message) and re-raised; a `BaseException` such as `KeyboardInterrupt` is not a capture error and propagates unrecorded. Either way the `finally` takes the call's backend artifacts (see "Taking the backend artifacts after every call" below). The test calls `call(model, torch.ones(2, 5))` on a `Linear(4, 4)`, catches the `RuntimeError`, and checks `failed.summary().complete` is false with exactly one `capture_errors` entry.

## The recording guard filter

A dropped guard does not fail at serving time; it silently widens what a graph is reused for, so the drops have to be inspectable. The session wraps `default_guard_filter_fn` (or the caller's filter) and, per compilation, records the decision for every `(guard_type, source)` slot:

```python
decisions = list(inner(entries))
default_kept = default_guard_filter_fn(entries) if self._custom_guard_filter else decisions
for keep, by_default, entry in zip(decisions, default_kept, entries):
    slot = (entry.guard_type, _normalize(strip_local_scope(entry.name)))
    enforced = keep or (_is_noop_guard_type(entry.guard_type) and global_state_kept)
    if enforced:
        self._kept_guards.add(slot)
    else:
        self._dropped_guards.add(slot)
        if rendered := " ; ".join(_render_code(entry.code_parts)):
            self._dropped_guard_code.setdefault(slot, rendered)
        if by_default or _is_risky_drop(entry, namespaces):
            self._risky_dropped_guards.add(slot)
    if entry.guard_type not in _UNMODELLED_GUARD_TYPES:
        facts.add(_GuardFact(guard_type=..., source=slot[1], code=..., value=_value_fingerprint(entry), enforced=enforced))
```

Every slot is normalized once, and `GuardFact.source` reuses `slot[1]`, so the dropped, risky and kept sets and the per-variant facts share one spelling and compare as equals. A dropped slot's rendered code is recorded only when it renders to something. A no-op guard type counts as enforced when `GLOBAL_STATE` is kept, since that is where its check lives. A drop the default filter would not have made (`by_default` true under a custom filter) is risky by construction: nothing here can say what the caller gave up. The test pins this with a custom filter that drops every `TENSOR_MATCH`:

```python
custom = precompile_capture(step, backend="eager",
                            guard_filter_fn=lambda es: [e.guard_type != "TENSOR_MATCH" for e in es])
with custom as call:
    call(model, x2)
("TENSOR_MATCH", "x") in custom.summary().risky_dropped_guards   # True
``` Unmodelled guard types are never compared, so they contribute no fact. One filter call is one compilation, and the package knows which frame is being compiled, so the fact set is filed under that frame:

```python
current = self._package.current_entry          # new property on CompilePackage
code = current.python_code
key = (code.co_name, code.co_filename, code.co_firstlineno)   # else ("<unknown>", "<unknown>", 0)
self._guard_sets.setdefault(key, []).append(frozenset(facts))
```

## `summary()`

`summary()` feeds the recorded sets to the landed `_summarize`, adding one more risk rule first: a dropped slot whose source held different values across a frame's variants is risky, because that guard was what told the variants apart and cannot pick between them at serve time. Merely being absent from one variant (a `MODULE_MATCH` a branch does not touch) is not. `test_a_dropped_guard_that_tells_variants_apart_is_risky` pins the rule: it rebinds the same-file global def `_act` (whose `CLOSURE_MATCH` the default filter drops) between two `dynamic=False` calls of `_through_act`, and `("CLOSURE_MATCH", "G['_act']")` is reported risky only when the def changed between the variants; it fails with the rule removed.

```python
risky = set(self._risky_dropped_guards)
for variants in self._guard_sets.values():
    values = {}
    for facts in variants:
        for f in facts:
            if not f.enforced:
                values.setdefault((f.guard_type, f.source), set()).add(f.value)
    risky |= {slot for slot, seen in values.items() if len(seen) > 1}
return _summarize(self._package.cache_entry(), dropped=..., kept=..., policy_dropped=set(),
                  risky=risky, truncated=frozenset(), capture_errors=..., guard_sets=..., dropped_code=...)
```

For the two-shape capture above the test checks:

```python
summary.complete                                  # True
(summary.frames, summary.resume_functions)        # (2, 1): step and its continuation
summary.guarded_codes >= 3                        # recompiled for the second shape
"MODULE_MATCH" in summary.dropped_guard_types     # the default filter's drop
("CLOSURE_MATCH", "G['torch']._dynamo.graph_break") in summary.dropped_guards
summary.kept_guards                               # non-empty
summary.risky_dropped_guards                      # ()
```

## Taking the backend artifacts after every call

The AOTAutograd cache records a bundled entry under each graph's backend id as the graph compiles, into a process-global list on `PrecompileContext`. After every call, in `_call`'s `finally`, the session moves this package's entries out of that list through the new `take_artifact`, a `pop` next to `serialize_artifact_by_key`; `__exit__` only marks the session finished and drops the compiled callable:

```python
@classmethod
def take_artifact(cls, key: str) -> BackendCacheArtifact[Any] | None:
    return cls._backend_artifacts_by_key.pop(_BackendId(key), None)

# PrecompileSession._take_backend_artifacts
for backend_id in self._package.cache_entry().backend_ids:
    if backend_id not in self._backend_artifacts:
        artifact = PrecompileContext.take_artifact(backend_id)
        if artifact is not None:
            self._backend_artifacts[backend_id] = artifact
```

Taking them as the capture goes keeps another capture's `PrecompileContext.clear()` between calls from losing them. Ownership moves to the session: once taken, an id is no longer found by `serialize_artifact_by_key`, as the `take_artifact` docstring says.

## `precompile_capture` and what it refuses

`precompile_capture` builds the session after three up-front refusals, each pinned by the test:

```python
precompile_capture(functools.partial(step, model))   # PackageError: "... cannot capture a partial ..."
precompile_capture(model)                            # PackageError: "... capture the function that CALLS the model ..."
precompile_capture(model.forward)                    # PackageError: "... cannot capture a bound method ..."
```

A `functools.partial` is refused because its bound arguments are not on the code object. A bare `nn.Module` is refused because Dynamo compiles it through its own wrapper frame, whose graphs close over the module, which a standalone artifact cannot rebuild; the message suggests a module-level `def step(model, x): return model(x)`. A bound method (`types.MethodType`) is refused because the artifact rebuilds `fn` from its code object, whose first parameter is the receiver: a captured `model.forward` would be served as `f(model, x)` instead of `f(x)`, so the message points at a module-level function that takes the receiver as an argument. `recompile_limit` defaults to 256, well above Dynamo's usual 8, because a precompile deliberately wants one compiled variant per condition, whereas the normal limit exists to catch runaway recompilation. Runtime guards stay intact during capture: `guard_filter_fn` applies only to the serialized guard state, so every call observes the same recompilation behavior as ordinary `torch.compile`.

## Scope

Rendering the session as an artifact, behind the coverage and guard gates, is the next commit (#198216). Not here, by design: the guard-drop invariance policy, the drift probe and the installed serving mode of the reference stack; `truncated` is always empty. `test_precompile_session_captures_variants_and_summarizes` pins everything above except the varied-value rule, which `test_a_dropped_guard_that_tells_variants_apart_is_risky` pins.

Test Plan:

`test_precompile_session_captures_variants_and_summarizes` captures a graph-breaking step at two shapes and checks the summary (frames, continuation, variants, dropped and kept slots), the inactive-session and re-entry refusals, a call that raised, a second session on the same function, a custom filter's drop reported risky, and the partial/module/bound-method refusals. `test_a_dropped_guard_that_tells_variants_apart_is_risky` rebinds a same-file global def between two static-shape calls and checks the dropped slot is reported risky only when the def changed (it fails with the varied-value rule removed).

message:
[ROCm] Fix test_lazy_init on hosts with more than 32 GPUs (#199036)

test_lazy_init sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES or HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES to the hard-coded index 32 after import and expects device_count() to be 0. Device 32 is a real device on a ROCm machine in CPX mode, which can expose 64 logical GPUs, so the child reports 1 and the assertion fails.

Use index 1024 instead. The parent's device_count() is not usable here: the test only runs when the parent sees fewer than 2 GPUs (@unittest.skipIf(TEST_MULTIGPU)), and the child checks the index against every GPU, so index 1 is still a real device when CPX mode exposes 64 logical GPUs.

The cuDeviceGetCount check was skipped on ROCm. hipGetDeviceCount cannot replace it, because that call initializes HIP itself. hipInit calls hsa_init, and hsa_system_get_info returns HSA_STATUS_ERROR_NOT_INITIALIZED until that happens. On Linux ROCm, query hsa_system_get_info on the libhsa-runtime64 torch already loaded (RTLD_NOLOAD). It must return 0x100B (HSA_STATUS_ERROR_NOT_INITIALIZED) after import and 0 (HSA_STATUS_SUCCESS) after torch.cuda.init(), so import torch did not call hsa_init.

Test Plan:
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 and HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 are required because test_lazy_init is skipped when more than one GPU is visible.

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python test/test_cuda.py -v TestCuda.test_lazy_init
```

message:
Fix teardown race in _test_rank_membership (#199026)

## Summary

test_gloo_rank_membership is flaky with:

>   RuntimeError: Gloo connectFullMesh failed with [.../gloo/transport/tcp/pair.cc:561]
>   Connection closed by peer

The test calls init_process_group() and then only does rank-local checks, so the ranks never sync after init. init_process_group() is not a barrier, and the Gloo TCP connect is asymmetric: the initiator reports its pair as connected once it has written the sequence number. It can do that while the listener is still polling FileStore for the peer address. The fast rank then finishes the test, destroys its PG and closes the socket. The slow rank picks up the already-closed connection, reads EOF, and init fails. Either rank can be the one that fails.

Fix by adding a dist.barrier() at the end of the helper, so no rank tears down before all ranks have finished init.

## Test Plan:

Tested on 8x MI300 (gfx942) with a torch 2.14 ROCm wheel; the helper and the Gloo pin are the same on main. Contention makes the race reproducible; run the test with 8 parallel workers pinned to 2 CPUs:

```
taskset -c 0,1 python test/distributed/test_c10d_gloo.py -v CommTest.test_gloo_rank_membership
```

Before: 4/80 failed with the error above (0/200 on an idle machine).
After: 0/398 failed. Reverting the fix brings it back (3/80).

Also passing with the fix:

```
python test/distributed/test_c10d_nccl.py -v CommTest.test_nncl_rank_membership
python -m pytest test/distributed/test_c10d_gloo.py -k CommTest
```

# Fixing an Issue

Before submitting, please review:

- [The Ultimate Guide to PyTorch Contributions](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/wiki/The-Ultimate-Guide-to-PyTorch-Contributions#getting-started-with-pull-requests)

## Issue

Fixes #198854

## Summary

The epsilon of `torch.float8_e5m2fnuz` is 0.125, which is supposed to be 0.25. And torch.tensor(1.0 + eps) should not be 1, but it is 1.0 in torch.float8_e5m2fnuz.

The new e5m2fnuz check fails on torch 2.10.0 (eps 0.125), and a standalone C++ program compiled with the patched header prints epsilon 0.25 / round_error 0.5. `test_type_info.py` has not been run against a build that includes this change.

Fix IndexError in tuned_addmm for 0-d scalar bias (#197214)

Fixes #197107

The `tuned_addmm` function was previously evaluating `inp.get_stride()[0] == 0` before confirming the tensor was actually 2D. Passing a 0-d scalar bias causes `get_stride()` to return `()`, which predictably triggers an `IndexError` when indexed.

This pull request makes a minor change to the condition order in the `tuned_addmm` function in `torch/_inductor/kernel/mm.py`. The logical order of the condition checking the input tensor's size and stride has been adjusted for clarity and possibly to avoid unnecessary computation.

* Refactored the conditional statement to check `len(inp.get_size()) == 2` before `inp.get_stride()[0] == 0` in the `tuned_addmm` function, improving code clarity and potentially preventing errors if the size check fails.
