author: mlazos
message:
Fix #195845: [inductor] mix-order reduction: split column sum ignores xmask, wrong results wh (#196565)

Human direction from @mlazos: Basically, when the row count is not a multiple of XBLOCK, pointwise can transform the fill value to a value other than the reduction identity, leading to silent incorrectness.

>
> ## Summary
>
> Fixes #195845.
>
> Correct mix-order split column reductions when the row count is not a multiple of `XBLOCK`. The change also makes heuristic, tuned, cached, and fixed configurations obey the split/block contract; preserves reduction-type and dtype invariants during later fusion; fixes Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) descriptor selection, reduction-store tracking, and metadata liveness; and adds focused code-generation and numerical regressions.
>
> ## Root cause
>
> Mix-order reduction computes each split's partial column reduction across X after running the fused pointwise body. Although masked loads use a fill value, pointwise operations can transform that value away from the reduction identity. The partial reduction did not apply `xmask` again, so padded rows could contribute to the result. With mask optimization, a singleton logical X extent had the same risk because a non-fixed mix-order kernel can still select `XBLOCK > 1`.
>
> `XBLOCK` must also be a positive power of two that divides `RSPLIT_SIZE`: programs are spaced by the split size while each loop iteration advances by the block size. Non-fixed heuristic, tuned, and cached candidates additionally have a maximum `XBLOCK` of 16; fixed configurations use the power-of-two and divisibility checks without that runtime-autotuning cap. These path-specific contracts were not enforced consistently. Cached configuration reconstruction also discarded non-`BLOCK` constexpr metadata, and fixed configurations could omit or contradict scheduled split metadata.
>
> During review, an explicit sum/product code-generation guard exposed two further invariant gaps. Later scheduler fusion could add `max` or `min` to the noncontiguous side without revalidation, and integer or wider floating-point reductions could enter a partial-accumulation path whose accumulator and shared workspace are float32. The former was an intermediate PR regression rather than a pre-existing compilation failure; the latter could silently round a large integer sum before its final cast.
>
> An intermediate version of this PR rejected tensor descriptors for fixed multi-stage kernels before deciding whether each descriptor would be created on the host or device. Only device-side descriptor construction is incompatible with that pipelined path, so the final implementation permits valid host-side TMA. Reduction-output stores also formatted tensor descriptors directly instead of using the shared descriptor-emission path. That bypassed host-descriptor registration and device-descriptor tracking. Because `uses_tma` remained false, the loop skipped `xoffset += XBLOCK`, causing a fixed two-stage kernel with only TMA-ineligible inputs but a TMA-eligible reduction-output store to repeatedly overwrite the first output rows.
>
> Conversely, descriptor eligibility was recorded once per kernel without being associated with the originating buffer before deferred stores were pruned. If fusion removed the only TMA-eligible intermediate reduction output, the surviving kernel still advertised TMA and retained its minimum-block constraint even though its emitted code contained no descriptor operation. During combo-kernel probing, `kernel.inductor_meta_per_kernel()` can be called while an unrelated kernel occupies `V.kernel`; checking removal through `V.kernel` then reads the wrong removal sets instead of those owned by the queried kernel.
>
> ## Fix
>
> Apply `xmask` immediately before every partial X-axis reduction and replace inactive lanes with the identity returned by `ir.Reduction.default_accumulator`. Keep the mask for singleton logical X extents in non-fixed kernels; a fixed `XBLOCK=1` can still omit it.
>
> Centralize mix-order configuration validation. Select a dividing heuristic block, reject invalid tuned and cached candidates, retain complete cached constexpr metadata, and honor TMA minimum-block and stage constraints. Create and normalize the kernel before split-size autotuning, skip that autotuning for fixed configurations, and pass the same kernel instance to final code generation. If a tensor descriptor cannot satisfy the mix-order constraints, fall back to ordinary loads or stores for that access only.
>
> Revalidate later fusion on the noncontiguous side so only sum/product reductions with float16, bfloat16, or float32 outputs use the float32 workspace. Unsupported operations and dtypes remain in separate kernels. For fixed multi-stage kernels, permit host-materializable descriptors while falling back from device-side descriptors. Route reduction-output stores through the shared descriptor-emission path so descriptor placement metadata and loop advancement remain consistent. Associate descriptor emission and minimum-block requirements with their buffers, and derive final metadata from the owning kernel's removal sets so only surviving accesses contribute.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> Applicability: Applicable
>
> Description: The change spans mix-order scheduling, Triton body generation, heuristic and coordinate-descent configuration, autotune-cache reconstruction, TMA descriptor selection, fixed-configuration normalization, workspace accumulation, and final wrapper reduction. It establishes four invariants at the relevant boundaries: inactive X lanes enter partial reductions only as the operation identity; every selected `XBLOCK` is valid for the scheduled `RSPLIT_SIZE`; only reduction operations and dtypes representable by the float32 workspace enter the noncontiguous mix-order path; and descriptor metadata reflects only live accesses. Descriptor placement is decided before applying the fixed multi-stage restriction, and reduction-output descriptors use the same placement and bookkeeping path as ordinary stores.
>
> Examples: For `RSPLIT_SIZE=18`, non-fixed selection may use `XBLOCK=2`, while a non-dividing value or a value above 16 is rejected before launch. A fixed configuration may exceed 16 but must still use a positive power-of-two divisor of `RSPLIT_SIZE`. A late `amax` remains separate from an already formed mix-order sum pair. A fixed two-stage kernel can use a zero-offset host TMA descriptor but falls back from a device-side descriptor. A `uint8` column sum remains outside mix order so its int64 result is not rounded through float32 workspace storage.
>
> ## Example
>
> ```python

message:
Route the riscv64 job back onto the cross-compilation code path (#194880)

The riscv64 cross build has not taken its own code path since #187821. That PR renamed the docker image to pytorch-linux-noble-riscv64-py3.12-gcc14-cross-build and narrowed the guards from *riscv* to *riscv*cross*, but the guards in .ci/docker/build.sh test the image name while the ones in .ci/pytorch/build.sh test BUILD_ENVIRONMENT -- and only the image name gained the "cross" marker. BUILD_ENVIRONMENT stayed linux-noble-riscv64-py3.12-gcc14, so `[[ "$BUILD_ENVIRONMENT" == *riscv64*cross* ]]` has been false ever since.

Everything in that block is skipped as a result: the crossenv at /opt/riscv-cross-env is never activated, so the build runs against the host interpreter; CMAKE_CROSSCOMPILING, CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME and CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR are never exported, so CMake never enters cross mode even though CC/CXX point at the riscv64 toolchain; and SLEEF_TARGET_EXEC_USE_QEMU and the workspace chown are missed too. #190887 later added an `elif *riscv64*` arm for the new native image, which is the branch this job has been taking.

Aligning BUILD_ENVIRONMENT with the image name is the smaller of the two possible fixes and matches the intent of #187821. Widening the guards back to *riscv64* would work for this job but would pull the native image, which is genuinely named linux-noble-riscv64-py3.12-gcc14, onto the cross path -- and that path exits 1 when /opt/riscv-cross-env is absent. The string is only consumed as $BUILD_ENVIRONMENT and as the build artifact name, so renaming it is contained; no other pattern in .ci/pytorch/build.sh matches the added "-cross-build".

This commit was authored with the assistance of an AI coding assistant.

The job is opt-in, so this needs a ciflow/riscv64 run to verify. It has been red since 2025-10 and the last run predates both #190887 and the scikit-build-core migration, so this is expected to uncover further breakage rather than turn the job green on its own -- in particular the crossenv is provisioned with `setuptools pyyaml typing_extensions wheel` only, while the build now invokes `python -m build --wheel --no-isolation`. Fixing that needs to be informed by a real run, since crossenv splits host and target environments and build backends belong in the host one.

Root cause confirmed from the last run's log
(https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/28817304405), which shows the guard evaluating false:

author: jansel
message:
[decomp] Fix _weight_norm_interface for 1-D inputs and half norm dtype (#198772)

Fixes #198676

Applying nn.utils.parametrizations.weight_norm to a 1-D parameter (e.g.
name="bias") under torch.compile with Inductor silently returned wrong
forward values and inf/nan gradients. backend="eager" and "aot_eager" were
unaffected because only Inductor applies the core decomposition table.

Root cause: the _weight_norm_interface decomposition builds keep_dim as
every dimension except dim and reduces with v.norm(2, keep_dim,
keepdim=True). For a 1-D v, keep_dim is the empty tuple, which is
PyTorch's legacy spelling for "reduce over all dims", so the norm came out
as a single ||v|| of shape [1] instead of ATen's per-element |v_i| of
shape [n] (the fused kernels allocate norm with g's shape and compute the
L2 norm of each length-1 slice). The forward was therefore v * g / ||v||
instead of v * g / |v|. The misshaped norm is also saved for backward:
AOTAutograd records _weight_norm_interface_backward(grad, v, g, result1,
dim) and Inductor lowers that op through the fused ATen fallback kernel,
which only checks contiguity and reads saved_norm[i] for every row of v.
On a one-element buffer that reads past the allocation, which is where the
inf/nan gradients came from.

A second mismatch sat on the same line. Both the CPU (WeightNorm.cpp) and
CUDA (WeightNorm.cu) kernels keep the norm in float when g is bfloat16 or
half, but the decomposition only promoted bfloat16 (#128956 predates the
CPU half support added in #148878, and no OpInfo covers this op). The
fused backward kernel reads the saved norm as float, so a compiled half
weight_norm with backward raised "expected scalar type Float but found
Half" on both devices at any rank. Half 1-D inputs would still crash
without this, so the dtype rule is fixed here as well.

Fix: when the reduction dims are empty the decomposition uses v.abs() as
the norm, and the norm dtype is promoted to float for half as well as
bfloat16. abs() is also what the rank-2-and-up branch compiles to for
single-element rows, because _refs.linalg.vector_norm special-cases
all-size-1 reductions to abs; the kernels' sqrt(v*v) differs only where
v*v under/overflows, where they return a 0 or inf norm. The promotion is
skipped on MPS: WeightNorm.mm allocates the norm with g's dtype and its
backward builds the MPSGraph ops from the saved norm's dtype, so a float
norm next to half tensors would not match that kernel (the bfloat16
promotion already disagreed with MPS before this change). The
post-decomposition Inductor graph is unchanged for float32, float64 and
bfloat16 at rank 2 and above on CPU/CUDA; only the 1-D, half and MPS cases
change.

Alternatives considered: reshaping so the reduction always has a real
dimension (unsqueeze/norm/squeeze, or mirroring ATen's norm_except_dim
with movedim/reshape) is correct but changes the traced graph for every
rank for no benefit, and switching to sum or linalg.vector_norm does not
help because they share the empty-dims-means-all-dims semantics. Left as
follow-ups: the decomposition computes v * (g / norm) in reduced precision
with three roundings where ATen rounds once, the C++ backward fallback has
no shape check on the saved norm, which is why this surfaced as silent
garbage rather than an error, and aligning the MPS kernel's norm dtype
with CPU/CUDA would let the device check go away.

Test Plan:

test_decomp.py::test_weight_norm_interface gains a 1-D case over float,
half and bfloat16 comparing both outputs against the ATen op (values,
shape and dtype); v is built with linspace so |v| is bounded away from
zero and the eager-mode half division cannot overflow. It also gains a
rank-2 half/bfloat16 case with atol=rtol=1e-2: the eager decomposition's
three roundings put ~20% of seeds outside the default half tolerance,
while 1e-2 passed 500 seeds per device.
test_torchinductor.py gains test_weight_norm_1d_and_reduced_dtypes, an
end-to-end compiled forward + backward check over float32, float16 and
bfloat16 at rank 1 and rank 2 that runs for CPU and CUDA and under the
dynamic-shapes variants; MPS runs float32 only since MPS eager keeps the
half arithmetic in half. Both the 1-D and the rank-2 half cases fail at
HEAD without the decomposition change. Compiled results matched ATen for
200 seeds per dtype, rank and device, bitwise for fp16 down to |v| = 6e-8.

```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" python -m pytest test/test_decomp.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k weight_norm
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0  python -m pytest test/test_decomp.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k weight_norm
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor_dynamic_shapes.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor_codegen_dynamic_shapes.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k weight_norm
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0  python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor_dynamic_shapes.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor_codegen_dynamic_shapes.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k weight_norm
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" python -m pytest test/test_decomp.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k DecompOneOffTests
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" python -m pytest test/test_nn.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k weight_norm
lintrunner -a torch/_decomp/decompositions.py test/test_decomp.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py
```

All passed on CPU and CUDA; lintrunner reported no issues.

message:
[inductor] Partition cross-device fallbacks from CUDA graphs (#190555)

## Summary

> - Split any extern kernel whose FX node reads or produces tensors on more than one device, ignoring meta tensors. This covers `FallbackKernel`, `ExternKernelOut` (custom ops with a `Tag.out` overload), `IndexPutFallback`, and multi-output ops together with their `MultiOutput` children.
> - Keep same-device kernels eligible for CUDA graph capture.
> - Rename and simplify the deterministic `device_put` regression.
> - Add regressions for a CPU-to-CUDA custom op, with and without a `Tag.out` overload, for multi-output ops with a CPU scalar input and with a CPU output, and for `index_put` with CPU indices. Each one checks results against eager and counts the recorded graphs.
> - Add a regression that SDPA with dropout stays in one forward and one backward CUDA graph, so the rule doesn't split attention over the RNG state its backward reads.

## Root cause

CUDAGraph partitions must not read tensor storage allocated outside the active CUDA memory pool. `Scheduler.should_partition` recognized explicit `ir.DeviceCopy` nodes, but a fallback kernel could report a CUDA output device while reading a CPU tensor input. That fallback passed the normal GPU-node check and could be recorded in a CUDA partition, where `check_memory_pool` rejected the CPU storage.

> The scheduler now checks the FX node behind each extern kernel: if the kernel's inputs and outputs span more than one device, it gets its own partition. Deciding on the FX node keeps a multi-output op and its `MultiOutput` children together, the way `is_cudagraph_unsafe_op` already does. Same-device kernels remain eligible for CUDA graph capture. The partition reason is now `cross-device ops`.

Issue #188677 is the earlier CI quarantine of this same regression; #190233 tracks the underlying failure.

Fixes #190233

Fixes #188677

## Test plan

- pre-fix counterfactual: the generic CPU-to-CUDA custom-op regression fails in `check_memory_pool`
- focused device-copy, `device_put`, generic cross-device fallback, and same-device fallback tests pass
- graph-partition subset: 58 passed, 2 skipped
- both positive regressions: 10/10 repeated passes with CUDA memory-leak checking
- `TRITON_OVERRIDE_ARCH=sm86`: both positive regressions pass
- targeted `spin lint` on both changed files, including NEWLINE, Pyrefly, Ruff, Flake8, ClangFormat, and the remaining configured linters
- `git diff --check`

> Re-verified after the FX-level change on an RTX 4080, against torch 2.13 with the rule patched in and Inductor caches disabled, since there was no CUDA build of main. The four new cases crash at record time without the rule and pass with it. A same-device custom op and SDPA forward and backward are not split. Details are in [this comment](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/190555#issuecomment-5842853141).
>
> The SDPA dropout test's body was run the same way. It passes with the rule, and fails when the rule sees the seed and offset on the CPU.

ROCm runtime was not available locally, so this PR does not claim ROCm execution coverage.

author: krastogi-in
message:
Add pattern matcher to deduplicate var and std calculation (#182945)

Fixes #180957

When both torch.var(x, dim) and torch.std(x, dim) appear on the same tensor, std's decomposition in torch/_refs/__init__.py explicitly casts the input to the compute dtype (e.g., float32) before calling var internally, while the standalone var call relies on Inductor's lowering to handle the dtype promotion. This produces two structurally different FX graph nodes:

```
%var   = aten.var.correction(%arg0_1, [-1], correction=1)
%cvt   = prims.convert_element_type(%arg0_1, torch.float32)
%var_1 = aten.var.correction(%cvt, [-1], correction=1.0)
```
These differ in two ways that prevent FX-level CSE from deduplicating them:

- **Different inputs:** %arg0_1 (float16) vs. %cvt (float32 cast of the same tensor)

- **Different correction types**: correction=1 (int) vs. correction=1.0 (float), due to set_correction() returning a float in std's decomposition path

After Inductor lowering, both produce identical WelfordReduction IR nodes (same inner_fn, ranges, and reduction type) because the lowering normalizes the dtype internally. The C++ codegen partially compensates by merging the reduction loop into a single Welford accumulator, but still writes to two separate output buffers and duplicates the downstream pointwise operations (division by N-1).

General CSE at the codegen level cannot resolve this because Welford reductions are multi-statement loop constructs, not single expressions — the existing CSE operates on individual expression strings and cannot recognize two structurally identical reduction loops as equivalent at the buffer level.

Fix

A post-grad pattern matcher pass (register_graph_pattern with MultiOutputPattern) detects when both a standalone var.correction(x, dims) and a var.correction(convert_element_type(x, dtype), dims) exist on the same base tensor with equivalent correction values. It rewrites the standalone var to derive its result from the higher-precision var via a cheap convert_element_type cast, eliminating the redundant Welford reduction entirely. The generated kernel then contains a single reduction, a single output buffer, and reuses the divided result for both var and sqrt(var).

author: egeboy35
message:
Reject overlapping out= tensors in aminmax (#195342)

Fixes #195338.

`torch.aminmax(x, out=(t, t))` silently returned a wrong result. The two outputs are written
independently, so when they share storage whichever write lands last clobbers the other:

```python
>>> torch.manual_seed(0); x = torch.randn(5)
>>> torch.aminmax(x)
torch.return_types.aminmax(min=tensor(-2.1788), max=tensor(1.5410))
>>> t = torch.empty((), dtype=x.dtype)
>>> torch.aminmax(x, out=(t, t))
torch.return_types.aminmax_out(min=tensor(1.5410), max=tensor(1.5410))
```

No error, no warning, and `min > max` is reachable the same way.

`TORCH_META_FUNC(aminmax)` validated each output's dtype but never compared their storage. This
adds that check, using the same `get_overlap_status` machinery `kthvalue` reaches through
`at::assert_no_overlap` (`Sorting.cpp:569`). It does not call that helper directly because its
message describes an *input* aliasing the output, which would point a user at the wrong tensor.
The check uses `TORCH_CHECK_VALUE`, so from Python the reproducer now raises

```
ValueError: aminmax(): the `min` and `max` out= tensors must not overlap.
```

### Why the predicate is `!= Partial && != Full` and not `== No`

`get_overlap_status` returns `TooHard` — not `No` — whenever a tensor has symbolic sizes/strides
or is not non-overlapping-and-dense (`MemoryOverlap.cpp`). Requiring `No` therefore rejects
non-contiguous `out=` tensors that provably do not overlap, and calls under dynamic shapes. Both
of these are correct today and must stay working:

```python
b1, b2 = torch.empty(6), torch.empty(6)
torch.aminmax(x, dim=1, out=(b1[::2], b2[::2]))     # separate storages, strided
b3 = torch.empty(6)
torch.aminmax(x, dim=1, out=(b3[0::2], b3[1::2]))   # one storage, interleaved, disjoint
```

Rejecting only `Partial` and `Full` is what `at::assert_no_overlap` itself does. Both cases are now
in the test, and there is a comment at the predicate, so this does not get tightened by accident.

### Tests

`TestReductions.test_aminmax_out_overlap` covers the same tensor twice, two partially overlapping
views, two disjoint contiguous views, and the two strided cases above. The overlapping case is also
registered in `error_inputs_aminmax_amax_amin`, so the generic `test_errors` harness exercises it
on every device the op is registered for, not just CPU. Both expect `ValueError`.

Two tests in `test/test_schema_check.py` passed the same tensor as both aminmax outs on purpose, so
this check broke them. They now use `aten.log_sigmoid_forward.output`, which also has two out= tensors
of the same dtype and gives SchemaCheckMode the same mutation and aliasing records. The second test's
expected value changes from `torch.amax(x, dim=0)` to `logsigmoid(x)`; like before, that is whichever
write lands last (the CPU kernel stores `output` after `buffer`).

```
python -m pytest test/test_reductions.py -k aminmax -q   # 7 passed

author: stmcgovern
message:
[symm_mem]: Add per-PG stream serialization for ops (#195947)

Partial fix for  #188005 - only for CUDA and NCCL backends.
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/196337 is opened to address the NVSHMEM backend.

This PR is a step on the way to implementing per-PG signal pads, which would resolve https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/192581

Replace the advisory warn_if_multi_stream diagnostic with an RAII GroupStreamGuard that enforces correct stream ordering across all built-in symmetric-memory operations that touch the signal pad.

Signal pad operations use a CAS-based protocol on shared slots. When two operations for the same PG execute on different CUDA streams, the second CAS can find the slot still set by the first, causing deadlock.

The guard holds a per-(group_name, device) mutex across the guarded scope. On stream change, an event is recorded on the previous stream and the current stream waits on it. Same-stream fast path: one mutex acquisition and one pointer comparison, no event overhead. State is validated via weak_intrusive_ptr to detect PG destruction/name reuse, and held via shared_ptr to survive concurrent map replacement. No-op during CUDA graph capture, matching ProcessGroupNCCL's pattern.

Covers barrier, put_signal, wait_signal, all six collective ops in CUDASymmetricMemoryOps.cu, and both signal ops in nccl_extension.cu.

author: amd-maradosa
message:
[inductor] Fix no-op config restriction in TestTemplateConfigPruning (#195461)

## Problem

`TestTemplateConfigPruning` pins the autotuner to a single GEMM config with `heuristic.mm_configs = [c]`, where `heuristic` is a `CUDA*TemplateConfigHeuristic` constructed directly in `setUpClass`. CUDA and ROCm heuristics are registered
mutually exclusively (`register=torch.version.hip is None` / `register=IS_ROCM`), and the compiler resolves its own cached instance from the registry, so on ROCm that assignment has no effect.

As a result, on ROCm:

- All 43 candidates are autotuned per iteration instead of 1, each under `fresh_cache()`, so every one is a cold compile.
- `captured_smem` comes from whichever unrelated kernel compiled last while `smem_estimation` is computed for `c`, so the final assertion compares mismatched quantities and passes vacuously.
- `triton_compilation_fails` is never `True` (something always compiles), so the no-false-negatives branch is unreachable.

`persistent_mm_template` was never disabled either, which keeps polluting `captured_smem` even once the registry issue is fixed.

## Fix

- Resolve heuristics via `get_registered_heuristic_class(uid, GPU_TYPE, op)`; skip when nothing is registered for the device.
- Pin the config through `override_template_heuristics()`, which swaps the registry entry and clears the heuristic cache.
- Disable every GEMM template except the one under test, via a `template_pairs()` helper that derives the disabled set by exclusion.
- Build the pinned subclass once per test: the heuristic base uses a singleton metaclass keyed on the class object, so a per-iteration class leaks entries.
- Normalize each config through the heuristic's `_filter_configs` before deriving the shared memory estimate and the `exceeds` prediction, so both are computed for the config that is actually compiled (on ROCm this rewrites `num_stages` to 2, which also collapses the `[4, 5]` stage axis into duplicates that are skipped).
- Assert at most one Triton choice reaches the autotuner, so the restriction cannot silently stop applying again (zero when a config overflowing shared memory is pruned before benchmarking).

The Blackwell branch now selects a template uid rather than a heuristic class, since `CUDABlackwell*` heuristics register under `blackwell_ws_persistent_tma_mm_template.uid`.

## Test

Validated on gfx1151 (ROCm) with the equivalent change on `release/2.12`, before the `num_stages` normalization was added (which further halves the ROCm iteration count):

- Choices per autotune: 43 -> 2 (aten fallback + the config under test)
- `test_shared_memory_pruning_mm_float32_...`: 2728s -> 220s
- Full `TestTemplateConfigPruning`: ~5h40m -> 30m04s, 33 passed
- Singleton cache entries from the pinned class: 32 -> 1
- Regression assertion fires (reports 7 Triton choices) when the restriction is deliberately removed

*Description updated by @jeffdaily (with the help of an AI assistant) to reflect the `num_stages` normalization and the upstream template rename.*

author: malfet
message:
[MPS] Fix mixed-dtype batch_norm aborts and accumulate in float (#198740)

Fixes #154887

`batch_norm` with a half input and float32 running stats -- the ordinary AMP combination, accepted by CPU and CUDA -- killed the interpreter, because MPSGraph fails its module verifier on a mixed operand pair and calls `abort()` rather than throwing.

Follow common pattern and  compute normalization in the accumulate type (`toAccumulateType(dtype, kMPS)`, i.e. float for half and bfloat16) in both forward and backward: the input, weight, bias and running/saved stats are cast to it on the way in, and the results are cast back to their own dtypes on the way out. Besides removing the aborts, this resolves the "Accumulate type?" TODO: mixed-precision training used to compute batch statistics in half and was a few ulps off both CPU and CUDA. Non-mixed half/bfloat16 now accumulates in float as well, as it does on CPU and CUDA.

`save_mean`/`save_invstd` are stored by CPU's rule (float only when the parameters are float and the input is not) rather than CUDA's (always the accumulate type), because `TestConsistency` requires MPS outputs to match CPU, dtype included.

The backward cache key now covers the dtypes of every operand. It used to record only input and weight, so a weightless call with float32 stats followed by one with float16 stats at the same shape shared a graph and fed f16 buffers into f32 placeholders.

Coverage mostly comes from test_nn, where the mixed-dtype batchnorm tests already existed but were skipped on MPS: `test_batchnorm`, `test_batchnorm_eval_mixed`, `test_batchnorm_affine_mixed`, `test_batchnorm_nonaffine_half_input` and `test_batchnorm_nhwc` drop `skipMPS`. The MPS-only test covers what test_nn cannot reach: eval-mode gradients against CPU, the weightless stats-dtype pair that exposes the cache key, and a direct `native_batch_norm_backward` call with float32 saved stats. `test_batch_norm_mixed_dtype` no longer needs its loosened tolerance, and `test_addbmm_mixed_dtype_errors` drops its `out=` check, which duplicates OpInfo's `test_out` now that addbmm's MPS xfail is gone.

Un-skipping `test_batchnorm` exposed a macOS 14 only bug in the 5D-to-4D flattening from #180335: the input was made NCHW-contiguous, but the channels_last_3d output was reshaped into a view with channels-last strides and bound with the strided API, which `Placeholder` only honors on macOS 15+. On macOS 14 the graph wrote NCHW-ordered data into an NHWC buffer. The input is now flattened in its own memory format (merging D and H turns channels_last_3d into channels_last, which the 4D path handles natively), and an `out=` tensor in a different layout goes through a temporary that is copied back.

[Testcase Refactoring] Add hardware classification to APoT linear tests (#192636)

## Change background

PyTorch test classes are being annotated with hardware classification metadata so that test selection can distinguish device-agnostic framework tests from accelerator or device-specific tests (tracked in #185590).

`TestNonUniformObserver` contains two tests that compare `LinearAPoT` forward results against a uniform `torch.nn.Linear` baseline. The tests do not use device-type test instantiation, device parameters, CUDA-only decorators, CUDA APIs, hard-coded device strings, or device-specific assertions; the tensors use the default device only as inputs to shared APoT logic. Therefore, per review feedback, no hardware decoupling or class split is performed: the tests are kept in their original form and only the hardware-classification metadata is added.

`LinearAPoT` and the experimental APoT implementation path (`torch/ao/quantization/experimental/*`) support CPU only (e.g. `Tensor.apply_()` is CPU-only), so the class is classified as `HardwareClassification.CPU`.

## Modification

- Import `HardwareClassification` from `torch.testing._internal.common_utils`.
- Add `hw_classification = HardwareClassification.CPU` to `TestNonUniformObserver`.
- Keep all test methods, inputs, expected values, assertions, and the `unittest`-based execution entry unchanged.

## Self-test

Environment:

- Windows, Python 3.14.3
- PyTorch 2.12.0+cpu
- No CUDA-capable GPU is available locally.

The installed wheel predates the `HardwareClassification` API and does not package the experimental quantization namespace, so a local-only pytest plugin registers the classification API and the checkout's pure-Python `torch/ao/quantization/experimental` package before collection; the compiled PyTorch runtime remained the official wheel. Tests were run from outside the checkout so the unbuilt `torch/` source directory does not shadow the installed wheel.

Commands (the plugin only shims the missing wheel APIs before forwarding to pytest):

```bash
python -m pytest -p hw_class_compat --rootdir <checkout> --collect-only -q test/quantization/core/experimental/test_linear.py
python -m pytest -p hw_class_compat --rootdir <checkout> -vv -ra test/quantization/core/experimental/test_linear.py
python -m pytest -p hw_class_compat --rootdir <checkout> -vv -ra test/quantization/core/experimental/test_linear.py --hw-classification CPU
```

CUDA is not run locally because no CUDA-capable GPU is available; CUDA validation is left to the upstream CI.

## Risks

Low. This change only adds test metadata; it does not modify test logic, device placement, or the collected test set.

author: egeboy35
message:
Fix the unbacked guard in linalg_cross's meta length-3 check (#195767)

`linalg_cross`'s meta kernel checks the length-3 requirement with a single `torch._check` and an `and`:

```python
torch._check(
    self.size(dim) == 3 and other.size(dim) == 3,
    lambda: (...),
)
```

Python's `and` has to decide the truthiness of its left operand, so it calls `bool()` on the first `SymBool`. On an unbacked size that is a guard, and tracing fails instead of recording the constraint:

```python
def fn(x):
    nz = x.nonzero()
    a = torch.ones(4, nz.size(0))   # last dim unbacked
    return torch.linalg.cross(a, a)

torch.compile(fn, fullgraph=True)(torch.tensor([1, 0, 1, 1]))
```

```
torch.fx.experimental.symbolic_shapes.GuardOnDataDependentSymNode:
Could not guard on data-dependent expression Eq(u0, 3) (unhinted: Eq(u0, 3))
```

`sym_and` combines the two without the bool cast. It is what the rest of the file already reaches for on compound conditions - `_padding_check_valid_input` and the pooling checks both do this.

### Only the left operand is the problem

`a and b` evaluates `bool(a)` and, if truthy, returns `b` untouched. So a symbolic *right* operand is fine, and the many `x.dim() == n and <symbolic>` checks in this file are correct as written. I measured each shape rather than assuming:

| written as | result |
|---|---|
| `a_sym and b` | guard error |
| `plain and a_sym` | traces cleanly |
| `a_sym` alone | recorded as a deferred runtime assert |
| `all(<symbolic> ...)` | guard error |
| `a_sym or b` | guard error |

I swept `_meta_registrations.py` for `torch._check` conditions combining `and`/`or` over `size`/`shape`, and 18 sites matched textually - but on this rule most are safe, and of the ones that are not, only `linalg_cross` turned out to be reachable in a way I could actually trigger. I am only claiming the one I can demonstrate.

One adjacent finding, offered as information rather than as part of this PR: `meta_upsample_bimode2d_aa` has the same shape (`input.numel() != 0 or all(size > 0 ...)`, symbolic on the left). Rewriting it does remove that guard, but the op still cannot trace with an unbacked channel dim because `utils.suggest_memory_format` then guards on `u0 > 1`. That is a much deeper change, so I left the op alone rather than ship a hunk whose benefit I could not show.

### Test plan

New regression in `test/inductor/test_unbacked_symints.py`, which makes the **last** dim unbacked.

```
python -m pytest test/inductor/test_unbacked_symints.py -k linalg_cross
```

before: `Could not guard on data-dependent expression Eq(u0, 3)`
after: `1 passed`

The unbacked OpInfo tests already reach this guard: `test/test_ops_unbacked.py`
and its DTensor variant mark every dim of size >= 2 unbacked, the length-3 one
included. `linalg.cross` sat in `ops_dde_xfail` for exactly this failure, so it
never showed; with the fix CI reported both as unexpected successes, and the
second commit removes the entry. The DTensor test imports the same set.

```
python test/test_ops_unbacked.py -k test_unbacked_op_db_linalg_cross_cpu_float32
```

```
without the fix, entry present:   OK (expected failures=1)
with the fix, entry present:      FAILED (unexpected successes=1)   # what CI saw
with the fix, entry removed:      OK
```

The check still rejects a bad length in eager:

```
python -c "import torch; a = torch.ones(4, 5); torch.linalg.cross(a, a)"
```

```
RuntimeError: linalg.cross: inputs dimension -1 must have length 3. Got 5 and 5
```

Surrounding suites:

```
python -m pytest test/inductor/test_unbacked_symints.py
python -m pytest test/test_ops.py -k linalg_cross
python -m pytest test/test_meta.py -k cross
```

130 passed, 154 skipped, 8 xfailed

author: jansel
message:
[inductor] Use shape env in ExpandView reindexer for symbolic size-1 dims (#198774)

Fixes #198379

With dynamic=True, F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=1/300) followed by
F.pad(y, (1, 0)) and torch.gt(padded, y) produced wrong results. The
interpolate output has symbolic size TruncToInt(0.00333*ToFloat(s0)), which
fake tensor broadcasting has guarded == 1, but which is not the literal 1.

ExpandView decided broadcast dims inconsistently. _normalize_size and the
realized-input stride path in create() use the shape-env-aware
sizevars.is_size_one_or_false, so realized inputs got stride 0 correctly.
make_reindexer, the only path an unrealized Pointwise input takes, used the
structural check `actual[i] == 1`, which is False for the symbolic size. The
broadcast operand's index was therefore never zeroed, and the fused kernel
computed the second copy of y from the padded output's loop index instead
of index 0, reading source position 449 instead of 149.5. Static shapes were
unaffected because the size is literally 1 there.

The reindexer now computes broadcast dims once with the same predicate
create() uses, so the two can no longer disagree. Fixing this in the
ShapeEnv instead was considered and rejected: replacements are keyed by
symbol and Eq(TruncToInt(0.00333*s0), 1) cannot be solved for s0, so
sizevars.simplify can never turn the size into a literal 1. Storing the
broadcast decision as a field set in create() was also considered, but it
changes the dataclass constructor for no extra safety since the predicate
is monotonic. An audit of the other structural `== 1` size checks in ir.py
and lowering.py found none with the same failure mode; they index over the
source's own size or fall through to symbolic paths.

The new test also exposed a pre-existing bug in the Halide backend. The
fused kernel loads the input twice with different dimension shapes: once
through the interpolate gather at index h1*s53 + tmp[h0], and once at the
constant index h1*s53 + 149 that the broadcast copy of y now resolves to.
HalideKernel.install_dims reconciles the two by calling
sizevars.evaluate_max on the dimension sizes, but the gather's size s53
comes from halide_vars in graph-symbol form while the constant load's size
is the stride ks0 taken from the renamed index, and the shape env raises
"vr must not be None for symbol ks0" on the latter. install_dims now maps
kernel arg names back to graph symbols before asking the shape env.

Test Plan:

New test fails before the fix in every variant (CPU index-out-of-bounds
assert, GPU device-side assert, dynamic-shapes 1/4 mismatch) and passes
after:

```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor_dynamic_shapes.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor_codegen_dynamic_shapes.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k test_broadcast_symbolic_size_one_dynamic_shapes
```

Related slices, all passing:

```
python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k "expand or broadcast or interpolate or upsample or pad"
python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor_dynamic_shapes.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k "expand or broadcast or interpolate or upsample or pad"
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k "(expand or broadcast or interpolate or upsample or pad) and GPU"

```

The Halide variant failed on the first CI revision with the ks0 assertion
above and passes after the install_dims fix. The Halide wheel is not in the
dev env, so it was installed into a scratch directory:

```

PYTHONPATH=agent_space/halide_site python -m pytest test/inductor/test_halide.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -k "not GPU"

author: jansel
message:
[dynamo] Fix deque.remove raising deque.pop() TypeError under compile (#198716)

Fixes #198682

collections.deque.remove(x) always raised under torch.compile, even when x
was present. With fullgraph=True this was a hard Unsupported error; with the
default mode it graph-broke on every call; and inside try/except Exception
it silently took the except branch and returned a wrong result. Deque
subclasses were affected the same way. This regressed in #189429 when the
deque "remove" entry was pointed at the shared BaseListVariable.list_remove.

Root cause: list_remove found the index and then dispatched
self.call_method(tx, "pop", [idx], {}). Every tp_methods dispatch goes
through Method.__call__, which derives the arity flags from the CPython
type's PyMethodDef ml_flags and checks them before running the handler.
deque.pop is METH_NOARGS, so passing an index raised
"TypeError: deque.pop() takes no arguments (1 given)" before
DequeVariable.pop ever ran. CPython's list_remove and deque_remove never
call the Python-visible pop (they use list_ass_slice and deque_del_item),
so the coupling itself was the bug. The same coupling also made
list.remove reuse index's not-found text, so [1].remove(9) under compile
raised "9 is not in list" where CPython raises
"list.remove(x): x not in list".

Fix: list_remove now searches, records the mutation, and deletes in place;
it never calls pop. The search body of list_index is extracted into
_index_or_raise, which takes the not-found message, so index and remove
each raise their own CPython text through the existing constant fast path
and polyfills.index fallback. DequeVariable overrides the remove message
with the same sys.version_info >= (3, 14) split used for index (CPython
changed both texts in 3.14) and adds a thin remove wrapper that bumps
self.state so live deque iterators raise "deque mutated during iteration",
following the existing pop/clear/insert wrappers.

The issue proposed a standalone deque-only remove. That would leave list's
remove coupled to pop and duplicate the search logic, so the shared base
handler was fixed instead. One known deviation remains: when a user
__eq__ mutates the deque mid-search, CPython raises IndexError while
Dynamo raises RuntimeError with the same message via the deque iterator.
Modeling that would require DequeVariable.remove to own its own search
loop, which is not worth it for that case.

Test Plan:

New RemoveTests class in test/dynamo/test_list.py comparing fullgraph
compiled output to eager for present and duplicate items, an input deque
whose mutation must be replayed, missing items on the constant and
polyfill paths, tensor items, a deque subclass, live iterator
invalidation, maxlen, wrong arity, and the list not-found message. With
the lists.py hunk reverse-applied, 8 of the 11 new tests fail.

```
python agent_space/repro_198682.py
python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_list.py -q
python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_iterators.py -q

message:
[FSDP2] Add gradient accumulation finalization API (#196640)

Add a public FSDPModule method, `finalize_gradient_accumulation`, that completes deferred gradient reduction on the caller thread. It reshards parameters and reduces the accumulated gradients into sharded `.grad`.

The autograd final callback runs on the autograd thread, so its stream waits cannot be captured in a CUDA graph. Reuse its cleanup on the caller thread, but track deferred reduction explicitly so finalization does not rerun post-backward or reduce zero gradients after a synchronized backward. Temporarily override gradient synchronization, all-reduce, reshard, and last-backward settings, then restore them.

A separate callback would duplicate iteration cleanup. The deferred-work flag keeps one cleanup path while gating the reduction. HSDP all-reduce-only deferral requires a separate collective and gradient view-out path, so reject it explicitly instead of silently skipping gradients.

author: TANGBUDU
message:
[inductor] Don't reinplace index_put when indices or values share storage with the input (#198637)

## Issue

Fixes #198567

## Summary

The reinplace pass turns `index_put(x, [idx], val)` into `index_put_` when `x` isn't used afterwards, but it doesn't check whether `idx` or `val` read `x`'s storage themselves. For `torch.put(r, r, r, accumulate=True)` the kernel then reads indices and values from the buffer it is writing to: the result is wrong on CPU, and on CUDA aten's overlap check raises. This adds `should_reinplace_index_put` as the `extra_check` for `index_put` / `_unsafe_index_put`, the same kind of check #198010 added for scatter. #198260 handles `auto_functionalized` ops and user Triton kernels and doesn't fix this case on its own. The check compares storages, so disjoint slices of the same buffer also stay functional, which is conservative.

Tests: a graph-level test on `reinplace_inplaceable_ops_core` (`index_put` / `_unsafe_index_put` x aliased indices / values that are a view of the input / no aliasing as the control), and an end-to-end test on `device`. On CPU the aliased graph-level cases fail before and pass after. On a T4 (nightly 20260924, cu130), `test_inplacing_pass.py` goes from 5 failed / 31 passed to 36 passed, and the index_put / scatter / reinplace tests in `test_torchinductor.py` are unchanged (45 passed, 4 skipped).

## Checklist

- [x] Passes lint (`spin fixlint`)
- [x] Added/updated tests
- [ ] Updated documentation (if applicable)
- [ ] Included benchmark results (for PRs impacting perf)

## BC-breaking?

No

author: alepot55
message:
[inductor] Count reads of an earlier mutation of the buffer in fusable_weak_dep (#198325)

Fixes #198270

`fusable_weak_dep` decides whether a reader of a buffer may be fused with a later mutation of it by comparing the reader's reads of `mutation_real_name[mutating_buf]` with the mutation's write. A read of an earlier mutation of the same buffer has another name (after `x.index_put_(...)`, reads of x go through the index_put_ output), so it wasn't counted: the check found no reads, skipped the same-index comparison and allowed the fusion. `x.index_put_(...); x.add_(x.flip(0))` then compiles to one kernel that reads x flipped while writing it.

This resolves each read through `mutation_real_name` before comparing.

Test plan: `test_inplace_flip_after_index_put` in test_torchinductor.py, which fails on CPU without the change. On 2.14 with CUDA (RTX 4070), with the change and without: test_torchinductor.py GPUTests on mutation, indexing, copies and views (341), test_inductor_scheduler.py, test_loop_ordering.py, test_cuda_repro.py, test_inplacing_pass.py, test_foreach.py and test_compiled_optimizers.py, with no new failure.

Metal reports command buffer execution failures (such as `MTLCommandBufferErrorOutOfMemory` when the resources referenced by a single command buffer exceed `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize`) only asynchronously, via `MTLCommandBuffer.status`/`.error` once it completes. When that happens, the whole command buffer is skipped and none of its outputs are written. `MPSStream` never inspected either field, so such failures were silent: `synchronize()` returned normally, and `.cpu()` returned whatever the freshly allocated output buffers contained (all zeros in the repro from the issue).

No unit test is added, as triggering this requires allocating more than the device's recommended working set size, which is not feasible in CI.

[ROCm] Remove -amdgpu-early-inline-all / -amdgpu-function-calls from CK SDPA build and Inductor CK builds (#195023)

**Summary:**
Removes the `-mllvm -amdgpu-early-inline-all=true` and `-mllvm -amdgpu-function-calls=false` flags from the two places that build Composable Kernel (CK) code on ROCm:
- `aten/src/ATen/CMakeLists.txt` — the `ck_sdpa` static library (`CK_SDPA_EXTRA_HIPCC_FLAGS`), built when `USE_ROCM_CK_SDPA` is on.

author: xinyazhang
message:
[ROCm][Windows] Patch AOTriton cdiv to fix clang-cl dllimport error (#198906)

ROCm Windows builds of PyTorch have failed since #197747 bumped `__AOTRITON_CI_COMMIT` to AOTriton `c11b5b88` (0.14.2b). That commit includes ROCm/aotriton#244, which makes `AOTRITON_API` expand to `__declspec(dllimport)` for consumers on Windows. `aotriton/util.h` applies `AOTRITON_API` to `cdiv`, a function template defined in the header, and clang-cl rejects dllimport on a non-inline function definition:

```
FAILED: caffe2/CMakeFiles/torch_hip.dir/__/aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/hip/sdp_utils.cpp.obj
torch/include\aotriton\util.h(41,1): error: dllimport cannot be applied to non-inline function definition
```

Only Windows is affected. It is the one platform that builds the AOTriton runtime from source at `__AOTRITON_CI_COMMIT`; Linux downloads prebuilt runtimes, and there `AOTRITON_API` is a visibility attribute. The failure was caught by TheRock's Windows nightly (ROCm/TheRock#8564). A ROCm Windows build job in pytorch/pytorch CI would have caught it on #197747 itself.

Fix: `cmake/External/aotriton-win32/` holds a patch that drops `AOTRITON_API` from `cdiv`, and on WIN32 `aotriton_build_from_source` applies it as the ExternalProject `PATCH_COMMAND` (`git checkout -- .` then `git apply`, so re-running the step is safe). This is a stopgap. Once the equivalent fix lands in ROCm/aotriton, bump `__AOTRITON_CI_COMMIT` past it and delete the patch directory.

Test plan: Windows build validation using TheRock.  See https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock/actions/runs/36458839016/job/109051989544 for the successful Windows build.

author: guilhermeleobas
message:
Remove `_base_vt` (#193679)

Consider the following example:

```python
class MyList(list):
    def append(self, item):
        super().append(item)
```

Dynamo represented this inheritance by storing a `_base_vt` object on `UserDefinedObjectVariable` (UDOV), pointing to a `ListVariable`. This composition-based approach had limitations:

* Storage lived in a separate location (`_base_vt`), while dispatch logic remained on the UDOV itself.
* The `_base_vt` object was unaware it was serving as the base for a user-defined object, which broke identity/equality semantics in edge cases like:

```python
>>> class F(frozenset): ...
>>> f = F()
>>> id(f) == id(f.copy())
False
>>> h = frozenset()
>>> id(h) == id(h.copy())
True
```

Because the underlying `_base_vt` had no notion of being wrapped by a user-defined object, Dynamo's `.copy()` incorrectly returned the same identity in both cases.

Rather than composition, this PR uses inheritance to directly extend the behavior of the base type. The VT inheritance for a class `class MyList(list)` is `UserDefinedList` -> `UserDefinedObjectVariable` -> `ListVariable` -> `VariableTracker`. The reason for this choice is:

* `UserDefinedObjectVariable` is the `PyHeapType` and knows how to redirect any custom method calls to the appropriate user-defined implementations.
* `ListVariable` contains the builtin behavior for a list type.
* Inheritance gives a single MRO instead of two separate objects, so `isinstance` checks and attribute/method lookup fall through naturally to the builtin behavior without needing a separate `_base_vt` redirect.

Each commit in this stack migrates a specific user-defined object from composition to inheritance, but only the top commit ([#193679](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/193679)) is relevant for CI. Before merging, I'll squash everything into a single commit.

author: weifengpy
message:
[FSDP2] Keep the reduce-scatter output alive for the all-reduce hook (#198804)

> Authored with Claude Code.
>
> With 1-D FSDP and set_all_reduce_hook, foreach_reduce runs the hook on the all-reduce stream, or on the stream passed to set_all_reduce_hook, and then runs the post-reduce division, the cast to orig_dtype and the gradient view-out on that stream too. The reduce-scatter output they read is allocated on the reduce-scatter stream, and without native HSDP nothing holds it: all_reduce_input stays None, so post_backward never sets _all_reduce_state. When reduce_dtype != orig_dtype, the cast rebinds reduce_output and drops the last reference to the reduce-dtype buffer; when the gradient is added into an existing one or offloaded to CPU, the last reference goes away when foreach_reduce returns. The caching allocator then gives the block to the next group's reduce-scatter output, and that reduce-scatter only waits on the compute stream, not on the hook stream. If the hook is still running, e.g. a custom all-reduce over a slower network, the next reduce-scatter overwrites the buffer before the hook and the cast read it, and the group that reduced first silently gets the next group's gradients. #140044 fixed the same race for native HSDP by holding the all-reduce buffer in _all_reduce_state; without native HSDP, the hook path never set it.
>
> After the hook, foreach_reduce now returns the reduce-scatter output as all_reduce_input, with an event recorded on the hook stream, so post_backward holds it in _all_reduce_state like native HSDP's all-reduce buffer. _wait_for_post_backward, finalize_backward and _reset_iter_state drop it only after the current stream waits on a post-reduce event that the hook stream records after the group's hook, cast and view-out. The next reduce-scatter allocates its output after reduce_scatter_stream.wait_stream(current_stream), so reusing the block is ordered after the hook stream is done with it. With native HSDP and a hook, all_reduce_input was already this tensor, and only its event moves from after the all-reduce to after the hook. That event is only waited on together with the later post-reduce event, so native HSDP behaves as before.
>
> The cost is memory: with a hook, each group's reduce-scatter output stays allocated until finalize_backward, or the group's next post-backward, as native HSDP's all-reduce buffer already does. That only adds memory when the sharded gradients aren't views into it: when reduce_dtype != orig_dtype, when adding into existing gradients, or with CPU offloading. Calling record_stream for the hook stream would free it sooner, but FSDP2 avoids record_stream, since the allocator then reuses the block only once it sees the hook stream's work finish, which makes memory use depend on CPU/GPU timing. Having the next reduce-scatter wait on the hook stream would avoid holding the buffer, but would serialize every reduce-scatter behind the previous group's hook and lose the overlap the separate stream exists for.
>
> Test Plan
>
> test_all_reduce_hook_buffer_lifetime_mixed_dtype in test_fully_shard_memory.py shards two Linear(512, 512) layers with 1-D FSDP, FP32 parameters and BF16 param and reduce dtypes. It runs a backward without a hook as the reference, then one where each layer's hook sleeps for 200 ms on the hook stream, and compares the gradients.
>
> On two H100s, the new test passes, and with the torch/ changes reverted it fails on both ranks: the second linear's gradient differs from the reference in more than 99.9% of its elements, while the first linear's matches. TestHSDPWithCustomHook in test_fully_shard_init.py passes (2 tests), and lint passes. The four-GPU test_ar_buffer_lifetime_mixed_dtype, the rest of test_fully_shard_memory.py and the other FSDP test files haven't been run.

> CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=6,7 /home/weif/.conda/envs/code-review/bin/python test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_memory.py -k test_all_reduce_hook_buffer_lifetime_mixed_dtype
> CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=6,7 /home/weif/.conda/envs/code-review/bin/python -m pytest test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_init.py -k TestHSDPWithCustomHook -q -rfs

message:
[ROCm][UT] Fix runOnRocmArch used in boolean context in test_cublas_baddbmm_large_input (#196314)

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/196572

## Summary

`runOnRocmArch()` is a decorator factory. It returns a function, which is
always truthy. In `test_cublas_baddbmm_large_input`:

```python
if runOnRocmArch(MI200_ARCH) and dtype == torch.float16:
```

The arch check is discarded and the condition reduces to
`dtype == torch.float16`. The relaxed MI200 tolerance was therefore applied on
every platform, including CUDA, and the strict `else` branch was unreachable
for fp16.

Use `TEST_WITH_ROCM` and `isRocmArchAnyOf(MI200_ARCH)`, the form already used in
this file for the Navi guard in `test_cublas_addmm`.

Scope of the behaviour change is narrow: `_DTYPE_PRECISIONS[torch.float16]` is
`(0.001, 1e-5)`, so both code paths use `rtol=1e-3` and the only difference is
atol, `1e-4` -> `1e-5`. MI200 is unaffected: it takes the relaxed path before
and after. Non-MI200 ROCm and NVIDIA fp16 move to the default atol.

Part of https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/196583.

The identity matmul under test (linear and baddbmm) is bitwise
exact, `max_abs = max_rel = 0.0`, on gfx1100 and gfx1200 for
`N in {100, 1000, 10000}` across fp16/bf16/fp32, so the tightened atol has
ample headroom on RDNA. `test_matmul_cuda` passes 12/12 on both GPUs.

author: albmalamd
message:
[ROCm] Make test_ddp_apply_optim_in_backward deterministic for BLAS (#198643)

`test_ddp_apply_optim_in_backward` and
`test_ddp_apply_optim_in_backward_grad_as_bucket_view_false` fail on gfx908 (MI100) with "Params not equal at iteration 3" (~1e-5 abs diff).

## Root cause:

The test compares a DDP model with a regular optimizer against a DDP model with the optimizer applied in backward, using default tolerances. The training loop rapidly amplifies numerical differences, so it only passes if both replicas compute bitwise-identical results. The test enabled determinism for cuDNN only. On gfx908, GEMMs use rocBLAS by default, and getCurrentCUDABlasHandle() sets HIPBLAS_ATOMICS_ALLOWED unless torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) is on. With atomics, fp32 GEMMs with K=1024 are not run-to-run reproducible, and the ~1e-7 noise at iteration 0 grows past atol by iteration 3. Two identical regular-optimizer replicas diverge by the same amount, so DDP / optim-in-backward is not at fault. cudnn.flags(deterministic=True) does not help because it only affects convolutions.

## Fix:

Run the training loop under DeterministicGuard(True) next to the existing cuDNN flags. Use strict determinism for the linear reproducers and warn-only for the optional ResNet50 model because AdaptiveAvgPool2d backward has no deterministic implementation. Tolerances are unchanged, and deterministic rocBLAS disables atomics so the replicas match bitwise. CUDA already provides a separate cuBLAS workspace per handle and stream, so it does not require CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG.

Changing the rocBLAS atomics default was rejected because it would cost GEMM performance globally, while determinism is opt-in via use_deterministic_algorithms by design.

## Test Plan:

On 2x MI100 (gfx908):

```
export PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_ROCM=1 BACKEND=nccl WORLD_SIZE=2 TEMP_DIR=/tmp/dist_barrier
mkdir -p $TEMP_DIR && touch $TEMP_DIR/barrier
cd test
python3 distributed/test_distributed_spawn.py \
  TestDistBackendWithSpawn.test_ddp_apply_optim_in_backward \
  TestDistBackendWithSpawn.test_ddp_apply_optim_in_backward_grad_as_bucket_view_false \
  TestDistBackendWithSpawn.test_ddp_apply_optim_in_backward_ignored_params -v
```

Before: FAILED (errors=2), mismatches at iterations 3-4.
After: OK, 3/3 runs. Also OK on 2x MI210 (gfx90a, ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1,3).

author: neevmodh
message:
Reject a bare set of params, consistent with set inside a param group (#198710)

## Summary
- `Optimizer.__init__` converts `params` via `list(params)` before checking whether the first element is a dict, so a bare set passed as `params` (e.g. `torch.optim.Adam(set(model.parameters()))`) is silently accepted, even though the exact same unordered set of tensors is correctly rejected when passed inside a param group (`torch.optim.Adam([{"params": set(model.parameters())}])`).
- The existing `add_param_group` check for `isinstance(params, set)` never sees the set type in the bare-params case, since it's already been converted to a list at the top level by the time `add_param_group` runs.
- Since optimizer state is matched to parameters positionally, an unordered bare-set input is exactly as unsafe as an unordered set inside a param group, and should be rejected the same way — before conversion to a list silently erases that information.

- [x] Added an `ErrorOptimizerInput` entry to `get_error_inputs_for_all_optims` in `common_optimizers.py`, so `test_errors` in `test_optim.py` exercises this for every registered optimizer.
- [x] Manually verified against the exact repro in the issue (torch 2.14.0): bare set is now rejected with the same message as a set inside a param group; normal list/dict usage is unaffected.

author: jansel
message:
[inductor] Wildcard symbolic size-list entries in retraced patterns (#198320)

The HUD compilers dashboard lost ~20% speedup and gained 3-5 s of compile
time on every BERT-family HuggingFace model under the cudagraphs_dynamic
config after #195383 relanded (9b6e45278f). Static configs and non-BERT
models were flat.

#195383 validates every pattern-matcher match by re-tracing search_fn
with the matched inputs and matching the resulting specific pattern,
built with fx_to_pattern(match_node_meta=True). In that mode size lists
are wildcarded elementwise and the op's output shape is pinned by an
expected_meta check instead, but _wildcard_size_list kept PatternExpr
entries literal. Under a symbolic batch, matmul's decomposition reshapes
q/k to [s0*heads, seq, head_dim], so the re-traced _sfdp_pattern_29
contains a sym-expr node CallFunction(operator.mul, KeywordArg('arg0_1'),
12, _users=4) inside its view size lists and matches it structurally,
users count included. The user graph has a single mul(arg, 12) sym node
shared by the views of all 12 layers, so the specific match failed with
"multiple_users" for every layer, SDPA fusion was silently dropped, and
the unfused softmax kernels cost the extra compile time. Static shapes
never produce such a node, which is why only the dynamic config moved.

_wildcard_size_list now also receives the raw fx size-list args and
requires every entry (an int, or a sym node's meta["val"]) to be -1 or
statically equal to the traced output dim, the rule already applied to
ints. When that holds the whole list is wildcarded, sym nodes included;
expected_meta still pins the output shape, so a mismatched size is
still rejected and the wrong-output cases #195383 fixed stay fixed. The
alternative of relaxing the users check on sym nodes would still match
their spelling (mul vs sym_size chains) and was not pursued. The sym
KeywordArg bindings the dropped nodes provided are not needed: check_fn
unflattens only the static argnames and re-traces the replacement from
the fake args. The fix is scoped to size lists: a shared sym node used as
a scalar SymInt argument (slice bounds, say) or in a stride list would
still be matched structurally, but no registered pattern does that.

Test Plan:

New regression test with two attention layers sharing the batch dim, run
in inference and training so both the fwd_only and joint_fwd_bwd
re-traces are covered; the dynamic variants fail before the fix with no

author: nWEIdia
message:
[c10d][nccl2] Make ranks 1/2 abort in test_work_reports_communicator_error (#198318)

## Summary

`test_work_reports_communicator_error` deterministically hung for ~300s: rank 0 deliberately aborts its communicator to simulate a fault, while ranks 1 and 2 just slept and fell through to `tearDown()`'s ordinary `destroy_process_group()`.

`ncclCommRevoke()`/`ncclCommAbort()` are local operations -- NCCL does not notify peer ranks. So ranks 1 and 2 ended up in an inconsistent state with rank 0: NCCL's `ncclCommDestroy()` barrier waits for every rank to enter destroy, but rank 0 already exited via abort and never will, leaving ranks 1 and 2 spinning until the test harness's timeout.

## Fix

Ranks 1 and 2 now also call `self.backend.abort()`, so all three ranks take the same (abort) path instead of a mismatched abort/destroy combination.

## Test plan

Reproduced the hang pre-fix and confirmed the fix resolves it on real multi-GPU hardware with RDMA:
- Pre-fix: test still hanging past 40s (expected ~300s hang).
- Post-fix: `test_work_reports_communicator_error` completes in ~13s and passes, with ranks 1 and 2 observed taking the abort path.
- Full `Nccl2FaultToleranceTest` suite (16 tests) run with the fix applied: all pass, no regressions (`Ran 16 tests in 237.109s, OK`).

author: kvshbg-aws
message:
[FSDP2] Record the consumer stream on the reduce-scatter output when a backend frees eagerly (#193686)

**Problem -**

In `foreach_reduce`, `reduce_output` is allocated inside `with device_handle.stream(reduce_scatter_stream)` and becomes the sharded gradient. That gradient is consumed on the caller's stream (optimizer / gradient accumulation), so the buffer is produced on one stream and read on another causing a potention memory hazard, since, `foreach_reduce` does not record the consumer stream on it.

**Why a backend would see use-after-free hazard?**

Backends that allow the user code to allocate and free/dealloc the buffer across multiple streams for efficient and better memory management and as `reduce_output` is produced on the reduce-scatter stream whereas its consumed on the caller's stream; it leads to deallocs getting scheduled and executed (on streamA) before the read/consumption finishes (on streamB) and hence we need to explicitly call `record_stream` on such tensors to mark the edge between the reads & frees.

Furthermore, some backends may have the `free`/dealloc op execution wherein they actually releases device memory (unlike for some backends where it stays mapped) and hence it becomes imperative to have the tensor recorded on a buffer that is used across streams. Using, `record_stream` is the standard primitive for that read-before-free edge ([ref](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.13/generated/torch.Tensor.record_stream.html)).

_(NOTE - The implementation of `record_stream` on such backends should guarantee FIFO ordering within streams, so that it is the most optimized way of expressing the tensor as being used by a consumer stream; this will force implicitly help keep the dealloc/free submitted right after the read completes on the same stream. Tightening it further would mean explicit event record/wait around the free, which can lead to negative perf implications hence `record_stream` is used)_

**Why upstream does not see this hazard?**

On upstream this is not a problem since the caching allocator's free is host-side bookkeeping, and the storage stays mapped and the only thing to guard is reuse by a later allocation, which the allocator handles by stream and is guaranteed by the FSDPv2 code implementation.

This PR proposes the following change that records the consumer stream on `reduce_output` **after the `orig_dtype` cast** -- so it also covers mixed precision, where `reduce_dtype != orig_dtype` and the sharded gradient aliases the post-cast buffer -- gated on a backend-advertised capability so it is a no-op for backends that don't set it -

```python
with device_handle.stream(post_reduce_stream):
    _div_if_needed(reduce_output, postdivide_factor)
    # When reduce_dtype != orig_dtype this rebinds reduce_output to a NEW
    # orig_dtype tensor; the sharded gradient (as_strided below) aliases THIS
    # post-cast buffer, so the consumer stream must be recorded here -- recording
    # the pre-cast reduce_dtype buffer would miss it under mixed precision.
    reduce_output = _to_dtype_if_needed(reduce_output, orig_dtype)
    if getattr(device_handle, "_needs_record_stream_on_free", False):
        reduce_output.record_stream(current_stream)
    # View out and accumulate sharded gradients
    ...
```

## Test

`TestFullyShardReduceScatterRecordStream` (multi-process `FSDPTest`) in `test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_comm.py` runs a real `fully_shard` backward and spies on `Tensor.record_stream`. No in-tree backend sets the flag, so it patches the capability on the device module and parametrizes over `{needs_record_stream: [True, False]} x {mixed_precision: [False, True]}`:
- with the flag set, it asserts `record_stream` fires on the reduce-scatter output that backs the sharded gradient -- the **post-cast** buffer (`orig_dtype`: `bfloat16` under mixed precision, not the `float32` reduce_dtype buffer);
- with the flag unset, it asserts `record_stream` is never called (no-op).

import statistics, time, torch

sync = torch.mps.synchronize

def cpu_median_ms(fn, warmup, iters):
    for _ in range(warmup): fn()
    times = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); fn(); times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return statistics.median(times) * 1e3

def mps_pipelined_ms(fn, warmup, iters, warm_seconds=0.5):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    while time.perf_counter() - t0 < warm_seconds:
        for _ in range(warmup): fn()
        sync()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(iters): fn()

    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / iters * 1e3

        cpu_ms = cpu_median_ms(lambda: torch.linalg.inv_ex(a_cpu, check_errors=False), warmup, iters)
        mps_ms = mps_pipelined_ms(lambda: torch.linalg.inv_ex(a_mps, check_errors=False), warmup, iters)
        digits = 4 if cpu_ms < 0.1 else 3
        print(f"| {batch}x{n}x{n} | {cpu_ms:.{digits}f} | {mps_ms:.{digits}f} | {cpu_ms / mps_ms:.1f}x |", flush=True)

author: weifengpy
message:
[FSDP2] Document that modifying parameters between forward and backward is unsupported (#198826)

This PR was authored with an AI assistant (Claude Code). The description below is AI-generated and is pending author review.

> The `reshard_after_forward` docstring said the parameters may be modified between forward and backward as long as the sharded parameters are registered. The stream ordering does not support this. A write to the sharded parameters between forward and backward runs on the current stream, but the backward all-gather copy-in runs on `all_gather_copy_in_stream` in `PRE_BACKWARD`, and that stream is last ordered after the current stream at the root post-forward (its wait on the last copy-out event). Nothing orders it after later current-stream work, so the backward copy-in can read the old values. Backward prefetches have the same gap. Forward does not, because `_root_pre_forward` makes both all-gather streams `wait_stream(current_stream)`.
>
> Two options: (1) support it by making both all-gather streams `wait_stream(current_stream)` once per backward, before any backward all-gather, or (2) document it as unsupported. This PR takes (2). Option (1) prevents the first backward all-gather from overlapping the forward tail. On 8xH100 with an 8-layer bf16 Transformer, it measured +0.3% to +0.5% step time when the last block reshards after forward and within noise otherwise. The docstring now states that modifying parameters between forward and backward is not supported, and a TODO at the once-per-backward point in `FSDPState._register_root_post_backward_final_callback` records how to add support later.
>
> Test Plan

> ```bash
> lintrunner -a torch/distributed/fsdp/_fully_shard/_fully_shard.py torch/distributed/fsdp/_fully_shard/_fsdp_state.py

> The perf numbers for option (1) came from an A/B benchmark that monkey-patches the wait into `_register_root_post_backward_final_callback` and interleaves 10-iteration blocks with and without it in one process:

message:
[OSDC] Remove map_ec2_to_arc.py (#198706)

With every workflow naming its pod, the mapper has nothing left to translate.
Its other behaviours are gone too: the ROCm and XPU passthroughs return their
input unchanged, and the H100 `mt-` forcing is now literal in the workflows.

One behaviour does disappear with it. The script dropped `config: "onnx"` from
every ARC matrix, so that job has not run since the ARC switch. The entry is
removed outright here rather than left behind commented out, and the reason it
is gone -- onnxruntime sizes its intra-op thread pool from
`hardware_concurrency()`, which reads `_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN` and counts the
node rather than the pod's cpuset -- is recorded in #198915, which fixes that
and restores the entry.

An earlier version of this change did leave a commented-out entry with a prose
comment above it, and that is what got it reverted. A test-matrix is a literal
block scalar, interpolated verbatim into a double-quoted shell argument:

    --test-matrix "{ include: [ ... ]}"

Every `"` inside toggles shell quoting. The live entries survive because their
quotes wrap tokens with no spaces, so the fragments re-concatenate into one
argument; the comment contained a quoted phrase with a space in it, the shell
split there, and filter_test_configs.py got a stray argument:

    error: unrecognized arguments: failed in a 24k-line log, and a

Letting onnx run first was still worth it, because it found a second reason it
could not have passed. The OSDC pod exports `HF_HOME=/mnt/hf_cache`, the
read-only mount, and .ci/pytorch/test.sh is what redirects it to the writable
`HF_CACHE` the workflow prepares -- except it skipped onnx, a carve-out from
#178928 when the old .ci/onnx/test.sh (which never set HF_HOME) was folded in.
On EC2 that was harmless, since HF_HOME was unset and huggingface fell back to
a writable home; on a pod onnx alone writes to the read-only mount and dies on
`[Errno 30]`. That carve-out is dropped: it is wrong for any config.

arc.yaml stays: it documents the naming scheme and the EC2 correspondence,
which is still worth having as reference.

author: bobrenjc93
message:
[dynamo] Lower the backward eagerly under the multi-graph capture config (#198215)

**Problem.** `_capture_config` only forced the backward to lower eagerly for `training=True`, but AOTAutograd does not save a grad-enabled graph to the bundled cache until its backward has been lowered, so an ordinary inference capture made outside `torch.no_grad()` compiled fine and then had nothing to put in the artifact.

**Fix.** Set `force_non_lazy_backward_lowering` unconditionally in the capture config and drop the `training` parameter it used to gate on.

**Summary.** `_capture_config(training)` added `force_non_lazy_backward_lowering` to its functorch patch only when `training=True`, leaving inference captures with AOTAutograd's default of lowering a graph's backward lazily on the first `.backward()`. The cache entry the bundled artifact is built from is saved only once the backward has been lowered, so a graph compiled with grad enabled whose backward was never lowered records no backend at all -- and that is the ordinary inference case, a capture made outside `torch.no_grad()` on a model whose parameters require grad. The flag is now set unconditionally, so a graph compiled with grad enabled carries its backward into the artifact, and a call served under that grad mode returns outputs with a `grad_fn` as eager does. A call made under `torch.no_grad()` still compiles an inference graph, because the flag only changes when a backward that AOTAutograd would build anyway gets lowered, not whether one exists. With nothing left for it to select, the `training` parameter goes, and the two `_capture_config` tests pin the unconditional flag and its scoping.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR is plumbing for the multi-call `DynamoTracer` capture (#198138): the capture config always lowers the backward eagerly, so a grad-enabled call records its artifact.

## The patch dict, before and after

The parent built the functorch patch and then appended the eager-lowering flag under a condition:

```python
# parent: torch/_dynamo/precompile_package.py
@contextlib.contextmanager
def _capture_config(training: bool) -> Iterator[None]:
    functorch_patch = {
        "bundled_autograd_cache": True,
        "bypass_autograd_cache_key": True,
    }
    if training:
        functorch_patch["force_non_lazy_backward_lowering"] = True
    ...
```

Now the flag is part of the dict itself and the parameter is gone:

```python
# now
@contextlib.contextmanager
def _capture_config() -> Iterator[None]:
    functorch_patch = {
        "bundled_autograd_cache": True,
        "force_non_lazy_backward_lowering": True,
        "bypass_autograd_cache_key": True,
    }
    ...
```

The rest of the scope is unchanged: `strict_autograd_cache` still follows `torch._dynamo.config.strict_precompile`, `allow_empty_graphs` is still patched on, and `force_disable_caches` still raises `PackageError` up front. The docstring now says why the backward lowers eagerly for every capture: a graph compiled with grad enabled whose backward was never lowered is never saved, so a capture that never makes one -- a training step, or an inference call made outside `torch.no_grad()` -- would record no backend at all.

## Why an inference capture was affected

AOTAutograd lowers a graph's backward lazily, on the first `.backward()`, and the bundled cache entry is saved only once that has happened. A capture that only runs forwards never triggers the lowering:

```python
model = torch.nn.Linear(4, 4)          # parameters require grad
with _capture_config(training=False):  # parent: no eager lowering
    compiled(model, x)                 # grad enabled -> joint graph, backward deferred
# parent: no .backward() ever ran, so the entry was never saved -> no backend in the artifact
# now:    the backward is lowered at compile time, the entry is saved, the artifact has a backend
```

Under `torch.no_grad()` there is no backward to lower, so that path compiles an inference graph exactly as before.

## Tests

Both `_capture_config` tests move to the parameterless call and pin the flag as unconditional. `test_capture_config_is_scoped_per_entry_and_per_thread` reads the four patched flags in order (`bundled_autograd_cache`, `bypass_autograd_cache_key`, `force_non_lazy_backward_lowering`, `allow_empty_graphs`) from an all-`False` ambient:

```python
# parent
with _capture_config(training=False):
    self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, False, True))
    with _capture_config(training=True):
        self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, True, True))
    self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, False, True))

# now
with _capture_config():
    self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, True, True))
    with _capture_config():
        self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, True, True))
    self.assertEqual(flags(), (True, True, True, True))
self.assertEqual(flags(), ambient)
```

The same test still checks that an exception inside the scope restores the ambient flags, and that a worker thread holding its own `_capture_config()` scope sees `(True, True, True, True)` while the main thread's flags are untouched. `test_capture_config_refuses_disabled_caches_and_honours_strict` keeps its `force_disable_caches` refusal and its `strict_precompile` -> `strict_autograd_cache` checks, now written as `with _capture_config():`.

Test Plan:

lintrunner -a torch/_dynamo/precompile_package.py test/dynamo/test_precompile_package.py
```
