message:
[rel-land] allow horizontal fusion of copies from dynamic inputs into concat operation (#195635) (#198294) (#198294)

Summary:

`ConcatKernel.create` drops any cat input with a symbolic size from the foreach operation
list, so `Scheduler.create_foreach_nodes` never groups the copies and each becomes its own
kernel launch. With static shapes the same op is one foreach kernel launch
(`triton_for_fused_*`).

The optimization for static shapes, is Not shape dependent ( there is no checks on sizes of inputs)
 hence there is no reason why not to enable it for dynamic shapes as well.

```python
# torch/_inductor/ir.py, ConcatKernel.create
and is_gpu(dev.type)
and not is_dynamic(input_buffer)      # <-- removed
```

The clause shipped in the original feature commit (`543dc757463a`, #111437, Oct 2023) with
no comment and no test. The other two producers of `register_operation_list`
(`foreach_group_loop`, `_foreach_map`) later gained an explicit dynamic-shapes escape hatch
via `config.combo_kernel_foreach_dynamic_shapes` (default `True`); this call site never got
the same update.

Found on a recsys job that moved from static batch 768 to variable batch size. One frame
stacked 299 tangents of `f32[768, 192]` in fwd and bwd: static emitted 3 foreach kernel
launches, dynamic emitted 299 — roughly **+590 kernel launches per iteration**, 589 of the
607 extra launches across the whole model.

Also removes the now-unused `is_dynamic` import (the other use in `ir.py` is a local in
`_pad_strides` that shadowed it).

## Numbers
[perf expirment done by AI]
`stack` of N x `f32[768, 192]`, H100, dynamic dim 0:

| N | launches before | launches after | ms before | ms after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 16 | 1 | 0.104 | 0.041 |
| 64 | 64 | 1 | 0.336 | 0.178 |
| 256 | 256 | 3 | 1.297 | 0.577 |

Benefit tapers with tensor size — 1.7x at 0.02 MiB/input down to 1.07x at 64 MiB, once each
copy saturates HBM. `N <= config.max_pointwise_cat_inputs` (8) is unaffected: no
`ConcatKernel` is built there.

<details>
<summary>Benchmark method</summary>

`torch.compile(lambda xs: torch.stack(xs, 0), fullgraph=True)` with `mark_dynamic(x, 0)` on
each input; launch counts from `run_and_get_code`, timing from CUDA events over 200 iters
after 50 warmup.

Run-to-run variance put the N=64 ratio at 2.4x-2.8x. The residual dynamic-vs-static gap
after the fix (~1.45x) is symbolic index arithmetic inside the kernel, not launch overhead.

```python
Benchmark for: restore foreach fusion for cat/stack under dynamic shapes.
Run once on unpatched torch and once with the ConcatKernel.create gate removed.
    python bench_cat_foreach.py            # table 1: launches + time vs N
    python bench_cat_foreach.py --sizes    # table 2: effect vs tensor size, N=12
"""
import re
import sys
import torch
import torch._dynamo
import torch._inductor.config as inductor_config
from torch._inductor.utils import run_and_get_code
# Without this the FX graph cache serves a prior compile and hides the difference.
inductor_config.force_disable_caches = True
def fn(xs):
    return torch.stack(xs, dim=0)
def measure(n, rows, cols, dynamic, iters=200, warmup=50):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    xs = [torch.randn(rows, cols, device="cuda") for _ in range(n)]
    if dynamic:
        for x in xs:
            torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(x, 0)
    compiled = torch.compile(fn, fullgraph=True)
    out, codes = run_and_get_code(compiled, xs)
    torch.testing.assert_close(out, fn(xs))
    call = re.search(r"^    def call\(self, args\):(.*?)(?=\Z)", codes[0], re.S | re.M)
    body = call.group(1) if call else codes[0]
    launches = len(re.findall(r"(triton_\w+)\.run\(", body))
    for _ in range(warmup):
        compiled(xs)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start, end = torch.cuda.Event(True), torch.cuda.Event(True)
    start.record()
    for _ in range(iters):

author: chen-jin021
message:
[fx] make update_deps_for_fusions linear in fusion group size (#198654) (#198654)

Summary:

`FxNetAccFusionsFinder` maps every member of a fusion group to the *same* set
object:

    for n in fusion_group.nodes:
        result[n] = fusion_group.nodes

So a group of size K has K entries in `self.fusions`, all pointing at one set.
`update_deps_for_fusions` then iterated per entry and, inside that, per member
again, doing K^2 set differences per group. It also unioned into `self.deps`
while reading from it, so each repeat operated on progressively larger sets.
The final result was unaffected (union is idempotent) but the work was redone
K times on growing data.

Process each group once instead, keyed by identity. O(sum K^2 * d) becomes
O(sum K * d).

Measured on an AOTI lowering of an ads ranking merge net: the enclosing
`lowering_graph_split` stage is 428 s on the shipped recipe and 1,246 s after a
quantization change that creates more and larger fusion groups. A `py-spy`
flamegraph over that stage put 91.75% of samples on the single line
`self.deps[node].update(self.deps[fused_neighbor] - fusion)` and 99.92% inside
this function.

Equivalence rests on one invariant worth stating: `FxNetAccFusionsFinder`
inserts a group's members contiguously into the result dict, so the old
per-entry loop was already effectively atomic per group. Reordering the work to
be explicitly per-group therefore cannot observe a partially-updated
neighbouring group.

previous per-member loop verbatim as a reference implementation and asserts both
produce the same dependency graph, then asserts the documented contract that
members of a fusion share their outer dependencies.

message:
[ROCm] Bump AOTriton to 0.14.2b (#197747)

Notable new features compared with 0.13b:

* New `flyc` backend: FlyDSL SDPA fp16/bf16 kernels for gfx950 and gfx1201, at
  parity with the Triton kernels and substantially faster on most head
  dimensions
  + See [AOTriton 0.14.2b Release Notes](https://github.com/ROCm/aotriton/releases/tag/0.14.2b)
    for measured performance improvments
* **API BREAKING, ABI STABLE** `VarlenBits` replaces the `VarlenType` enum
  + Q and K now choose their sequence addressing independently, along three
    axes: tensor shape, how lengths are given, and how offsets are given
  + 0.14b library keep working with applications built for 0.13b; only
    the source-level params struct changed
* Triton bumped to 3.8.0; tuning databases re-tuned for gfx950 and gfx1100
* ROCM 10 (HIP 7.16) support is added to the package list

Bug Fixes:

* `bwd_kernel_fuse` used `Out`'s strides for `dO`
* Causal masking wrote `+inf` LSE out of bounds
* Attention bias was not cast to fp32 before scaling with `ln(2)`
* `attn_fwd` persistent dynamic mode early exits on certain mask pattern
* Runtime: device is taken from the stream, and several entry points no
  longer assume GIL being hold.
* Triton bwd kenels now handle `scale <= 0` cases correctly.

PyTorch-side changes:

* `seqused_k` uses the `INDIVIDUAL` length + `ARRAY` position pairing the new
  API can express. The per-launch `cumsum` is no longer needed.
* Split `mk_aotensor` into `mk_input_aotensor`/`mk_output_aotensor` so
  read-only Q/K/V go through `const_data_ptr()`. `data_ptr()` aliases
  `mutable_data_ptr()`, which materialized lazily-cloned (COW) inputs
  + This enables `TestCompositeComplianceCUDA.test_cow_input`
* `USE_ASAN` branch is removed. ASAN support is being reworked.
  + Previous ASAN package was not built against ROCM ASAN.
* `test_mem_eff_attention_single_query_tail`* tests are disabled on gfx11
  + They require hdim = 256 which is unsupported by gfx11 right now

UT enablements (previously skipped on ROCm):

* `torch.ops.aten._efficient_attention_forward` OpInfo: dropped
  `skipCUDAIf(TEST_WITH_ROCM, "Efficient attention on ROCM doesn't support
  custom_mask_type==2")`.
  + The support is added in AOTriton >= 0.10 but not enabled

*Other changes are intentionally left out: they consist mainly of internal
refactoring that is not perceivable to pytorch users.*

message:
[CUDA] Expose SM partitions and disjoint green-context splitting (#198278)

> Authored with an AI assistant.

>

> a, b = GreenContext.split(
>     num_sms=(24, 40), coscheduled_sm_count=(8, 4), device_id=0

Queried partitions retain their originating context, and contexts own their native handles.

author: Arindamsamanta2004
message:
[Test] Skip test_checkpointing_without_reentrant_dataparallel on CPU (#198640)

Fixes issue : https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/198636
### What fails and why ?

`TestAutogradDeviceTypeCPU::test_checkpointing_without_reentrant_dataparallel_cpu`
fails on any machine with CUDA and more than one GPU:

```
RuntimeError: module must have its parameters and buffers on device cuda:0
(device_ids[0]) but found one of them on device: cpu
```

The device-generic refactor replaced the old `if torch.cuda.is_available(): .cuda()` guards with `device=device` / `.to(device)` but left the bare `DataParallel(...)`. So the CPU variant wraps a CPU model in a DP defaulting to `cuda:0`. Before the refactor the guards moved everything to CUDA on such machines, so this never tested CPU+DataParallel there — the only real CPU runs were on CPU-only hosts where DataParallel is a passthrough.

### Fix

DataParallel needs CUDA, so skip the CPU variant:

```python
@skipCPUIf(True, "DataParallel requires CUDA")
def test_checkpointing_without_reentrant_dataparallel(self, device):
```

The CUDA variant (the actual coverage) and the existing XPU skip are untouched.

### Test plan

```
python test/test_autograd.py TestAutogradDeviceTypeCPU.test_checkpointing_without_reentrant_dataparallel_cpu
python test/test_autograd.py TestAutogradDeviceTypeCUDA.test_checkpointing_without_reentrant_dataparallel_cuda
```

- CPU variant: previously FAILED, now skipped
- CUDA variant: still passes

message:

## Summary
Removes the `skipIf(torch.version.hip is not None, "CUDA-only")` from `TestStandaloneInductor.test_aoti_cuda_cmake_uses_multi_arch_gencode_flags` and `TestStandaloneInductor.test_aoti_cuda_save_kernel_recompiles_for_target_arch` so the same test IDs run and pass on both CUDA and ROCm. This is a test-only change; there is no product code change.

- `test_aoti_cuda_cmake_uses_multi_arch_gencode_flags`:
  - **CUDA** behavior is unchanged: `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=7.0;8.0;8.6;9.0` with compile target sm_80 emits `-gencode` for 80/86/90 and drops 70 and the mocked live 100a.
  - **ROCm** links the prebuilt multi-arch `.o` bundle from `compile_multiarch_bundle_from_llvm_ir` directly, so the generated CMake project has no GPU toolchain. The test asserts there is no `enable_language(CUDA)`, `-gencode`, or `embed_gpu_kernel` in the CMake output, and that `get_rocm_target_archs()` (the bundle's arch list) resolves to the patched `PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH`. `torch.cuda.is_available` is mocked to False so the live GPU arch is not appended, which makes the result the same on any runner.

- `test_aoti_cuda_save_kernel_recompiles_for_target_arch`:
  - **CUDA** behavior is unchanged: with `aot_inductor.emit_multi_arch_kernel=True`, a mismatched `cuda.arch` triggers a Triton recompile (`cc_override`) and packages the target cubin/PTX, and an unset `cuda.arch` keeps the current-device binary.

the model to the list. A dedicated per-model tolerance would avoid affecting
other opt-ins, but would duplicate the mechanism already intended for this kind
of small noisy output.

author: LiRunGuo
message:
Fix int32 overflow in cdist CUDA backward kernel (#198452)

Fixes #128791. The forward half of that issue was already fixed by #188006; this fixes the same crash in the backward kernel. I reviewed the diff and the new test, and the tests below were run on our H200 server.

The description below was drafted with Claude Code and reviewed by me:

> The forward crash reported in #128791 was fixed by #188006, which caps the cdist/pdist forward grid and grid-strides over the outputs. The backward kernel still fails at the same scale: on the 2026-09-23 nightly (H200), `torch.cdist(x1, x2, p=1)` backward raises `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` once either of two quantities reaches 2^31:
>
> ```
> (b, r, m) = (2, 8191, 32)   OK
> (b, r, m) = (2, 8192, 32)   illegal memory access   # r1 * r2 * m = 2^31
> (b, r, m) = (31, 8192, 1)   OK
> (b, r, m) = (32, 8192, 1)   illegal memory access   # dist.numel() = 2^31
> ```
>
> ### Root cause
>
> `cdist_backward_kernel_cuda_impl` computes its indices in `int`, while the forward kernel already uses `int64_t` for the same quantities:
>
> - `y = (blockIdx.y * gridDim.z + blockIdx.z) * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y`. The launcher rounds the grid up, so when `dist.numel()` is 2^31 the extra threads have `y >= 2^31`. That wraps negative, gets past the `y >= count` guard, and reads `grad[y]` / `dist[y]` out of bounds.
> - `l_size = r_size * m` is the per-batch stride of the `(batch, r2, r1, m)` scratch buffer. When `r1 * r2 * m` reaches 2^31, it wraps, so `buffer + l * l_size` points before the buffer for every batch `l >= 1`.
>
> ### Fix
>
> Make `y`, `l`, `k` and `l_size` `int64_t`, casting at the first multiply. They are computed once per thread before the inner loop, so the loop itself keeps its existing pointer-increment form. An alternative was to template the kernel on `index_t` and dispatch on `canUse32BitIndexMath`, but that doubles the number of kernel instantiations to save a few 64-bit multiplies per thread, and it would differ from the forward kernel, which already uses `int64_t` unconditionally.
>
> The launch configuration itself is fine: `grid_y`/`grid_z` are already split to stay under 65535, so they only overflow when `dist.numel()` exceeds about 6.9e10.
>
> ### Test plan
>
> New test `test_cdist_backward_large_index` in `test/test_torch.py` covers both overflows (`largeTensorTest('32GB')`; measured peaks are 16.1 GiB and 24.3 GiB). It compares the last batch against the same batch computed on its own, which stays within int32. Integer-valued `grad` with p=1 makes the reductions exact, so the comparison is bitwise and not order-dependent.
>
> On 1x H200, CUDA 12.8, `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=9.0`:
>
> ```
> python test/test_torch.py -k test_cdist_backward_large_index -v                       # nightly without fix: illegal memory access; with fix: OK
> python -m pytest test/test_torch.py -k "pdist or cdist" -q                            # 29 passed, 11 skipped
> python -m pytest test/test_ops.py -k "cdist or pdist" -q                              # 80 passed, 16 skipped, 5 xfailed
> python -m pytest test/test_autograd.py test/test_nn.py -k "cdist or pdist or pairwise" -q   # 31 passed, 2 xfailed
> compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck python sanitize_case.py 2 1024 2048                # 0 errors
> compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck python sanitize_case.py 32 8192 1                  # 0 errors
> ```
>
> Backward timing before/after (median, `torch.utils.benchmark`, H200), same build with only `DistanceKernel.cu` swapped. The differences are within run-to-run noise:
>
> ```
> p  b   r1    r2    m     before     after
> 1  1   1024  1024  64    0.558 ms   0.552 ms
> 1  8   1024  1024  64    4.071 ms   4.020 ms
> 1  4   4096  4096  16   21.583 ms  21.875 ms

author: hknsahin97-coder
message:
[dynamo] Trace __get__ for user descriptors in a class's own __dict__ (#198410)

Before this PR, guards accessed the descriptor through normal attribute access (`Cls.attr`), so its `__get__` ran again and again and the result was wrong without any error. I reproduced this myself: eager gives `(10, 20)`, compiled gives `(90, 90)`. That it fails silently is what makes this fix important to me. The test checks two things because the returned values can happen to match even when `__get__` ran the wrong number of times.

_(My comment above was written in Turkish and translated with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Accessing `Cls.attr`, where `attr` is a user-defined descriptor with a Python `__get__` stored in `Cls.__dict__`, silently produced wrong results under Dynamo. `resolve_cls_descriptor` built a VariableTracker for the raw descriptor while attaching `AttrSource(Cls, "attr")`, whose runtime value is `descriptor.__get__(None, Cls)`. Guard building, guard evaluation and output reconstruction all re-evaluate that source, so `__get__` ran many times at compile/guard time and the returned value came from reconstruction: with a counting descriptor, `return G.d, G.d` gave `(90, 90)` instead of `(10, 20)`. CPython's `type_getattro` calls `__get__(None, type)` exactly once per access.
>
> The fix routes own-`__dict__` descriptors through `invoke_cls_descriptor_get` (the path inherited descriptors already use, which traces `__get__`), and makes that path source the descriptor object through `get_source_by_walking_mro` (a lookup in the defining class's `__dict__`, as the property/member/staticmethod branches already do), so neither guards nor reconstruction invoke the descriptor protocol. The torch-internal clause is kept, so `torch.FloatStorage.dtype` still defers to runtime without a compile-time deprecation warning.
>
> This also covers the Enum item from #195901 ("Enum's metaclass makes a property/method-shadowing member break guard construction ... sometimes silently computes a wrong value"): an Enum member that shadows an inherited `@enum.property` is stored in the class `__dict__` as an `enum.property` whose `__get__(None, cls)` returns the member. Previously `list(E)[0] is E.first` was silently `False` and `E.first.value` failed.
>
> **Updated after review.** If the traced `__get__` hits something Dynamo cannot handle (e.g. a `torch._dynamo.graph_break()` inside it, as in the reviewer's reproducer), the generic `_load_attr` fallback caught the `Unsupported` and, because a class is a python constant, called `getattr(cls, name)` at trace time. That ran `__get__` during compilation and installed an `EQUALS_MATCH` guard on `C.a`; evaluating the guard called `__get__` again, and a stateful `__get__` failed with "Guard failed on the same frame it was created". The follow-up fix that was planned as a separate PR is now included (second commit): the fallback re-raises when the object is a class and the attribute resolves through its MRO to a descriptor with a Python `__get__`, so the attribute load graph-breaks instead. The check is limited to that case so the fallback keeps working for other python-constant objects.
>
> Cost: three CPython test_enum tests (`OldTestFlag`, `OldTestIntFlag`, `TestSpecial` `test_multiple_mixin`) now graph-break and get expected-failure markers. Their `classproperty` getter does `cls.ALL = ...` / `cls.MAX = ...`, a setattr on `EnumType` that Dynamo cannot trace; they passed only because the fallback ran the getter, class mutation included, once at compile time.
>
> **Tests**
>
> - `test_tp_getattro.py::test_user_descriptor_get_on_class`: compares both the returned values and the number of `__get__` calls with eager, for a descriptor on the class and on a subclass. Fails without the fix, passes with it.
> - `test_tp_getattro.py::test_user_descriptor_untraceable_get_on_class`: a `__get__` that calls a skipped function; checks value and call count against eager (nested graph breaks off and on) and that `fullgraph=True` raises `Unsupported`.
> - `test_tp_getattro.py::test_user_descriptor_get_on_class_graph_break`: the reviewer's reproducer (`graph_break()` inside `__get__`, different value on each call). Runs with `nested_graph_breaks=False`, the default outside the test harness; with nested graph breaks on, the reproducer does not reach the fallback. Fails with only the first commit (the regression the reviewer found), passes with the second; main never had the bug.
> - `test_enum.py::test_enum_member_shadows_property`: the Enum shadowing case. Fails without the fix, passes with it.
> - CPython `test_enum.py` under Dynamo: 140 tests go from ERROR to ok, and their expected-failure markers are removed; the three `test_multiple_mixin` tests above go from ok to graph-breaking and get markers. `test_descr`, `test_property`, `test_functools`, `test_super`, `test_builtin` are unchanged.
>
> ```
> python test/dynamo/test_tp_getattro.py -k test_user_descriptor
> python test/dynamo/test_enum.py -k test_enum_member_shadows_property
> PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_enum.py -v

author: aorenste
message:
Construct streams on the runtime CooR device (#196939)

After tensor devices became runtime-relative under compile_on_one_rank, Dynamo
could no longer pass x.device through the stream constructor's constant-only
example path. Converting it to the tracing rank's device without retaining its
origin would instead reconstruct the stream on the wrong rank.

Build the example stream from the device's index-less form, which resolves to
the tracing rank's current device, while keeping the runtime-relative device
for reconstruction. This preserves both positional and keyword construction for
generic and CUDA streams.

An explicit device index -- Stream(0), Stream("cuda:0"), device_index=0 --
names the compiling rank's GPU and would be reconstructed as that GPU on every
rank. Under compile_on_one_rank it is now refused with
CompileOnOneRankUnsupported, matching how explicit-index device contexts are
refused.

torch.Event(device=x.device) goes through the same constant-only path and is
not fixed here.

author: aorenste
message:
Preserve rank-relative devices in Dynamo device contexts (#196938)

Tensor device observations use a runtime-relative device under
compile_on_one_rank. Device context constructors previously required a Python
constant, so passing x.device either failed during tracing or tempted callers to
freeze the compiling rank's index.

Represent these contexts explicitly as CurrentDeviceContextVariable. CooR gives
a rank a single accelerator, so entering the current device is a no-op and no
index reaches the graph.

That no-op is sound only while nothing moves the current device mid-frame, and
two paths could. Both are now refused. Entering a device context with an
explicit index is refused because, with a no-op enter,
`with torch.cuda.device(1)` wrapped around a rank-relative context did not
switch back on entry and silently allocated on the wrong GPU under
fullgraph=True. That includes the compiling rank's own index: the artifact runs
on every rank, so `torch.cuda.device(0)` compiled on rank 0 would name the wrong
GPU everywhere else. Calling set_device (cuda, xpu, mtia, or
accelerator.set_device_index and its deprecated set_device_idx alias) while
tracing is refused because a no-op exit restores nothing, so the move would
leak past the region and leave every rank-relative device in the frame denoting
the wrong GPU. The refusal is unconditional, even for the device the rank is
already on, so whether a frame compiles doesn't depend on which rank compiled it;
set_device outside compiled code, e.g. the usual set_device(local_rank) at
startup, is unaffected. set_device_idx is marked skipped in trace_rules because
the warnings.warn in its deprecation wrapper graph-breaks, which ran the wrapped
set_device_index eagerly without ever reaching the check.

An index-less constant device (e.g. `torch.device("cuda")` or None), when the
context manager matches the rank's accelerator type, becomes a
CurrentDeviceContextVariable as well, rather than resolving through
GenericDeviceVariable.create. That covers the index-less form Dynamo's own
reconstruct emits at a graph break, and is what keeps a resumed frame portable:
create() resolves the index at trace time, so tracing the resume frame baked in
the compiling rank, and since that artifact is shared across ranks every rank
ran the resumed region on the compiling rank's GPU.

The alternative to refusing set_device was to keep real exchange nodes and make
their operand rank-relative, preserving eager's restore-on-exit semantics. That
is more machinery to serve a call that violates CooR's single-accelerator
premise anyway, so refusing it is the simpler contract.

the compiling rank's own index and each set_device variant but mtia).

message:
[RAWTHROW][15] torch/csrc/jit/tensorexpr: 294 conversions, the burn-down list is empty (#198500)

## Author Notes

Bulk migration of tensorexpr.

## Agent Notes

Written by Claude Code:

> The last burn-down entry: removes `'torch/csrc/jit/tensorexpr/**'` from
> RAWTHROW's `exclude_patterns`, together with the "Burned down later in this
> stack" block it was the last member of. What remains are the seven permanent
> entries (vendored code, forks, and the c10-free qnnpack headers).
>
> 294 raw throws in 35 files under `torch/csrc/jit/tensorexpr` (NNC) become
> `TORCH_CHECK`. 208 of them threw NNC's own classes from `exceptions.h`
> (`malformed_input` 118, `unsupported_dtype` 54, `malformed_ir` 21,
> `unimplemented_lowering` 14, `out_of_range_index` 1), the rest
> `std::runtime_error` (82) and `std::logic_error` (4). Where an `if` guarded
> the throw and held nothing else, it is collapsed into the check, and
> if/else-if chains in which every branch threw become the same checks in
> sequence (176 sites). The other 118 are `TORCH_CHECK(false, ...)` in
> `default:`/`else` branches or in if/else-if chains that also have
> non-throwing branches.
> Three of the collapses are inside `TYPE_CASE`/`VALUE_AS_*DISPATCH` macros,
> where clang-format then realigns the whole macro's backslash column; those
> hunks are larger than the change in them.
>
> **Messages are byte-identical.** Each NNC class prefixed its `what()` with
> its category and pretty-printed the IR node it was handed, so each site
> spells out exactly what the constructor used to build:
>
> ```
> throw malformed_input("bad dtype in CompareSelect", v);
> TORCH_CHECK(..., "MALFORMED INPUT: bad dtype in CompareSelect - ", std::to_string(v));
> ```
>
> `std::to_string` rather than passing `v` to `c10::str` is load-bearing:
> there is no `operator<<` for `ExprPtr`/`StmtPtr`, so `c10::str(v)` would
> print a pointer. `exceptions.h` itself is untouched: nothing in-tree throws
> those five classes any more, but it is a public `TORCH_API` header and
> deleting them is not throw-handling.
>
> **Exception types.** Python-visible: `RuntimeError` before and after, on
> both paths. The `HANDLE_TH_ERRORS` path already flattened every
> `std::exception`, and the bare pybind bindings in `tensorexpr_init.cpp` map
> `std::runtime_error` and `c10::Error` both to `RuntimeError`. The NNC
> classes derive from `std::runtime_error`, so `out_of_range_index` was a
> `RuntimeError`, not an `IndexError`, and becomes plain `TORCH_CHECK`, not
> `TORCH_CHECK_INDEX`. `std::logic_error` has no distinct pybind mapping
> either (established in `[12]`). C++-visible: `std::runtime_error` becomes
> `c10::Error`, which is the "fine for TorchScript" decision already applied
> in `[10]`-`[12]`. There are no C++ NNC tests left (`test/cpp/tensorexpr`
> went in #158928), and no Python test matches on these types or messages.
>
> **One catch had to move with them.** `evalInt` (`eval.cpp`) caught
> `std::runtime_error` and returned `nullopt`, and its only caller,
> `FunctionInliner` (`loopnest.cpp`), relies on that `nullopt` to decline
> inlining a producer whose store index is neither a `Var` nor a constant. The
> evaluator throws "could not find Var in context" for such an index (and
> the converted dtype checks in `eval.h`, `ir.h` and `types.h` sit on the same
> path), so after the conversion those would have escaped `evalInt` and
> `computeInline` would throw instead of declining; `TensorExprKernel`'s
> `catch (...)` would not mask it because fallback is off by default. The catch is widened to
> `const std::exception&`. One side effect: the pre-existing
> `TORCH_CHECK(rhs != 0, "Division by zero")` in the same evaluator used to
> escape this catch and now also becomes `nullopt`, i.e. the inliner declines
> instead of throwing for an index that divides by a constant zero.
>
> **Code no build here compiles.** `llvm_codegen.cpp` (29 sites) is under
> `TORCH_ENABLE_LLVM`, and nothing in OSS CI sets `USE_LLVM`, so it is only
> compiled internally. `cuda_codegen.cpp`/`.h` (18) are compiled by CUDA CI
> but not by the local CPU build. Those were reviewed line by line instead.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> ```
> spin lint -- --skip CLANGTIDY
> spin lint -- --take RAWTHROW --all-files
> bash -ic 'BUILD_CONFIG spin develop'
> python test/test_tensorexpr.py
> python test/test_tensorexpr_pybind.py
> python test/test_jit_fuser_te.py
> python test/test_static_runtime.py
> ```
>
> plus a positive control for the `evalInt` catch: a script that builds a
> producer storing to `A[i + 1]` and calls `LoopNest.compute_inline(A)`
> declines without raising, and with only the catch reverted it raises
> `RuntimeError: MALFORMED INPUT: could not find Var in context - i`.
>
> This change was authored with the help of an AI assistant (Claude Code).

[RAWTHROW][14] the last two c10/util carve-outs (changes one exception type) (#198268)

## Author Notes

A couple simple fix, and adding a test for currently untested code.

## Agent Notes

Written by Claude Code:

> This is the plan's phase 9: the two files earlier PRs parked in a
> "converting this changes the Python-visible exception type" block, kept out
> of the mechanical PRs so that each of those stayed provably mechanical.
> **This is the only PR in the stack that changes an observable exception
> type**, which is why the title says so.
>
> The two files do not want the same answer.
>
> `c10/util/SmallVector.cpp` (2 `std::length_error`, 3 `std::bad_alloc`) moves
> to the permanent vendored block rather than being converted. It is
> `llvm/ADT/SmallVector.cpp` carried verbatim under Apache-2.0 WITH
> LLVM-exception, with a three-line delta recorded at the top of the file, so
> its throws are upstream's contract in exactly the sense that block already
> applies to `flat_hash_map.h`. Converting them would also diverge the fork for
> no gain, because **no c10 type preserves `bad_alloc`'s `MemoryError`**:
> `torch.OutOfMemoryError` derives from `RuntimeError`, not `MemoryError`
> (measured, not assumed). An honest permanent entry beats a silent behaviour
> change. The plan anticipated this outcome: "if any of them turns out to be
> load-bearing, it keeps its per-file exclude with a comment saying why".
>
> `c10/util/StringUtil.cpp` (3 `std::range_error`, malformed UTF-16 in the
> `wchar_t` overloads of `c10::str`) is a real conversion, to
> `TORCH_CHECK_VALUE`, and its exclude entry is deleted. Neither macro
> preserves both binding paths: under `HANDLE_TH_ERRORS` these are
> `RuntimeError` today, while through a bare pybind binding `std::range_error`
> maps to `ValueError`. `TORCH_CHECK_VALUE` keeps the pybind path exact and
> moves the `HANDLE_TH_ERRORS` path from `RuntimeError` to `ValueError`.
> **That is the behaviour change.** It follows the same resolution Skylion007
> gave on #194378 for the memory-format lookups, and malformed UTF-16 is a
> value error on the merits. Blast radius is small: the throwing
> `_strFromWide` is inside `#ifndef _WIN32`, and the only in-tree wide-string
> callers are the Windows-only JIT fuser, so nothing in-tree reaches it on
> Linux.
>
> Measured on a built `libc10`, before and after, rather than reasoned about:
>
> ```
>                         before                       after
>   unpaired high         std::range_error             c10::ValueError
>   unpaired low          std::range_error             c10::ValueError
>   bad second unit       std::range_error             c10::ValueError
>   valid surrogate pair  no throw                     no throw
>   plain ascii           no throw                     no throw
> ```
>
> All three messages are byte-identical across the change. The two no-throw
> rows are the control: they confirm the inverted conditions
> (`low >= 0xDC00 && low <= 0xDFFF`) did not turn valid input into an error.
> Nothing in the repo catches `std::range_error` or asserts on these message
> strings.
>
> `c10/test/util/string_util_test.cpp` gains a case pinning all four rows, so
> the behaviour change is covered by a test rather than only by the table
> above -- those three branches had no coverage at all before. It is guarded
> `#ifndef _WIN32` to match the code it covers. Checked with a positive
> control: reverting the conversion makes it fail.
>
> One caveat on the table, pre-existing macro behaviour rather than anything
> this PR introduces. Under `-DSTRIP_ERROR_MESSAGES`, `TORCH_CHECK_WITH_MSG`
> discards its `error_t` and throws a plain `c10::Error`
> (`c10/util/Exception.h:502`), so in a strip build these become
> `RuntimeError` on both paths rather than `ValueError`. That applies to every
> `TORCH_CHECK_VALUE` already in the tree.
>
> After this, `exclude_patterns` is eight entries: seven permanent vendored ones
> and `torch/csrc/jit/tensorexpr/**` as the only burn-down item left. The
> "behaviour change pending" block is gone. Note that the burn-down list will
> therefore never reach zero -- seven vendored entries are the intended end
> state, not remaining debt.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> ```
> spin lint -- --skip CLANGTIDY
> CMAKE_GENERATOR=Ninja USE_CUDA=0 USE_DISTRIBUTED=0 BUILD_TEST=0 \
>     pip install -e . -v --no-build-isolation
> ```
>
> plus `c10/test/util/string_util_test.cpp`, which is not built under
> `BUILD_TEST=0`, compiled and run by hand against the built `libc10`: 13/13
> pass, including the new surrogate case.
>
> ```
> g++ -std=c++20 -I. -Ibuild -Iaten/src -Ibuild/aten/src -Itorch/include \
>     -Itorch/csrc/api/include -Ithird_party/googletest/googletest/include \
>     c10/test/util/string_util_test.cpp gtest-all.o gtest_main.o \
>     -Lbuild/lib -lc10 -Wl,-rpath,$PWD/build/lib -lpthread -o /tmp/t && /tmp/t
> ```
>
> This change was authored with the help of an AI assistant (Claude Code).

message:
[RAWTHROW][13] widen include_patterns: 20 conversions, 11 that must not be (#198231)

## Author Notes

Pretty simple stuff

## Agent Notes

Written by Claude Code:

> RAWTHROW's `include_patterns` were only `**/*.cpp` and `**/*.h`, so every
> raw throw in a `.cc`, `.cu`, `.cuh`, `.hpp` or `.mm` file was invisible to
> it. Emptying the exclude list without fixing that would leave the check
> narrower than it looks, which is why this lands before the last two PRs of
> the stack rather than after them.
>
> **This is the only PR after phase 0 that deletes no `exclude_patterns`
> entry.** Widening `include_patterns` is the equivalent strengthening move:
> the new coverage is what enforces the 31 sites below, and the whole-tree
> RAWTHROW run is the acceptance test. Calling it out because "every PR
> deletes at least one exclude entry" is otherwise a hard rule in this stack.
>
> Adding `.cc`, `.cu`, `.cuh`, `.hpp`, `.inl` and `.mm` brings 34 raw throws
> into the linter's view. Three of those already pass, covered by
> `ALLOWED_EXCEPTION_TYPES` entries that earlier PRs added:
> `c10::AcceleratorError` in `aten/src/ATen/mps/MPSStream.mm`, and two
> `NCCLException` in `torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/nccl2/ProcessGroupNCCL.hpp`
> -- the plan predicted that second one, since `[9]` allow-listed a type whose
> macros live in a `.hpp` the linter could not yet see. That leaves 31
> findings in 14 files: 20 conversions and 11 annotations.
>
> `.m` is not added because no `.m` file is tracked. `.inl` is added for
> completeness; its one tracked file has no throws. `**/*.cc` newly matches
> the amalgamated vendored perfetto SDK, so `third_party/perfetto/sdk/**` goes
> into the permanent vendored block -- it is clean today, but a future perfetto
> roll could otherwise turn RAWTHROW red with no legitimate in-repo fix. The
> glob covers both halves of the amalgamation, since `perfetto.h` was already
> in scope via the pre-existing `**/*.h`.
>
> Review order: the `.lintrunner.toml` hunk first, then the 11 annotations
> (they are the argument), then the 20 mechanical conversions.
>
> **The 11 annotations are claims that the throw is correct, not that it was
> awkward.** Two of the three groups would have been silent breakage:
>
> - `c10/cuda/test/impl/CUDAAssertionsTest_*.cu`, 7 sites. The throw sits
>   inside `try { device_synchronize(); throw ...; } catch (const c10::Error&)`,
>   and is how the test reports that the device-side assertion it expected did
>   not fire. The handler asserts on the device-assertion text with a run of
>   `ASSERT_THAT(err_str, HasSubstr(...))`. A `TORCH_CHECK` there raises
>   `c10::Error`, so it would be caught by that handler and the test would fail
>   on a substring mismatch against this sentinel string instead of on the
>   assertion never firing. The test still fails either way -- what is lost is
>   the diagnostic, which would point at the wrong thing.
> - `benchmarks/static_runtime/test_static_runtime.cc`, 1 site. The
>   `maybe_throw` test op feeds four `EXPECT_THROW(..., std::runtime_error)`
>   assertions in the `ModelCrash*` tests. `c10::Error` derives from
>   `std::exception`, not `std::runtime_error`, so those four stop matching.
>   The same file uses `EXPECT_THROW(..., c10::Error)` elsewhere, so the
>   distinction is deliberate rather than incidental.
> - `test/cpp/c10d/TestUtils.hpp`, 3 sites. `std::system_error` carrying
>   `errno` as a `std::error_code`, which `TORCH_CHECK` cannot express. Same
>   reason and same wording as the annotation already on
>   `test/cpp/c10d/FileStoreTest.cpp`, which landed in [6].
>
> The 20 conversions, and what each one had to be checked against:
>
> - `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/RowwiseScaledMM.cu`, 9 sites, three identical
>   cutlass status blocks. Plain `TORCH_CHECK`; the file already uses it 39
>   times.
> - `aten/src/ATen/native/mps/OperationUtils.mm`, 4 sites. Three plain, plus
>   one `c10::SyntaxError` that becomes `TORCH_CHECK_WITH(SyntaxError, ...)`
>   so the Python-visible `SyntaxError` is preserved. One of the three ends a
>   non-void function; `TORCH_CHECK(false, ...)` is safe there because the
>   condition is a literal, so the compiler folds the branch and
>   `torchCheckFail` is `[[noreturn]]`. Same shape as
>   `aten/src/ATen/NestedTensorImpl.cpp:278` and `OperationUtils.mm:736`.
>   One caveat on "preserved", which is pre-existing macro behaviour rather
>   than anything this PR introduces: under `-DSTRIP_ERROR_MESSAGES`,
>   `TORCH_CHECK_WITH_MSG` discards its `error_t` and throws a plain
>   `c10::Error` (`c10/util/Exception.h:502`), so in a strip build that site
>   raises `RuntimeError` rather than `SyntaxError`. That is equally true of
>   every `TORCH_CHECK_WITH` and `TORCH_CHECK_VALUE` already in the tree.
> - `torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/Utils.hpp`, 5 `std::invalid_argument` ->
>   `TORCH_CHECK_VALUE`. **Disclosure:** `assertSameType`, `assertSameSizes`
>   and `assertSameSizeAndType` have no callers anywhere in this repo, so the
>   `RuntimeError` -> `ValueError` question is unobservable in-tree. This is a
>   shipped header, so out-of-tree C++ catching `std::invalid_argument` from
>   them would still break.
> - `test/cpp/aoti_abi_check/cuda/test_kernel_utils.cu`, 1 site, to
>   `STD_TORCH_CHECK`. That tree exists to prove `torch/headeronly` builds
>   without c10, so it cannot reach for `TORCH_CHECK`. `STD_TORCH_CHECK`
>   throws `std::runtime_error`, so the C++ type is unchanged; only the
>   `__func__, __FILE__:__LINE__` prefix is added, which is the same accepted
>   trade as #194378 and #194773. The linter's per-directory macro hint is
>   taught about this directory in the same commit, with two unit tests, since
>   the widening is what made it scannable.
> - `torch/csrc/jit/backends/coreml/objc/PTMCoreMLBackend.mm`, 1 site.
>   `COREML_THROW_IF_ERROR` built a `c10::Error` with an explicit
>   `{__func__, __FILE__, __LINE__}`, which is exactly what `TORCH_CHECK`
>   captures on its own. Unlike `METAL_THROW_IF_ERROR`, which had to stay raw
>   because buck compiles it with `-DSTRIP_ERROR_MESSAGES`, this file has no
>   buck build at all -- it is CMake-only. One non-throw delta worth naming:
>   the original wrote `if C10_LIKELY(error)`, marking *error present* as the
>   likely branch, which reads like a typo for `C10_UNLIKELY`. `TORCH_CHECK`
>   marks the failure branch unlikely, so the hint flips. That is inherent to
>   the conversion rather than a drive-by edit, but it is a behavioural delta
>   in an otherwise mechanical hunk.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> ```
> spin lint -- --skip CLANGTIDY
> python -m pytest tools/test/test_raw_throw_linter.py -q
> CMAKE_GENERATOR=Ninja USE_CUDA=0 USE_DISTRIBUTED=0 BUILD_TEST=0 \
>     pip install -e . -v --no-build-isolation
> python -c "import torch; print(torch.randn(3).sum())"
> ```
>
> Lint clean, whole-tree RAWTHROW goes from 31 findings to 0 under the wider
> globs, 72 linter unit tests pass, build exits 0.
>
> **What the local build does not cover.** With `USE_CUDA=0`,
> `USE_DISTRIBUTED=0` and `BUILD_TEST=0` it compiles none of the files touched
> here, so it only shows nothing else broke. To narrow that, two translation
> units were compiled directly against the built tree: one instantiating all
> three converted `c10d/Utils.hpp` helpers, one exercising `STD_TORCH_CHECK`
> with the exact argument shapes of the new `CUDA_ASSERT_OK`. Both are clean,
> and the first was run with a positive control (break the macro name, confirm
> the compile fails, restore). `RowwiseScaledMM.cu` needs CUDA and
> `BUILD_ROWWISE_FP8_KERNEL`, and `OperationUtils.mm` needs macOS, so both
> rest on CI. `PTMCoreMLBackend.mm` is gated on `IOS AND USE_COREML_DELEGATE`
> with no iOS workflow in `.github/workflows`, so nothing in OSS compiles it,
> CI included; that one rests on review.

author: andriy-ca
message:
[ROCm][Inductor] Advance CK pin, Generate ck/config.h for the CK wheel and re-enable CI tests (#195658)

Advances the `rocm-composable-kernel` pin and generates the one CK header the wheel
does not ship. Restores CK autotuning in CI disabled due to stale pin.

## Motivation

ROCm 7.14 stopped installing the CK headers system-wide, so the inductor CK backends
now compile against what the `ck4inductor` wheel ships. Every header they `#include`
is checked into CK except one: `ck/config.h` is generated by CK's build from
`include/ck/config.h.in`, so it exists in neither ROCm nor the wheel's source tree.
Without it every CK choice fails to compile and is silently discarded, so the CK backends
contribute no autotune candidates at all rather than reporting a missing header.

Scope: this restores CK autotuning in CI. The ROCm CD path has routed through the
Python build pipeline since #182696 and has no CK step.

## Changes

**Generate `ck/config.h`** (`.ci/pytorch/rocm_utils.sh`, `.ci/pytorch/generate_ck_config_h.cmake`)

`build_rocm_ck_wheel()` now generates the header for `gfx90a;gfx942;gfx950` and packages it
with the rest of `include/ck`. This replaces the `ck_tile` `pyproject.toml` patch, which the new
pin makes a no-op.

CK's own CMake cannot produce it in the wheel-build container: `CMakeLists.txt` calls
`find_package(ROCM)`, `find_package(hip REQUIRED)` and `enable_language(HIP)`, and the
image has `hipcc` but no ROCm CMake packages. `config.h.in` substitutes only plain
variables, so the helper sets them and runs the same `configure_file` in `cmake -P`
script mode.

The helper mirrors CK's arch rules rather than referencing them, so it assigns every
variable unconditionally — `"ON"` or empty — instead of only in the true branch.
Leaving one undefined would be indistinguishable from a deliberate OFF, which both
defeats the drift check and makes the script reject any target list that does not
happen to enable everything.

> **Note for CI:** this step shells out to `cmake -P`, so the wheel-build image must
> provide `cmake`.

**Pin bump** `4266f867` → `e2daf442`

The outgoing pin is from February. The new one packages the `ck_tile` headers in
`pyproject.toml`, which makes the patch #189646 added to `rocm_utils.sh` a no-op. It
also makes instance enumeration deterministic and duplicate-free, so a given wheel
offers the same candidates on every machine instead of depending on filesystem order.

This pin is also a prerequisite for follow-up PRs adding gfx1250 WMMA support.

**Re-enable version-skipped tests** (`test/inductor/test_ck_backend.py`)

Removes seven `skipIfRocmVersionAtLeast([7, 14])` decorators, added in #188593 (and
one in #188429) for known 7.14 failures. The predicate is `>=`, so on ROCm 10.x it
evaluates true and these subtests are skipped on every current ROCm CI job rather than
only on the 7.14 release they were written for.

## Test plan

Verified on hardware with both wheels built from this branch — the CK wheel by the
real `build_rocm_ck_wheel()`, so the code under test is what produced the artifact.

| Arch | Collected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| gfx942 (MI300X) | 84 | 76 passed, 8 skipped |
| gfx942 (MI325X) | 84 | 76 passed, 8 skipped |

The 8 skips are the `scaled_mm` cells, skipped upstream for unrelated reasons.

message:
[MPS] Check that 1D/2D/3D dispatch grid dims fit in uint32 (#198592)

`thread_position_in_grid` can only be a 32-bit (or 16-bit) value per axis; the Metal compiler rejects `ulong` for that attribute. `dispatchThreads:` silently truncates the grid width to its low 32 bits

Add a `TORCH_CHECK` in `mtl_dispatch1DJob` and per-axis ones in `mtl_dispatch2DJob` and `mtl_dispatch3DJob`, so any caller exceeding the limit raises instead of producing silently wrong results. Callers that need more threads must split the work (chunks with a base offset, a multi-dimensional grid, or a grid-stride loop).

message:
[dynamo] Match CPython repr for self-referential sets and set subclasses (#198476)

This fixes the set part of my claim on #195901: Dynamo printed the wrong placeholder for self-referential sets and dropped the class name for set subclasses. I traced both bugs to how the set VariableTrackers implement repr, and checked the fix against CPython's `set_repr`.

> AI-assisted PR description:
>
> ## Issue
>
> Towards #195901. Implements the set item of my [claimed self-referential container repr subtask](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/195901#issuecomment-5800751713) (`test_set.py::_TestJointOps::test_cyclical_repr`). The `UserList` / `UserDict` items have a different root cause in `generic_repr` and will be a separate PR.
>
> ## Summary
>
> ```python
> w = ReprWrapper(); s = SetSubclass([w]); w.value = s
> repr(s)  # eager:  SetSubclass({SetSubclass(...)})
>          # dynamo: {...}
> ```
>
> CPython's `set_repr` prints `"%s(...)"` with the type name on a cycle, and `"%s({...})"` for anything that is not an exact `set`. Two bugs:
>
> 1. **set / frozenset**: `SetVariable` and `FrozensetVariable` did not override `repr_recursive_sentinel()`, so a cycle printed the `VariableTracker` default `"..."`. They now return `"<type name>(...)"`.
> 2. **set subclasses**: `UserDefinedSetVariable` is not a `SetVariable` subclass; it wraps one in `_base_vt`. Its repr was dispatched to `_base_vt`, which only knows its type as `set`/`frozenset`, so the subclass name was lost even without a cycle (`repr(SetSubclass([1]))` printed `{1}`). It now formats its repr with its own type name and overrides `repr_recursive_sentinel()`. Subclasses that define their own `__repr__` keep the existing path, using the same `_base_methods` check as `UserDefinedDictVariable.tp_repr_impl`.
>
> I did not add `set` to the fixed sentinel table in `generic_repr`, because the placeholder depends on the type name. I also did not put the override on `BaseSetVariable`, because `dict_keys` correctly prints `"..."`.
>
> The four `test_cyclical_repr` expected-failure markers are removed.
>
> Note: this adds `parametrize` / `instantiate_parametrized_tests` to `test_repr_protocol.py`. #196902 adds the same imports, so whichever PR lands second needs a trivial conflict resolution.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> Run in a Python 3.13 environment on CPU. The new `test_self_ref_set_repr` cases use `fullgraph=True`, because a graph break would fall back to eager and hide the wrong output. Without the `SetVariable`/`FrozensetVariable` change, the `set`/`frozenset` cases fail; without the `UserDefinedSetVariable` change, the two subclass cases fail.
>
> ```bash
> python test/dynamo/test_repr_protocol.py -v -k test_self_ref_set_repr
> python test/dynamo/test_repr_protocol.py
> python test/dynamo/test_sets.py
> PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_set.py -v -k test_cyclical_repr
> PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_set.py
> lintrunner -a torch/_dynamo/variables/sets.py torch/_dynamo/variables/user_defined.py test/dynamo/test_repr_protocol.py
> ```
>

>
> - [x] Passes lint (`lintrunner -a`)
> - [x] Added/updated tests
> - Documentation: not applicable
> - Benchmarks: not applicable
>
> ## BC-breaking?
>
> No.

message:
[dynamo] Fix isinstance() with unions/tuples of runtime_checkable Protocols (#196124)

Fixes #195969

The description below was drafted with an AI assistant (Claude Code) and is quoted as such; the diff and the tests were reviewed by the PR author.

> **Problem.** `isinstance(o, HasPorts | HasFoo)` and `isinstance(o, (HasPorts, HasFoo))` compile to a constant `False` when `HasPorts` is a `@runtime_checkable` Protocol with a data (non-method) member, while eager returns `True`. No graph break, no warning; `fullgraph=True` takes the wrong branch.
>
> **Root cause** (`BuiltinVariable.call_isinstance`). The metaclass-hook path only fired when the classinfo object itself had `__instancecheck__` in its metaclass `__dict__`. For a union that metaclass is `types.UnionType`, for a tuple it is `tuple`, so the branch was skipped and the check fell through to `issubclass(arg_type, members)`. `_ProtocolMeta.__subclasscheck__` raises `TypeError` for Protocols with non-method members, and the `except TypeError` fallback then compared the class object by identity against the members (`arg_type in members`), which is `False` for any real program. Ordering a method-only Protocol first only worked because `issubclass()` short-circuits left to right.
>
> **Fix.** Mirror CPython's `object_recursive_isinstance`. Nested tuples and unions are flattened onto a work list, and members are validated and checked left to right, stopping at the first match. A member whose metaclass supplies `__instancecheck__` -- resolved through the metaclass MRO, as CPython's `_PyObject_LookupSpecial` does, so an inherited hook counts -- is evaluated with the real `isinstance()` whenever Dynamo can reconstruct the argument (`VariableTracker.get_real_python_backed_value()`), which also yields CPython's exact-type fast path for free; a `TypeError` from such a hook becomes an observed, catchable exception. Plain classes stay on the `issubclass()` path, so a lazy constant keeps its weaker type-only guard until a hooked member is actually reached.
>
> When there is no reconstructible object and `issubclass()` raises, the argument's exact type is still known, and a representative instance can stand in — but only under two conditions, both required. The argument's type must be one of the builtins in `_VALUE_INDEPENDENT_TYPES`, whose instances cannot carry per-instance attributes (membership is exact-type, never `issubclass`, since a subclass may add a `__dict__` or a `__getattr__`). And the hook must be one that provably ignores the instance value: `typing._ProtocolMeta.__instancecheck__`, which looks only at attribute presence, or `typing._BaseGenericAlias.__instancecheck__`, which is `self.__subclasscheck__(type(obj))`. A hook that reads the value — a metaclass doing `instance[0] == 1` — would otherwise be answered from an empty list, which is wrong and can raise. Everything else graph breaks with a registered `gb_type` rather than guessing.
>
> The same pair decides whether the object is consulted at all. A class based hook (a plain class, or `abc.ABCMeta`) reads only `type(obj)`, and for those exact builtins an attribute based hook cannot see per-instance state either — nor can they spoof `__class__`, the one thing `ABCMeta`'s hook sees that `issubclass()` does not. In both cases the type answers, so a lazy constant is never realized and keeps its `TYPE_MATCH` guard instead of specializing once per value. This also settles a contradiction inside the file: `_uses_custom_classinfo_check` already excludes `abc.ABCMeta`.
>
> **Review order.** The six commits are meant to be read in sequence: the first fixes the reported bug, the second restores CPython's left-to-right short-circuit after review feedback, the third flattens nested classinfo and widens test coverage, the fourth adds the type-only probe after CI showed the graph break firing for a `SymNodeVariable` under dynamic shapes, where `main` had answered correctly, the fifth resolves the hook through the metaclass MRO, gates the real-`isinstance()` path on `get_real_python_backed_value()` and restricts the probe to value-independent hooks, and the sixth stops consulting the object when the type already answers, so constants no longer specialize.
>
> **Behavior changes** (all toward eager):
>
> | Case | eager | before | after |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | `isinstance(obj, HasPorts \| HasFoo)`, `(HasPorts, HasFoo)`, `HasPorts \| None`, `(int, HasPorts)` | True | **False** | True |
> | `isinstance(3, DataProto)` (constant arg) | True | **False** | True |
> | `isinstance(n, DataProto)` (unspecialized int) | as eager | as eager | as eager, no graph break |
> | `isinstance(None, HasPorts \| None)` | True | True (by coincidence) | True, no graph break |
> | `isinstance(MyError, (type, 1))` (invalid member after a match) | True | **TypeError** | True |
> | `isinstance(o, ((HasPorts,), HasFoo))` (nested tuple) | True | **TypeError** | True |
> | `isinstance(obj, NotRuntimeCheckable \| HasFoo)` | raises TypeError | **False** | observed TypeError |
> | `isinstance(obj, NotRuntimeCheckable)` | raises TypeError | InternalTorchDynamoError | observed TypeError |
> | `isinstance([x], (list, HasPorts))` | True | **False by identity** | True, no graph break |
> | `isinstance([x], HasPorts)` (no wrapped object) | False | **False by identity** | False, from the type |
> | `isinstance([x], typing.List[int])` | raises TypeError | **False by identity** | observed TypeError |
> | `isinstance(traced_fn, HasPorts)` (no object, has a `__dict__`) | False | False, by class identity | graph break |
> | `isinstance(v, HasReal)` / `isinstance(v, Sequence)` over 4 distinct strings | 1 frame | 1 frame | 1 frame |
> | `isinstance(lst, M)`, `M.__instancecheck__` reads `instance[0]` | True | **False by identity** | True, from the real object |
> | `isinstance(obj, typing.List[int])` (inherited hook) | raises TypeError | graph break | observed TypeError |
>
> Three `dynamo_expected_failures` markers are removed, each CI- or locally-confirmed as an unexpected success: `test_patma.py`'s `TestTypeErrors.test_regular_protocol` and `TestTypeErrors.test_positional_patterns_with_regular_protocol`, because a non-`runtime_checkable` Protocol's `TypeError` is now observable, and `test_isinstance.py`'s `TestIsInstanceIsSubclass.test_isinstance_with_or_union`, which the union handling fixes.
>
> **Deliberately not fixed here.** The `isinstance()` result is constant-folded without guarding the attributes a data-member Protocol reads, so two instances of one class that differ in whether the attribute is set share a cache entry. That hole predates this PR and is present on `main` for the single-class path as well, so widening or papering over it here would be the wrong call; it is filed separately as #196127. Also unchanged: objects created inside the compiled region carry an uninitialized `.value`, so Protocol checks depending on attributes set in a traced `__init__` still return `False`.
>
> **Review focus.** (1) Whether evaluating the real `isinstance()` on the reconstructed object is the right trade-off given #196127. (2) The two membership sets behind the probe — the claims are that no instance of those exact types can carry an attribute a Protocol probe would see, and that those two hooks never read the instance value. (3) The `abc.ABCMeta` arm of the type-answers rule, which is deliberately narrowed to the exact builtins so the real-object path that `main` used for user-defined objects (where `__class__` can be spoofed) is untouched.
>
> **Test plan.** `test_isinstance_runtime_checkable_protocol_classinfo` is parametrized over ten classinfo spellings and five argument kinds; `test_isinstance_protocol_with_unspecialized_int` pins the `SymNodeVariable` case; `test_isinstance_protocol_member_order_effects` pins the short-circuit and that neither member order specializes; `test_isinstance_does_not_specialize_value_independent_constant` and `test_isinstance_instancecheck_raises_non_str_args` pin the last two; `test_isinstance_value_reading_instancecheck_on_traced_list` pins the value-reading metaclass; `test_isinstance_inherited_instancecheck_metaclass` and `test_isinstance_protocol_on_nn_module` pin the MRO lookup and the widened value gate; `test_isinstance_tuple_short_circuits_before_invalid_member`, `test_isinstance_protocol_without_issubclass_graph_breaks` and `test_isinstance_non_runtime_checkable_protocol_raises` cover the remaining paths. All of them fail before the corresponding commit. Full `test_misc.py` matches the recorded unmodified `main` failure set; full `test_dynamic_shapes.py` is unchanged across the commits of this PR.

message:
Move the remaining py3.10 CI test jobs to 3.11 (#198531)

Follows #198271 (pull, trunk) and #198501 (periodic, slow, periodic-strict), covering the 32 workflows those two did not touch.

## What moves

The inductor, rocm, h100, xpu, docs, dtensor, native-aot and microbenchmark families. Job ids, display names, `build-environment`, `needs` references, `${{ needs.<job>.* }}` interpolations and `python-version` all move together, following the convention the two earlier PRs established.

The only versioned image any of these workflows names is `pytorch-linux-jammy-py3.11-clang21`, which is already defined in `.ci/docker/build.sh` and listed in `docker-builds.yml`.

## Also: a guard that would have lost coverage silently

`.ci/pytorch/test.sh` gates a test on the build-environment *name*:

```bash
# Remove dill to test that serialization works without it
if [[ "$BUILD_ENVIRONMENT" == *py3.10-gcc11 ]]; then
  pip uninstall -y dill 2>/dev/null || true
fi
```

\#198271 renames that environment to `py3.11-gcc11` but does not touch this guard. Once it lands the branch stops matching, dill is never uninstalled, and the without-dill serialization coverage disappears — no failure, just a test that no longer runs. Fixed here since it is the same migration.

## Deliberately left alone

| file | why |
|---|---|
| `lint.yml` | needs `pytorch-linux-jammy-cuda13.0-cudnn9-py3.11-linter`; `.ci/docker/build.sh` has no case for that tag, so the image cannot be built yet |
| `.github/scripts/test_trymerge.py` | `py3.10` appears in historical job names used as test fixtures |
| `linux_binary_build_workflow.yml.j2`, `_binary-test-macos.yml` | `py3_10` appears in comments and input descriptions about **binary** wheels. The binary matrix still ships 3.10 on the test and release channels; only nightly dropped it |
| `job-filter.yml` | the reference is inside a commented-out example |

## Verification

- All 32 workflows parse as YAML.
- Every `needs:` entry and every `${{ needs.<job>.* }}` interpolation resolves to a job defined in its own file — **0 dangling references**. That is the failure mode a blind rename produces, since job ids carry the version.
- `bash -n` clean on `test.sh`.
- The diff is symmetric at 357 insertions / 357 deletions, and mapping `3.11` back to `3.10` pairs every added line with a removed one — i.e. nothing changed but the version.

## Follow-up needed elsewhere

Three py3.11 images have no case in `.ci/docker/build.sh`:

```
pytorch-linux-jammy-cuda13.0-cudnn9-py3.11-clang20
pytorch-linux-jammy-cuda13.4-cudnn9-py3.11-clang20
pytorch-linux-jammy-cuda13.0-cudnn9-py3.11-linter
```

That is why `lint.yml` is excluded here. It also affects #198501, which renames `docker-image-name` to the two clang20 tags and updates `docker-builds.yml` to match — that PR will request images that cannot be built until `build.sh` defines them.

message:
[dynamo] Leave plain functions unbound when super() is bound to a class (#198435)

When `super()` is bound to a class (e.g. zero-arg `super()` in a classmethod), CPython calls the descriptor with `obj=NULL`, so a plain function from the MRO stays unbound ([typeobject.c](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.0/Objects/typeobject.c#L11162-L11166)). Dynamo always passed `objvar` as the first argument, which can silently change the result:

```python
class Parent:
    def greet(*args):
        return len(args)

class Child(Parent):
    @classmethod
    def greet(cls):
        return super().greet()  # eager: 0, compiled: 1
```

`SuperVariable.call_method` now leaves the function unbound when `objvar` is a class. This enables `test_super.py::TestSuper::test_reassigned_new` and `test_mixed_staticmethod_hierarchy` and removes their expected-failure markers.

In a metaclass method, `super(Meta, A)` binds to `A` even though `A` is a class. That case goes through the real `super()` fallback in `_resolved_getattr_and_source`, which already applies the descriptor, so it never reaches the new branch unbound. `test_super_metaclass_method` covers it, including a staticmethod on the parent metaclass that was previously called with `A` prepended.

Towards #195901.

message:
[Sigmoid] Stabilize AOTI inplace weight identity (#197430) (#197430)

Summary:

Resolve AOTI constants by exact or unique wrapper-normalized FQN for compatibility with existing snapshots whose generated _run_on_acc/_run_on_gpu wrapper changed.

The `_run_on_acc_<n>` and `_run_on_gpu_<n>` components are generated by lowering partitioning, so wrappers may be added, removed, or renumbered when graph partitioning or ordering changes between otherwise compatible snapshot publishes. In the observed `1140807405/4 -> /17` transition, the cold-loaded AOTI delegate retained `merge.submod_0._run_on_acc_0...ln.weight`, while the replacement archive exposed the same tensor as `merge.submod_0...ln.weight`. The prior exact lookup therefore raised `<wrapper-qualified FQN> not found in Weights` and aborted the update before snapshot 17 became ready.

Also index each packed parameter, buffer, and tensor constant by its namespaced archive storage key. AOTI delegates retain that compatible-snapshot identity from the source snapshot and prefer it during inplace updates, so lowering-wrapper renames do not control weight matching. Storage-key ambiguity is derived directly from the multimap, and canonical ambiguity is derived directly from the current weight set, eliminating separately maintained ambiguity state.

Every update logs an exhaustive resolution breakdown: storage key, exact FQN, canonical FQN fallback, and optional constants retained. Constant metadata is read for both cold-loaded and cached-weight executors, so buffers, tensor constants, and empty parameters retain AOTI optional-update semantics in the child process while missing required parameters still fail.

This is runtime-only and requires no model input or publishing-config change.

author: jansel
message:
Fix export move_to_device_pass device rewrites (#185105)

`move_to_device_pass` rewrites device-bearing FX nodes and tensor metadata, but it did not recompile the affected GraphModules. Generated Python could therefore retain stale `_assert_tensor_metadata` device arguments and fail when the moved graph ran directly through `ep.graph_module`.

Recompile every GraphModule touched by the pass so its callable code matches the rewritten graph. Export also supports interpreter-only graphs whose in-memory custom objects cannot be emitted as Python, so keep that existing fallback by ignoring only the same `SyntaxError` raised during code generation.

An earlier version tried to preserve parameter identity with `.data`. Freshly exported state aliases the source module, so that moved source parameters while replacing buffers and left the source module mixed-device. It also corrupted traceable wrapper subclasses by moving only the outer TensorImpl. Retain the existing out-of-place state movement instead, with regressions covering source-module reuse and wrapper-subclass children.

I considered overriding `GraphModule.to()` so it rewrites graph IR, but exported graphs are device-specific and `move_to_device_pass` is the supported graph-casting path. Keeping the fix in that pass avoids changing general FX `GraphModule.to()` semantics.

Fixes #163323

message:
[inductor] Codegen backed SymInt input runtime asserts (#185588)

When prefer_deferred_runtime_asserts_over_guards=True, Dynamo records backed-SymInt shape checks as deferred runtime asserts instead of guards. FX materializes those backed-only checks as input-graph aten._assert_scalar nodes, but regular Inductor lowering dropped those nodes. Only the AOTI full-runtime-assert path converted input-graph _assert_scalar nodes into wrapper AssertScalar operations, and the unbacked-symbol deferred assert path had no binding point for backed-only expressions.

This teaches Inductor to codegen input-graph _assert_scalar nodes when the assertion expression has backed free symbols and no unbacked symbols. Assertions with unbacked symbols continue to use the existing deferred path so they are emitted only after their unbacked inputs are bound. The fix preserves the existing AOTI full-runtime-assert behavior while covering the regular torch.compile path from the issue.

The alternative was to reject prefer_deferred_runtime_asserts_over_guards under torch.compile, but that would leave the underlying assert codegen gap in place. Emitting the missing wrapper assert fixes the root cause and keeps the config usable.

message:
Fix no-tensor-aliasing recompile reason for stale sources (#184793)

NO_TENSOR_ALIASING guard failure reporting re-evaluates the tensor source
expressions recorded by the first compile. When a later invocation changes a
container that held tensors into a value such as None, sources like
L['data'][0] no longer evaluate. The guard had already failed correctly, but
the diagnostic path raised TypeError before Dynamo could report the failure and
recompile.

Handle source-path lookup failures while building the no-tensor-aliasing
recompile reason. Sources that still evaluate are grouped for duplicate alias
reporting, while unavailable sources are included in a separate reason.
TypeError handling is limited to subscription/indexing failures so unrelated
evaluation bugs still propagate.

I considered only skipping failed sources, but reporting them keeps the
recompile reason actionable and preserves information about the stale guard
sources.

message:
[dynamo] Constant-fold unbound int/float/complex methods on constants (#198482)

I reproduced this myself with a small script. With the old build, `complex.__radd__` and `int.__radd__` gave up with `Unsupported`, `float.__rsub__(3.0, 1)` crashed inside Dynamo, and only `float.__neg__(3.0)` worked. The reason is that the old float branch passed on only the first argument and lost the second one; `__neg__` takes a single argument, so it was not affected. With the fix all of them give the correct result. Computing these calls at compile time is safe because they are deterministic: however many times you run them, there is no counter or other outside factor, so the result is always the same.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Calling a numeric builtin method through its type, e.g. `complex.__radd__(3j, 4.0)` or `float.__rsub__(3.0, 1)`, reaches `BuiltinVariable.call_method`. For int and complex there was no handler, so it graph broke with "Unsupported method call". For float there was a branch, but it called `getattr(float, name)(args[0])` with the receiver only, dropping every other positional and keyword argument. Any float method taking an argument therefore failed at trace time with an internal `TypeError: expected 1 argument, got 0`.
>
> This PR generalizes that branch to int, float and complex: when all arguments are `ConstantVariable`s, it calls the real unbound method on the Python constants and wraps the result. Exceptions raised by the call are re-raised as observed exceptions, so CPython behavior is preserved: operands of the wrong type return `NotImplemented`, a receiver of the wrong type raises `TypeError`, and `float.__rtruediv__(0.0, 1)` raises `ZeroDivisionError`. Non-constant arguments still fall through to the existing graph break. Adding per-dunder handlers was the alternative, but it would duplicate what the slot wrappers already do.
>
> Not covered here: `ClassPropertiesAndMethods.test_compattr` in CPython's test_descr still fails. The straightforward fix for it produced a silently wrong result for a descriptor that mutates its own state, so it is left for a separate change.

author: malfet
message:
[MPS] Use atomic counters for histogram/histogramdd and drop the eps slack (#198416)

Extends #192164 from `histc` to the remaining two bin-selection algorithms.

`histogramdd_kernel_impl` gave every thread its own `[numel, *hist_sizes]` slice and reduced with `at::sum_out`, so the temporary scaled with the product of input size and bin count -- 4.2 GB for a million elements into a thousand bins. Unweighted counts are integers, so all threads can accumulate into one `uint32` histogram with 32-bit atomics and the result stays order-independent; the counter is converted to the output dtype by the `copy_` that already had to happen, since `histogram` returns the input's dtype. Weighted sums stay on the per-thread path deliberately: float atomics would make the result depend on completion order, and that path is deterministic today.

The kernel also widened its range test by `eps = 4e-6` on both sides. The CPU kernel it was ported from compares against the edges exactly, so MPS counted elements that both CPU and numpy drop, and on the linear paths an element inside the slack could derive an index outside the histogram. Removing the slack restores the invariant that `upper_bound` never returns `first` for an in-range element; `pos` is now clamped to the valid range rather than only having its top edge folded down, which also covers the narrow-range case on the two linear paths. Both kernels share a `histogramdd_index` helper so the weighted and unweighted paths cannot drift apart.

Element offsets are now computed inline. Every input reaching these kernels is already 2-D (`histogramdd` reshapes to `[M, N]`, `histc` to `[numel, 1]`), so an element's offset is just `row * stride(0) + dim * stride(1)` in 64-bit arithmetic. That removes `kernel_index_offset`, the `[numel]` offsets buffer and the extra dispatch that preceded every call, along with the size guards that buffer needed, and collapses `histc`'s dense and strided kernel variants into one.

Finally, integral inputs are no longer accepted, and their kernel instantiations are dropped. CPU dispatches `histogram` over floating types only, and since the output carries the input's dtype, integer histograms silently overflowed. `histc` keeps its integer support, which matches CUDA.

Apple M5 Pro, `range=` supplied so neither column pays the bin-edge readback:

| op | elements | bins | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| histogram | 1,024 | 100 | 0.0722 ms | 0.0103 ms |
| histogram | 65,536 | 100 | 0.1964 ms | 0.0141 ms |
| histogram | 1,048,576 | 100 | 4.0947 ms | 0.0739 ms |
| histogram | 1,048,576 | 1000 | 37.6526 ms | 0.0748 ms |
| histogramdd | 4,096 | 16^2 | 0.0566 ms | 0.0240 ms |
| histogramdd | 262,144 | 16^2 | 2.3294 ms | 0.0525 ms |

Runtime no longer scales with bin count, and strided inputs now cost the same as contiguous ones. Weighted, which keeps the per-thread path, is essentially unchanged at ~1.4 ms.

`torch.histogram(x, bins=N)` without an explicit range still costs ~0.33 ms regardless of size, because `histogram_select_outer_bin_edges_kernel` reads the min and max back with `.item()`. That is a separate sync, not addressed here.

author: jansel
message:
Make SDPA backend checks safe for unbacked head dims (#184983)

`torch.export` can trace models that build repeat counts as tensors and
pass them to `repeat_interleave`. Without an explicit output size,
`repeat_interleave` creates unbacked symbolic sizes for the repeated K/V
head dimension. The fused SDPA backend selectors then used normal
`SymInt` comparisons such as `query_size_last == key_size_last`,
`head_dim <= max`, and alignment tests while deciding whether flash,
mem-efficient, or cuDNN kernels are viable. Those bool conversions guard
on the unbacked expressions before SDPA can fall back to math, producing
`GuardOnDataDependentSymNode` errors like `Eq(128, u0)`.

Switch those eligibility predicates to `sym_*` expressions evaluated with
`TORCH_GUARD_OR_FALSE`. Concrete and guardable symbolic inputs keep the
same result, while unbacked or unknown predicates conservatively reject
the fused backend and let the existing math fallback handle export. This
keeps the fix in backend selection instead of special-casing
`repeat_interleave` or SDPA export.

The main alternative would be requiring users to add `torch._check(...)`
for these repeated dimensions, but the backend picker only needs to know
whether a fused kernel is definitely legal. Treating unknown fused-kernel
preconditions as not viable is the narrower framework fix.

author: jeffdaily
message:
[ROCm] Honor depthwise_kernel="native" where the native kernel applies (#198221)

torch.backends.cudnn.flags(depthwise_kernel=...) is only consulted inside use_cudnn_depthwise(), which returns false when cuDNN is absent. On ROCm _select_conv_backend then took the next branch and picked MiopenDepthwise for "auto", "cudnn" and "native" alike, so asking for the native depthwise kernel had no effect unless MIOpen was disabled altogether. That is also why test_Conv2d_depthwise_kernel_flag was skipped on ROCm: all three modes ran the same kernel, so the comparison was meaningless.

The MIOpen depthwise branch now goes through ConvParams::use_miopen_depthwise(), which skips MIOpen when the flag is NATIVE and the native kernel can actually serve the input. "auto" and "cudnn" keep MIOpen unchanged.

What the native kernel can serve is taken from that kernel rather than from cuDNN's predicate. It is 2-D only, so a 5-D depthwise convolution stays on MIOpen: conv_depthwise3d has never run for fp32, fp16 or bf16 on ROCm, carries tighter numel <= INT32_MAX limits, and stages its grad_weight block reduction in scalar_t after accumulating in accscalar_t. It also indexes with 32 bits, and the tensors it range-checks are the input and the output, not the weight, in all three directions: the forward checks input and output, grad_input checks grad_input and grad_output, and grad_weight checks input and grad_output. A channel multiplier makes the output k times the size of the input, so an input just under INT_MAX can produce an output over it; the guard therefore tests input, weight and output element counts, taking the output count from conv_output_size(). Element counts are sufficient here because the backend contiguous-ifies before the kernel runs. Finally, a channels-last input stays on MIOpen when MIOpen is the one asked to suggest NHWC.

The remaining conditions cuDNN applies are deliberately not mirrored. On CUDA the flag is consulted only inside kernel_cond, which additionally requires fp16, at least 32 channels, no dilation and a square or 1-D stride, because those are the shapes cuDNN has a depthwise kernel for. MIOpen serves every dtype use_miopen() accepts and the native kernel handles all of them correctly, so "native" is a wider switch on ROCm than on CUDA.

With the test comparing two different kernels, fp16 needs a wider tolerance on ROCm. For fp16 depthwise 3x3 MIOpen selects the Winograd solver ConvBinWinogradRxSf2x3, whose output against an exact fp64 reference is off by up to 4.1e-3 over 50 seeds (about two fp16 steps at these magnitudes), while the native kernel stays at 9.8e-4; that gap is the same on gfx950, gfx942 and gfx90a and is reported as ROCm/rocm-libraries#12334. Across 500 seeds the largest MIOpen-to-native difference was 5.9e-3, so the ROCm atol is 1e-2; CUDA keeps 1e-3.

The tolerance is not what makes the test meaningful. Comparing numerics alone cannot fail in the state the test exists to catch: when "native" is not honored, all three modes run the same deterministic MIOpen kernel and return bitwise identical tensors, which passes at any tolerance. The test now asserts the selected backend, and a second test covers the 2-D restriction.

Test Plan:

On gfx950 (MI355X, ROCm 10.0), 533 passed, 343 skipped, 24 xfailed:

```
python -m pytest test/nn/test_convolution.py -k "depthwise or Depthwise or conv_backend"
```

Backend selection on a 4-D contiguous input returns CudaDepthwise2d for "native" and MiopenDepthwise for "auto" and "cudnn". A 5-D input stays on MiopenDepthwise under "native". A channel multiplier whose output exceeds INT_MAX while its input does not stays on MiopenDepthwise and runs, where routing it to the native kernel instead fails that kernel's own canUse32BitIndexMath(input) && canUse32BitIndexMath(output) check. torch.compile(dynamic=True) with the flag set matches eager across several batch sizes.

The tolerance measurements above were repeated on gfx942 and gfx90a, where MIOpen picked the same Winograd solver with the same 4.12e-3 error, so the fp16 gap is a property of the solver rather than of one architecture. The backend-selection changes have been exercised on gfx950 only.

message:
[ATen][ROCm] zero_: keep the memset fast path outside graph capture on ROCm 7.0.x (#198565)

Summary:
D120460087 reverted `zero_cuda_` to the `fill_` kernel for ROCm [7.0.0,
7.1.0) because `hipMemsetAsync` recorded into a HIP graph leaves stale
bytes (ROCm runtime bug, fixed in ROCm/clr 3038c4c3 and clean on 7.1.0).
That blanket revert also degrades every NON-capturing workload: an A/A
serving comparison on MI350X (same model, same host, good = pre-guard
build vs bad = post-guard build) shows `aten::zero_` switching from ~181
driver memsets to ~145 single-block `FillFunctor` kernel launches per
forward, and the resulting launch/contention storm inflates every kernel
on the box by 15-75% at identical grids — GPU time per forward 53ms ->
75ms (+42%), a direct serving QPS regression on the rocm70 fleet. Full
trace analysis: P2519416887.

The corruption requires an ACTIVE stream capture; outside capture the
memset is sound. So gate the fallback on capture status instead of
reverting wholesale: on ROCm 7.0.x, `zero_cuda_` takes the memset fast
path when `at::cuda::currentStreamCaptureStatus()` is `None` and falls
back to `fill_(0)` only while capturing. Same pattern as the capture
check in `Copy.cu`; `currentStreamCaptureStatus()` is context-safe (no
primary-context creation) and the pre-guard fast path already performed
an equivalent per-call capture-status query (`hipStreamIsCapturing`)
with no measurable cost. CUDA and other ROCm versions are unchanged
(`constexpr` short-circuit).

Behavior vs D120460087: identical under capture; restores the
D117790729 fast path (including `bits*`/`Float4_e2m1fn_x2` `zero_`
support) outside capture.
