author: A-Kokolis
message:
[torch][inductor] Extend KernelContextGuard profiling to template and combo kernels (#198433) (#198433)

Summary:

With `TORCHINDUCTOR_CPP_ENABLE_KERNEL_PROFILE=1` and `enable_kernel_context_guard`, AOTInductor opens each kernel call's `{ ... }` block with a `KernelContextGuard`, which publishes the kernel's name and stack trace on a thread-local for the duration of the launch. The previous diff in this stack extends that to the wrapper-level fallbacks. This one extends it to the template and combo kernels, and makes the profiling block a real C++ scope, which the template wrap needs to produce code that compiles.

 # Template and combo kernels

`codegen_template` writes its call line directly, and so does the combo-kernel path:

- `SIMDScheduling.codegen_template`, both the single-kernel branch and the `SizeHintMultiKernel` branch
- `SIMDScheduling.codegen_combo_kernel`
- `CppScheduling.codegen_template`
- `CUTLASSScheduling` and `ROCmCppScheduling`

Under max-autotune the template kernels are where most of the GPU time goes, so this was the largest gap in guard coverage. Each site takes the same change the non-template paths already use -- `kernel_profile_scope(kernel_name, node_schedule)` around `call_kernel`, directly after the `codegen_comment` that names it.

The guard rather than `profiled_kernel_scope`, because all of these already carry a `RAIIAtenRecordFunctionHandle`: a Triton kernel in its generated launcher and a C++ template from `CppTemplateKernel.maybe_codegen_profile`. A second handle at the call site would record them twice. (CUTLASS and ROCm get theirs from the next diff in the stack, on the `triton=False` branch of `CppWrapperGpu._generate_kernel_call_helper`.)

The `SizeHintMultiKernel` branch names its guard with `MultiKernel.launched_kernel_name()`. Under cpp_wrapper the choice among subkernels is made at compile time and the generated code calls the chosen `triton_*` kernel directly, so the dispatcher's `multi_kernel_N` never reaches the output; `call_kernel` takes its launch name from the same method, so the guard and the call cannot disagree.

The remaining `codegen_template` implementations are deliberately left alone, on one criterion: the backend cannot run under the C++ wrapper, so the scope would be a no-op there. `FlyDSLScheduling` says so outright -- its template returns `NotImplementedError("FlyDSL does not support AOT wrappers")` when `cpp_wrapper` or `aot_mode` is set. `CuteDSLScheduling` and `NVUniversalGemmScheduling` say it by construction: both call `generate_kernel_call(triton=True)` with no `triton_meta`, which `CppWrapperGpu` needs to build a launcher, and neither emits C++ for its kernel body. The same holds for the Helion `ExternalTritonTemplateKernel` that `SIMDScheduling`'s template branch can dispatch to, whose `call_kernel` writes Python.

For NVUniversalGemm the wrap would be worse than a no-op: its `call_kernel` calls `codegen_allocation` for the `local_reduce` primary output, a real graph buffer read after the call, so a block around it would scope that declaration away the day the backend does support the C++ wrapper. Helion's is the same shape and larger -- it codegens whole unfused epilogue nodes from inside `call_kernel` -- but it sits on a branch that is already wrapped, inert for the same reason.

 # Making the block a scope

The block is a real C++ scope, but the wrapper treated its braces as two strings in a flat line list, so every memo that decides whether a declaration is emitted reached across them. That produces generated code that does not compile, in two ways:

- Buffer reuse. `memory_plan_reuse` resets its `MemoryPlanningState` only at a subgraph boundary, so a workspace allocated and freed inside one block was handed to the next block's allocation as `auto workspace_3 = std::move(workspace_2);`, naming a variable the first block had destroyed. Two persistent-TMA matmuls are enough once the template call is wrapped: `error: use of undeclared identifier 'workspace_2'`.
- Lifetime. A `ZERO_PER_GRAPH` workspace -- the cooperative reduction semaphores -- is allocated once at first use and never freed, so its declaration lands inside whichever block asks for it first while every later block names it: `error: use of undeclared identifier 'semaphores_cuda_0'`. This one reproduces on the base revision, with none of the wraps in this stack, through the block the Triton launch path already opens.

`EnterKernelProfileScopeLine` / `ExitKernelProfileScopeLine` replace the two strings and bracket the state the way `EnterSubgraphLine` / `ExitSubgraphLine` already do for subgraphs: a fresh `MemoryPlanningState` in `memory_plan_reuse`, and a snapshot of `computed_sizes` and `codegen_int_array_var_cache`. The two memos are saved at different times on purpose -- `ensure_size_computed` runs while lines are being collected, `codegen_int_array_var` while they are being emitted -- so one is bracketed in `__post_init__` and the other in `codegen`. The per-graph workspace cannot be fixed by scoping at all, so `generate_workspace_allocation` emits it through `writeline_outside_kernel_profile_scope`, which inserts in front of the block instead of appending.

The cost is that a workspace no longer participates in buffer reuse while profiling is on. Ordinary buffers are unaffected: the scheduler allocates them before the block opens and frees them after it closes, so only the workspaces `call_kernel` allocates internally are inside one.

`CppWrapperCpuArrayRef` plans its allocations with its own copy of `memory_plan_reuse` rather than the base one, so it has to learn the two bracket lines separately. Nothing reachable puts a memory-planning line between those braces on a CPU ArrayRef compile today -- every CPU block wraps only `call_kernel`, the scheduler emits frees after it, and every workspace allocated inside a `call_kernel` is GPU-only -- so this is a divergence rather than a live miscompile. It is fixed anyway because the copy rots silently. Hoisting the shared body instead was considered and rejected here: the base loop swaps `estimate_peak` per subgraph and the ArrayRef one does not, and `codegen_while_loop` on that wrapper really does emit subgraph lines, so unifying them would change generated code for `while_loop` models under it -- a separate change wanting its own test.

`config.memory_planning` plans through `MemoryPlanner` instead of `memory_plan_reuse`, and `MemoryPlanner` does not see the bracket, so a pool first created inside a block would be declared there and named after it. Rather than teach `MemoryPlanner` about the markers -- which means hoisting `pool.codegen_create` out of open blocks -- profiling is disabled under it: `kernel_profile_enabled()` and `kernel_profile_scope` both return false when `config.memory_planning` is set.

 # Not covered

- The mix-order reduction call in `SIMDScheduling`, which passes `deallocate_ws=False` precisely because the workspace outlives the call. The scope bracket does not help there: the allocation and the free straddle the brace rather than sitting inside it. It also has no kernel name to give a guard -- it calls `codegen_comment` with `None`.
- The JIT cpp_wrapper stream declaration, which `write_get_raw_stream` emits inline under an `lru_cache`, so a stream first declared in one block is named by kernels in another. AOT mode takes the stream as a function parameter. The next diff in the stack hoists the JIT declaration to the entry prologue.

 # Behaviour

Profiling off, generated code is unchanged: `kernel_profile_scope` writes nothing when `cpp.enable_kernel_profile` is false and is a bare `yield` on the Python wrapper, so neither bracket line is constructed, the hoist index stays None, and `writeline_outside_kernel_profile_scope` degenerates to the `writeline` it replaced.

With profiling on and `config.memory_planning` set, no profiling record or block is emitted, including the C shim records that already existed. That combination produced C++ that did not compile, so this is a deliberate behaviour change to it.

Test Plan:
Run from `fbcode/`, on this diff (the previous diff applied, the next one not):

```
buck2 test mode/dev-nosan fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:test_aot_inductor -- \
  --regex 'test_aoti_profiler|test_kernel_profile|KernelProfileNumelScope|KernelProfileScopeMemoryPlanning'
buck2 test mode/opt fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:aot_inductor_arrayref_cpu_local -- \
  --regex 'test_aoti_profiler|test_kernel_profile'
buck2 test mode/dev-nosan fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:combo_kernels
```

64 passed / 0 failed (28 skipped), 35 passed / 0 failed, and 177 passed / 1 failed. The one combo failure, `test_combo_kernel_dynamic_scale_rblock`, fails identically in the full suite on the base revision with no diff in this stack applied. `mode/dev-nosan` because the default sanitizer config cannot initialize CUDA and silently skips every GPU variant.

 # What the new tests pin, and how each was shown to fail

Template wraps. With `simd.py` and `cpp.py` reverted to the previous diff and everything else kept, all six non-skipped variants fail:

- `test_kernel_profile_template_kernel` compiles a bias-free `nn.Linear` under max-autotune with ATEN excluded, so the template kernel is the whole graph, and asserts exactly one guarded kernel (on CPU an ordinary fused kernel shares the `cpp_` prefix and is guarded upstream). Fails with `expected one guarded kernel: []`.
- `test_kernel_profile_every_kernel_has_context` asserts, for a graph mixing a max-autotune template, a pointwise kernel and a reduction, that every kernel the wrapper launches is named by a `KernelContextGuard`. Launches are read off the `call_` launcher on GPU and the `extern "C"` symbol on CPU, so a template's internal micro-gemm helpers -- which the kernel body calls, not the wrapper -- are out of scope. Fails with the template named: `['triton_tem_fused_add_mm_relu_t_0']` on cuda, `['cpp_fused_add_mm_relu_t_0']` on cpu.

Scope machinery. Each piece was disabled by a one-line mutation that leaves every class defined, so the test module still imports and a test can only fail on its own assertion. All six non-skipped variants fail, each for its own reason:

- `memory_plan_reuse` ignoring the bracket: `test_kernel_profile_scope_is_a_scope_for_workspace_reuse` (two persistent-TMA matmuls) fails with `error: use of undeclared identifier 'workspace_2'`. It asserts a workspace is present, so a path that stops emitting one cannot pass with nothing exercised, and that no `std::move` reuse names a source declared in an earlier block.
- The workspace hoist degraded to an append: `test_kernel_profile_scope_hoists_per_graph_workspace` (two cooperative reductions) fails with `error: use of undeclared identifier 'semaphores_cuda_0'`. It also asserts the semaphores declaration precedes the first guard. This test fails on the base revision too, with no diff in this stack applied.
- The ArrayRef copy ignoring the bracket: `KernelProfileScopeMemoryPlanningTest` drives `CppWrapperCpuArrayRef.memory_plan_reuse` directly with a probe `MemoryPlanningLine` inside and outside a bracket pair, and fails with `unexpectedly identical: <MemoryPlanningState ...>`. An end-to-end test cannot reach this: nothing puts a memory-planning line inside those braces on a CPU ArrayRef compile, so a model-level test would pass with and without the change.
- The `memory_planning` veto removed: `test_no_block_is_emitted_under_memory_planning` fails with `The length of the sequences mismatch: 2 != 0`, i.e. a block was emitted.

`KernelProfileNumelScopeTest` builds a real `CppWrapperCpu` over an empty graph instead of hand-setting the attributes those paths happen to read, so a path that starts reading a new one exercises it rather than raising `AttributeError` and quietly testing nothing; its nesting test now codegens the collected lines and checks both memo stacks are balanced afterwards.

With the rest of the stack applied: the same profiler suite 76 / 0, `:gpu_cpp_wrapper` 335 / 0, the full `:aot_inductor_arrayref_cpu_local` 278 passed with one failure, `test_multi_device_cpu_with_stack_allocation`, which fails identically on the base revision, and `:control_flow` under `cpp_wrapper` 114 / 15, where the same 15 CPU tests fail identically on the base revision.

author: bvillasen
message:
CUDA: unrolled kernels for upsample_linear1d forward/backward when grid is small (#180885)

**Summary**
Adds alternative CUDA implementations for upsample_linear1d forward and backward that map each output sample to its own thread (unrolled over batch × channel × output width). The existing kernels parallelize only over output_width and loop over batch and channels inside each thread; the new path improves occupancy when ceil_div(output_width, block_size) is small by launching enough blocks to cover all (n, c, w) samples.

**Implementation**
`upsample_linear1d_out_frame_unrolled`: same math as `upsample_linear1d_out_frame`, but one interpolation per thread for a unique (batch, channel, output_index).
`upsample_linear1d_out_frame_backward_unrolled`: same adjoint logic as the original backward kernel, with atomic adds into grad_input preserved for overlapping source pixels.

**Heuristic**
If ceil_div(output_width, 512) < 128, the launch uses the unrolled kernels with grid size ceil_div(batch × channels × output_width, 512). Otherwise behavior is unchanged, and the original kernels are used.

**Motivation**
Wide, shallow launches (few blocks × 512 threads) often leave GPU underutilized; expanding parallelism across batch and channels targets those cases without changing numerics on the default path.

**Testing**
Performance has been measured to improve by a factor of 5-25x, depending on the size of the arrays.
Outputs have been tested to give the same numerical results.

[ROCm] Fix the NaN-check tests on boxes with core dumps enabled (#197885)

## Summary

The detecting tests in `test_c10d_nan_check.py` exit with `-6` instead of `6` on ROCm, with an `HSA_STATUS_ERROR_EXCEPTION` naming the `checkForNaN` kernel.

`CUDA_KERNEL_ASSERT` does compile to a device-side `abort()` on ROCm when `USE_ROCM_KERNEL_ASSERT` is OFF, but whether that kills the process is decided by the core-dump limit, not by the assert. The HIP queue-error callback, [`callbackQueue`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-systems/blob/9e915c90dc5550b173464949dc527ada64ac8767/projects/clr/rocclr/device/rocm/rocdevice.cpp#L4491-L4508) in ROCm/rocm-systems, does

```cpp
const bool should_abort =
  (is_oom || invalid_dispatch)
    ? !HIP_SKIP_ABORT_ON_GPU_ERROR
    : (amd::Os::DumpCoreFile() || !HIP_SKIP_ABORT_ON_GPU_ERROR);

if (should_abort) {
  abort();
}
```

The trap raised by the assert reports `HSA_STATUS_ERROR_EXCEPTION`, so the second branch applies. `DumpCoreFile()` is true when the soft `RLIMIT_CORE` is nonzero, and `HIP_SKIP_ABORT_ON_GPU_ERROR` defaults to true. With core dumps enabled the runtime aborts deliberately so a GPU core file can be written. With them disabled it keeps a sticky error that surfaces as an `AcceleratorError` at the next sync, exactly as a CUDA device-side assert does.

Upstream ROCm CI already runs with `--ulimit core=0` (`.github/workflows/_rocm-test.yml`), which is why these tests are green there and red on a developer box that inherits an unlimited core size. So this is a test-environment gap, not a defect in the NaN checker.

## What this changes

Tests that expect a catchable device error now run the code that provokes it inside a new `core_dumps_disabled()` context manager, which lowers the soft `RLIMIT_CORE` to 0. The runtime reads the limit at fault time, so this works after the GPU context already exists and needs no ROCm-specific branch. The fault is processed asynchronously, so the block stays open through the sync that surfaces the error. On exit the previous soft limit is restored, so a caller in a worker reused across tests (as in `MultiProcContinuousTest`) does not leave core dumps off for later tests. On Windows, which has no `RLIMIT_CORE`, the helper is a no-op. The ROCm carve-out in `ProcessGroupNCCLGroupTest.setUp` is removed because both platforms now exit `6` by the same mechanism.

## Test Plan

On 8x MI355X (gfx950), HIP 7.16.26362, under `ulimit -c unlimited`, which is the configuration that reproduces the report.

The three tests from the report, which fail with "Expected 6 but got -6" without this change and pass with it:

```
cd test && ulimit -c unlimited && PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_ROCM=1 python3 \
  distributed/test_c10d_nan_check.py \
  NcclLegacyNanCheckHookTest.test_env_var_auto_attach \
  Nccl2NanCheckHookTest.test_nan_in_input_detected \
  NcclLazyNanCheckHookTest.test_nan_in_input_detected
```

The full suite, green under both an unlimited and a zero core limit:

```
cd test && PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_ROCM=1 python3 distributed/test_c10d_nan_check.py
```

`test_nan_assert` is skipped on Linux upstream by six flakiness issues (166066, 164426, 177006, 166067, 177007, 176975). With those skips temporarily lifted all six dtype variants pass, covering the FP8 specializations and the 1G-element float16 buffer:

```
cd test && PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_ROCM=1 python3 -m pytest \
  distributed/test_c10d_nccl.py -k nan_assert
```

To confirm the helper is what fixes the tests rather than something else, the three tests from the report and the six `test_nan_assert` variants were rerun with `core_dumps_disabled()` stubbed out to a no-op; all of them fail again with "Expected 6 but got -6".

CI exercises less of this than the green checks suggest. All six `test_nan_assert` variants are skipped on Linux by the stacked `IS_LINUX` skips, and unittest skips before `setUp` runs, so neither `core_dumps_disabled()` in that test nor the changed `TEST_NAN_ASSERT_RETURN` is evaluated there; the `SIGABRT` expectation on ROCm rests on the local run above with the skips lifted. Since `_rocm-test.yml` already passes `--ulimit core=0`, the `test_c10d_nan_check.py` change is a no-op in CI. The green ROCm jobs show that nothing regressed, not that the fix works.

author: pearu
message:
torch/_native: less per-call work in the chunked linear_cross_entropy loop (#196134)

Three changes independent of the kernel's own arithmetic: `grad_linear_weight`
is no longer zeroed before the loop, because the first chunk writes it outright;
the kernel emits each row's loss contribution instead of the two statistics it
was built from, so the per-chunk loss arithmetic disappears; and the kernel's
staging default becomes `(512, 8)`. Together they are about 6% on top of the
kernel path on an H100 and about 10% on a B200, with every gradient bitwise
unchanged.

> None of the three changes what the loop computes. The first two remove work
> that existed only because of how the loop was written; the third changes only
> how the kernel schedules the work it already does.
>
> `grad_linear_weight` was allocated with `zeros` and then accumulated into,
> so the first chunk read back a (C, F) buffer that was known to be zero, after
> a (C, F) fill that nothing consumed. The first chunk now writes it with
> `mm(out=)` and later chunks accumulate as before, which drops a fixed
> `2 * C * F` bytes per call -- independent of the batch, the chunk size and the
> chunk count, so it reads as a share of call length: 4.8% at N=1024, 1.0% at
> N=16384. The accumulator is still zeroed when there is no first chunk to
> write it, which is the empty-batch early return.
>
> The kernel emitted `lse` and the target logit, and the caller then formed
> `scale * (lse - target_logit)` and reduced it, per chunk, on (Bc,) data:
> four launches moving 2 KB each. Both values are already in registers where
> the row's statistics are finished, so the kernel forms that product itself
> and writes one vector; the caller keeps one slot per row of the call and
> reduces once, after the loop, with `sum(out=loss)`. Nothing else read the two
> statistics, so they are gone from the kernel's signature. That slot is the one
> buffer here that is not a chunk, so the forward-only path -- which forms the
> loss chunk by chunk and never reads it -- does not allocate it.
>
> The staging default moves from `(512, 4)` to `(512, 8)` -- eight column tiles
> staged per barrier in pass 2 rather than four. `tiles_per_stage` does not
> reach pass 1's reduction, so this is a scheduling change and nothing else.
> Measured by calling the kernel directly from a captured CUDA graph, so that no
> GEMM time is in the number, over seven `(Bc, V)` chunk shapes -- `V` in
> {4096, 8192, 16384, 32000, 65536} at `Bc = 4096`, plus `Bc` in {1024, 2048} at
> `V = 32000` -- in both dtypes on an H100 and a B200, so 28 points: `(512, 8)`
> is faster at every one, by 1.4% to 12.2%, and uses less energy at every one,
> by 3.3% to 8.5%.
>
> Energy is worth reporting separately because it does not follow from the time.
> Per-call joules come from NVML's total-energy counter read over windows
> aligned to its updates, with the idle gaps subtracted at measured idle power.
> Where the board is not power-limited the faster setting draws 2-4% more power,
> so it saves less energy than time -- on B200 fp16, 9.1-12.2% faster for
> 6.9-8.5% less energy. Where the board is at its limit the two coincide: B200
> bf16 at `V >= 32000` runs both settings at ~1000 W, and there the energy win
> equals the time win. On H100 bf16 the faster setting also draws less power,
> 673 W against 691 W at `V=65536`, so it saves more energy (4.0%) than time
> (1.4%). Neither metric prefers `(512, 4)` at any point measured.
>
> That kernel is 4-25% of a chunked call and the rest is three cuBLAS GEMMs, so
> the retune is worth 0.1-2.9% end to end, largest where `in_features` is small
> relative to `num_classes`.
>
> Measured through the op's 12-shape sweep, paired per point across three
> repetitions -- the two states differ only in two Python files, so the arms are
> swapped in place at each point and a pair is measured seconds apart in one
> session.
>
> |                                    | H100 bf16 | H100 fp16 | B200 bf16 | B200 fp16 |
> | ---------------------------------- | --------- | --------- | --------- | --------- |
> | geomean                            | 1.058     | 1.065     | 1.095     | 1.099     |
> | min                                | 1.015     | 1.025     | 1.029     | 1.024     |
> | max                                | 1.143     | 1.160     | 1.377     | 1.390     |
> | above 1.0 in all three repetitions  | 11/12     | 12/12     | 12/12     | 12/12     |
>
> The maxima are at `in_features=1024` on the B200 and `V=4096` on the H100,
> where the fixed costs dominate; the minima are at `in_features=8192` and
> N=16384, where the surrounding GEMMs are largest. The single point not above
> 1.0 in every repetition is H100 bf16 at N=16384: 1.037 over a 0.992-1.042
> spread.
>
> Peak memory moves by at most the one new buffer, the (N,) fp32 loss terms:
> 0 to +48 kB measured, never more than `N * 4` bytes and sometimes nothing at
> all where the allocator reuses a freed block.
>
> The loss's summation order changes -- one reduction over N rather than a
> partial sum per chunk -- so the value is deterministic but not guaranteed
> bit-identical to a per-chunk accumulation. Measured against the previous path
> at four shapes spanning one to four chunks, in both dtypes, `grad_input`,
> `grad_linear_weight`, `grad_linear_bias` and the loss all came back bitwise
> identical.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> The kernel's isolation test asserts the loss term against a torch reference
> rather than against `lse` and the target logit separately. That pins the
> difference only: the row max cancels out of the term, and out of `g`, so what
> those assertions see of it is its effect on the row sum and not its value.
> Its other job, keeping `exp` in range, is pinned by
> `test_a_lone_high_column_pins_the_row_max`, where the row's maximum sits
> alone in one thread's column and a partial lost at either reduction stage
> takes the row out of fp32. The uniform-logit test became a stronger invariant
> in the process (`term == scale * log(V)`, whatever the logit value), and the
> aliased-buffer test still pins that the target logit is read before any write
> can occupy its bytes, since the term is now the only path by which that logit
> reaches an output.
>
> ```
> python test/python_native/test_lce_fused_grad_logits_kernel.py
> python test/python_native/test_linear_cross_entropy_override.py
> python test/test_nn.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> OPINFO_RESTRICT_TO_DSL=cutedsl python test/test_ops.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> lintrunner -m origin/main
> ```
>
> All pass on an H100 (sm_90) and a B200 (sm_100): 55 kernel tests, 31 override
> tests, 226 test_nn linear_cross_entropy tests, and the DSL-restricted test_ops
> run over its 5 OpInfo entries.

message:
torch/_native: one CuTeDSL kernel for the chunked linear_cross_entropy backward (#195829)

Per chunk the chunked path is three cuBLAS GEMM calls plus a set of pointwise
passes over the `(Bc, V)` logits buffer. This commit collects those passes into
one CuTeDSL kernel which also writes the dense gradient of logits into the
logits buffer itself, so the `index_add_` scatter and one buffer disappear.
Measured on an H100, the call takes 0.61-0.87 of eager's time at a lower peak
memory; on a B200, 0.30-0.78. The kernel is verified on sm_80, sm_90 and
sm_100, with its block knobs tuned on H100. Accuracy is level or better in
fp16; in bf16 the weight gradient's error runs 1.02x to 1.10x of eager's at the
same chunk size, from the same accumulation count.

> The `torch_nn::_linear_cross_entropy_batch_chunked` override stops delegating
> and computes the loss and gradients itself for the slice its `cond` claims.
> Per chunk: one cuBLAS matmul for the logits, one CuTeDSL kernel, and two more
> matmuls for the gradients.
>
> The kernel is what the change is about. Eager walks the `(Bc, V)` logits buffer
> five more times after the matmul -- row max, subtract, gather, `exp_`, row sum
> -- and then scatters the one-hot correction into `grad_linear_weight` with
> `index_add_`. Here one launch reads the raw logits twice (an online
> max-and-sumexp pass, then an apply pass) and writes the dense
> gradient-of-logits `g[n, v] = s_n * (softmax(z)[n, v] - [v == T_hat_n])`,
> emitting the two `(Bc,)` statistics the loss needs. Forming `g` densely is what
> makes both parameter gradients plain matmuls -- `grad_input = g @ W`,
> `grad_linear_weight = g^T @ X` -- so the scatter disappears: the backward is
> deterministic where eager's was not, and the separate `scatter_add` override
> stops being reachable from this path.
>
> `g` is written into the logits buffer's own storage rather than a second
> buffer, so a chunk costs one `(Bc, V)` buffer. That needs ordering, because
> `g[n, j]` occupies the bytes of `z[n, j / 2]`: pass 2 stages a group of column
> tiles in registers, synchronizes, and only then writes them, which is safe
> because a group's writes reach at most halfway into the columns it just read.
> The alternative that reaches the same footprint -- keeping the logits at low
> precision, as eager does for fp16 -- was measured and rejected for bf16: bf16
> stores `z` with absolute error ~|z| * 2^-9 while the softmax depends on
> DIFFERENCES of z, so gradients degrade once |z| reaches the tens, which is the
> regime a trained head operates in. At fp16 the buffer follows eager down to two
> bytes per element, since that is eager's own choice there and matching its
> footprint is the compatibility contract; the exponential and the scaled
> gradient still stay in fp32 registers, so this path is strictly more accurate
> than eager's at an identical footprint.
>
> Review `cutedsl_impl.py` first: it holds the eligibility predicate and the
> implementation, and it replaces the delegating implementation the routing commit
> installed. Eligibility is shapes, dtypes and device only, so it is safe under
> FakeTensor tracing; an input outside it never enters the override at all and the
> router falls back, which keeps "the kernel ran" observable rather than hidden
> behind an internal delegation. Its architecture condition is the DSL runtime's
> floor, which is also where this path's own arithmetic becomes available -- the
> logits matmul asks cuBLAS for an fp32 output from low-precision inputs, rejected
> below 8.0 -- and it lives in one predicate that `cond` and the tests both call.
> Holding out for a measurement on every capability would keep the kernel off
> hardware it runs on perfectly well; what is unmeasured below sm_90 is
> performance, not correctness.
>
> The implementation re-runs every check the op would have run -- an override
> installed at a backend key replaces the body that ran them, and the checks below
> it too -- by calling the op's own check functions, and it takes the per-row
> target correction and gradient weight the same way. Nothing about the op's
> contract is restated here; the previous commit moved each of those pieces out
> so this one could call them.
>
> Then `fused_grad_logits_kernel.py`: one block per row, because a row's own
> maximum and sum must be complete before any element of it can be written, and a
> block is the largest unit that can share them without a grid-wide barrier.
>
> Its two shape knobs -- the block width, and how many column tiles pass 2 stages
> per barrier -- are keyword arguments rather than constants, so a tuner or a
> caller with measured shapes can choose them without editing the file, and each
> combination compiles its own kernel. The defaults were measured on an H100 over
> a 3 x 5 grid at 20 chunk shapes, which the comment beside them summarizes: no
> setting wins everywhere, (512, 4) is never the worst and at most 1.39x behind
> the per-shape best, and since the chunked loop spends ~85% of its time in
> cuBLAS at the shapes where that share can be measured cleanly, the best setting
> at the loop's own chunk shapes is worth under 2% end to end. Their legal ranges
> are enforced, and one of them is a correctness limit rather than a preference
> -- above 32 warps per row the cross-warp combine would silently drop the
> surplus partials.
>
> Not covered here. The forward-only path (no gradient requested) has no `g` to
> write and keeps eager's statistics. `reduction='none'` keeps its own op and
> implementation. Probability targets, label smoothing, `acc_policy='accurate'`
> and fp32 input fall back through the router. One accuracy trade is worth
> naming: the dense `g` puts O(1) target-row contributions and O(1/V) off-target
> ones through a single matmul where eager keeps the scales apart, which costs
> ~14x on `grad_linear_weight` in isolation -- visible as ~15% at fp16 with
> `reduction='sum'`, invisible at bf16 where other error sources dominate. It
> buys the deleted scatter, the determinism and the speed.
>
> What the kernel buys, measured on an H100 through the op's own 12-shape sweep,
> in two comparisons.
>
> Against the op's own chunked path, at the same shapes and the same chunk size
> -- identical work, so this isolates the kernel: in bf16 the call takes
> 0.61-0.87 of eager's time (1.14-1.63x faster) at 0.77-0.97 of eager's peak
> memory; in fp16, 0.63-0.89 of the time at 0.86-1.00 of the peak.
>
> Accuracy splits by dtype. In fp16 the override is at least as accurate as
> eager everywhere: `grad_linear_weight` error is equal, 0.996-1.001 of
> eager's, and `grad_input` error is below it, 0.824-0.975. In bf16 the weight
> gradient is the one that gives ground -- 1.018-1.100 of eager's error,
> largest at `num_classes=16384` -- while `grad_input` stays level at
> 1.000-1.021. The dense `g^T @ X` accumulates in a different order than
> eager's `index_add_` scatter, which is where that comes from.
>
> The three matmuls are the same shapes at the same chunk size in both paths,
> so the whole win is in what surrounds them. Per chunk, eager makes five
> passes over the (Bc, V) logits buffer -- row max, subtract, exp, row sum, scale
> -- and then scatters the one-hot correction into grad_linear_weight with
> index_add_. Here one kernel reads the buffer twice and writes the dense
> gradient-of-logits once, and the dense form makes the scatter part of an
> ordinary matmul: less traffic and about a third of the launches (611 -> 195 per
> call at D=1024). The gain tracks how much of eager's time those passes were:
> 1.56x where the matmuls are cheap relative to the buffer (D=1024), 1.14x where
> they dominate (D=8192). Memory: one (Bc, V) fp32 buffer per chunk, with the
> gradient written into the same storage, replaces eager's logits buffer plus its
> downcast copy and its (Bc, D) scratch.
>
> Against liger-kernel 0.8.2, at constant memory: for each shape the override's
> chunk size is set so its peak matches liger's where that is reachable
> (0.997-1.025 of liger's peak at those points; elsewhere the whole batch fits
> one chunk and the peak stays at 0.48-0.87 of liger's). At that budget the
> override runs 1.25-6x faster than liger in bf16 (0.17-0.80 of its time) and
> 1.25-7x in fp16 (0.14-0.80), and 1.2-4x faster than eager at its default chunk
> size. The extra factor over the same-shape comparison is the memory itself: the
> override needs one (Bc, V) buffer per chunk where liger materializes more, so
> at equal peak it runs a chunk several times larger -- fewer chunks, fewer re-
> accumulations of grad_linear_weight, matmuls with a longer inner dimension. The
> chunk size stays under the caller's control; this comparison shows what the
> design returns when given liger's memory.
>
> This kernel's module imports the CuTeDSL runtime at import time, so the two
> tests that import every module under `torch/` --
> `test_public_bindings::test_modules_can_be_imported` and
> `test_testing::TestImports::test_circular_dependencies` -- need it in their
> optional-runtime ignore lists, where the other `_native` DSL kernels already
> sit. Both entries name the module rather than the package, so `cutedsl_impl`
> and the package `__init__` stay checked -- they import without the runtime
> and should keep having to.
>
> The new test files need the CuTeDSL runtime, so the B200 smoke job is the only
> place they can run at all -- nothing else collects them. That job already
> discovers every `test/python_native/test_*.py`, so they are picked up without
> being named. Added to it explicitly: `test_nn -k linear_cross_entropy`, the
> op's own accuracy harness. It compares fp16/bf16 against an fp64 reference
> with tolerances the op's author calibrated, and it runs in every CUDA job
> already -- but only where the DSL is installed does it measure this kernel
> instead of eager, so this job is where it earns its keep. The `-k` lines have
> to be named because `test_ops` and `test_nn` sit outside what that discovery
> reaches.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> The numbers above come from the out-of-tree benchmark harness, one process per
> configuration, over the same 12 shapes in both dtypes; the commands below are
> the in-tree correctness checks.
>
> ```
> python test/python_native/test_lce_fused_grad_logits_kernel.py
> python test/python_native/test_linear_cross_entropy_override.py
> python test/python_native/test_override_declarations.py
> python test/python_native/test_registry.py
> python test/test_nn.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> python test/test_ops.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> spin lint
> ```
>
> All of the above pass -- 54 kernel tests, 30 override tests -- including the
> two upstream batteries: `test_nn.py` runs 226 linear_cross_entropy tests and
> `test_ops.py` 191, both clean. Tests that
> need the kernel to be eligible skip where it is not, so a machine below its
> architecture floor reports skips rather than failures.
>
> The kernel's numerics are checked three ways. Against a torch expression of its
> contract, on its own, for three output dtypes across shapes that cross the block
> width and the staging group, including both aliasing ratios -- an fp32 buffer
> with narrower gradients, where a write lands halfway back, and the fp16 buffer
> where it lands on the column just read -- and including logits large enough
> that an unshifted exponential would overflow. End to end by the op's own
> fp64-referenced harness, which this change routes into the job that has the
> DSL. And two identical runs are required to produce bit-identical gradients,
> with `index_add_` asserted never to run, so the determinism the deleted scatter
> bought is pinned rather than asserted in prose.
>
> The op-level tests cover the paths a caller can reach rather than the kernel
> alone: the forward-only branch, which reimplements the loss with eager ops and
> which any `no_grad` call takes; `reduction='sum'`, a class weight and an
> `ignore_index` that fires, which are the four `_neg_weight_target` branches the
> row scale is built from; the empty batch, where the one allocation left
> unwritten has to be zeroed; and an out-of-range target, which traps as
> eager's index assert does, checked in a child process because the trap takes
> the CUDA context with it.

[benchmarks/dynamo] Use small-output accuracy policy for SigLIP (#197367)

## Summary
The next Triton pin bump will include https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11189, which updates Triton’s bundled CUDA libdevice. This change is not included in PyTorch's current Triton pin.

In particular, the Triton PR changes the implementation used for float32 `erf` (`__nv_erff`). On A10G, we observed that the updated `__nv_erff` changes GELU rounding in `vit_base_patch16_siglip_256`. This causes the benchmark’s synthetic training loss to fail its accuracy check:
  - Failing test: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35206051520/job/105174646954
  - Eager RMSE against FP64: 0.13545
  - Compiled RMSE against FP64: 0.47106
  - Ratio: 3.48×
  - Current limit: 3×

The failure is limited to the synthetic scalar loss that the benchmark creates to run backward. Inference and all other training results still pass with the existing thresholds.

This PR adds SigLIP to the existing small-output policy similar to what has been previously done (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/177042 for example) to allow a larger multiplier for small tensors.

author: simranbarnwal
message:
Make the aten.polar ref functional so it can be used as a decomposition (#198300) (#198300)

Summary:

The `aten.polar` ref has been unusable as a decomposition since it was added in #100345, and nothing caught it: `aten.polar` is not in `core_aten_decompositions()`, so Inductor calls the ATen kernel instead.

The bug: It builds its result and writes the halves into it, emitting `aten.copy_` into an intermediate. A decomposition is inlined into a graph that must stay functional, and `assert_functional_graph` allows `copy_` only into a graph input.

```
# before
result = torch.complex(abs, angle)
result.real = abs * torch.cos(angle)
result.imag = abs * torch.sin(angle)
return result

# after
return torch.complex(abs * torch.cos(angle), abs * torch.sin(angle))
```
Other changes:
- The dtype check moves onto the inputs and is shared with the `complex` ref: checking the products instead would let `cos`/`sin` promote an integral input to float. `aten.polar` is deliberately not added to `core_aten_decompositions()`.

- DTensor derives `polar`'s placement from the decomposition, so two `Partial()` inputs now give `Partial(sum)` rather than `Replicate()` -- correct, and one collective cheaper. `test_misc_ops_with_no_sharding_rules` updated.

Test Plan:
Registering the ref as an Inductor decomposition and compiling `torch.polar`.

**Before**, every case failed the same way on CPU (`float32`, `float64`, 0-d, broadcast) and on an NVIDIA A100 (`float32`, `float64`):

```
AssertionError: n=copy__1, n.args[0]=imag, placeholders={arg1_1, arg0_1}
```

On the A100 the tracer names the lane view `select_1` rather than `imag`; same defect.

**After**, all pass, plus `float16` (`complex32`) and Triton codegen on the A100.

buck2 test @//mode/opt fbcode//caffe2/test:test_ops -- --regex 'conversions_polar|conversions_complex'

```bash

7 passed.

`test_polar_decomposition_is_functional` is added to `caffe2/test/test_decomp.py` (OSS CI only). It decomposes `torch.polar` through the registered table and asserts the result is functional. Checked against both bodies: the old leaves two `aten.copy_` nodes, the new none.

author: joshuuuasu
message:
[ATen] Don't let a failed event record escape CachingHostAllocator::free (#198426) (#198426)

Summary:

`CachingHostAllocatorImpl::free()` records a CUDA event per stream the block was
used on. `record_stream()` goes through `CUDAEvent::record()`, which takes a
checked device guard (`ExchangeDevice`), so once the device context is poisoned
every record fails and `free()` throws.

`free()` is reached from `~StorageImpl`, so the throw crosses a `noexcept`
destructor and calls `std::terminate()`. Observed on an AMD MI300X predictor,
where the sticky `hipErrorLaunchFailure` left by an earlier asynchronous fault
turned response teardown into an abort:

```
PredictionResponse::~PredictionResponse()
 torch::distributed::WireMessage::~WireMessage()
  folly::IOBuf::~IOBuf()                      IOBuf.cpp:1112   <- noexcept
   folly::IOBuf::freeExtBuffer()              IOBuf.cpp:1249
    c10::TensorImpl::~TensorImpl()
     c10::StorageImpl::~StorageImpl()
      CUDACachingHostAllocatorImpl::free(void*)
       ...::record_stream(...)                CachingHostAllocator.h:473
        c10::cuda::CUDAEvent::record(CUDAStream)
         c10::cuda::ExchangeDevice()          -> throws c10::AcceleratorError
```

The `IOBuf` frame is incidental — any pinned-host tensor destroyed with a
poisoned context hits this, and the same crash has been seen with `StorageImpl`
at the top and no `IOBuf` involved.

This catches around the record loop. The block is not lost silently: the earlier
`event_count_ += streams_.size()` stays elevated, so the block is never
recycled, which is the same deliberate leak the stream-capture branch just below
relies on. Leaking one pinned block is preferable to aborting the process, and
it lets the caller's own sticky-error handling run instead of being pre-empted
by `terminate()`.

author: jeanschmidt
message:
[CI] Lower @claude job timeout to 55 minutes to match credential life time (#198521)

**Impact:** CI only, `@claude` review jobs on pytorch/pytorch
**Risk:** low

## What
Drops `timeout_minutes` for the Claude Code workflow from 120 to 55. The comment now explains the real limit.

## Why
#196537 raised the timeout to 2 hours so large reviews could finish. That can't work. Two credentials are minted at job start, last exactly 1h, and are never refreshed: the AWS STS session (IAM max is 3600s) and the Claude GitHub App token that posts the review. Past about 60 minutes the job can't call Bedrock or post the review. Between Sep 10 and Sep 22, 239 of 252 failures were 403s at 61-64 minutes. Those runs used up to an extra hour of runner time and posted nothing.

55 minutes keeps the kill a few minutes ahead of expiry. At exactly 60, some cancels still land after the session is gone.

# Notes
- A job-timeout kill shows up as `cancelled`, not `failure`. Alerts that count failures will go quiet, but long reviews still won't post. To track them, query for `cancelled` runs whose duration is at or above the cap.
- Raising the STS session duration by itself doesn't help, because the App token still expires at 1h. Reviews longer than 55 minutes would need token refresh in test-infra's `_claude-code.yml`, which is out of scope here.

author: desertfire
message:
[inductor] Detect uncaptured graph partitions for backward static inputs (#197438)

When the forward is graph-partitioned, saved activations produced outside a
CUDA Graph are reallocated every call, so the backward must not classify them
as static inputs. That condition was detected by counting partition maps, but
compute_graph_partition_maps drops partitions marked skip_cudagraph, so a
forward lowering to [uncaptured][captured] reports a single map and the
backward treated its eager-allocated activations as static. Record on the
lowered graph whether any partition stayed outside a CUDA Graph, and test that
instead of the map count.

The count is not merely incomplete, it is redundant: graph_partition groups
runs of nodes sharing a should_partition verdict, so two captured partitions
are never adjacent and more than one map already implies an uncaptured
partition. The remaining partition_maps check still matters, rejecting a
forward where every partition was skipped.

This change was authored with the assistance of an AI coding agent.

author: laithsakka
message:
[re-land] avoid re-allocation of base views when generating example inputs. (#198398) (#198398)

Summary:

### What changed since revert:
pdating test_pad_non_zero_cpp_wrapper in test_inplace_padding.py to expect the new _autotune_storage_N = generate_example_value(...) + torch.as_strided(...) codegen form (the test that caused the revert), and adding a GPU peak-memory regression test for the concat autotuning case.
### Summary

Compile-time autotuning currently generates each tensor argument independently. For concat foreach kernels, output slices have large strides but share one physical output allocation at runtime. Generating each slice independently can therefore allocate nearly the full concat storage for every argument and cause a compile-time CUDA OOM.
This change identifies the canonical owning buffer for each supported tensor argument. It creates one synthetic backing allocation per owner and reconstructs each logical argument with torch.as_strided, preserving its size, stride, and offset.
Both allocation modes retain their existing behavior. Per-kernel mode shares backing storage within one kernel and deletes it afterward. Wrapper-wide mode caches logical arguments and backing storage across kernels.
The implementation supports ordinary owning tensors, direct views, mutation targets, and nested MutationLayoutSHOULDREMOVE or NonOwningLayout aliases that do not introduce another view transformation. Unsupported layouts, dtype-reinterpreting views, TMA descriptors, multiple nested ReinterpretView nodes, and other chains requiring offset composition continue using independent synthetic allocations.

message:
[BE] Refactor reductions on MPS (#198494)

Refactor reductions on MPS.

I believe code is now better readable and more concise. `ReductionKernel` which defines what kind of kernels we have, `ReductionLayout` which is a struct for the layout of the reshaped tensor. As an example given a tensor of `[128, 128, 1024, 64, 32, 16].sum(dim=2)`  we reshape it in a following way -> `[outer_size, dim, inner_size]`, where `outer_size` is prod of all numbers before dim=2, i.e. being `128 * 128` here and inner_size being `64 * 32 * 16` (i.e. prod of all shapes after dim=2), so shape before reduction would be `[16384, 1024, 32768]`.

author: jeffdaily
message:
[ROCm] Run the SDPA view-grouping test at ieee fp32 precision (#198289)

test_pattern_fails_with_mismatched_view_grouping_gpu has failed deterministically on rocm-mi300 on every trunk run since #195383 landed. The failure is the numeric assert in the test's second _check_common, not the pattern matching the test is about, and it is bit-identical every run: greatest absolute difference 0.0011501904809847474 at index (2, 1, 14, 7), against atol=1e-3.

TestSDPAPatternRewriterTemplate.setUp sets fp32_precision="tf32". On NVIDIA that keeps both sides of the comparison at the same precision. On ROCm it does not: hipBLASLt honors the flag as XF32 on gfx942 and gfx950, so the eager bmm reference is degraded, while the fused path lowers to AOTriton, which computes in full fp32 whether the flag says "ieee" or "tf32". The test compares a reduced-precision reference against a full-precision kernel, with the thing under test being the more accurate of the two. Measured against an fp64 gold on gfx942: under "ieee" the eager reference is 2.41e-06 from gold and the fused result 2.46e-06; under "tf32" the reference is 6.04e-03 while the fused result is unchanged. This pattern is more exposed than its neighbours because it applies no 1/sqrt(d) scaling and adds a mask, so the scores are large and softmax amplifies the XF32 error.

setUp sets tf32 because fuse_attention.py:970 gates the fp32 SDPA fusion on it, but that gate does not reach this pattern. _sfdp_pattern_24 is registered with _sfdp_extra_check passed uncalled (fuse_attention.py:1338), unlike every neighbour, so the matcher gets the factory's inner closure back as a truthy value and _sfdp_params_check never runs. Confirmed at runtime: the pattern fuses under "ieee" with the fuse_attention counter at 1 and the two sides agreeing to 1.18e-06. That uncalled check is a separate upstream defect worth fixing on its own; note that fixing it will make this test stop fusing under "ieee" and fail loudly on has_fuse_pattern, at which point the gate's ROCm premise needs revisiting too, since the ROCm fused kernel is exact and the gate still refuses it under "ieee".

Given that, run this test at "ieee" on ROCm. Both sides are then exact and atol is left alone. recover_orig_fp32_precision restores the flag, which is required because TestCase.tearDown's fp32 leak detector runs before this class's own tearDown restore. The condition is device-gated so the cpu variant bound from the same body is unaffected.

The alternative was a ROCm-conditional tolerance bump, matching the precedent at test_fused_attention.py:188-190. It was rejected: the divergence needs atol=2e-2 to clear, and on a tensor whose elements are ~0.3 that leaves the numeric assert testing essentially nothing, so it would accept a genuinely broken fusion.

Test Plan:

    python -m pytest test/inductor/test_fused_attention.py -k "test_pattern_fails_with_mismatched_view_grouping" -q -p no:randomly
    python -m pytest test/inductor/test_fused_attention.py -q -p no:randomly

On gfx942 the CI failure reproduces exactly before the change (both GPU variants fail with the same bit-identical difference as CI) and all 4 variants pass after. Whole file after the change: 158 passed, 8 skipped, 0 failed, matching the baseline.

Arch coverage for the claim that the ROCm fused path is fp32-exact wherever XF32 exists: gfx90a and gfx1100 have no XF32, so the reference is unaffected there either way; gfx942 and gfx950 were both measured with a standalone probe driving eager bmm and F.scaled_dot_product_attention at the test's shapes, and both select EFFICIENT_ATTENTION with a fused error of 2.456e-06 under either flag. Worth recording: gfx950 has XF32 but degrades far less than gfx942, 7.44e-05 against 6.04e-03, so its worst diff clears the existing atol and this test passes on gfx950 even unfixed. MI355X CI would not have caught the regression.

Not a regression from this change: with TORCH_ROCM_FA_PREFER_CK=1 the fp32 SDPA falls back to the MATH backend and both GPU variants of this test already fail on unmodified main, on the "aten._scaled_dot_product not found" assert rather than numerics. That configuration is unaffected either way.

This PR was authored with the assistance of an AI agent (Claude). The analysis and test results were verified by hand.

author: David-Wu1119
message:
Fix two log messages that print a literal %s (#198244)

Two log calls have a `%s` placeholder and no argument to fill it, so the placeholder is printed verbatim.

**`torch/_dynamo/package.py`** — the disk-cache load failure:

```python
except Exception:
    counters["dynamo_cache"]["dynamo_cache_error"] += 1
    logger.warning("Failed to load package from path %s", exc_info=True)
```

`exc_info=True` is a keyword argument, so it does not feed the format string. The warning reads `Failed to load package from path %s` and never names the path, which is the one thing it is there to report. `path` is computed five lines above, so it is passed now.

**`torch/_inductor/select_algorithm.py`** — the CUDA autotuning handler:

```python
except CUDACompileError:
    if not isinstance(choice, CUTLASSTemplateCaller):
        log.exception(
            "CUDA compilation error during autotuning: \n%s. \nIgnoring this choice."
        )
```

Here the `except` binds no exception, so there is nothing to interpolate, and any user whose kernel fails to compile under `max_autotune` sees a bare `%s` at ERROR level. Since `log.exception` already prints the exception and its traceback, the placeholder is dropped from the message rather than binding the exception, which would trip `TRY401` (redundant exception object in a `logging.exception` call).

This shape is invisible to lint: ruff's `PLE1206` only fires when at least one positional argument is passed, so a message with a placeholder and none is never flagged. Both lines are message-only changes with no behavior change.

`ruff check` reports the same 3 pre-existing findings on these two files before and after, and `ruff format --check` is clean.

Found with an AST scan for messages that have `%` placeholders and no arguments; written with AI assistance and reviewed line by line.

author: egeboy35
message:
Treat an engaged-but-undefined optional weight as no weight in rms_norm (#195574)

`aten::rms_norm` declares `Tensor? weight=None`, but `rms_norm_composite` gates the weight multiply on `weight_opt.has_value()` alone. A C++ caller forwarding a possibly-undefined Tensor where an optional is expected produces an engaged optional holding an undefined tensor, and that reaches `upcasted_result.mul(<undefined>)`:

```
Expected a proper Tensor but got None (or an undefined Tensor in C++) for argument #1 'other'
```

`at::layer_norm` accepts the same call, because `math_native_layer_norm` also checks `.defined()`. That asymmetry is the bug.

The MPS branch of `rms_norm_symint` had the same gate and would have handed an undefined weight to `_fused_rms_norm_mps`, so it is fixed here rather than left as a twin of the one being removed. I have no MPS hardware; that half is reasoned from the source and left to CI.

### Test

The failure is only reachable from C++ — Python cannot construct an engaged optional holding an undefined tensor — so the regression test is a gtest in `undefined_tensor_test.cpp`, which `aten/tools/run_tests.sh` already runs. It went there rather than `math_kernel_test.cpp`, which is built but appears in no runner list and so would not have gated this PR.

This machine's Device Guard policy refuses to launch freshly linked gtest binaries, so the assertions were exercised through a `cpp_extension` against a locally built `torch_cpu`. Same harness before and after:

```
before:  engaged-but-undefined  : THREW -> Expected a proper Tensor but got None ...
after:   engaged-but-undefined  : ok, numel=6
```

and the test's own assertion, plus a check that a real weight is still applied:

```
equal(undef, nullopt)  : true
max abs diff           : 0
weight still applied   : true
```

### Related

#193936 adds `torch::nn::RMSNorm` and currently works around this by converting an undefined weight to `std::nullopt` before calling `at::rms_norm`. If this lands first, that conversion and its comment can be dropped there.

Developed with AI assistance (Claude); I reproduced the failure, wrote the fix and ran the checks above.

message:
Validate input/hidden dimension consistency in RNN cells (#191232)

Fixes #175978

## Summary

LSTMCell, GRUCell, and RNNCell segfault when input and hidden state have different numbers of dimensions (e.g. 1D input with 2D hidden). The is_batched flag is determined solely from input.dim(), so when hidden states disagree on rank, they get incorrectly unsqueezed into 3D tensors that cause out-of-bounds memory access in GEMM.

## Changes

1. torch/nn/modules/rnn.py: Add dimension consistency checks in all three cell forward methods
2. aten/src/ATen/native/RNN.cpp: Add defense-in-depth dim check in check_rnn_cell_forward_hidden
3. test/test_nn.py: Test all 6 mismatch cases across all three cell types

Prior PR #176070 was approved in concept but went stale. This fix addresses the root cause (Python batching logic) across all three cell types and adds a centralized C++ check per the review suggestion on #176070.

author: tvukovic-amd
message:
[ROCm][Windows] Audit license-files: explicit enumeration + audit test (#183434) (#185813)

Fix for [pytorch/pytorch#183434](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/183434).

The PEP 639 migration (#180237) replaced the old concatenated `LICENSE` blob with per-file `license-files` in `pyproject.toml`. The existing recursive globs:

```toml
license-files = [
    "LICENSE",
    "third_party/**/LICENSE",
    "third_party/**/LICENSE.txt",
    "third_party/**/LICENSE.rst",
    "third_party/**/COPYING.BSD",
]
```

matched **107 files** in the source tree, but only **~59** represent code that actually ships in the wheel. The remainder are over-collection from nested submodule vendoring — tests, docs, bindings, build tools, and dynolog transitive deps.

This caused two concrete problems:

1. **Windows `MAX_PATH` failures** — PEP 639 copies each license into the wheel under `.dist-info/licenses/`, doubling path length. Deep dynolog paths (up to **135 characters** relative) exceeded Windows limits during packaging.
2. **Incorrect license surface** — including files like `cpr/test/LICENSE` (GPL-3.0) in the distribution metadata, even though that code is never compiled or linked into PyTorch.

## How the explicit list was derived

The 59 paths in `pyproject.toml` were **not** picked manually one-by-one. They are the output of a repeatable audit that mirrors the issue author's "conservative exclusion" (which estimated ~61 paths on ~108 glob matches; this tree yields **107 discovered → 59 shipped**).

### Step 1 — Start from the old glob universe

Run the same patterns PyTorch used before the audit:

```toml
LICENSE
third_party/**/LICENSE
third_party/**/LICENSE.txt
third_party/**/LICENSE.rst
third_party/**/COPYING.BSD
```

This finds every candidate license file the recursive globs would have collected (**107 files** in the current tree).

### Step 2 — Apply exclusion rules

Each candidate is classified using structural rules in `test/test_license.py`. Paths that match non-shipping trees — tests, docs, googletest, bindings, dynolog transitive deps, deep nested vendoring — are **excluded**.

### Step 3 — Whatever survives = explicit list

The shipped set is computed directly from discovery minus exclusion:

```python
shipped = [path for path in discovered if not is_excluded(path)]
# → 59 paths
```

Those 59 paths are what go into `pyproject.toml` `license-files`. The list is the **output of the audit**, not a separate manual pick.

### Step 4 — Test locks it in

`test_pyproject_license_metadata` asserts:

```python
project["license-files"] == shipped
project["license"] == spdx_from(shipped)
```

If a submodule is added or moved, the test fails until `pyproject.toml` and the exclusion rules are updated together.

author: fegin
message:
[FSDP2] Add gradient accumulation finalization API (#196640)

Add a public FSDPModule method, `finalize_gradient_accumulation`, that completes deferred gradient reduction on the caller thread. It reshards parameters and reduces the accumulated gradients into sharded `.grad`.

The autograd final callback runs on the autograd thread, so its stream waits cannot be captured in a CUDA graph. Reuse its cleanup on the caller thread, but track deferred reduction explicitly so finalization does not rerun post-backward or reduce zero gradients after a synchronized backward. Temporarily override gradient synchronization, all-reduce, reshard, and last-backward settings, then restore them.

A separate callback would duplicate iteration cleanup. The deferred-work flag keeps one cleanup path while gating the reduction. HSDP all-reduce-only deferral requires a separate collective and gradient view-out path, so reject it explicitly instead of silently skipping gradients.

message:
[XPU] Register linalg._powsum and _foreach_powsum.Scalar for XPU (#189238)

Registers the XPU dispatch keys for `linalg._powsum` and `_foreach_powsum.Scalar` so the kernels added in torch-xpu-ops (PR: https://github.com/intel/torch-xpu-ops/pull/4195) can be reached.

#### Changes

No new ops or schemas are introduced; this only wires existing op definitions to the XPU backend in `aten/src/ATen/native/native_functions.yaml`:
- `linalg__powsum`: add `XPU` to the existing `CPU, CUDA` dispatch list (shared host function).
- `_foreach_powsum.Scalar`: add `XPU: foreach_tensor_powsum_xpu`.

#### Testing

With the torch-xpu-ops kernels built in, the upstream `test_powsum*` / `test_foreach_powsum*` tests in `test/test_linalg.py` pass on the XPU device (6 passed, 1 skipped `@onlyCPU`).

author: A-Kokolis
message:
[torch][inductor] Extend KernelContextGuard profiling to the fallback kernel paths (#179699) (#179699)

Summary:

With `TORCHINDUCTOR_CPP_ENABLE_KERNEL_PROFILE=1`, AOTInductor emits a kernel
call inside a `{ ... }` block, and with `enable_kernel_context_guard` on top of
that the block opens with a `KernelContextGuard`. The guard publishes the
kernel's name and stack trace on a thread-local for the duration of the launch,
which is what lets a consumer attribute a launch back to the operator that
issued it. It is a different thing from the `RAIIAtenRecordFunctionHandle` that
gives a trace event its External id: a Triton kernel already gets one of those
in its generated launcher, and an extern kernel from the C shim path.

The guard reached only the kernels emitted through `codegen_node_schedule` and
`CppScheduling.flush`. Every other path that writes its own kernel call had
none. This diff covers the wrapper-level fallbacks; the template and combo
kernel paths are in the next diff in the stack.

 # Wrapper-level fallbacks

These bypass `generate_c_shim_extern_kernel_call` and emit their own call line:

- `_generate_scatter_fallback` (`aten::scatter_`, `scatter_reduce_`)
- `_generate_index_put_fallback` (`aten::index_put_`)
- `codegen_device_copy`, from both `DeviceCopy` and `InplaceCopyFallback`
(`aoti_torch_copy_`)

Nothing records these at all, so they get `profiled_kernel_scope`: the guard
plus a `RAIIAtenRecordFunctionHandle`, which is what the C shim path already
emits for an extern kernel. `profiled_kernel_scope` delegates the block to
`kernel_profile_scope` rather than opening it itself, and keeps its own gate --
`kernel_profile_enabled()`, which also requires a platform where the handle
exists -- passing it down so the block opens on exactly that condition.

Every reference a fallback's call needs is computed before its block opens, so
nothing inside one declares a variable that a line after the block could name.

 # Argument metadata

`write_record_function_handle` takes the same ordered
`profiling_args: list[str | None]` the C shim path uses -- one entry per
operator schema argument, a tensor handle or a placeholder. Both build the
conversions through `_profiling_ivalue_lines`, so the two cannot drift on the
order, the independent numbering of tensors and placeholders, or the variable
names; the shim path keeps its `out` entry by passing the output handle.
`scatter_reduce.two` records `[self, dim, index, src, reduce, include_self]`.

Three call sites reorder their arguments on the way to the kernel, so the
shared builder cannot derive the list for them, and they pass it themselves via
`make_profiling_args`: scatter keeps `dim` between its tensors, index_put's
index list is spread across the node's inputs and carries a None per unindexed
dimension, and `DeviceCopy`'s destination is the node's own output rather than
one of its inputs. `InplaceCopyFallback` is not one of them -- its inputs are
already `[dst, src]`, so the shared builder gets `copy_`'s schema order right
and it passes nothing. Each entry is derived separately from the IR node rather
than reusing the expression handed to the kernel: a reinterpret view's
expression owns the handle it names, so using it twice would free it once too
often.

`make_profiling_args` builds nothing unless the wrapper will record it, which is
what `records_profiling_args()` reports. That matters on
`CppWrapperCpuArrayRef`: an `ArrayRefTensor` is not an `AtenTensorHandle`, so
the ivalue conversion cannot be called on one, and deriving the list anyway
would make a reinterpret view mint a handle with no owner.

`scatter_fallback_kernel_name` gives the record and the emitted call one name:
`CppWrapperCpu` appends `_out` to the C shim symbol, the Python wrapper leaves
the resolved name alone. Trace consumers key on the emitted name, so recording
the ATen symbol instead would have kept scatter out of the analysis.

 # Not covered

- `generate_fallback_kernel_with_runtime_lookup`. Its three JIT variants
(`_nopython`, `_boxed`, `_python`) emit `RAIIAtenTensorHandle <output>;` at
the caller's scope and fill it inside their own block, so a profiling block
around the call would scope the fallback's outputs out of the code that
consumes them. The AOT proxy-executor variant carries no such declaration,
but the guard needs a kernel name and a node to take stack traces from, and
neither reaches `generate_fallback_kernel_with_runtime_lookup_aot`.

 # Behaviour

Profiling off, generated code is unchanged: `profiled_kernel_scope` reads its
gate once and puts both the block and the record behind it, and
`make_profiling_args` returns before it can emit codegen for a reinterpret
view. `kernel_profile_scope` writes nothing when `cpp.enable_kernel_profile` is
false and is a bare `yield` on the Python wrapper.

Test Plan:
Run from `fbcode/`, on this diff alone (the next diff not applied):

```

  --regex 'test_aoti_profiler|test_kernel_profile|KernelProfileNumelScope'
buck2 test mode/opt fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:aot_inductor_arrayref_cpu_local -- \

 # What the new tests pin, and how each was shown to fail

With this diff's `wrapper.py`, `cpp_wrapper_cpu.py`, `cpp_wrapper_cpu_array_ref.py` and `ir.py` reverted to the base revision and the tests kept, every non-skipped variant of the four new tests fails (11 of 16; the other five are MPS, and the device copy on CPU, which needs a non-CPU device):

author: jansel
message:
[dynamo] Graph break on shape-changing differentiable Tensor.data assignment (#186512)

DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 style forward hooks gather partitioned parameters by
assigning a full-sized tensor to Parameter.data before a submodule runs,
then repartition the same parameter back to an empty tensor in a forward
hook. Dynamo traced those hook-side mutations into the same graph as the
module compute.

AOTAutograd builds backward graphs from the original metadata of differentiable
graph inputs. If a traced .data assignment changes an input's shape, later
forward operations can produce gradients with the replacement shape for an
input whose original shape is different, causing an invalid-gradient failure.
This invariant applies to ordinary differentiable tensors as well as Parameters.

Fix this by graph breaking before shape-changing .data mutations on
differentiable tensors. Fake shapes are compared with sym_eq and
statically_known_true, so symbolic equality is not guarded and unbacked SymInts
are not evaluated. If equality cannot be proven, Dynamo conservatively breaks;
provably same symbolic shapes and non-differentiable assignments remain
traceable. The check does not depend on ambient grad mode because a mutation
inside a local no_grad block can be followed by differentiable use.

A fully traced alternative would require AOTAutograd-safe semantics for changing
differentiable input metadata. This patch uses the narrower correctness
boundary and lets Dynamo resume on the tensor compute after the mutation.

Fixes #115484

message:
[Lowering Memory] Release the allocator pool after constant serialization (#197659) (#197659)

Summary:

Hands the caching allocator's pool back to the driver once graph constants have
been serialized to host. The constants were just copied out, but the blocks they
occupied stay reserved; packaging then allocates on top of that slack and sets a
new high-water mark.

**Why this is at a different stage from the autotune offload (D120287672), and
has to be.** The offload is a context: it frees the constants for the duration of
autotuning and restores them on exit. Immediately after autotuning they are live
on device again, so there is nothing to hand back at that point. Constant
serialization is the first moment they have been copied to host and are genuinely
dead on device. The offload shrinks the live set *during* autotuning; this returns
the resulting free-but-reserved slack *after* the constants are gone for good, and
before packaging allocates on top of it.

Note that by this diff itself, peak memory might not see any reduction due to there being other bottlenecks during lowering.

author: malfet
message:
[BE] Compute linspace/logspace step in the opmath type for half and bfloat16 (#198415)

`range` (RangeFactories.cpp:156) and `arange` (RangeFactoriesKernel.cpp:23) already widen the step via `at::acc_type`, and CPU `logspace` computes its step and `pow` in double. CPU `linspace`, and CUDA `linspace` and `logspace`, kept everything in `scalar_t`, so for half and bfloat16 the step was rounded to the output dtype before being multiplied by the index, and CUDA `logspace` also evaluated `pow` in half. For `linspace(0, 10, 38)` element 3, CPU returned 0.810546875 where the correctly rounded half value is 0.811035156.

The step type was written with integer range in mind (See #27957: "step should be of double type for all integral types"), and #43578 later added bfloat16 by editing only the dispatch macro line. Delete `NOTE [Linspace+Logspace precision override]` in `test_tensor_creation_ops.py` that recorded "our Linspace and logspace torch.half CUDA kernels are not very precise", but #31962, which introduced it, only checked that the output matched PyTorch 1.2.0 and pinned the measured error as a 0.0039 tolerance without root-causing it.

`at::opmath_type` rather than `at::acc_type`: `acc_type<float>` is `double` on CPU but `float` on MPS and CUDA, which would newly desynchronise float32, and `acc_type<c10::complex<float>>` is `c10::complex<double>`, which has no `operator+` with `c10::complex<float>` and does not compile under this dispatch macro. `opmath_type` promotes exactly half and bfloat16 and leaves float, double and complex bit-identical.

Summary:

Inference effect-token insertion shifts `static_input_indices` by the number of tokens. When `unlift_effect_tokens` removes those leading inputs, the metadata keeps the shifted indices. Inductor can then classify an ordinary runtime tensor as static and omit its alignment check, allowing a valid offset view to reach a kernel specialized for 16-byte alignment.

```
Original: [weight, data], weight is input 0
Add log token: [token, weight, data], weight is input 1
Remove token: [weight, data], BUG: still says input 1
```

Restore the indices when the inference graph removes its token arguments. The correction stays in the inference path because joint training does not apply the insertion offset. Add a CPU compiler-metadata regression for both retained and removed tokens, checking that static indices still identify the parameter and buffer.

author: Nicoshev
message:
Enable Sleef in the NNC LLVM codegen on aarch64 (#198002) (#198002)

Summary:

NNC's LLVM backend only ever reached Sleef on x86. Two things blocked aarch64,
and either one alone was sufficient:

- `intrinsic_symbols.cpp` registers the `Sleef_*` symbols with the JIT inside a
  `#if !defined(_MSC_VER) && defined(__x86_64__)` block, so on aarch64 the JIT
  knew about no vector math symbols at all.
- `getSimdFunction()` gated vectorized lowering on the target feature string
  containing `+avx`, which is never true on aarch64.

This diff registers the Advanced SIMD entry points and replaces the `+avx` test
with `targetTriple.isAArch64() || +avx`. Advanced SIMD is mandatory on aarch64,
so there is no runtime capability to probe; x86 keeps its existing AVX gate.
Sleef emits the unsuffixed `Sleef_logf4` names as aliases for the `advsimd`
implementations (`ENABLE_ALIAS`, generated by `mkalias.c` from the same shared
`funcList` as x86), so the names and ULP suffixes match the x86 block exactly.
That alias is off for Apple and Windows targets, hence the extra guard.

The lane count needed a second fix. `LoopNest::vectorizeInnerLoops()` splits
inner loops at 8 with a 4-wide tail, and `getSimdFunction()` bakes that width
straight into the symbol name, so it asked for `Sleef_logf8`. Advanced SIMD
tops out at 4 floats / 2 doubles, so the lookup would have missed and every
transcendental would still have fallen back to one scalar libm call per lane.

Rather than shrink the loop vectorization width -- which would also halve the
unroll factor for plain arithmetic kernels that have nothing to do with Sleef
-- `getSimdFunction()` now searches downward from the requested width and
reports the width it settled on, and the new `emitSimdCall()` slices the
operands and concatenates the results. An 8-lane float body therefore calls
`Sleef_logf4` twice in a row. Loop widths in `loopnest.cpp` are unchanged.

This also picks up `double` on x86, which never had an 8-wide entry point
either: `lanes == 8` used to scalarize to 8 libm calls and now issues two
`Sleef_logd4` calls.

The 0-3 element scalar residue that `vectorizeInnerLoops()` leaves behind is
unaffected and still calls libm, on every platform, as before.

Test Plan:
Positive control that the new guard is actually live in this build -- a
temporary `#error` inside the aarch64 block failed the compile, confirming the
TU is built for `cfg:dev-linux-arm64-fbcode-platform010-aarch64-clang21` and
that the guard is not silently false:

```
fbcode/caffe2/torch/csrc/jit/tensorexpr/intrinsic_symbols.cpp:134:2: error: AARCH64_SLEEF_BLOCK_IS_ACTIVE
```

This mattered: `AT_BUILD_ARM_VEC256_WITH_SLEEF`, the macro ATen uses to guard
its own Sleef usage, is applied only to the `_ATen-cpu` target's
`compiler_flags` and is not in `_libtorch`'s `propagated_pp_flags_cpu`, so
gating on it here would have compiled to nothing.

With the control removed:

```
buck2 build fbcode//caffe2:_libtorch
```

`fbsource//third-party/sleef:sleef` is an unconditional `exported_dep` of
`_ATen-cpu`, so the symbols resolve when libtorch is linked.

New test `test_llvm_sleef_aarch64` in `test_tensorexpr_pybind.py` (aarch64
Linux only). For `log` (unary) and `atan2` (binary), in float32 and float64, it
builds a 20-element kernel, runs `vectorize_inner_loops()` and lowers it with
the LLVM backend. 20 elements = two 8-lane bodies (the new split path, 2x
`Sleef_*f4` / 4x `Sleef_*d2` per body) plus one 4-lane tail (exact-width path)
and no scalar residue. It then checks that the optimized IR from
`get_code_text()` calls `Sleef_{log,atan2}{f4,d2}`, contains no scalar libm call
(`logf(`, `log-meta-apac(`, ...) or `llvm.<op>.` intrinsic, and compares the output
against eager `torch.log` / `torch.atan2`.

```
buck2 test fbcode//caffe2/test:tensorexpr -- -r 'test_tensorexpr_pybind'
Tests finished: Pass 18. Fail 0. Timeout 0. Fatal 0. Skip 0.
```

Negative control: with `intrinsic_symbols.cpp` and `llvm_codegen.cpp` reverted
to the parent, all 4 subtests fail, e.g.

```
AssertionError: Regex didn't match: 'call [^
]*Sleef_logf4\(' not found in ...
```

and the IR shows the old lowering: 20 scalar `logf` / `atan2f` / `log-meta-apac` /
`atan2` calls, one per lane.
