author: aorenste
message:
Guard tensors against the current device index under compile_on_one_rank (#196150)

A TENSOR_MATCH guard records a tensor's device type in its DispatchKeySet and
its device index separately. Under compile_on_one_rank, an input on the current
accelerator should use a rank-relative index guard so that another rank can
reuse the compiled artifact. The device type stays exact, and an input on a
non-current accelerator is refused rather than guarded (see below).

Nothing here guards a device value that Python reads back. Under CooR the index
carries no information -- every accelerator tensor is on the current device --
and the preceding commit makes that explicit by handing back an index-less
"cuda" from x.device, so a read cannot observe the compiling rank's index in
the first place. Adding an exact guard for those reads would defeat the point:
it pins the artifact to the one rank whose device it recorded, turning the
divergence into a recompile rather than preventing it.

The relative-versus-exact decision has two halves. Which tensors qualify is
derived: it turns only on whether the tensor is on an accelerator, the same
answer on every rank, so a guard rebuilt from a state loaded elsewhere reaches
it without consulting the saving rank -- whose device is the one thing a reload
must not read. Whether the relaxation applies at all is recorded, as
compile_on_one_rank on the saved graph state, because that half is not
portable: loading rebuilds the guard through the same builder, so a relaxed
guard reloaded with the setting off would come back pinned to the saving rank's
index and reject the device it was saved to accept, and an exact one reloaded
with it on would come back relaxed and accept a device it was saved to reject.

What makes the derived half hold is refusing the case that would otherwise
differ: an input on an accelerator other than the current one cannot be made
rank-portable, so tracing now rejects it, in wrap_to_fake_tensor_and_record.
The make_fx backends already refused such a graph via
_coor_check_current_accelerator, but Dynamo builds tensor guards before any
backend runs, so an eager-backend compile reached the guard with a device only
the tracing rank has.

The recursive-dict-tag fast path keeps a TensorCheck snapshot of its own, and
an unchanged tag lets it answer without running the TENSOR_MATCH leaf, so that
snapshot has to be taken in the same relative form. Pinned, it accepts a
parameter left behind on a device the leaf rejects. The root guard manager
carries the mode for that path to read. It shows up only with
use_recursive_dict_tags_for_guards on, and only while the tag holds: busting
the tag forces the leaf to run and the guard rejects correctly again.
clone_manager copies the mode too, so a cloned root snapshots the same way.

Checking a relative guard needs the current accelerator index. Cache that value
once per root guard evaluation so guard sets containing thousands of tensors do
not make thousands of runtime device queries. The recorded-index path stays
call-free: TensorCheck short-circuits rather than resolving a current device it
would not use.

TensorCheck holds the choice in one field -- an optional index, unset for "the
current one" -- rather than an index plus a flag deciding whether to read it.
Unset means the current accelerator, never "any device": both forms compare the
tensor's index against something. The pybind default now matches the C++
constructor's, so out-of-tree callers of add_tensor_match_guard still compile.

Guard mismatch diagnostics report both the runtime current-device index and the
actual tensor index. The exact-index path also casts DeviceIndex to int before
formatting, fixing the pre-existing behavior where its int8_t representation
was emitted as a character.

Cover the refusal directly, and keep pinning that the runtime guard rejects a
tensor on a non-current device -- relaxing the index must not mean ignoring it.
The dict-tag fast path gets a case of its own, since it answers without the
leaf, and the serialization test covers a load under the opposite setting in
both directions. The get_device test compiles with fullgraph and counts frames,
because the original code object's cache entries would miss the resume frames a
graph-breaking implementation compiles under their own code objects.

python test/dynamo/test_guard_manager.py
python test/dynamo/test_guard_serialization.py
python test/dynamo/test_modules.py

author: aorenste
message:
Make tensor device observations rank-portable under compile_on_one_rank (#196151)

Dynamo specializes tensor device metadata before make_fx runs. Under
compile_on_one_rank, baking the current accelerator index into a guard, an FX
constant, or Tensor.get_device() makes the artifact rank-specific: another rank
can either recompile unnecessarily or silently observe the tracing rank's index.

Classify an indexed accelerator as runtime-relative only when it is the current
accelerator under CooR. x.device uses a dedicated variable that keeps the
accelerator type static and resolves index-dependent observations at runtime.
Tensor guards still check the exact index at this commit; #196150 relaxes them
to check against the runtime current device using the same classification.
Tensor.get_device() uses the same coor::current_device_index SymInt operator as
x.device, whose fake implementation leaves the index unbacked until execution.

An exact index guard would preserve eager specialization but defeat CooR by
creating one artifact per rank. Returning only an index-less device works for
factory and .to() passthrough but loses observable index semantics. The runtime
index representation preserves both: device passthrough remains portable, while
arithmetic reads the executing rank's index and data-dependent control flow
graph-breaks rather than specializing to the tracing rank.

The index observation is cached per tracer, not per graph. A higher-order op
traces each subgraph with its own tracer, and a proxy created under a sibling
cannot be lifted into this one -- both branches of a torch.cond reading
x.device.index otherwise trip the root-tracer assertion in
lift_tracked_freevar_to_input.

torch.device(d) copies d: the result is equal to it but a distinct object, so
the call hands back a fresh rank-relative device rather than d itself, and the
device= keyword form is accepted as well. Handing back a distinct variable is
what keeps `torch.device(d) is d` False the way it is eagerly, so identity
comparison is taught that two of these are never the same object -- the same
rule a bound method already follows, and the same reason `x.device is x.device`
is False.

Equality reports one equal to an explicit cuda:N whenever N is the running
rank's index, so its hash has to agree with every cuda:N. Under CooR both it and
a constant torch.device hash as the index-less device, so all devices of one
type share a bucket and equality decides: two rank-relative devices are the same
key (which is what _group_tensors_by_device_and_dtype, and so
clip_grad_norm_, needs), and against an explicit cuda:N the key comparison reads
the runtime index -- a data-dependent error under fullgraph, a graph break
otherwise, the same as `x.device == torch.device("cuda:N")`. Refusing to hash
was the alternative, but it made clip_grad_norm_ fail to compile under CooR.

CompileOnOneRankUnsupported, for a construct CooR cannot express at all, is
raised by later commits in the stack; it propagates whether or not graph breaks
are allowed, which is why it is its own type rather than an Unsupported or a
UserError -- convert_frame soft-fails both of those.

The tensorless index operator is assigned a CPU lowering device because
FallbackKernel otherwise has no tensor from which to infer one.

author: aorenste
message:
Anchor a property descriptor's guard source at the type (#197585)

`object_generic_getattr` computes one instance-anchored source and hands it to
`_resolve_descriptor_get` for every kind of descriptor. That anchor is wrong
for a `property`: the descriptor lives on the type, and `PropertyVariable`
derives its `fget` source from it, so the guard reads `L['obj'].attr.fget` --
which evaluates the getter and then asks the resulting value for `.fget`:

    AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'fget'

Reaching it takes a `property` on an object Dynamo wraps as a
`ConstantVariable`, which in practice means `torch.cuda._CudaDeviceProperties`:

```python
props = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0)
torch.compile(lambda x: x + props.multi_processor_count)(torch.randn(2, device="cuda"))
```

Point the source at the descriptor `mro_lookup` actually returned. Naming it
`type(obj).attr` is not enough: that reads back through `type.__getattribute__`,
where a data descriptor on the metaclass beats the class chain, so a metaclass
`property` of the same name reproduces the very same `.fget` error one level up.
Index the owning class's `__dict__` instead, walking the MRO to find it and
guarding that the classes ahead of it still do not define the name.

Only the `property` branch moves: `staticmethod` and `classmethod` keep the
instance anchor, since reading those through the type unwraps them. A
pure-Python property resolves through `UserDefinedObjectVariable` and never gets
here, and `torch.finfo` / `torch.iinfo` expose getset descriptors rather than
properties.

That MRO walk already existed three times over -- in
`AutogradFunctionVariable._get_raw_attribute_source` and in both
`get_source_by_walking_mro` methods -- so it becomes one `mro_attr_source` next
to `mro_lookup`, and the callers keep only what differs: their extra guard and
what a miss means. Three discrepancies had to be settled to share it. The
absent-guard loop runs `range(idx)` everywhere now, so the `user_defined`
callers guard MRO index 0 the way `misc` already did -- otherwise setting the
attribute on `type(obj)` later moves the owner while the guard still reads
`__mro__[idx]`. `mro_source_cache` is keyed on the owning class rather than the
descriptor: one descriptor object can sit in several unrelated classes, and a
source through one of them does not notice the attribute being reassigned on
another. Keying on the owner still lets instances and subclasses that reach the
same owner share one source, so they do not pick up an OBJECT_ALIASING guard.
And entry 0 is spelled as the class itself only after checking that it is the
class -- every MRO CPython computes puts it there, but a metaclass overriding
`mro()` can not, and now that index 0 is guarded the mismatch would fail a guard
on the frame that created it.

`TestConstantTypeProperty` covers the `common_constant_types` path: a plain
property, one shadowed by a metaclass descriptor, one inherited from a base,
one shadowed on the subclass after the first compile (which has to recompile),
and one on a class whose metaclass reorders `__mro__`. The
`_CudaDeviceProperties` case moves to `TestConstantTypePropertyAccelerator`, so
both classes carry a `hw_classification` and survive `--hw-classification`.
Two tests in `test_repros.py` pin the cache key from both sides: a descriptor
shared by unrelated classes recompiles when one of them reassigns it, and two
instances reaching the same class attribute get no OBJECT_ALIASING guard.

python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_misc.py test/dynamo/test_repros.py \
    test/dynamo/test_functions.py test/dynamo/test_autograd_function.py
python -m pytest test/distributed/tensor/test_compile_on_one_rank.py

author: jhou-jpg
message:
[pytorch][aten] make isinf/isfinite work for fp8 dtypes that cannot encode infinity (#197444) (#197444)

Summary:

This replaces https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192008 (D114427404), which
went stale. Same fix, plus vkuzo's review feedback from that PR and the
regression test he asked for.

To fix `TORCHINDUCTOR_NAN_ASSERTS` to work with FP8 types. Inspired by
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/178376 as that PR was closed unmerged.

`torch.isinf()` raises `NotImplementedError` for `Float8_e4m3fn` (and
`e4m3fnuz`/`e5m2fnuz`/`e8m0fnu`): `isinf` dispatches through
`_AT_DISPATCH_INF_TYPES`, which only covers Double/Float/Half/BFloat16/Float8_e5m2,
so the other fp8 dtypes fall through to the dispatcher's default and throw. Simply
adding them to the macro does not compile, because
`std::numeric_limits<Float8_e4m3fn>` has no `infinity()` member at all.

`Float8_e5m2` is the only fp8 dtype with an infinity encoding, so for the rest
`isinf` is trivially false. Return `zeros_like` before the dispatch, mirroring the
existing integral-type guard. `isfinite` shares the same macro and throws
identically; with no infinity representation it reduces to "not NaN", i.e.
`self == self`, which routes through the fp8-capable `eq` kernels.

Per vkuzo's review, that decision is now spelled out one dtype at a time in
`is_fp8_type_without_inf()` instead of being written as
`isFloat8Type(t) && t != kFloat8_e5m2`. The old form was already right only by
luck: `c10::isFloat8Type()` has since grown a fifth member, `Float8_e8m0fnu`,
which got swept into the predicate without anyone deciding it should be. Naming
each dtype makes a newly added one trip the `TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT` rather than
silently inherit an answer. The helper is written as a `||` chain mirroring
`c10::isFloat8Type()` itself rather than as a `switch`: a `switch` over
`ScalarType` covering only the fp8 cases trips `-Wswitch-enum` on the other ~40
enumerators, and a `default:` arm does not silence that one.

`isfinite`'s `self == self` carries a `NOLINTNEXTLINE(misc-redundant-expression)`.
clang-tidy flags any syntactically identical `x == x`; here `operator==` is
`Tensor`'s, and the comparison is the not-NaN test the adjacent comment
describes. Same suppression as `c10/util/intrusive_ptr.h` uses for the same
false positive.

Authored and iterated on with Claude Opus.

Test Plan:
**The bug.** Before this change, `torch.isinf()` on an fp8 tensor of any dtype
other than `Float8_e5m2` raised:

```lang=text, counterexample
NotImplementedError: "isinf" not implemented for 'Float8_e4m3fn'
```

`torch.isfinite()` failed identically (`"isfinite" not implemented for
'Float8_e4m3fn'`) because both dispatch through the same `_AT_DISPATCH_INF_TYPES`
macro. `torch.isnan()` was unaffected: it is `self != self`, and the `ne` kernels
already cover fp8.

**New regression test.** `test_isinf_isfinite_float8` in
`test/test_unary_ufuncs.py`, parametrized over all five fp8 dtypes:

```
python test/test_unary_ufuncs.py -k test_isinf_isfinite_float8
```

It derives the expectation from a float32 reference tensor rather than hardcoding
it, and feeds `Float8_e5m2` a `[1.0, inf, -inf, nan]` input so the new fast path
cannot mask a genuine infinity. `Float8_e8m0fnu` is exercised for `isinf` but
carved out of the `isfinite` assertion, because `isfinite` has a separate
pre-existing early return that reports every `Float8_e8m0fnu` value as finite,
NaN included. That inconsistency is untouched here and addressed in the diff
stacked on top.

message:
[MPS] Add heaviside (#195265)

I have built this branch standalone and run its tests locally on Apple silicon before submitting.
The description below was drafted with an AI assistant, so it is quoted rather than presented as my own prose.

> ## Why this is needed
>
> Requested on #141287, where a user reports `aten::heaviside.out` missing and states that `torch.heaviside` on MPS-like devices would be useful for their astronomy work.
>
> ## Change
>
> Adds a native Metal kernel for `heaviside`, which so far only had CPU, CUDA and
> XPU implementations and was listed as unimplemented in the MPS xfail list.
> `heaviside` and `heaviside_` are structured delegates of `heaviside.out`, so
> registering the MPS kernel against `heaviside_stub` covers all three.
>
> Unlike most of the binary functors already in `BinaryKernel.metal`, which are
> special functions registered for floating point only, `heaviside` is dispatched
> with `AT_DISPATCH_ALL_TYPES_AND3(kHalf, kBool, kBFloat16)` on the other
> backends, so it is registered with both `REGISTER_FLOAT_BINARY_OP` and
> `REGISTER_INTEGER_BINARY_OP` and the functor stays type-generic rather than
> promoting to float.
>
> The gradient test needs an `XFAILLIST_GRAD` entry. That is not an MPS gap:
> `aten::heaviside` has no derivative on any backend, and the grad test only
> passed before because entries in `UNIMPLEMENTED_XFAILLIST` also end up on the
> grad test's OpInfo copies. Removing the forward xfail exposed that, so the
> grad leg is now xfailed for the reason it actually fails, alongside the
> existing `histogram` and `floor_divide` entries.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> Removing the `heaviside` entry from `UNIMPLEMENTED_XFAILLIST` enables
> `test_output_match`, which runs the OpInfo on MPS and on CPU and compares the
> results for every supported dtype.
>
> ```
> python test/test_mps.py -k "heaviside" -v
> ```
>
> 12 tests, 10 passing and 2 expected failures (the grad legs described above).
>
> Also checked against CPU over the cross product of the two arguments for every
> supported dtype, so that the `a == 0` branch and NaN and infinite inputs are
> covered rather than left to the OpInfo samples:
>
> ```
> python - <<'PY'
> import torch
> vals = torch.tensor([-1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, float('nan'),
>                      float('inf'), float('-inf')])
> for dt in (torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16, torch.int32,
>            torch.int64, torch.uint8, torch.int8, torch.bool):
>     if dt.is_floating_point:
>         a = vals.to(dt)
>     elif dt == torch.bool:
>         a = torch.tensor([False, True])
>     else:
>         a = torch.tensor([-1, 0, 1, 2], dtype=dt)
>     b = torch.tensor([True, False]) if dt == torch.bool else torch.full_like(a, 7)
>     x, y = (t.contiguous() for t in torch.meshgrid(a, b, indexing='ij'))
>     torch.testing.assert_close(torch.heaviside(x.to("mps"), y.to("mps")).cpu(),
>                                torch.heaviside(x, y), equal_nan=True)
> PY
> ```

## Summary

[Testcase Refactoring] Decouple TestDeprecatedJitQuantized for out-of-tree backends (#194192)

## Background

Ascend for PyTorch community test-case decoupling task, issue Ascend/pytorch-ecosystem#18.

`test/quantization/jit/test_deprecated_jit_quant.py` gates test discovery on backend availability: `test_quantization_modules` is defined inside a class-body `if "fbgemm" in torch.backends.quantized.supported_engines:` branch. On any backend that does not provide FBGEMM the method is never defined, so the same file collects a different number of tests depending on the backend it runs on. ## Changes

1. Import `HardwareClassification` from `torch.testing._internal.common_utils` and set `hw_classification = HardwareClassification.GENERIC` on `TestDeprecatedJitQuantized`. The class instantiates no device and contains no accelerator-specific logic, so it is device independent.
2. Remove the class-body `if "fbgemm" in torch.backends.quantized.supported_engines:` guard around `test_quantization_modules` and mark the method with `@skipIfNoFBGEMM`, the decorator already used by the other three tests in this file.

Test method names, inputs, assertions and execution order are unchanged; no test case is added or removed. Guard semantics for community-supported configurations are unchanged: with FBGEMM available the branch was always taken, so `test_quantization_modules` is still executed, in the same order, and the collected set is identical.

None.

message:
Remove unload_xpu_triton_pyds() to fix fatal access violation in Windows+XPU inductor tests (#194217)

Windows+XPU inductor tests were crashing the test worker with an access violation (0xC0000005) during test teardown, inside fresh_cache()'s call to unload_xpu_triton_pyds(). See intel/torch-xpu-ops#4950.

The function manually dropped the last Python reference to the native spirv_utils "utils" object (`del driver_mod.driver.active.utils`) to force an immediate unload of spirv_utils.pyd. This could happen while native code from that same module was still on the call stack, unmapping the DLL out from under itself and causing the fatal access violation.

This manual unload is no longer needed: #159025 already added ignore_errors=is_windows() to the shutil.rmtree() call in fresh_cache(), so a still-mapped Triton .pyd no longer fails test cleanup. This PR removes unload_xpu_triton_pyds() and its call site entirely, letting the object be released normally by refcounting/GC.

author: SrijanSuresh
message:
Add tiled CUDA kernel for dense 2D transpose copies (#194310)

Addresses #113560.

`t().contiguous()` on CUDA goes through the generic TensorIterator elementwise kernel, which can't coalesce both the read and the write of a transpose. This adds a shared-memory tiled kernel for copies that TensorIterator reduces to a 2D transpose, including sources with a row pitch larger than the row (narrowed or strided outer dims).

## Kernel

- 128-bit global loads and stores for aligned 1-, 2- and 4-byte elements. Byte and halfword copies are packed into 32-bit words, shared memory transposes the words, and `__byte_perm` handles the 4x4 / 2x2 transpose inside each word.
- 64x64 tiles for vectorized fp32, 128x128 and 64x64 for packed byte and halfword copies.
- The scalar tiled kernel is kept as a fallback when pointer alignment, dimensions or row pitch rule out wide accesses, and for 8-byte elements.
- The grid-stride loop over tile rows is only compiled in when `tiles_y` exceeds `maxGridSize[1]`. Running it unconditionally cost 10-48% on Hopper for shapes that never needed it.
- Dispatch cutoff is 256 KiB for vectorized 1- and 2-byte copies, 4 MiB otherwise.

## Results

GB200, fixed 256 MB transposes, against a plain contiguous copy as the ceiling:

| dtype | tiled GB/s | contiguous copy GB/s |
|---|---|---|
| fp32 | 5910-6191 | 6168-6220 |
| fp16 | 5615-5660 | 5578-5660 |
| uint8 | 4816-5011 | 4855-5023 |

RTX 4060 (sm_89): fp32 goes from 127 to 225 GB/s against a ~230 GB/s bus limit. Vectorization is neutral there since the scalar kernel was already bus-bound, and the 256 KiB cutoff shows no regression against the generic path (within noise at 256-512 KB, 1.1-2.95x from 1 MB up).

## Tests

`test_copy_transpose_tiled` covers uint8/fp16/bf16/fp32/fp64/complex64 across square, non-square and non-multiple-of-32 shapes, plus narrowed and strided sources, all bitwise. `test_copy_transpose_tiled_rejects` covers broadcast and dtype-converting sources. Additional tests cover the dispatch boundary, alignment fallbacks, pitched rows and large-h grid-stride iteration.

Vectorized path and tile sizing by @ngimel.

author: bobrenjc93
message:
[precompile] Apply a make_fx capture's in-place updates once (#198243)

**Problem.** A make_fx capture ran the caller's `fn` twice, once to trace it and once to serve the rendered artifact. Every in-place update in `fn`, such as a BatchNorm's running stats or an `x.add_(1)`, landed twice. The hazard comes from the commit directly below, which added `capture()` and its serve; the two land together.

**Fix.** Restore the buffers and tensor inputs the trace changed, so the serve is the one execution the caller sees. Refuse a `fn` that updates a parameter in place, detected from the traced graph.

**Summary.** `_MakeFxCapture.__call__` traces `fn` with make_fx, then serves the freshly rendered artifact on the real arguments so the caller gets exactly what serving returns. A static trace runs on the real example tensors, though, so one captured call of a training-mode BatchNorm left `num_batches_tracked == 2` and a `x.add_(1)` added 2. The trace now snapshots the modules' buffers and the tensor arguments, and after tracing copies back any value that changed, the same treatment `_capture` already gives `.grad`; changed values are found by comparing values, because under make_fx the batch-norm kernel's running-stat update does not bump the buffer's version. Parameters are not snapshotted, because that would clone every parameter up front, so a `fn` that updates one in place (an optimizer step) is refused with a `PrecompileError`, found by scanning the traced graph for a write into a parameter placeholder rather than by version counter, which a write through `p.data` does not bump. An unbacked (`mark_unbacked`) capture traces on fake tensors, so it skips the snapshot and the scan entirely.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR fixes the `MakeFxTracer` capture from #198135 so in-place updates in `fn` land once, not twice.

## Before and after

```python
import torch
from torch.compiler.precompile import capture, MakeFxTracer

def step(m, x):
    y = m(x)
    x.add_(1)
    return y.sum()

m = torch.nn.BatchNorm1d(4).train()
x = torch.zeros(3, 4)
with capture(step, artifact_path="a.py", cache_path="a.cache", tracer=MakeFxTracer()) as cap:
    cap(m, x)

m.num_batches_tracked   # parent: 2   now: 1
x[0, 0]                 # parent: 2.0 now: 1.0
```

Measured on both `backend="eager"` and `backend="inductor"`, with the same numbers on each.

## How the trace is kept side-effect free

```python
def _trace_without_side_effects(self, args):
    if _has_unbacked_marks(args):
        self._module._compile(args)          # traces on fakes; only the serve touches the reals
        return
    mods = [a for a in args if isinstance(a, torch.nn.Module)]
    leaves = pytree.tree_leaves(args)
    # a parameter also passed as a plain argument is snapshotted like any input
    params = {id(p) for m in mods for p in m.parameters()} - {id(t) for t in leaves}
    tensors = [*(b for m in mods for b in m.buffers()), *leaves]
    saved = {id(t): (t, t.detach().clone()) for t in tensors
             if isinstance(t, torch.Tensor) and id(t) not in params}
    try:
        self._module._compile(args)          # the make_fx trace
    finally:
        with torch.no_grad():
            for t, value in saved.values():
                if not torch.equal(t, value):  # by value: BN does not bump _version
                    t.copy_(value)
    if _writes_a_parameter(self._module._gm, len(self._module._param_names)):
        raise PrecompileError("MakeFxTracer cannot capture a fn that updates a parameter in place ...")
```

The restore runs in `finally`, so a trace that raises also leaves the caller's buffers and inputs as they were.

A parameter passed to `fn` both inside its module and as a plain tensor argument (`cap(model, model.lin.weight, x)`) is traced as that user input, so the parameter scan below would not see a write to it. It is therefore left out of `params` and snapshotted and restored by value like any other input, and the serve applies its update once.

## How a parameter write is detected

The params are the first `len(_param_names)` placeholders of the traced graph. `_writes_a_parameter` looks for an op whose schema marks an argument `alias_info.is_write`, and walks that argument back to its base through `_aliased_input`:

```python
# A write can reach a parameter placeholder in several graph shapes:
w.add_(1)                                  # add_ directly on the placeholder
w.data.add_(1)                             # add_ on aten.alias(placeholder)
w.chunk(2)[0].add_(1)                      # add_ on getitem(split(placeholder))
for row in w.unbind(0): row.mul_(0.9)      # mul_ on getitem(unbind(placeholder))
torch._foreach_add_(list(m.parameters()), 1)  # a Tensor(a!)[] argument, walked per element
```

`_aliased_input` steps through `operator.getitem` to the list it indexes. For a schema op it follows the argument whose alias set matches the return's, so an `out=` overload walks to `out`, not to its first argument; `torch.mul(w.detach(), 2, out=buf).add_(1)` with `buf` an input still captures. `split`/`unbind`, whose alias set sits on the list elements, follow their one aliased argument.

The graph is used rather than `p._version` because a write through `.data` bumps no counter the parameter shares: with a version check, `p.data.add_(1)` in `fn` was captured silently and the weight ended up +2. Checking fake-tensor storage (`StorageWeakRef` on each node's `meta["val"]`) was also tried and rejected: in a real-mode trace a view's fake value does not share its placeholder's storage, so `.data`, `chunk` and `unbind` writes were missed. `p.data = new` (a rebind) leaves no op in the graph at all; that is a pre-existing make_fx limitation this PR does not change.

```python
def step(model, x):
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.lin.weight.add_(1)   # an optimizer-style in-place update
    return model(x)

with capture(step, ..., backend="eager") as cap:
    cap(model, x)
# PrecompileError: MakeFxTracer cannot capture a fn that updates a parameter in place
# (e.g. an optimizer step): serving the capture would apply the update a second time,
# and the trace has already applied it once. Step the optimizer outside the captured fn.
```

## Alternatives rejected

- **Return the trace's own outputs and drop the serve.** An unbacked capture traces on fake tensors and has no real output to return, and `.grad` reaches the caller's model only through the served artifact.
- **Document the double update.** That would leave the default MakeFxTracer silently wrong for any model with batch norm.
- **Snapshot and restore parameters too.** That clones every parameter up front on every capture; the refusal costs nothing on the common path.

## Tests

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| `test_a_capture_applies_in_place_updates_once` (inductor, eager) | result, `num_batches_tracked`, running mean and `x` match a single eager step |
| `test_a_capture_refuses_an_in_place_parameter_update` (direct, `.data`, `chunk`, `unbind`, `_foreach_add_`; inductor, eager) | the refusal, and that no artifact is written |
| `test_a_parameter_passed_as_an_argument_is_updated_once` (inductor, eager) | a parameter also passed as a plain argument is updated once, not refused |
| `test_a_trace_that_raises_leaves_buffers_and_inputs_as_they_were` | the restore runs when `fn` raises, and nothing is written |

Test Plan:

`test_a_capture_applies_in_place_updates_once` (both backends) captures a BatchNorm step that also does `x.add_(1)`, and checks the result, `num_batches_tracked`, the running mean and `x` against a single eager step. `test_a_capture_refuses_an_in_place_parameter_update` pins the refusal, for a direct write, a write through `.data`, a write through a `chunk` or `unbind` piece, and a `_foreach_add_` over the parameters, on both backends, and checks that nothing is written. `test_a_parameter_passed_as_an_argument_is_updated_once` covers a parameter that `fn` also receives as a plain tensor argument: it is snapshotted with the inputs, so the serve applies its update once. `test_a_trace_that_raises_leaves_buffers_and_inputs_as_they_were` checks the restore also runs when `fn` raises.

```

author: bobrenjc93
message:
[precompile] Add capture() with the MakeFxTracer over an on-disk artifact pair (#198135)

**Problem.** `torch.compiler.precompile` can `load` an on-disk `(python_code, cache)` pair but nothing in the module writes one: there is no public way to capture `fn` and produce the artifact `load` expects.

**Fix.** Add `capture(fn, /, *, artifact_path, cache_path, tracer=MakeFxTracer(), backend="inductor")`, a `Capture` context manager that traces one call with make_fx, serves it through the freshly rendered artifact, and writes the pair on clean exit or on `cap.save()`.

**Summary.** With `load` in place, this adds the producing half of the module: `capture(...)` returns a `Capture`, and entered as a context manager and called like `fn`, it runs the call through the freshly rendered artifact, so the caller gets exactly what serving returns, and writes the `(python_code, cache)` pair to the two paths when the block exits cleanly or whenever `cap.save()` is called inside it. The make_fx front-end is the only tracer here: `_MakeFxCapture` takes exactly one positional call and refuses a second, since the trace records one execution, and a `MakeFxTracer(decompositions=...)` table is forwarded into that trace. A step that calls `.backward()` captures its parameter gradients, which the artifact scatters onto the runtime model; the trace runs with grad enabled and the drivers pin their own grad mode, so there is no grad-mode knob. The capture must be entered before it is called and is over once its block exits, so a `cap(model, x)` outside the `with` block, before or after, raises instead of running the whole trace and writing nothing; the rendered pair is recorded only once the serve has returned, so a call whose serve raised can be retried and a clean exit never writes a pair known not to run; a block that raises, or never calls the capture, writes nothing; and a capture is single-use, with `save()` refused outside its block. `capture()` validates the arguments its callee cannot (a tracer of the wrong type is a `TypeError`, and so is a `functools.partial`; a bad `backend` stays the `ValueError` `PrecompiledModule.__init__` already raises), the self-load goes through `_runnable_from_pair(..., _trusted=True)`, a keyword added here with its only caller, so the exec warning a load of untrusted source emits is suppressed for source rendered in-process a moment ago, and `capture` is re-homed to `torch.compiler.precompile` beside `load`, with the API reference and user guide showing the capture/load pair.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR adds `capture()` as the context manager, with `MakeFxTracer` as its only tracer so far. The one-call limit here is `MakeFxTracer`'s (one ATen trace records one execution), not the API's: the multi-call `DynamoTracer` capture arrives in #198138 and becomes the default in #198217.

## The capture/load pair

`capture` is caller-driven: it returns a `Capture` and runs nothing until the block calls it. The call inside the block is served by the artifact, and the two files land when the block exits.

```python
from torch.compiler.precompile import capture, load, MakeFxTracer

with capture(lambda model, x: model(x), artifact_path="m.py", cache_path="m.cache") as cap:
    y = cap(model, x)          # served through the rendered artifact, == model(x)

f = load("m.py", "m.cache")   # PrecompiledRunnable; f.installed is False
f(model, x)                    # == model(x)
f(other, x)                    # == other(x): no weights are baked in
```

`test_capture_and_load_round_trip` pins this on both backends: the call result, the load, the weight swap onto a structurally identical `_FilesModel`, and that the standalone artifact's `with f:` and `f.unload()` are no-ops. `capture()` validates only the arguments its callee cannot; the `backend` check is not duplicated, since `PrecompiledModule.__init__` already raises the `ValueError` when `_MakeFxCapture` builds its module (`test_capture_validates_backend_and_tracer`):

```python
capture(fn, ..., backend="nope")           # ValueError from PrecompiledModule: precompile backend must be 'inductor' or 'eager'
capture(fn, ..., tracer="make_fx")         # TypeError: precompile.capture tracer must be a MakeFxTracer
capture(functools.partial(fn, model), ...) # TypeError: ... takes the function itself, not a functools.partial
```

The partial is a `TypeError` like the bad tracer: the artifact rebuilds the call from the function's own parameters, so a pre-bound model or argument would not be one of them. Pass the underlying function and give them as call arguments. Both paths may be `os.PathLike`, and the tracer may be left at its `MakeFxTracer()` default: `test_capture_takes_pathlike_paths_and_the_default_tracer` captures into `pathlib.Path(self.dir) / "sub" / "m.py"` and `.../"m.cache"` and loads the pair back with the same `Path` objects; the same test pins `capture()`'s `backend` default to `"inductor"`.

## One positional call, only inside the block, and nothing written on a bad block

`_MakeFxCapture` is single-shot: a make_fx trace records the ATen ops of one execution, and there is no notion of guards or recompiled variants here, so a second call could add nothing. Arguments are positional only, as the loaded artifact takes them.

```python
with capture(_files_fn, artifact_path=..., cache_path=..., backend="eager") as cap:
    cap(model, x=x)     # ValueError: positional arguments only
    cap(model, x)       # traced and served
    cap(model, x)       # PrecompileError: captures a single call ...
```

The capture must be entered before it is called and is over once its block exits. Outside the block nothing would be written at exit, so `__call__` refuses up front rather than running the whole trace for a missing artifact; `__enter__` arms `_entered` and `__exit__` clears it whether the block exited cleanly or raised, so a call after the block is refused the same way as a call before it:

```python
cap = capture(_files_fn, artifact_path=..., cache_path=..., backend="eager")
cap(model, x)           # PrecompileError: capture is not active: enter it with a `with` block ...
# artifact_path does not exist

with cap:
    raise RuntimeError("boom")   # propagates
cap(model, x)           # PrecompileError: capture is not active; still nothing on disk

with capture(_files_fn, ...) as cap:
    cap(model, x)                # pair written at exit
cap(model, x)           # PrecompileError: capture is not active
```

The pair is assigned to `self._rendered` only after the serve has returned, so a call whose serve raised leaves the capture retryable and gives exit and `save()` nothing to write; `test_a_serve_that_raises_leaves_the_capture_retryable` patches `torch._precompile._runnable_from_pair` to raise, asserts the artifact does not exist, then makes the same call again and gets `model(x)` back with the pair on disk after exit:

```python
with capture(_files_fn, ..., backend="eager") as cap:
    with mock.patch("torch._precompile._runnable_from_pair", side_effect=RuntimeError("serve failed")):
        cap(model, x)            # RuntimeError: serve failed; artifact does not exist
    cap(model, x)                # == model(x): the capture was not consumed
# artifact exists
```

`__exit__` writes only on a clean exit that captured a call. A block that raises writes nothing it has not already saved, and one that never called the capture leaves both paths untouched; the empty block surfaces as `PrecompileError("nothing was captured ...")` from the exit-time `save()`, rather than writing an empty artifact, and the `Capture` docstring now documents both.

```python
with capture(_files_fn, ...):
    pass                       # PrecompileError: nothing was captured; no files

with capture(_files_fn, ...) as cap:
    cap(model, x)
    raise RuntimeError("boom") # propagates; artifact and cache do not exist
```

Pinned by `test_a_make_fx_capture_takes_exactly_one_positional_call`, `test_a_capture_must_be_entered_before_it_is_called`, `test_a_capture_is_over_once_its_block_exits` (both the raising and the clean exit), `test_a_serve_that_raises_leaves_the_capture_retryable` and `test_a_block_without_a_call_or_that_raises_writes_nothing`.

## `save()` checkpoints the pair mid-block

`Capture.save()` joins the contract: it writes everything captured so far to the same two files without ending the capture. For a make_fx capture there is nothing further to fold in, so `save()` and block exit write identical bytes.

```python
with capture(_files_fn, ..., backend="eager") as cap:
    cap.save()                        # PrecompileError: nothing was captured
    cap(model, x)
    cap.save()                        # pair on disk; load(...) already works here
    saved = open(artifact, "rb").read()
# exit rewrites the same bytes: open(artifact, "rb").read() == saved
```

`test_save_checkpoints_the_pair_exit_rewrites` reads the file after `save()`, loads and runs it inside the block, and asserts the exit rewrite is byte-identical.

## A capture is single-use, and only its block writes

`__exit__` writes through a private `_write()`, and the public `save()` refuses outside the block, so a block that raised cannot have its withheld pair published afterwards. `__enter__` refuses a capture that is already entered or has exited, so a nested `with` cannot disarm the outer block and a second block cannot silently rewrite the previous trace's bytes. A failed write surfaces as a `PrecompileError`, with the previous pair left in place. The messages match the ones `_DynamoCapture` uses higher in the stack, except that a call or `save()` after the block has exited says so ("its block has already exited, and a capture is single-use; call capture() again for a fresh one.") instead of telling the caller to enter a `with` block that `__enter__` would then refuse. `__enter__` after the block has exited gives the same message. A call whose serve raised records nothing, so if the block swallows that error, the exit raises "nothing was captured: the capture's call raised, so there is no pair to write." A block that never called the capture still gets the "call the capture with your example arguments" message. The `Capture` and `capture()` docstrings state that a capture is single-use, including after a failed write at exit: the spent capture does not keep its pair, so the caller fixes the path and captures again. `Capture.save` documents that it raises outside the block.

```python
cap = capture(_files_fn, ..., backend="eager")
try:
    with cap:
        cap(model, x)
        raise RuntimeError("boom")    # exit writes nothing
except RuntimeError:
    pass
cap.save()                            # PrecompileError: capture is not active: its block has
                                      #   already exited, and a capture is single-use; ...
with cap:                             # PrecompileError: this capture has already been entered;
    ...                               #   capture() returns a fresh capture per call.
```

`test_save_after_a_raising_block_is_refused`, `test_a_capture_is_over_once_its_block_exits` ("already exited" after a raising and a clean exit), `test_a_capture_must_be_entered_before_it_is_called` (a call and a `save()` before the block), `test_a_swallowed_serve_failure_is_named_at_exit`, `test_a_capture_is_single_use` (nested and second block) and `test_an_exit_time_write_failure_raises_precompile_error` (an `OSError` from `_write_artifact` during `__exit__`) pin these.

## Decompositions reach the trace

`tracer` carries the tracer-specific configuration; `capture()` unpacks `tracer.decompositions` into the `PrecompiledModule` it builds, so a decomposition table given to `MakeFxTracer` is the one make_fx traces with.

```python
called = []

def my_relu_decomp(x):
    called.append(True)
    return (x > 0) * x

tracer = MakeFxTracer(decompositions={torch.ops.aten.relu.default: my_relu_decomp})
with capture(_files_fn, ..., backend="eager", tracer=tracer) as cap:
    y = cap(model, x)          # called == [True]; y == model(x)
```

`test_decompositions_forward_through_the_tracer` asserts the decomposition ran and the served result still matches eager.

## A backward step is captured without a flag

There is no grad-mode knob: the trace runs with grad enabled and the drivers pin their own grad mode, so the caller's ambient mode is not consulted. A step that calls `.backward()` therefore captures its parameter gradients, and the artifact scatters them onto whichever model is passed at runtime, returning `fn`'s own result (`None` here).

```python
def train_step(model, x):
    model(x).sum().backward()

with capture(train_step, ..., backend=backend) as cap:
    cap(model, x)                      # returns None; model.lin.weight.grad populated

load(artifact, cache)(runtime, x)      # runtime.lin.{weight,bias}.grad == eager grads
```

`test_a_backward_step_scatters_grads_onto_the_runtime_model` runs on both backends and compares both the captured model's and a fresh runtime model's grads against an eager `_FilesModel` with the same state dict.

## The trusted self-load, recorded after the serve

The call inside the block is served by the same path `load` takes, so what the caller gets back is exactly what serving produces (invariants checked, grads scattered onto the model). `python_code` is built once and threaded into `to_cache_bytes` so `code_hash` covers exactly the bytes written. The pair is assigned to `self._rendered` only after the serve has returned: a serve that raised leaves the capture retryable, and neither exit nor `save()` has a pair known not to run to write (the retry is exercised above).

```python
# torch/_precompile.py, _MakeFxCapture.__call__
self._module._compile(args)
python_code = self._module.to_python_code()
rendered = (python_code, self._module.to_cache_bytes(python_code))
result = _runnable_from_pair(*rendered, _trusted=True)(*args)
self._rendered = rendered
return result
```

`_runnable_from_pair(python_code, cache, *, _trusted=False)` is the shared core of `load` (which reads the pair off disk first) and this self-load. `_trusted` is added here with its only caller: the source was rendered in-process a moment ago, so it is not untrusted input, and the keyword forwards as `_make_inlined_forward(python_code, warn=not _trusted)` to suppress the per-load exec warning. `load` itself keeps the default and still warns. The round-trip test asserts the suppression with `assertNoLogs("torch._precompile", level="WARNING")` around the captured call. `Callable` also leaves the `TYPE_CHECKING` block in this PR and becomes a runtime `from collections.abc import Callable` import in `torch/_precompile.py`.

## Re-homing and docs

`capture` joins `load` in the `__module__ = "torch.compiler.precompile"` loop at the bottom of `torch/_precompile.py`, so introspection (test_public_bindings, Sphinx, `help()`) resolves both under the public path; both are re-homed where they are defined because a function's annotations resolve through its own globals, not its `__module__`. `torch/compiler/precompile.py` exports `capture` and its docstring now points at `capture` and `load` rather than listing the types. The API reference gains `.. autofunction:: torch.compiler.precompile.capture` and `:members: save` on `Capture`, and both it and the user guide show the capture/load block above. `test_precompile_public_members_are_the_exported_types` adds `"capture"` to the pinned export list.

Test Plan:

`TestPrecompileCapture` in test/test_precompile.py: the round trip on both backends (call result, load, weight swap, no-op enter/unload), the one-call/positional-only refusals, the not-entered and after-exit refusals, a serve that raises leaving the capture retryable with nothing written, `PathLike` paths into a new directory with the default tracer, nothing written on a raising or empty block, `save()` mid-block, backend/tracer/partial validation, a `MakeFxTracer(decompositions=...)` table reaching the trace, and a `.backward()` step on both backends whose grads match eager on the captured and on a runtime model.

```
python test/test_precompile.py
lintrunner -a torch/_precompile.py torch/compiler/precompile.py test/test_precompile.py docs/source/torch.compiler_api.md docs/source/user_guide/torch_compiler/torch.compiler.md
```

message:
[precompile] Add load() over an on-disk artifact pair (#198213)

**Problem.** After the switch from a callable to a module, `torch.compiler.precompile` had no entry point: a capture could write its `(python_code, cache)` pair to disk, but nothing public could read that pair back and run it.

**Fix.** Add `torch.compiler.precompile.load(artifact_path, cache_path)`, the consuming half, over the loader core the switch kept.

**Summary.** The module switch left `torch.compiler.precompile` with no entry point, so the on-disk pair a capture writes could not be reloaded through any public name. This commit adds the consuming half first: `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` reads the pair with `_read_artifact` (already in place) and hands it to `_runnable_from_pair`, the loader core the switch kept from the callable API's `load`, which validates the source as a precompile artifact through `_parse_artifact_metadata`, refuses a cache whose `backend` or `code_hash` does not pair with the source, degrades a foreign format/version envelope to JIT'ing from the source, primes the inductor kernel caches from the bundle, and exec's the inlined driver. `load` reads the source's `BACKEND` and checks the cache's `backend` tag against it; the cache is acceleration only, primed when it carries a bundle. `load` is re-homed where it is defined rather than in the loop that re-homes the types, because a function's string annotations resolve through its own globals rather than its `__module__`. The loader's messages stop saying `precompile()` -- a pair is now from a `capture`, and the warnings name `torch.compiler.precompile` rather than one entry point, since the capture-time self-load above will run the same code -- and the module Note's invariant 7 follows.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR adds the serving half, `load(artifact_path, cache_path)`. The capture half comes next in #198135.

## The entry point

```python
import torch
from torch.compiler.precompile import load, PrecompiledRunnable

# A capture wrote the pair; in the suite, TestPrecompileLoad writes it with
# _precompile_pair(_files_fn, model, x, backend=...) + _write_artifact.
f = torch.compiler.precompile.load("m.py", "m.cache")
isinstance(f, PrecompiledRunnable)   # True
f.installed                          # False: a standalone artifact installs nothing
f(model, x)                          # same argument structure _files_fn took: (model, x)
```

`load` is two lines over what was already there:

```python
def load(artifact_path, cache_path) -> PrecompiledRunnable:
    torch._C._log_api_usage_once("torch.compiler.precompile.load")
    python_code, cache = _read_artifact(artifact_path, cache_path)
    return _runnable_from_pair(python_code, cache)
```

`_runnable_from_pair` is unchanged in what it does: it validates the source as a precompile artifact through `_parse_artifact_metadata`, reads the source's `BACKEND` and checks the cache's `backend` tag against it, unpickles the envelope with `weights_only=True`, primes the inductor kernel caches through `torch.compiler.load_cache_artifacts` when the cache carries a bundle, and exec's the inlined driver with `_make_inlined_forward`. Its docstring now calls it the core of `load`, which reads the pair off disk first, instead of "the loader core the module's `load` builds on".

The round trip is pinned by `test_load_round_trips_the_pair` on both backends: the served result equals eager `model(x)`, no weights are baked in, so a structurally identical `_FilesModel()` with other weights serves its own answer, and the handle's context manager and `unload()` are no-ops. `test_load_in_a_fresh_process` saves the model's `state_dict`, `x` and the eager `expected = model(x)` with `torch.save`, then runs `_FRESH_PROCESS_LOADER` under `sys.executable`, which rebuilds the model from the `state_dict`, calls `torch.compiler.precompile.load(artifact, cache)` and `assert_close`s the served result against that eager `expected`.

## What load refuses, and what it only warns about

```python
load("m.py", "other.cache")           # cache from a different capture (same backend)
# PrecompileError: cache does not match python_code (its code_hash ... != sha256(python_code) ...);
#                  the cache and python_code came from different precompile captures. ...

load("m.py", "missing.cache")         # a missing cache
# PrecompileError: precompile could not read the artifact pair (artifact_path='m.py', cache_path='missing.cache'): ...
```

Both are `test_load_refuses_a_pair_from_two_captures_or_a_missing_cache`, which writes a second pair with `x=torch.randn(3, 4)` and pairs the first artifact with its cache. A cache whose `format`/`version` does not match is not fatal: the cache is acceleration only, so `load` logs a warning and degrades to JIT'ing from `python_code`, as does an envelope it cannot read or a bundle it cannot prime.

Those messages are reworded. Where the parent said `"came from different precompile() calls"` and `"Pair each cache with the python_code from the same precompile() call"`, the refusals now say `"different precompile captures"` and `"the same capture"`, and the three `log.warning` calls that began `torch.compiler.precompile.load ...` now begin `torch.compiler.precompile ...`: the capture-time self-load above runs the same core, so naming one entry point would be wrong there. The two sentences of Note [precompile programming model] invariant 7 that said `precompile() calls` follow the same wording.

## Export, re-homing and docs

```python
# torch/compiler/precompile.py
from torch._precompile import Capture, load, MakeFxTracer, PrecompiledRunnable, PrecompileError
for _t in (Capture, MakeFxTracer, PrecompiledRunnable, PrecompileSummary):
    _t.__module__ = "torch.compiler.precompile"       # classes: re-homed here (parent)
__all__ = ["load", "Capture", "MakeFxTracer", "PrecompiledRunnable", "PrecompileSummary"]

# torch/_precompile.py
__all__: list[str] = []                               # the private module exports nothing
...
load.__module__ = "torch.compiler.precompile"         # function: re-homed where it is defined
```

`load` joins `__all__` as its first name; the four types were exported and re-homed by the parent. `load` is re-homed where it is defined, since a function's string annotations resolve through its own globals rather than its `__module__` (`test_precompile_public_members_resolve` pins that every export's annotations resolve, and `test_precompile_public_members_are_the_exported_types` pins the now five-name `__all__`). The private module's `__all__` stays empty, with its comment rewritten to say the public surface (`capture`, `load` and their types) lives in `torch/compiler/precompile.py` and `PrecompileError` in `torch/compiler/__init__.py`, so `test_public_bindings` sees one public location. The API reference in `docs/source/torch.compiler_api.md` renders `load` with `autofunction` ahead of the types, and its lead-in now says it documents the module's `load` and its public types.

Test Plan:

`TestPrecompileLoad` writes pairs with the suite's `_precompile_pair` plus `_write_artifact` and loads them: the round trip on both backends (weight swap, no-op enter/unload), a fresh-process load through `sys.executable`, and the mismatched-pair and missing-cache refusals; the fresh-process load compares the served result against eager.

```
python test/test_precompile.py
lintrunner -a torch/_precompile.py torch/compiler/precompile.py test/test_precompile.py docs/source/torch.compiler_api.md
```

message:
[precompile] Make torch.compiler.precompile a module and retire the callable API (#197993)

> **Landing note: this PR is not usable on its own.** After this commit `torch.compiler.precompile` exports only types (`Capture`, `MakeFxTracer`, `PrecompiledRunnable`, `PrecompileSummary`, and a re-exported `PrecompileError`). There is no `capture()` and no `load()` yet, and the callable is gone, so `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, x)` raises `TypeError: 'module' object is not callable` and `torch.compiler.precompile.load(...)` raises `AttributeError`. Landed alone, this is a regression against main, which ships the v2.14 callable. The smallest landing unit that leaves a usable API is #197993 through #198135: `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` arrives in #198213 and `capture(..., tracer=MakeFxTracer())` in #198135, which together bring back the callable's single-call make_fx capture, now over two files. The multi-call `DynamoTracer` is usable from #198138 and becomes the default tracer in #198217. #198213 and everything above it currently carry `[no-ci]` titles, so they need CI turned on before they can land with this PR.

**Problem.** `torch.compiler.precompile` is a callable object, a `_PrecompileApi` singleton: `precompile(fn, *example_inputs, backend=, tracer=, decompositions=)` traces `fn` once, on inputs you hand it up front, and returns a `(python_code, cache)` pair that `precompile.load(python_code, cache)` reloads. The API this stack replaces it with is a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, you call it on as many different example inputs as you like (each graph break and recompiled variant they exercise is folded in), the artifact is written to two files when the block exits, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. A callable singleton cannot also be the module those two entry points and their types live in.

**Fix.** Retire the callable and make `torch.compiler.precompile` a real submodule, `torch/compiler/precompile.py`, that exports the four public types (`Capture`, `MakeFxTracer`, `PrecompiledRunnable`, `PrecompileSummary`) and re-exports `PrecompileError`. The entry points (`capture`, `load`) are deliberately NOT in this commit; they arrive in the next commits, so this is the one commit in the series where behaviour changes for a caller.

**Summary.** Until this commit `torch.compiler.precompile` was an instance of `_PrecompileApi` in `torch/_precompile.py`, whose `__call__` traced `fn` on example inputs and whose `load` method reloaded the returned pair. That shape cannot host the caller-driven API, whose `capture` and `load` take the caller's own calls and file paths and need a module namespace to live in together with their types, so this is deliberately the point in the stack where behaviour changes. With everything else the callable carried already moved down the stack (argument validation and the test helpers in #198283, its docstring caveats in #198284), this commit deletes `_PrecompileApi` and adds `torch/compiler/precompile.py`, which imports the four types from the private modules, resolves their string annotations with `typing.get_type_hints` into `__annotations__`, and sets their `__module__` to `torch.compiler.precompile`, so pickle, Sphinx and `test_public_bindings` all find them at the public path. The re-homing has to be a loop in this module, after the classes exist, because `@dataclass` dereferences `sys.modules[cls.__module__]` while decorating and `torch.compiler.precompile` is not yet imported when the class bodies in `torch/_precompile.py` run. Anyone calling `torch.compiler.precompile(...)` today gets a `TypeError` after this commit; the API is a documented prototype with no deprecation cycle, but this is a breaking change for current callers and the commit to hold back if that is not yet acceptable.

## The new API, end to end

This PR is the first step of the replacement, so here is where the stack ends up (the top PR, #198217, where `DynamoTracer` is the default tracer):

```python
import torch.compiler.precompile as precompile

# Capture: YOUR loop makes the calls; every input it exercises is folded in.
with precompile.capture(step, artifact_path="m.py", cache_path="m.cache") as cap:
    for x in example_inputs:     # different shapes/branches -> recompiles, graph breaks
        y = cap(model, x)        # runs for real and returns step(model, x)
    cap.save()                   # optional: checkpoint the pair mid-block
    print(cap.summary())         # coverage, recompiles, dropped guards
# the (python_code, cache) pair is written to m.py / m.cache on exit

# Serve, in a fresh process:
f = precompile.load("m.py", "m.cache")    # PrecompiledRunnable
out = f(model, x)                         # dispatches among the captured variants by guards;
                                          # an input no variant covers raises
```

`capture(..., tracer=MakeFxTracer())` keeps a single-call, make_fx-traced front-end for code with no graph breaks: it takes exactly one call, since one ATen trace records one execution. The stack adds the pieces bottom-up, and it lands as a unit, so no landed state exposes the gap between this PR and the entry points:

| PR | Adds |
|---|---|
| #198283 | groundwork: `backend`/`tracer` validation moves into `PrecompiledModule.__init__`, and the test helpers drive the internals directly |
| #198284 | groundwork (docs-only): the callable's `shape_id` and threading caveats move into the Note, and private names leave `PrecompileSummary`'s docstring |
| #197993 (this) | `torch.compiler.precompile` becomes a module; the callable API is retired |
| #198213 | `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` |
| #198135 | `capture()` as a context manager, with the one-call `MakeFxTracer` |
| #198137, #198216 | `PrecompileSession`, the multi-graph capture underneath, and its artifact |
| #198138 | `DynamoTracer`: a multi-call `capture()` |
| #198227 | `save()` checkpoints and `summary()` for Dynamo captures |
| #198217 | `DynamoTracer` is the default tracer; docs |

The old-to-new mapping for a current caller:

```python
# old: trace once, on inputs passed up front; the pair comes back in memory
python_code, cache = torch.compiler.precompile(step, model, x)
f = torch.compiler.precompile.load(python_code, cache)

# new: the caller's own calls drive the capture; the pair goes to files
with torch.compiler.precompile.capture(step, artifact_path="m.py", cache_path="m.cache") as cap:
    cap(model, x)
f = torch.compiler.precompile.load("m.py", "m.cache")
```

## Before and after

```python
model, x = torch.nn.Linear(2, 2), torch.ones(1, 2)

# parent: a callable singleton that traces on the inputs you pass
python_code, cache = torch.compiler.precompile(lambda m, x: m(x), model, x)
f = torch.compiler.precompile.load(python_code, cache)
out = f(model, x)

# now: a module
import torch.compiler.precompile as p
type(p)                                   # <class 'module'>
p.__all__                                 # ['Capture', 'MakeFxTracer', 'PrecompiledRunnable', 'PrecompileSummary']
p.MakeFxTracer, p.Capture, p.PrecompiledRunnable, p.PrecompileSummary
p.PrecompileError is torch.compiler.PrecompileError   # True, re-exported
torch.compiler.precompile(lambda m, x: m(x), model, x)
# TypeError: 'module' object is not callable

from torch.compiler._precompile_types import PrecompileSummary

for _t in (Capture, MakeFxTracer, PrecompiledRunnable, PrecompileSummary):
    _t.__annotations__ = typing.get_type_hints(_t)   # resolve strings against the DEFINING module first

First, the order: `torch/_precompile.py` uses `from __future__ import annotations`, so a class's annotations are strings, and `typing.get_type_hints` resolves them in the namespace of `sys.modules[cls.__module__]`. Re-homing first and resolving later would make `get_type_hints` look up any non-builtin name (a `Callable`-typed field, say) in the new module's namespace and fail. Today every class-level annotation resolves anywhere -- `MakeFxTracer`'s is `dict | None`, `PrecompiledRunnable`'s is `installed: bool`, and `Capture` has none, so for it the loop is the `__module__` assignment alone -- and resolving before the re-homing keeps that true for whatever is added later. [precompile] Move the callable's shape_id and threading caveats into the Note and keep internals out of PrecompileSummary's docstring (#198284)

**Problem.** Two caveats of `torch.compiler.precompile` (a shared `shape_id` for `mark_unbacked` dims that must be equal, and which part of a capture is thread-serialized) are written down only in the callable's `__call__` docstring, which #197993, the next PR up, deletes along with the callable; separately, `PrecompileSummary`'s docstring names private implementation that would end up on the public docs page once #197993 renders it with `autoclass`.

**Fix.** Move both caveats into Note [precompile programming model] in `torch/_precompile.py`, leaving a one-line pointer to each in the docstring, and restate `PrecompileSummary`'s docstring in public terms with the private cross-references moved into code comments.

**Summary.** The callable's `__call__` docstring is the only place that says two `mark_unbacked` dims which must be equal at runtime need a shared `shape_id`, and that concurrent `backend="inductor"` captures are serialized by an internal lock while the make_fx trace and `backend="eager"` are not. #197993 deletes that docstring with the callable, so without this commit both caveats would vanish from the source, and the equal-dims one guards against a silent wrong result: independently marked dims bake an equal-size assumption because the capture's deferred `Eq(u0, u1)` runtime assert is not harvested yet. This commit moves the first caveat under invariant 3 of Note [precompile programming model] and the second beside the Note's backend paragraph, now naming the lock as `_COMPILE_LOCK` in `torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/to_standalone_python.py`, where every surface that survives the retirement points, and leaves a one-line pointer to each in the docstring for the commits in between, with the shape_id pointer still stating that independently marked dims fail silently. It also strips private names (`OutputGraph.bypass_package`, `FrameExecStrategy`, `_pins_a_value`, `default_guard_filter_fn`, `_INVARIANT_DROPPABLE_GUARD_TYPES`, `Guard.code_list`, `allow_empty_graphs`, and the "added by this stack" paragraph) from `PrecompileSummary`'s docstring, which becomes public once #197993 renders it on the docs page, and moves those cross-references into comments in the class body and in `complete()` so a maintainer still finds the producer's rules, and gives `GuardFact.source` and the `_precompile_types.py` module docstring the same treatment. It is docs-only: no code changes, and the one test edit is a reworded comment.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR is docs-only groundwork split out of #197993 so each PR is small enough to review: it gives the callable's last two docstring-only caveats a home that outlives the callable, and makes `PrecompileSummary`'s docstring fit for the public page #197993 renders it on.

## The two caveats move into the Note

Parent: the callable's `__call__` docstring carries both.

```python

        THREADING: the inductor lowering step drives process-global compiler state
        and is serialized by an internal lock, so concurrent ``backend="inductor"``
        calls lower one at a time. The make_fx capture phase and the ``backend="eager"``
        path are NOT serialized.
        ...
        Dims that MUST be equal at runtime (e.g. two inputs combined by a broadcast that
        requires equal sizes, ``model(a) + model(b)``) MUST be given a SHARED ``shape_id``
        so a mismatch is rejected; marking two such dims INDEPENDENTLY currently bakes a
        SILENT equal-size assumption and a runtime mismatch does NOT raise the loud failure
        eager gives (invariant 3). This is a harvesting gap, not an inherent limit of the
        standalone artifact: the capture ShapeEnv DOES record the equality (as a deferred
        runtime assert, e.g. ``Eq(u0, u1)``), but precompile does not yet harvest/enforce
        those relational asserts in the driver -- only the decorator's declared min/max feed
        the runtime bound checks. A shared ``shape_id`` is the way to get the check today.

author: huydhn
message:
Make largeTensorTest's host-memory check cgroup-aware (#198327)

`_has_sufficient_memory` gates CPU-side allocations on `psutil.virtual_memory().available`, which reads `/proc/meminfo` and therefore reports the **host's** memory. In a container that is not the ceiling the OOM killer enforces.

On a CI pod capped at 41GiB but scheduled onto a 64–768GiB node, the gate sees hundreds of gigabytes free and admits tests that cannot possibly fit:

```python
@largeTensorTest("180GB", "cpu")  test_pool3d_large_size_int64
@largeTensorTest("64GB", "cpu")   test_warp_softmax_64bit_indexing
@largeTensorTest("30GB", "cpu")   test_invalid_input_csr_large
```

Each then allocates until the cgroup kills it, so a test written to *skip* on small machines instead takes down the shard with a bare SIGKILL. Which of them run depends on which node the pod landed on, which is why these read as flaky.

This clamps the figure to what the cgroup will actually allow — cgroup v2 `memory.max`/`memory.current`, falling back to the v1 pair. Where the cgroup is uncapped (`"max"` on v2, the ~2^63 sentinel on v1, or the files absent) the helper returns `None` and the psutil value stands, so bare-metal runs and containers without a memory limit behave exactly as before.

Verified the helper against all four shapes:

| case | result |
|---|---|
| 41GiB limit, 8GiB used | 33GiB |
| v2 uncapped (`max`) | `None` → psutil |
| v1 uncapped sentinel | `None` → psutil |
| usage > limit | `0`, not negative |

Found while migrating the 1-GPU CUDA jobs to smaller OSDC runners (#197326), where six such tests accounted for 23 of 31 failures — but the bug is not specific to that change: any containerised runner with a memory limit below its host's has always been affected.

author: mlazos
message:
[inductor] Use the symmetric kernel for X @ X.T (#194178)

Human commentary from the author: "and add architecture descriptions and examples to each PR to make it clear"

> AI-assisted change description:
>
> ## Summary
>
> Teach Inductor to recognize eligible contiguous `X @ X.T` and batched
> `bmm(X, X.mT)` expressions and lower them to the symmetric CuTeDSL kernel.
> Unsupported or unprofitable cases keep the existing matrix multiplication
> path.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> The integration is split between graph recognition and kernel execution:
>
> ```text
> FX graph containing mm/bmm(X, permute(X, transpose_dims))
>                           |
>                           v
> post-grad pattern and eligibility checks
>                           |
>                           v
> inductor::quack_symmetric_mm(X)
>                           |
>                           v
> symmetric_mm lowering -> gemm_symmetric(X, X.mT, out=out)
> ```
>
> The matcher verifies that the right operand is the matrix transpose of the
> same FX value used as the left operand. For an input `X` shaped `(M, K)` or
> `(B, M, K)`, it currently selects contiguous BF16 inputs on NVIDIA GPUs with
> compute capability major version 10 when Inductor can statically prove that
> `M >= 4096`, `K >= M`, and both dimensions are multiples of eight. CuTeDSL
> must be available, and C++ and FX wrapper modes remain on the existing
> `mm`/`bmm` lowering.
>
> The custom op has fake-tensor support for tracing and returns a full, dense
> `(M, M)` or `(B, M, M)` result. Its lowering enforces a contiguous input
> layout. The runtime implementation defensively falls back to
> `torch.matmul` when CuTeDSL is unavailable, on unsupported or HIP devices,
> for noncontiguous inputs, and when the input data pointer is not 16-byte
> aligned. The pointer-alignment guard preserves correctness because alignment
> is not represented in the compiled graph's cache key. QuACK compilation
> artifacts are stored below the configured Inductor cache directory.
>
> ## Example
>
> Callers continue to write ordinary PyTorch:
>
> ```python
> def gram(x):
>     return x @ x.T
>
> compiled_gram = torch.compile(gram, fullgraph=True)
> x = torch.randn(4096, 14336, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
> result = compiled_gram(x)
> ```
>
> On an eligible input, the post-grad graph contains
> `torch.ops.inductor.quack_symmetric_mm.default`, whose lowering invokes the
> triangular CuTeDSL implementation. The Python API and mathematical operation are unchanged, and results agree
> with the existing path within the BF16 test tolerances.
>
> ## Benchmark results
>
> Author-provided, independently unverified measurements from a GB200 BF16
> shape sweep showed why compiler selection is shape-dependent:
>
> | `X` shape | symmetric kernel | cuBLAS | speedup vs cuBLAS |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|
> | `(1024, 8192)` | 0.045 ms | 0.024 ms | 0.53x |
> | `(2048, 7168)` | 0.043 ms | 0.042 ms | 0.98x |
> | `(5120, 8192)` | 0.160 ms | 0.269 ms | 1.68x |
> | `(7168, 18432)` | 0.600 ms | 1.037 ms | 1.73x |
>
> Shapes below the `M >= 4096` cutoff therefore stay on the existing GEMM path,
> while the rewrite targets the large shapes where computing one triangle is
> profitable. The matcher also conservatively excludes `M > K`. These
> development microbenchmarks are not performance guarantees.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> These commands were run against the complete stack on an NVIDIA GB200
> (SM100). The symmetric-MM suite completed successfully with 48 tests; the
> eligible SM100 kernel cases executed rather than architecture-skipping. The
> author-local helper points the existing editable Conda build at this worktree:
>
> ```text
> CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES=1 /home/mlazos/.conda/envs/pytorch-3.12/bin/python agent_space/run_worktree.py test/inductor/test_symmetric_mm.py
> spin quicklint torch/_inductor/kernel/symmetric_mm.py torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py test/inductor/test_symmetric_mm.py
> ```
>

author: warrendeng
message:
[benchmarks/dynamo] Use small-output accuracy policy for SigLIP (#197367)

## Summary
The next Triton pin bump will include https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11189, which updates Triton’s bundled CUDA libdevice. This change is not included in PyTorch's current Triton pin.

In particular, the Triton PR changes the implementation used for float32 `erf` (`__nv_erff`). On A10G, we observed that the updated `__nv_erff` changes GELU rounding in `vit_base_patch16_siglip_256`. This causes the benchmark’s synthetic training loss to fail its accuracy check:
  - Failing test: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35206051520/job/105174646954
  - Eager RMSE against FP64: 0.13545
  - Compiled RMSE against FP64: 0.47106
  - Ratio: 3.48×
  - Current limit: 3×

We isolated the failure to the updated `__nv_erff`; when we restored only its previous implementation, the accuracy failure disappeared. We also verified that the updated implementation remains within 1 ULP of correctly rounded FP64 (while CUDA permits up to 2 ULP) so this is expected numerical variation from the new implementation.

The failure is limited to the synthetic scalar loss that the benchmark creates to run backward. Inference and all other training results still pass with the existing thresholds.

This PR adds SigLIP to the existing small-output policy similar to what has been previously done (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/177042 for example) to allow a larger multiplier for small tensors.

## Test plan

  - `erff` accuracy sweep:
