author: dmitrivMS
message:
sessions: fix renderer OOM from workspace file count telemetry (#337889)

SessionsTelemetryContribution computed workspaceFileCount with an unbounded
file search and restarted it on every send, because the prewarm bypassed the
per-session cache. When a session's workspace is a very large folder such as
the home directory, every file URI was materialized in the renderer until the
V8 heap ran out, and the next send after reopening crashed it again.

- Cap the count at 20,000 files, searching one folder at a time with the
  remaining budget so the cap holds across folders and schemes.
- Cache the pending or completed count per workspace URI and folder roots so
  each set of folders is scanned once per window.
- Skip the scan when usage telemetry is off, since the event is not sent.

Fixes #325919

author: bhavyaus
message:
agentHost: show live HydraFusion phase work in its phase chat (#337635)

* agentHost: show live HydraFusion phase work in its phase chat

Runtime #21218 sends a provisional copy of each phase message and tool call
as it happens, then replays the committed phase with a commitId. Show the
copies live in the phase chat when the phase is known, and skip the
committed replay of anything already shown. A phase's answer still waits
for its commit, so a rejected draft never becomes the response.

Requires an SDK built on a runtime that contains #21218.

* agentHost: route every HydraFusion phase message to its phase chat

A phase's text is routed by its model call, not by whether each message
carries tool requests. Live, everything a phase says goes to its chat,
including its answer, so a rejected draft's answer is visible there. On
commit, a model call that ends in tool requests is phase work and one
that ends without them is the answer; earlier chunks wait for the last
one, so text before a reasoning boundary no longer leaks into the
response and displaces the real answer. Review phases still show their
critique on completion.

Also define renderMessage before the handler that uses it.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* agentHost: preserve Fusion phase chunks and completion routing

Share whole-call classification between live events and history, retain every complete Fusion chunk, and keep phase completion summaries out of the root response. Cover missing call IDs and non-Fusion rendering regressions.

author: thc1006
message:
e2e_node: fix GCE instance readiness polling

Return the instance that passed both VM and runtime readiness checks. Report the latest failed readiness check without retaining failures superseded by newer progress. A describe or probe that the deadline cuts off saw nothing, so it does not replace the last observation.

Bound readiness commands with the polling context and recheck the runtime after cloud-init or kernel updates. When the context can be canceled, the ssh and gcloud commands get a WaitDelay, so a descendant that inherited their pipes, such as a ProxyCommand, cannot hold the call open past the deadline. Calls that cannot be canceled still wait for the pipes, because WaitDelay also turns a normal exit that leaves them open into an error.

author: Siddhanthguptaa
message:
test/e2e/dra: remove flaky WaitForPodRunningInNamespace from extended resource cleanup test

The DRA extended resource cleanup tests were flaking because they
attempted to observe pods in the Running phase, but the pods completed
so quickly (2-second sleep) that they transitioned directly to
Succeeded before the wait function could observe Running.

The WaitForPodRunningInNamespace call used BeRunningNoRetries() which
treats PodSucceeded as a permanent failure with gomega.StopTrying,
causing the test to fail when API server delays, race detection, or
network issues delayed observation.

The test does not actually need to observe the Running phase. It
verifies:
1. Extended resource claim is created (proves pod started and consumed
   the resource)
2. Pod reaches terminal state (Succeeded or Failed)
3. Extended resource claim is cleaned up

Removing the WaitForPodRunningInNamespace call eliminates the timing
dependency while preserving the test's purpose: verifying that extended
resource claims are properly cleaned up when pods complete or fail.

author: pohly
message:
resource.Quantity: make String and encoding read-only operations

Most of the time, String for a resource.Quantity as returned by ParseQuantity
is safe to use concurrently, but not always: when the input string isn't
already in the canonical form, then the instance has no cached string and
String mutates it when first called, leading to data races. This also happens
when encoding as protobuf because Size() (another conceptually read-only
method) mutates the instance when calling String. Encoding as JSON or CBOR
don't do this.

Because it is not predictable for callers when String or encoding are safe when
done concurrently, it is better to make both read-only, which matches the
normal expectation.

To mitigate potential performance regressions during decode + encode,
ParseQuantity now always caches a string on all return paths. OTOH, this itself
can cause a performance regression when the generated cached string isn't
used. The expectation is that non-canonical input is the exception, so
hopefully this won't matter.

Changing the behavior of resource.Quantity is visible in unit tests which
compare the unexported field.

author: krishhna24
message:
resource: reject qualified names with more than one slash

Both the handwritten validateQualifiedName and the declarative
resourcesQualifiedName split on "/" and switch on the number of parts,
handling only one and two. A value with two or more slashes matched
neither case and was returned with an empty error list, so it skipped
every check the two-part case performs, including the empty-prefix and
empty-name checks. "a/b/c", "/a/b" and "a//b" were all accepted on
resource.k8s.io/v1 objects.

Names that reach the DRA CEL environment are split on the first slash
only, so a stored two-slash attribute key yields an identifier that
still contains a slash, which device selectors cannot address.

Add the missing default case to both functions so the two stay
equivalent, and bound the split at three parts. Also check the format
of NodeAllocatableMapping.capacityKey before the capacity lookup, so a
malformed key is reported as such instead of "not found". That field is
behind the alpha DRANodeAllocatableResources gate and needs no
ratcheting.

Validation added after an object was stored should not have to be
satisfied retroactively. spec.devices is an atomic list, and the
generated validation revalidates every device once anything in the list
changes. Ratchet the handwritten device validation at the same level,
replacing the per-device comparisons of capacity and taints. Node
selection depends on perDeviceNodeSelection as well, so move it into
its own function that runs when either input changes; otherwise
flipping that field on an unchanged list trips the declarative
validation mismatch metric.

author: antcybersec
message:
resource: keep decoding out-of-int32 exponents written before 1.38

#141203 started rejecting a decimal exponent that does not fit the int32
scale. A <=1.37 apiserver accepted those spellings, narrowed the exponent
and stored the object with the text it was given, so master cannot read
them back: ParseQuantity fails, and the etcd3 store fails an entire LIST
on the first object it cannot decode.

Narrow the exponent the way 1.37 did instead of rejecting it, so
cpu: 1e4294967296 decodes to 1 again. The one spelling that stays
rejected is a scale landing exactly on math.MinInt32, and it is rejected
in ParseQuantity now rather than in the suffix handler: negating that
scale overflows int32, and 1.37 hung while canonicalizing such a
quantity rather than writing one, so no stored object carries it.
Fraction digits move the scale off MinInt32, so 1.25e2147483648, which
1.37 did store, decodes again as well.

The new test pins what 1.37 did on the decode and the encode paths, for
JSON and protobuf, and passes unchanged against v1.37.1. The interpret
bounds and the parse error baseline move back to the narrowing they
described before #141203.

author: antcybersec
message:
client-go/util/cert: let callers choose the self-signed key algorithm

GenerateSelfSignedCertKeyWithOptions hardcoded a 2048 bit RSA key for
both the CA and the serving certificate, so the apiserver's --cert-dir
and loopback certificates could not be post-quantum even once the rest of
the stack could.

Add a GenerateKey option, defaulting to the existing RSA key so current
output is unchanged. Key encipherment is asserted only for RSA, since
ECDSA and ML-DSA sign only, which settles the note left in this function
by #142273. Encoding goes through keyutil.MarshalPrivateKeyToPEM, which
already covers the three supported key types.

Covers RSA, ECDSA P-256 and ML-DSA-65: each generates, parses back
through keyutil, carries the expected key usages and public key
algorithm, and the serving certificate verifies against the generated CA
while carrying the exact key the generator returned.

author: pohly
message:
test: remove tCtx.Cancel workarounds

Since commit "ktesting: cancel the TContext as soon as the
test is done", a TContext created by ktesting.Init is automatically
canceled as soon as the test binary considers the test done, before
any t.Cleanup callback runs. Previously, many tests had to explicitly
call tCtx.Cancel(...) at the end of the test (typically via defer) to
stop tCtx-driven background goroutines (controllers, informers,
schedulers) because automatic cancellation only happened during
Cleanup, i.e. too late. That workaround is now redundant and is
removed throughout the codebase.

Three different patterns had to be handled, depending on what the
removed Cancel call was ordering:

 - Bare "defer tCtx.Cancel(...)" with nothing else depending on it:
   simply deleted. This wasn't necessary in the first place.

 - "tCtx.Cancel(...)" followed by dependent code in the same
   defer/closure (e.g. wg.Wait(), informerFactory.Shutdown(),
   runtime.WaitForShutdown()): kept the dependent code but moved it
   (without the Cancel call) into tCtx.Cleanup(...), since Cleanup
   callbacks now reliably run only after the automatic cancellation.

 - "tCtx.Cancel(...)" was ordering a *separate* deferred teardown
   function (e.g. "defer closeFn()" or "defer server.TearDownFn()")
   registered *earlier* in the same function. Because Go defers run
   LIFO, the old code relied on Cancel (registered later) running
   before that teardown (registered earlier), guaranteeing
   tCtx-driven goroutines stopped before the apiserver they talk to
   was torn down. Simply deleting the Cancel call would break this
   ordering: the deferred teardown would now run immediately when the
   test function returns, while the goroutine keeps running
   unconstrained until the (now later) automatic cancellation during
   Cleanup - risking connection errors or a "Log in goroutine after
   Test has completed" panic. These sites were fixed by converting the
   deferred teardown into a t.Cleanup/tCtx.Cleanup registration.

   In some cases the teardown can be removed entirely by directly
   registering the corresponding operation inside the setup function.

Left untouched: Cancel calls used for legitimate mid-test, explicit
timing (e.g. servicecidr's migration test cancels the first
controller before switching to a second apiserver), and self-contained
helpers that synchronously call Cancel as their own first action
regardless of ktesting's automatic timing (e.g. resourceclaim's
stopInformers, invoked both via defer and explicitly mid-test).

author: reckless-sherixx
message:
e2e: do not modify the caller's URL in OpenWebSocketForURL

OpenWebSocketForURL rewrote the scheme of the *url.URL it was given:
"https" became "wss", anything else became "ws". Called a second time
with the same URL, the scheme was already "wss", which is not "https",
so it was rewritten to "ws" and the dial spoke plaintext HTTP to the
TLS port. Go's server answers that with "400 Bad Request" before the
request reaches any handler, and the websocket client reports it as
"bad status".

The "Pods should support retrieving logs from the container over
websockets" conformance test builds the URL once and retries the
websocket read with gomega.Eventually. Whenever the first attempt
succeeded but the container had not flushed its output yet, every
retry then failed with "bad status" until the timeout, which is the
signature of the flake in #142284: exactly one hijacked request in the
apiserver log, no further requests, and a final Gomega message noting

author: thc1006
message:
e2e_node: add image_exclude_regex to drop images by name

The Ubuntu node-e2e configs force cgroup v2 by dropping the -cgroupsv1
image with image_regex ".*[^-cgroupsv1]$". That is a negated character
class, so it also drops normal images whose name ends in one of
-cgroupsv1's characters, and the run can fall back to an older image.

This adds an image_exclude_regex that drops images whose name matches it,
so a config can write "-cgroupsv1$" and match only the suffix. It refines a
positive selector, so it needs an image_regex or image_family, and an
explicit image still takes precedence. Both filters are compiled into an
imageSelector before the gcloud listing, so a malformed regex returns an
error instead of paying for the listing first.

message:
cel: cover the 19 digit int64 boundary for quantity()

ParseQuantity takes the fast integer path for 19 digit values since #141938,
so a quantity at the int64 rails is backed by an int64 and isInteger() and
asInteger() can answer for it. Nothing at the CEL layer pinned that: the
existing cases stop at "50k" and a 37 digit value, leaving the whole boundary
that changed uncovered.

Cover MaxInt64, MinInt64, one step past each rail, and a plain 19 digit value.
Setting maxInt64Factors back to 18 fails six of these. isQuantity() is pinned
alongside them, because a value past the rail still parses and it is only the
int64 conversion that gives up.

Pin the overflow boundaries the saturated cases do not reach

The oversized cases for calculateCPUMaximum and CalculateTimeoutForVolume

author: reckless-sherixx
message:
kubectl describe node: fix per-pod resource percentages

The per-pod rows in "Non-terminated Pods" had two problems that the
"Allocated resources" totals right below them did not:

1. The percentages were computed with an unguarded division by the
   node's allocatable CPU/memory. On a node that has not reported
   capacity or allocatable (kubelet has not posted status yet, a
   hand-created Node object, some virtual nodes), the float division
   yields +Inf/NaN and the int64 conversion prints
   -9223372036854775808% for every pod. The totals guard the same
   division and print 0%.

2. Since 97f00d18eeb the rows are computed with UseStatusResources
   (the resources actually allocated to the containers), but the
   totals still used the pod spec only. While a pod is being resized
   in place the rows and the totals disagree, e.g. a row shows
   500m (50%) while the totals show 100m (10%) for the same pod.

Guard the per-pod division with a small helper and use the same
resource accounting options for the totals as for the rows.

author: reckless-sherixx
message:
kubectl describe: fix "+ 0 more..." endpoints suffix for not-ready endpoints

formatEndpointSlices marks the endpoint list as truncated as soon as it
visits a fourth endpoint, but it decides that before it applies the
readiness filter and only counts ready endpoints. When a service has
exactly three ready endpoints followed by one or more not-ready
endpoints, the not-ready endpoint sets the "more" flag without being
counted, and describe prints:

  Endpoints:  10.0.0.1:80,10.0.0.2:80,10.0.0.3:80 + 0 more...

Derive the suffix from the number of ready endpoints instead, so the
count and the truncation decision always agree. The headless (no ports)
branch had the same defect.

author: antcybersec
message:
apiserver: build the pod-aware ServiceAccount storage exactly once

GenericConfig.NewRESTStorage built a generic serviceaccounts storage that
legacyProvider.NewRESTStorage then destroyed and replaced with a pod-aware one
whenever an issuer is configured, so a real cluster stood up two etcd watch
caches for the resource and did two LISTs at startup.

Build each storage inside the if-block that decides whether its resource is
served, keeping the order the storages are constructed in today, and let the
legacy provider pass an APIResourceConfigSource that reports core/v1
serviceaccounts as not enabled when it is going to build that storage itself.
It then errors if the storage turns up in the map anyway instead of destroying
it.

The ServiceAccount storage reads secrets to mint legacy tokens, so the secret
store is handed to it when secrets are served, and built on demand when they
are not.

author: oscrx
message:
kubectl explain: add auto completion (#140058)

* Add kubectl explain auto completion

* kubectl explain: address review feedback on auto completion

- Reuse completion.CompGetResourceList (exported, with configurable verbs)
  instead of duplicating the apiresources listing logic
- Depend on genericclioptions.RESTClientGetter instead of cmdutil.Factory
- Fix license boilerplate header and gocritic offBy1 lint hint
- Test resourceFieldCompletionFunc directly rather than command wiring

* kubectl explain: export a CompletionFunc type

The completion helpers all spell out cobra's completion signature by hand,
which makes the functions returning them hard to read. Export the signature
as a type in pkg/util/completion and use it for explain's completion
function.

* kubectl explain: honor --api-version in field completion

Reading the flag off the cobra command tied the completion function to
explain, or to any command happening to define a flag of that name, and
returned an empty string everywhere else without saying so. Take the value
as a parameter instead, evaluated once the flags have been parsed.

The flag was also only used to pick the parser, and then dropped. The
resulting GroupVersionResource keeps the version the RESTMapper prefers,
so completing "deployments.spec." with --api-version set offered the fields
of the default version rather than the requested one. Apply the pinned
group/version to the parsed resource, the way Run already does before
rendering.

* kubectl explain: complete fields from the OpenAPI v3 schema

Field completion parsed the OpenAPI v2 document, which the apiserver is
proposed to stop serving (kubernetes#141455) and which does not always carry
complete CRD fields. Walk the v3 document instead: resolve the kind through
the RESTMapper, fetch the group version's spec, and traverse
components/schemas, following $ref, the single-element allOf Kubernetes
generates next to a description, and array items. Map fields stay leaves, as
they were with v2.

The version the v2 document served could differ from the one the RESTMapper
resolved, so the lookup used to try the group's preferred version as well.
The v3 documents and discovery come from the same source, so the mapper's
version is always served; drop the fallback rather than let it hide a
--api-version that the cluster does not serve.

The tests move to the v3 testdata the other explain tests already use, and
build their RESTClientGetter from TestConfigFlags and a fake discovery
client instead of the test factory, so nothing here blocks dropping
cmdutil.Factory. Serving autoscaling in two versions lets them cover
completing a pinned --api-version that is not the preferred one.

author: semx
message:
limitranger: skip unchanged pod resources on resize

On a resize, LimitRanger validated the whole pod against the LimitRange
again, including containers and init containers the resize did not
touch and the pod-level totals. A stored value is valid by definition,
so a request or limit the update leaves unchanged must not be rejected
by a constraint it no longer satisfies.

Pass the stored pod into PodValidateLimitFunc and skip the min, max and
limit-to-request ratio checks for a container resource whose request
and limit both match the container of the same name in the stored pod,
and for a pod-level resource whose totals match. Values the resize
changes are checked as on create; create itself is unchanged.

author: thc1006
message:
core/validation: keep stored ResourceQuota values out of update checks

ValidateResourceQuotaUpdate checks the whole new spec.hard, and the
status update checks every status.hard and status.used value, without
looking at the stored object. The integer check for those values became
stricter in c09332890d6. A value past the milli range that the wrapped
milli projection used to accept is rejected now, so a quota that stores
one cannot be updated at all, not even to change a label. A v1.31
apiserver accepted spec.hard[pods]=18446744073709551616m, because the
milli projection wrapped to 0.

Compare each value with the one the object already stores under the same
key and skip the value checks when the two are equal. Equal means
Quantity.Cmp returns 0, the comparison the semantic equality for
quantities uses. Names are still checked for every entry, scopes and the
scope selector as before, and a create is checked in full. A value the
update adds or changes is checked as on create. spec.hard is compared
with the stored spec.hard, status.used with the stored status.used, and
status.hard with the stored status.hard or the stored spec.hard. The
quota controller writes spec.hard into status.hard whenever the two
differ, and admission enforces status.hard. A status the controller
cannot write would leave the quota with an empty or stale limit. Only
the integer check has changed over time, and a negative value could not
have been stored, so nothing new gets in this way.

The test that pinned the lock-out now pins this behavior, with the
fractional fixture from that commit and the update and status cases
around it.

Signed-off-by: thc1006 <84045975+thc1006@users.noreply.github.com>

author: thc1006
message:
limitranger: skip min/max on an unchanged PVC request on update

LimitRanger re-admits a PersistentVolumeClaim on every update and
checks its requests against the min and max of the range without
looking at the stored claim. A request that was accepted when the
claim was stored, or that a LimitRange created later no longer
allows, therefore fails every update of that claim, even one that
only touches labels, and #141348 widened that to requests that used
to pass only because both sides were rounded to whole units. For a
bound claim the request cannot go down to status.capacity or below,
so when the max sits at or under the capacity nothing satisfies both.

Pass the old object into ValidateLimit and, for a claim, skip the min
and max checks on a request that the update leaves as it was stored.
A request that is changed, added or removed, and any other resource
in the range, is checked as before; so is a create. This is the same
reasoning #62673 applied to pod updates in 2018.

Signed-off-by: thc1006 <84045975+thc1006@users.noreply.github.com>

author: pohly
message:
GitHub: remove "Additional documentation" section from PR template

Reasons for removing it:

- Having to deal with this part of the PR template is additional work and/or
  causes confusion ("I initially put the release note in the docs section by
  mistake.").
- Contributors typically don't know what to put there, reducing its usefulness.
- When contributors stop reading past that section they miss the AI disclosure section.

My subject impression is that this section is not used or not used correctly.
To verify, I ran an analysis of the PRs that went into 1.37.

- No docs code block at all: 497 PRs (43.4%) — e.g. http://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136271
- Empty docs block (blank/only comment): 453 PRs (39.5%) — e.g. http://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117119
- docs block = only a placeholder (N/A/None/-): 105 PRs (9.2%) — e.g. http://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129079
- docs block = a single KEP link: 64 PRs (5.6%) — e.g. http://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134639
- docs block = multiple KEP links, nothing else: 15 PRs (1.3%) - e.g. http://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138759 (three KEP links)
- docs  block = KEP link(s) plus other non-KEP info (Usage docs, etc.): 5 PRs (0.4%) — e.g. http://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140052 (KEP + sysctl Usage doc)
- docs  block = other info, no KEP link at all: 7 PRs (0.6%) - e.g. http://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140033 (note about a docs typo fix)

This was first suggested on
Slack (https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C2C40FMNF/p1788427548615859) two
weeks ago, with no objections and several people supporting the proposal.

author: zylxjtu
message:
Refuse UNC symlink targets in Windows subPath resolution

The subPath symlink resolver on Windows only treated the \?\ and \.device forms as non-followable and let ordinary UNC paths such as
\attacker\share through. Following such a target makes the node open an
SMB session and automatically send its credentials, enabling forced NTLM
authentication (MITRE ATT&CK T1187) via an attacker-controlled subPath.

Treat any path beginning with \ as a device/UNC path so it is never
followed. Add TestIsDeviceOrUncPath covering the UNC, device and volume
forms plus a local-path negative case.

author: yongruilin
message:
validation-gen: add --validation-extensions-file for project-defined formats

A YAML file the stock binary reads at generation time, declaring formats by
name with a pattern, a message and docs. The flag may be repeated, and each
file is one document.

Every file is validated up front, so a mistake names its source rather than
surfacing at the first use of the tag. A project may not redefine a built-in
format, nor take a name under the reserved "k8s-" prefix, so a tag means the
same thing everywhere it is recognized.

Formats sit under a "formats" key rather than at the root, and a pattern is
one field rather than the whole format, so that other kinds of extension and
other backings can be added later without changing files already written.

author: pohly
message:
DRA testing: separate creation of counters and capacity

Counters (from the partitionable devices feature) and capacity (original device
attribute for use in CEL, extended by consumable capacity) are different
concepts. Lumping them together when constructing test slices via
`fromCounters` made tests hard to understand because helpers had unexpected
behavior. It also wasn't clear that withCapacityRequest is a request for one
particular capacity.

Counters are not qualified. Using the same names for capacities led to tests
for consumable capacity which don't cover using fully-qualified names and
probably contributed to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140650.

Counters and capacity names are now clearly separated. All capacity gets
declared explicitly if (and only if) needed. Several test cases created slices
with capacity without doing anything with it. Those now use simpler slices.

The new withAttribute and withCapacity helpers replace passing attributes and
capacity to the device constructor. They simplify writing test cases because
they remove the need for constructing maps and pointers. The same could also be
done elsewhere, but that's left for later.

author: pohly
message:
e2e podlogs: fix handling of network issues

The Pods watch loop had two issues when the apiserver becomes
temporarily unreachable:
- the periodic ticker case did not call check(), so a missed watch
  event was never noticed
- once the watch's result channel closed, receiving from it never
  blocks again, causing a busy loop of reconnect/List calls

Fix both by using a RetryWatcher, which reconnects with a minimum
delay between attempts, and by calling check() from the ticker case.

The TestCopyPodLogsAPIServerTemporarilyDown integration test covers this
scenario. Without the fix, the test fails with:

    podlogs_test.go:182: FATAL ERROR: I0914 17:38:30.045924]
                got 8015 list calls while quiet for 5s, expected at most 3: watch reconnects are not being rate-limited (busy loop)

    FAIL    k8s.io/kubernetes/test/integration/podlogs      10.319s

author: DoraGlinderzaldosh
message:
scheduler: fix data race in activeQueue.len()

activeQueue.len() called aq.queue.Len() without holding aq.lock.
All write paths (add, delete, pop) hold aq.lock.Lock() and every
other read path (has, get, list, schedulingCycle) holds aq.lock.RLock().
This inconsistency is a data race under the Go memory model.

Fix by adding aq.lock.RLock()/defer aq.lock.RUnlock() to len(),
matching the pattern already used by all other read methods on the
struct. backoffQueue.len() already takes its lock correctly; this
brings activeQueue.len() in line.

Add TestLenDataRace to reproduce the race reliably. The test runs
add() and delete() concurrently with len() and triggers a DATA RACE
report under -race before this fix. It passes cleanly after.

Signed-off-by: Samiksha Agarwal <agarwalsamiksha88@gmail.com>

author: krishhna24
message:
resource: widen the golden corpus and pin protobuf

The fractional class has suffixed, exponent-form and negative members
that reach the same fast path, so #138166's guard flips those too. Pin
them next to the plain decimals rather than leaving that part of the
flip unmeasured.

The fast path also caches spellings carrying no fractional part at all:
a leading "+", leading zeros, an upper-case exponent marker, a "+" or a
zero exponent. #138166's guard is on the denominator and leaves those
as they are, so they name #141166 instead.

Marshal is a fourth entry point and the one the apiserver persists for
built-in types. Its payload is String(), so only the framing was
unpinned. Round-trips now check the decoded value as well as the bytes;
byte stability alone accepted the pre-#140459 behaviour.

author: Fedosin
message:
test/e2e/autoscaling: merge-patch CR status.replicas in GetReplicas

The CRD variant of ResourceConsumer.GetReplicas stands in for the
controller a real CRD would have: on every poll it mirrors the child
Deployment's ready replicas into the custom resource's status.replicas.
It did so with a full read-modify-write (Get, SetNestedField, Update)
on the main resource.

The HPA controller writes spec.replicas to the same object through the
/scale subresource on its own 15s sync period. When that lands between
the Get and the Update, the Update carries a stale resourceVersion and
fails with 409 Conflict. framework.ShouldRetry does not treat 409 as
retryable, so HandleRetry wraps it in gomega.StopTrying and
WaitForReplicas aborts on the spot, roughly 14 minutes short of its
15 minute budget:

  timeout waiting 15m0s for 2 replicas: Told to stop trying after 60.095s.
  Unexpected final error while getting int: Operation cannot be fulfilled
  on testcrds.autoscalinge2e.example.com "foo-crd": the object has been
  modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again

This fails "[Feature:HPA] ... Should scale with a CRD targetRef" in
about 3.7% of upstream runs (13 of 355 over three months across the
four jobs that run [Feature:HPA]); every failure of that test in the
window is this conflict.

Replace the Get/Update pair with a JSON merge patch of only
status.replicas. A merge patch carries no resourceVersion, so it cannot
collide with the HPA's /scale write, it no longer writes spec.replicas
(the HPA's field) back at all, and it saves one API call per poll.

See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142094 for the CI data.

Signed-off-by: Mikhail Fedosin <mfedosin@redhat.com>

author: antcybersec
message:
kubeadm: stop TestWriteKubeletConfigFiles sharing one directory

The four subtests of TestWriteKubeletConfigFiles ran against a single
t.TempDir(), so the files written by an earlier subtest decided the outcome
of a later one. That made "missing instance config file" pass for a reason
unrelated to its name, and fail whenever the wall clock happened to tick.

The case expects an error, but its InitConfiguration is identical to the one
in "write kubelet config file successfully", which expects none. The error it
was getting came from CreateTimestampDir: that names the backup directory to
the second and creates it with os.Mkdir, so the call fails EEXIST once an
earlier subtest has made the same-second directory. Cross a second boundary
before the subtest runs and the Mkdir succeeds instead, instance-config.yaml
is already on disk from the first subtest, nothing else errors, and the
assertion fails:

    postupgrade_test.go:162: expected error: true, got: false, error: <nil>

A missing instance configuration is not an error to begin with. Per the stat
in WriteKubeletConfigFiles, it is the trigger for writing one with defaults so
the upgraded kubelet has something to start with.

Give each subtest its own directory and let the table carry optional setup and
verify hooks, then cover both sides of that stat: a missing instance
configuration is created, and an existing one is left alone. The other three
cases keep their expectations and now reach them on their own merits.

```release-note
NONE
```

author: thc1006
message:
pod: ratchet a stored pod-level hugepages value that no longer validates

usesIndivisibleHugePagesValues decides whether an update may keep a hugepages
value that fails the divisibility check because the stored object already
holds it. It scanned the containers and spec.overhead but not pod-level
spec.resources, which goes through the same check, so a pod carrying such a
value there failed every update that validates the spec, a label-only one
included (status updates are not affected), while the same value in a
container was kept.

Such a pod can exist. Before Value() saturated (#141305), a request of 2^64
bytes wrapped to zero and passed as a multiple of 2Mi, at the pod level as
well as in a container; since then it saturates to MaxInt64 and fails. A
cluster that stored one on v1.37 cannot update it after the upgrade unless
the pod level is ratcheted like the containers.

Scan spec.resources too, and fold the three scans into one helper.

Signed-off-by: thc1006 <84045975+thc1006@users.noreply.github.com>

author: thc1006
message:
core/helper: read hugepage divisibility through the checked accessors

IsHugePageResourceValueDivisible reads the page size and the request through
Value() and MilliValue(), which saturate at the int64 limit since #141305 and
give the caller no overflow signal. The check then rejects an oversized page
size only because MaxInt64 is not a multiple of 1000, and a positive oversized
request only because MaxInt64 is not a multiple of any power-of-two page size
above one byte.

Read both through AsMilliInt64 and AsScaledInt64 and reject on overflow
explicitly. Accepted and rejected inputs stay as on master, except that a
request past int64 is now always rejected. Before, it passed when the
saturated int64 happened to be a multiple of the page size: a positive one for
a page size dividing 2^63-1, which is odd, so no real page size does
(hugepages-7 in the test); a negative one, already rejected as negative, for
any power-of-two page size, so those now get the divisibility error as well.

The rounding of both operands to whole bytes before the comparison is kept,
so a request a fraction of a byte below a page is still accepted as before;
changing that is a validation decision, not an overflow fix.

Part of #141166.

Signed-off-by: thc1006 <84045975+thc1006@users.noreply.github.com>

message:
kubelet: cpumanager: add metrics tests for pod-level allocation restore

Cover the exclusive allocation gauges across the restore paths: full and
partial restore on re-admission, release on a failed restore, cleanup of
stale pod-level CPU sets (overlapping and non-prefix), and a full
allocate-restart-restore-release cycle.

Signed-off-by: Lukasz Wojciechowski <l.wojciechow@partner.samsung.com>

author: lukaszwojciechowski
message:
kubelet: cpumanager: add detailed tests for pod-level allocation restore

Cover the checkpoint states the kubelet may leave behind when it stops
while admitting a pod with pod-level resources:

- complete checkpoint: everything is restored as-is, even when a fresh
  allocation would pick different CPUs, and restoring is idempotent;
- partial checkpoint: the checkpointed assignments are restored
  untouched and the missing ones are carved out of the restored
  pod-level CPU set, honoring the CPU reuse rules of regular init
  containers (also with multiple init containers), the sidecar
  exclusivity rules (a missing sidecar next to a restored one declared
  earlier in the spec, a missing app container next to a restored
  sidecar), and the recomputed pod shared pool for non-guaranteed
  sidecars and init containers;
- leftovers of an interrupted cleanup: container assignments which do
  not form a prefix of the pod's containers in spec order are released
  in full and the pod is allocated from scratch, and so is a stale
  pod-level entry overlapping the default CPU set (interrupted
  release); a failed completion releases every CPU held by the pod
  back to the default CPU set, so no CPU is leaked;
- pod-scope topology hints are regenerated from the restored pod-level
  CPU set: on a dual-NUMA topology the preferred hint must carry the
  NUMA affinity of the restored CPUs, not the affinity a fresh
  computation from the default CPU set would prefer;
- pod-scope topology hints are never regenerated from a stale
  pod-level CPU set, and the fresh hints generated instead account for
  the CPUs about to be released: both for an entry overlapping the
  default CPU set (interrupted release) and for non-prefix leftovers,
  including a leftover assignment of a non-guaranteed container, whose
  shared pool CPU set never matches its zero exclusive request;
- CPU accounting stays consistent across restarts with multiple
  pod-level pods, and with a pod-level pod sharing the node with a
  guaranteed pod managed at container scope.

Signed-off-by: Lukasz Wojciechowski <l.wojciechow@partner.samsung.com>

author: lukaszwojciechowski
message:
kubelet: cpumanager: don't re-allocate restored pod-level CPU allocations

allocatePodForAdd used to allocate CPUs for a pod with pod-level
resources unconditionally, even when the pod already had a pod-level
CPU set restored from the state checkpoint (pod re-admission after a
kubelet restart). The re-allocation either rejected a running pod
("not enough cpus available to satisfy request") or moved it to
different CPUs, leaking the previously assigned exclusive CPUs.

Restore the checkpointed allocation instead, mirroring what the
container-scope path already does:

- if the pod-level CPU set and all the container assignments were
  checkpointed, everything is restored as-is, without re-allocation;
- if the kubelet stopped after checkpointing the pod-level CPU set but
  before checkpointing all the container assignments, the checkpointed
  assignments are restored as-is and only the missing ones are
  computed, carved out of the restored pod-level CPU set with the same
  partitioning logic used by the initial allocation (including the CPU
  reuse rules for init containers and the sidecar exclusivity rules);
- if a missing assignment cannot be satisfied, the pod admission fails
  with a regular allocation error and every CPU held by the pod is
  released back to the default CPU set, so the union of the default
  CPU set and of the pod-level CPU sets keeps covering all the CPUs
  and nothing is leaked. The release updates the default CPU set
  before dropping the pod-level entry, so a crash between the
  checkpoint writes cannot leave CPUs unaccounted for and fail
  validateState at the next startup.

The restore relies on the container assignments in the state forming a
prefix of the pod's containers in spec order, which is exactly what
the allocation paths produce: the assignments are written in spec
order, one checkpoint write at a time, so a partially checkpointed
admission always leaves such a prefix. State contents which do not
match that shape can only be leftovers of the interrupted cleanup of a
previous, already terminated instance of the pod (removeStaleState
deletes the assignments of an inactive pod in no particular order, and
e.g. a static pod re-created from an identical manifest reuses the
same UID) - they are released in full during re-admission and the pod
is allocated from scratch, like a pod-level entry left overlapping the
default CPU set by an interrupted release.

Also regenerate the pod-scope topology hints from the restored
pod-level CPU set, so the Topology Manager does not reject the pod
during re-admission before the CPU manager gets a chance to restore
the allocation. The hint generation shares the staleness
classification with the allocation path, because the Topology Manager
merges the hints of all the providers before calling AllocatePod: were
the hints regenerated from a pod-level CPU set which is about to be
released, they could conflict with another provider under the
restricted policy and get the pod rejected before the cleanup ever
runs - and since the cleanup only happens during the allocation, the
rejection would repeat on every retry. Hints for a stale pod-level CPU
set are therefore generated for the pool as it will look after the
release, that is the default CPU set plus the CPUs about to be
released, minus the reserved ones; the equally stale container
assignments are ignored for the same reason.

Signed-off-by: Lukasz Wojciechowski <l.wojciechow@partner.samsung.com>

author: lukaszwojciechowski
message:
kubelet: cpumanager: add tests for pod-level CPU restore after restart

Add a regression test reproducing kubernetes/kubernetes#140989: when a
pod with pod-level resources is re-admitted after a kubelet restart, the
static policy re-allocates the pod-level CPU set instead of restoring
the allocation checkpointed in the state file. Depending on the amount
of allocatable CPUs, the re-allocation either rejects the pod ("not
enough cpus available to satisfy request", e.g. on a 4 CPU node) or
silently moves the pod to different CPUs and leaks the previously
assigned ones (e.g. on a 6 CPU node).

The unit test fails until the fix lands. The e2e_node test covers the
same scenario on a real node with a real kubelet restart.

While at it, refactor the pre-existing TestCPUManagerRestoreState to
share the new newRestoreTestManager helper with the added test, and
tighten its restored pod-level CPU set assertion to compare by equality
instead of by size. The new test runs on Windows behind the
WindowsCPUAndMemoryAffinity feature gate, following the pattern of the
cpu_manager_test.go tests, instead of being skipped.

Signed-off-by: Lukasz Wojciechowski <l.wojciechow@partner.samsung.com>

author: krishhna24
message:
resource: pin Quantity's serialized form across String, JSON and CBOR

TestJSON and TestQuantityRoundtripCBOR fuzz a Quantity, encode it,
decode it and compare with Cmp. That asserts the value survives the
round trip, not the form it travels in, so a change to canonicalization
passes both untouched. Their fuzzer also draws Int63 at scales
3-Intn(15), so none of the boundary inputs tracked in the overflow
burndown reach it.

The serialized form is API-visible: MarshalJSON is what writes a PVC's
storage request into etcd. Pin it, for the inventory the burndown
already enumerates, with each row carrying today's bytes for String,
MarshalJSON and MarshalCBOR. All three share one canonicalization,
since MarshalCBOR is cbor.Marshal(q.String()) and MarshalJSON emits the
same bytes quoted, so a single table drives them.

Three properties beyond the byte pins:

Cache agreement. MarshalJSON has two paths, the cached q.s fast path
and CanonicalizeBytes. For a decimal with exactly 3n fractional digits
the parse fast path caches the input verbatim, so "1.441" and the
identical value reached any other way ("1441m") are two wire forms of
one value. Those rows carry a TODO naming what #138166 should produce.

No-op arithmetic. Add clears the cached string, so adding zero to a
stored request rewrites "1.441" as "1441m" without changing its value.

Byte-stable round trips. Decoding and re-encoding, which an apiserver
does on every read-modify-write, must reproduce the same bytes.

Tests only, no production change. Rows pin today's behavior and are
green on master; applying the #138166 guard locally flips exactly the
three TODO rows and nothing else.

Serialization is architecture-independent even for inputs whose int64
accessors are not (golang/go#45588), because String formats from the
decimal representation rather than through int64(math.Pow10(n)), so
rows are pinned exactly rather than arch-split.

author: yongruilin
message:
validation-gen: stop lifting child-type short-circuits into subfield

A subfield validation belongs to the parent, so a short-circuit in the
child's type must not suppress it. Reverts the inheritance from #139564
and the opaque registries and tests that only served it.

author: yongruilin
message:
validation-gen: scope subfield cohorts to the validated path

The cohort is the short-circuit scope, but subfield named it after the hop
rather than the path validated, so chains through a common hop collapsed
into one and suppressed each other. Name it for the whole chain:
subfield(inner)=subfield(value) becomes "inner.value".
